en: Preface to the Essential Outline of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The sūtras spoken by the sages of the West are vast and overflowing; were it not for those who are superior practitioners of the Mahāyāna, [they could not be mastered].

Even one endowed with the ocean of hearing and retention would be insufficient to receive it; for this is not the ordinary literature of the world, but rather the celestial Dharma of the ultimate truth that transcends the world.

During the Age of Semblance Dharma, the Great Being Nāgārjuna, by means of the fierce power of his wisdom and eloquence, went directly to the palace of the great dragon king and exhausted the entirety of the collected Dharma-treasury.
There he beheld three versions of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, including the chapters of the Upper Version.
The verses are all calculated by the number of atoms (*paramāṇu*). The middle version also consists of over a thousand fascicles and approximately five hundred thousand verses.
These two versions were considered beyond the mental capacity of those in Jambudvīpa to uphold; consequently, they were rolled up and kept hidden, not transmitted to the world.
The eighty-one fascicles currently circulating in China are but a small portion and are not yet complete. Alas!

The River Lord gazes out at the vast ocean, while the wren bounds about the ground; by this we know that the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings and the ocean of the Buddha’s words cannot be fathomed by those of limited or petty vision.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles constitutes one great [scripture].
It is the crown of the Tibetan canon. Yet its chapters are fixed in number and its verses are fixed in count;
it possesses titles and colophons, and may be held, observed, read, and recited. Nevertheless, those who peruse it in Zen monasteries or lecture halls are truly few.
Is this not because they fear its prolixity, preferring instead the eighty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka*, which still has those who chant and recite it? By this, one may infer the dragon’s [intent].
The Master Shu’s words—“I am able to thoroughly fathom the faculties and understandings of sentient beings according to their regions and customs”—were no mere idle claim.

As my years have passed and I have retired from the service of the imperial altars, I have spent my time until evening briefly revealing one or two points. When several eminent bhikṣus saw this, they laughed and said:
"Why do you exert yourself so diligently for this? A gentleman has three precepts; once his vital energy has declined, he must guard against greed. How much more so now!"
Among the ranks of the venerable elders, what do you hope to achieve by exerting yourself so diligently?
I was just now holding a sutra and did not respond, knowing in my heart that you were sparing my physical strength, yet we have simply not shared the same resolve. How profound it is!

How difficult it is to hear the deep sutras and how hard it is to plant the seeds of Bodhi. For this reason, I have composed the *Treatise on Honoring the Sutras and Expelling Heresy* to rescue the world during the final age.
The layman Ge Gongyi was delighted upon seeing this and struck his palm in approval.

Indeed, because the phrases and sentences of this scripture were heaped up like mountains and as vast as the sands of the Ganges, difficult to calculate, Ge Gongyi had resolved to abridge it so that it might be easily upheld and received.
That he arrived at this independently is a coincidence; he sent a letter with gifts and brought his draft to me for correction. I sighed and said: "As the saying goes, 'the magnet stone...'"
It attracts iron; a fine awl draws out thread. This is to say that moisture flows toward dryness, for all things follow their own kind.

I and Master Ge had been strangers to one another throughout our lives, yet through this matter we have come together. Master Ge has finally won my heart, and I am likewise able to communicate with his will.
It seems that in the past we were both among those gathered in the assembly of Prajñā. Thus, I opened the sutra and contemplated it.

The essential principles and systematic organization are arranged with meticulous order. He condenses a text of approximately six hundred fascicles into five volumes; herein lie the essential principles, and herein lies the entirety of the scripture.

In pruning the redundancies and streamlining the repetitions, he exercised his pen with great deliberation and profound reflection. The six sections on the origins of the work are recorded at the beginning of each volume.

It appears that the Master had long aspired to transcend the mundane world since his youth, and having witnessed the vicissitudes of time through his maturity, he has drawn extensively from the annals and histories.
Furthermore, rising at the crowing of the cock, he applied himself with tireless diligence, just like an old monk in a secluded mountain valley who recites this sutra as his daily practice.
This is truly what is meant by "right faith is rare. Ancient sages have said that the five perfections are like the blind, while Prajñā is like a guide.
The sublime diction and wondrous eloquence of this sutra appear in successive layers; its exposition of the Buddha’s wisdom is profound, vast, subtle, and mysterious, and is truly a supreme Dharma.
This is the essential method for practicing the gates [of the Dharma], and it is from this that the Great Treatise of Nāgārjuna was composed.
It is to be lamented that among the learned monks of today, there are those with white hair who have neither heard nor seen it, let alone understood its meaning.

Consequently, they sit by and watch as young novices of yellow mouths constantly mock the Buddha, while laypeople with broad foreheads all presume to expound upon Chan. Is this not Mara manifesting as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?
Alas! Alas! Those born into this world weary themselves within the mundane realm, abandoning their own spiritual roots. Though their hair may be short, their minds are exceedingly long;
they are all skilled at preserving life, yet do not know the source from which life arises. Some are adept at worldly wisdom, yet lack the wisdom of *prajñā*;
moreover, they do not realize that both the sutras and dhyāna flow from a single Buddha—that outside the Buddha there is no dhyāna, nor are there any sutras.
Within this middle realm of existence, there was originally no sign of written characters; how, then, could there be a divergence between Chan and the Teachings?

Indeed, worldly phenomena are impermanent and the heavens are difficult to trust. How many times has the water of Mount Penglai become shallow and clear? How many times have the Golden Immortal Statues shed tears within a single dream?
If one can indeed be perfumed by the hearing of Prajñā and serve the King of Emptiness, then the palace of Susa and the city of Gandhavatī need not be sought elsewhere.
One should cultivate the contemplation of difference. The site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the realm of defects likewise merge into a single characteristic.

Thus, the *brahmā-ghoṣa* chants of Jetavana and the zither songs of the Zhusi [Confucian] tradition are ultimately nothing other than a single sound. I know that Mr. Ge, rising at dawn and retiring at dusk, has devoted himself to the profound scriptures;
what he has attained must be much. When the oboe blows and the flute responds, there are those with a shared heart—how could one not be moved and give rise to contemplation?
Thus I beheld the Dharma assembly on Vulture Peak. This serves as the preface.
Written on the full moon day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Kangxi era (Xinhai), by the old man Chu-sou Tongmen Mochun of Gunan, at the rainy window of Lanzhai.
A Brief Preface to the Essentials of Prajñā:

Now, as for *prajñā*, it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects; it is utterly transcendent of the middle and the extremes, surpassing all limitations.
Fierce flames cannot tolerate being approached; a thunderclap leaves no time for reflection. When one investigates its source, not even a single word or character can be found.

Thus, throughout the entire Tripitaka—one that has been exhaustively surveyed across its various categories up to as many as six hundred fascicles—is it not the case that there is a vast disparity between the *prajñā* of words and letters and the principle of the contemplation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
He asked: "Why is this so? [The Master] replied: "Since the time of our patriarchs, it has indeed been said that 'no reliance is placed on words and letters.

He asked: 'Is it not the case that there is a separate transmission and direct pointing? [The Master] replied: 'However, to engage in practice apart from the teachings or to attain enlightenment apart from the teachings is something the former worthies did not permit.'"

They take silence and wordlessness as the ultimate goal, claiming that the moment one opens the mouth, one falls into the "present age" (the realm of conventional time), which is what Mahamati condemned as the "heretical meditation of silent illumination.
Thus, although they possess mouths, those mouths are fit only to hang on a wall; yet this does not hinder their horizontal or vertical preaching.
Although they forbid others from recording their words, those who skillfully expound the essentials of the Dharma may speak even a single word.
A half-phrase. Extending throughout the world and throughout space, it continues without interruption as an inexhaustible treasury.

If one interprets written words as mere words, or interprets the absence of words as the absence of words, one will either stumble within the tangles of conceptual entanglement or hide beneath the black mountain;
in either case, one cannot escape the censure of being "carrying a single board," falling into two extremes, and failing to recognize the essence of the School.

As for those who have attained the goal: although the Great Master of Caoxi showed that he was illiterate, he nonetheless suddenly penetrated the source of the mind through half a verse of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, the Patriarch Huineng once encouraged people to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Today, this sutra circulates most widely.

Both the wise and the foolish practice this; it was thus initiated within the assembly at Huangmei. Therefore, when contracted, the single phrase "no abiding" encompasses the entirety of Prajñāpāramitā without being deficient;
when expanded, the entire six hundred fascicles of the sutra do not exceed its scope even when dissected down to a minute particle.
Thus, even unto the myriad phenomena of the universe, the ocean of meaning shines brilliantly; clouds drift and birds fly.
As the wind moves and dust arises, various phenomena manifest before one; yet all are the foremost *pāramitā*.

Those whose minds dwell upon quantity—reckoning things as few or many—have not reached the source of the Dharma and merely produce frivolous discourse (*prapañca*). This treasury is the original section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
In total, there are six hundred fascicles. Among the *sūtras* as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of worlds, they occupy no more than the tip of a hair;
yet our mental capacities are dull and inferior, leaving us unable to even gaze upon the vast ocean. We cannot even discern their titles, let alone penetrate their underlying meaning.
My friend, Layman Fukan (whose alternative name is Qikong), has spent many years in the diligent investigation of the Great Dharma; regarding the ultimate pivot of the Way, he has transcended words.
In the intervals between my swimming, I devoted myself all the more to its study and refinement. I spent three years unraveling it from beginning to end.

I reflected that because the volumes were so numerous, few could complete the work; furthermore, within them, meanings were often identical and texts repetitive, making it difficult to reach a definitive conclusion.
Although the subtle words of the Great Sage may be either elaborate or concise, they are not easily fathomed by ordinary intellects. Yet, lacking the power to circulate them, I opened [the text]...

Having observed many hardships regarding the conditions for engaging with sentient beings, and fearing that there might be deficiencies in my reverence, I have exhausted my thoughts and efforts to provide a summary of the essential points in ten fascicles.
This work briefly provides a grand overview, so that all who behold this compilation may ascend to the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).

Yet the light of the Dharma constantly shines forth. Entering the swirling ocean of the Dharma-stream, one comes to possess the full flavor of the ocean. Such is the earnest and urgent resolve to propagate the Dharma.

Should those who increase their arrogance within the stream of Chan further gather up these fragmentary words and claim that our school is devoid of phrases and sentences—[this would be a grave error].
Furthermore, not a single dharma has been given to anyone. I venture to ask: regarding these ten scrolls of profound texts, are they words or are they not words?
Is there a dharma being given to others, or is there no dharma being given to others? I pray that those with the discerning eye will examine and judge this.
Written by Dharma-brother Zhang Lilian, a student of the Jì school, in homage to his fellow students.
**Preface to the Essentials of Prajñā** What is *prajñā*?
The *Prajñā* section is the foremost of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*). [The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*...]
Furthermore, it stands as the foremost of the Prajñāpāramitā sections; this is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The scripture comprises six hundred fascicles in total, with every word expounding upon the fundamental principle. Its text is vast and extensive; herein, I shall present the essential outline to clarify its central tenets.
In the past, Master Yongming compiled the Great Canon as the "Mirror of the Source" (Zongjing), yet he did not preserve the designations of "scriptures" (jing) and "teachings" (jiao).
Thus, it is clear that those who later categorized scriptures as mere teachings would have been rebuked by this master.

This is all the more so for the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, which are the most honored and supreme; they employ provisional verbal expressions to reveal the wordless and the ineffable, thereby clarifying names.
By means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they reveal the single characteristic of non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*), ultimately dissolving everything back into non-existence and unattainability.

What, then, is the subject matter of their discourse? To treat it as if it were merely words is to bury it alive; to interpret the scriptures while failing to understand the scriptures is truly a self-imposed obstruction.
Later patriarchal sayings—such as the four propositions and hundred negations, or the "having a word" and "not having a word"—are all considered the Patriarch’s [teaching].
The Master founded [this school] as a tradition that does not rely on written words, yet he was unaware of this one Great Scripture, which Śākyamuni Tathāgata proclaimed with his own golden mouth.
Indeed, that by which the Tathāgata established his teaching and that by which the Patriarchs established their school are non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata—the saint among saints—how could he have been unaware that later, written words would proliferate?

Yet, from the outset, they fell into the trap of verbal expression, acting as its instigator. That they could not dispense with written characters to establish their teaching implies that they could not help but rely on written characters to establish their core tenets.

Although the great scriptures are divided into six hundred fascicles, totaling tens of thousands of leaves, with names and characteristics analyzed in detail and doctrines established or refuted, they do not serve to provide a guiding framework or extract the essential points. How can a reader help but feel disappointed?

Yang: Even if one were to complete the entire volume, it would still be difficult; how much more so for contemplating, practicing, and realizing its meaning? It would merely become a bookshelf ornament, and one could never finish perusing it.
For a great scripture such as this, to possess it with reverence is superfluous, yet to hear it directly is insufficient.

This is not the way to assist in propagating the Holy Teaching or to enlighten those at the beginning stage of their practice. It is just like the "Twenty Additional Volumes" within the sutra, which state that all phenomena are unobtainable. Furthermore—
The words themselves are also ungraspable. Having discerned their ultimate aim, I have composed a mere three lines that provide a stable summary.

Furthermore, regarding the *Śrī-vimala-prabhā-śāstra* in one hundred and thirteen fascicles, which mutually integrates all dharmas and interweaves the one and the many, I have likewise reached a state of certainty by grasping the five-leaved framework.
The extraction of the entire scripture follows this same model. Thus, while the scriptural text is concise, its meaning remains without error.
I leave it to you; there is no need to wait for extensive research before one can exhaustively fathom the profound purport.

First, a detailed examination of the principles: having already presented the essential framework, I shall now clarify the specific principles. The essential framework serves to elucidate the fundamental tenets.
This systematic arrangement serves to clarify the underlying mechanisms of the teaching. Within the sutras, there are instances where a bodhisattva asks a question and the Tathāgata answers;

instances where the Tathāgata poses a challenge and a bodhisattva responds; and instances where bodhisattvas engage in mutual inquiry and debate, while the Tathāgata offers encouragement and praise for them.
He provided them with attestations and records. There were also occasional inquiries concerning the future Bodhisattva Maitreya, to which the Tathāgata likewise provided testimony and verification.
These were arranged in successive order, their thematic threads mutually elucidating one another; each follows its original source, returning to its own beginning and conclusion.
There are instances of one question and one answer; there are instances of several questions and several answers; and there are instances of dozens of questions and dozens of answers.
The phrasing has its origins, and the meaning is without interruption.
First, to follow the scriptural text according to the words of the sūtra: I once read the *Biography of Master Ci'en*. At that time, the translated scriptures were voluminous;
in order to comply with the wishes of the assembly, they had removed redundancies and repetitions. That night, he was warned in a dream to return to a full translation.

When the other masters requested that no omissions or deletions be made, how much less would an ordinary person like myself dare to attempt such editing? It would be no different from a base scholar attempting to circulate [the teachings].

I am deeply mindful. My practice in the mountains and fields has left my body withered and my sinews withered; with such meager resources, it was difficult to obtain [the opportunity] to propagate the Sūtra.

For a time, I joyfully heard its profound meanings, and through various skillful means, I finally resolved to seek out this pearl. Having received this humble sincerity, I have redoubled my efforts toward vigilance and reverence.

Not a single character of the Sūtra’s text has been misplaced, nor has a single word of the original manuscript been altered. I shall only strive to regulate my health and carefully preserve the continuity of the transmission. I have now read [it].
Those who are already capable of irrigating the sprouts of enlightenment need only hold the precious case and recite it in its entirety.

For this reason, the titles and colophons are recorded in full detail across the volumes; the essential tenets are marked at the beginning of each fascicle, and the divisions are listed in the margins.

This is like having a table of contents for the *Tongjian*, while the complete history itself remains intact, allowing one to explore by consulting the map and seek out passages by following the lines across several leaves, as if guided by a needle through a thread.
Like a torch leading through darkness, do not exhaust yourself in exhaustive retranslation;

once you have reached your destination, there is no need to record both the positive and the negative aspects of a single question-and-answer session. Do not omit or neglect solitary phrases that stand alone.

When the scriptural text contains detailed questions followed by repetitive answers, or when there is a reverse statement followed by a restatement of the original, these are intended as earnest exhortations and instructions.

Repetition serves to make the phrasing and intent all the more refined; by applying both the provisional and the ultimate, and through the interplay of affirmation and negation, the underlying meaning overflows.

Although this constitutes a double presentation, what fault is there in such earnestness? Yet, as the volume of texts gradually increases, one should instead emphasize the principle of "holding fast to the concise.

In questions and answers, do not merely present two opposing views; let affirmation and negation open up but a single path. Whether responding to those far or near, the response is as swift as a needle piercing a mustard seed; the meanings are blended like water and milk.
Iron is attracted by the magnet; yet when it comes to single words and solitary phrases, their origins pass by in obscurity and their linguistic currents are profound and subtle.
To investigate and realize these true dragons, one must not wound the soaring cranes.

The *Heart Sūtra* constitutes the essential core of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. While the full text of the *Prajñāpāramitā* consists of six hundred fascicles, the *Heart Sūtra* comprises only some two hundred characters;

though they differ in their degree of elaboration, the latter is indeed the essential core. Within it, there is both establishment and refutation, surging like waves and rising like clouds, yet all ultimately returns to "no wisdom and no attainment.
Like a divine jewel reflecting with perfect clarity, the *Heart Sūtra* addresses the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the eighteen elements.
From the initial discourse up to the Bodhisattva, the Prajñā of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is identical.
Yet, within this interval, the names and characteristics of various dharmas—the six perfections and myriad practices—involve layers of establishment and refutation that exceed several hundred.

Nevertheless, having swept away all rules and eliminated all traces without leaving even the slightest mark, the divine source and the precious jewel do not transcend the two principles of "no wisdom" and "no attainment. This is the Heart Sūtra.
Regarding these phrases, they are summarized solely by the three meanings of arising-and-ceasing, defilement-and-purity, and increase-and-decrease.

As recorded in the Prajñā[pāramitā] scriptures—whether concerning the permanent or the impermanent, pleasure or suffering, and so forth, extensively up to existence or non-existence, and union or dispersion—the texts are not of a single type;
each contains profound significance. Although these three pairs of opposites differ in their breadth or brevity, they are in fact already contained therein.
The *Heart Sūtra* states that all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness, and within emptiness there is no form and so forth;

yet the *Prajñāpāramitā* repeatedly enumerates what is non-existent and unobtainable. The *Heart Sūtra* distances itself from inverted dreams and delusions, whereas the *Prajñāpāramitā* exhaustively analyzes the demonic activities of bodhisattvas.
The *Heart Sūtra* concludes with a divine mantra, thus being both esoteric and exoteric, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* divides [the teaching] according to the six pāramitās.

The six assemblies of discourse summarize the entire text. For while mantras constitute the gateway of total retention (*dhāraṇī*), the six perfections (*pāramitās*) likewise constitute the total retention of all phenomena;

their meanings are precisely equivalent. The opening passage of the Heart Sūtra illuminates the emptiness of the five aggregates and does not further address other dharmas, yet it immediately speaks of crossing over calamities, culminating in the conclusion of the sūtra which removes suffering—this is truly not false. The internal correspondences are complete and subtle.
The Prajñāpāramitā begins and ends by clarifying that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and even like cities of Gandharvas;

yet, for the sake of sentient beings, it redirects the source of spiritual awakening, extensively opens the ocean of vows, and brings about the attainment of Buddhahood and the liberation of beings—such is its meaning.
Now, regarding the vast literature of the thirteen thousand [lines], this Great Sūtra summarizes the essential framework in no more than a few fascicles; thus, the Heart Sūtra is concise.
These are subsumed within two hundred and thirty characters. Is it not that the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind?
Over these past two years, when expanded, they comprise the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; when condensed, they comprise the two hundred characters of the *Heart Sūtra*.
From much comes little; from little comes much. With each recitation and retention, new meanings emerge; the inconceivable Dharma cannot be fully extolled.
These are the essential outlines, not numerous, yet the entire scripture is perfectly contained within them. This comprises five hundred and seventy-seven fascicles.
The "Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā" section is the circulated text of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The term "Vajra" (Diamond) serves as a metaphor; its meaning is indicated [as follows]:
The Middle Way, the very marrow of Prajñā, is found in these two sutras; I shall not further enumerate them here, as their titles alone suffice to manifest their significance.
This chronicler is a withered stump of a man. In youth, he aspired to transcendence; in maturity, he became stubborn and clumsy.

Since the years of Shen (1912) and You (1913), he has taken the complete history preserved in his family collection and read it through once. As the years and months passed and the four seasons of furs and flaxen garments changed, he reached the final volume.
In the evening, he sighed deeply and said with profound emotion: "For over four thousand years, from top to bottom, all matters of rise and fall, gain and loss, have been contained herein.
From this point on, I shall conceive a sense of weary detachment toward the world, realizing that things arise as illusions and perish as illusions, possessing no ultimate reality.

My Way is certainly not a matter of rise and fall or gain and loss. Unconsciously, he moved from the study of history into Chan meditation, seeking a single truth; he came to believe that such a thing truly exists.
Yet his haughty spirit remained strong and his five passions had not yet been stilled. Although he read extensively, it was merely a pursuit of literary elegance;
though he felt deep remorse and self-reproach, his efforts were inconsistent and lacked unity. As the years passed and seasons changed, his recitation and retention of the scriptures increased daily.

His habitual afflictions gradually lightened and became peaceful, and his entanglements in worldly bonds slowly dissolved. Suddenly mindful of impermanence, he turned his heart toward Prajñā, and then reflected on the coarseness [of his former state].
Having purified my body and speech, I was finally fit to unroll the scroll and receive its teachings.

I hesitated for two years until the spring and summer of the Wushen year, when after six months of continuous attendance at lectures, I was able to cease consuming meat and blood. Consequently, from the beginning of the new year in the Jiyou year until the end of the first month in the Gengxu year, I have completed [the recitation].
During this interval, though I suffered from carbuncles and skin sores, my mind never ceased its engagement with this Great Sūtra.
It was exactly two years, yet when calculated by the watches of the night, it was actually three years.

During this period, no distracting thoughts whatsoever entangled my mind, and I continued to study other sutras concurrently. Consequently, I fell frequently ill and constantly contemplated impermanence;

I vowed to achieve thorough penetration and, day and night, cast off the hindrance of sleep. During the summer season at dawn, I would sit in the dew upon the courtyard steps and rinse my mouth with cold spring water.
He then opened his scroll again; as the sun shone upon his desk and mat, he moved it inside the door. During a winter night, after one deep sleep, he blew out the lamp and sat up;
the crowing of the cock and the moonlight were experienced with great intimacy. At times, the paper windows appeared blue while the short desk-lamp emitted a red glow.

He threw down his pen and rose. In his daily life, he kept his door bolted, restricting himself to the threshold; only during the two periods for rice gruel and meals would he rest for a brief moment.
Even when attending to the two purifications (the calls of nature), he did not go far from his side. The grass in the back garden and the sounds near his chamber were ever-present;

yet he remained aloof like a guest. Those close to him wondered at this. Once his tasks were finished, he was suddenly released from his diligent toil, and his chest felt as if it had been unburdened.

Upon discarding one thing, body and mind find great rest; it is truly refreshing and exhilarating. That evening, several liters of sediment suddenly settled at the bottom [of the vessel], yet my spirit remained entirely free from fatigue.
I reflected that over six hundred scrolls of the Great Sūtras had been read over a period of no less than six hundred days.
Relying on this light of wisdom, immeasurable accumulated transgressions have been illuminated and beginningless karmic obstructions eliminated—this is indeed a great gain.
I felt profound joy. Thinking that this could not have occurred without the power of repentance, I invited my fellow practitioners to present offerings before the complete canon of scriptures.

As the ritual implements were arrayed like clouds, we reverently practiced the methods of repentance; yet, both the one who performs the prostrations and the object of those prostrations were found to be utterly ungraspable.

Thereafter, my vital blood was finally exhausted and a spleen ailment followed. I wished to record these origins, but once again time slipped away. Together we were struck with alarm as my head and eyes grew heavy and dark. From myself—
Delighted, I looked back and saw it clearly. I briefly set aside my medicinal bundle and quickly wrote down what I had been contemplating.

I have composed six illustrative cases as an introduction appended to the end of the scriptural text. Like an ant shaking a tree, my efforts are ultimately laughable for their frailty; yet like a quail or a mouse drinking from a river, my own belly is already full.
May future gentlemen rectify these omissions and straighten these constraints, so that they do not slightly impair the scripture, nor consider this [work] merely [a triviality].

This penetrates the teachings; may it assist in the flourishing of our school’s tradition. I, Ge [Ding*Hui] of Kunshan, respectfully compose this preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Essentials*, following the *Introduction to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

For what reason does the Buddha preach the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra?
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which does not move without cause or for minor reasons. Answer: Within the Tripiṭaka, various analogies are extensively cited.

He preached the Dharma for the śrāvakas and did not speak of the bodhisattva path. Although the *Madhyama Āgama* records that Maitreya will become a buddha, it likewise does not explain the various practices of a bodhisattva.
Now, wishing to extensively expound the bodhisattva practices for the sake of Maitreya and others, he therefore speaks this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. Because the Buddha wishes to cause them to attain further increase in this samādhi, he has taught the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, mindful of his original vows and his great loving-kindness and great compassion, emitted a great radiance at the time of his birth,
uttered the lion’s roar, left the household life to practice the Way, engaged in six years of asceticism, abandoned that place of asceticism,
proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree, sat upon the adamantine seat, and having subdued the hosts of Māra, immediately attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Brahma King and Śakra invited the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma. Having accepted their invitation, the Buddha preached the Dharma.
That which is most profound among all dharmas is the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, he preached the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, there are those who doubt that the Buddha has attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
To sever the doubts of all sentient beings, the Buddha himself uttered this sincere word: "I am an all-knowing person. For this reason, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are ready to be delivered; yet because the Buddha’s great merit and wisdom are immeasurable, they are difficult to know and difficult to understand.
Consequently, they are deluded by evil teachers and their minds sink into false teachings. The Buddha, with the hand of great compassion, pulls them out and causes them to enter the Buddha-way.
Desiring to proclaim the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and to sever the knots of doubt for all sentient beings, he [preaches this].

While the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra was being preached, furthermore, there were wicked and heterodox persons who, harboring feelings of jealousy, slandered it, saying: "The Buddha’s wisdom does not transcend that of ordinary men."
To sever that haughty and perverse arrogance, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* itself proclaims his immeasurable divine virtues:
he is uniquely honored throughout the three realms and serves as a refuge for all. Should one give rise to even a single thought of malice, one incurs immeasurable transgression;
yet by giving rise to a single moment of pure faith, one enjoys the bliss of humans and devas and will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of causing people to have faith and accept the Dharma;
furthermore, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to rejoice that this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra is spoken.

The Great Teacher endowed with the Ten Powers is difficult to encounter; you have now met him. I shall, according to the occasion, expound the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and other teachings.
This profound treasury of Dharma is open for you to gather from at will.
Furthermore, all sentient beings have been afflicted by the disease of the fetters since the beginning of birth and death;
until now, no one has been able to cure this illness. I have now appeared in the world as the Great King of Physicians; therefore, I speak of the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the *Pāramitā-sūtras*, there are those who think:
"The Buddha is the same as humans; he too undergoes birth and death, and truly experiences hunger, thirst, cold, heat, old age, and illness.
Desiring to sever such thoughts, the Buddha speaks this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to demonstrate: [as follows].

My body is inconceivable. Even Brahmā, the Heavenly Kings, the various devas, and the ancestral spirits, though they sought to measure my body and investigate my voice for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were unable to fathom them; how much more so my wisdom and samādhi?
Furthermore, there are those who are ready for deliverance: some, lacking wisdom, seek only physical pleasure;

others, for the sake of the Path, cultivate and become attached to asceticism. Desiring to uproot these two extremes and lead them into the Middle Way, the Buddha therefore preached the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, in order to distinguish between the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and [to explain] the karmic fruit of making offerings,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was preached (as explained in the "Chapter on Seeing the Śarīra Stūpa").
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to speak of the *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva and the characteristics of the *avaivartika*;
furthermore, because he wishes to speak of the illusions of Māra, the counterfeits of Māra, and the deeds of Māra;
furthermore, for the sake of providing future generations with the causes and conditions for making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*; and furthermore, because he wishes to bestow [the prediction].
Because [the Buddha] bestows the predictions of enlightenment upon those of the three vehicles,
he speaks this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Furthermore, because the Buddha wishes to expound the first-principle *siddhānta* (there are four kinds of *siddhāntas*,
as seen later), he speaks this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra was spoken in order to inspire faith in the Buddha-dharma within great dialecticians such as the brahmin Dīrghanakha.

Furthermore, the Buddhas have two ways of teaching the Dharma: first, observing the minds of people according to their capacity for deliverance; second, observing the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Now, the Buddha wishes to explain the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); therefore, he preaches the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of teaching: first, that concerning the locus of dispute; second, that concerning the locus free from dispute.
The locus of dispute has already been explained in other sūtras; now, wishing to explain the locus free from dispute, I shall therefore speak the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, other sūtras frequently teach the Dharma by means of three categories: namely, the category of the wholesome, the category of the unwholesome, and the category of the indeterminate.
Now, wishing to explain the characteristics of all dharmas that are neither wholesome, nor unwholesome, nor indeterminate, he therefore preaches the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, in other sūtras, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught in accordance with the Dharma of the śrāvakas.
Now, wishing to teach the four foundations of mindfulness by means of a different method, he therefore speaks the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Furthermore, in other sūtras, the Buddha has taught that the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self-characteristic;
now, wishing to explain the five aggregates by means of a different method, he therefore teaches the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Just as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless, so too the causes and conditions for explaining the Mahāprajñāpāramitā are immeasurable and boundless.
Because this matter is vast, the brief explanation of the causes and conditions for the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is now concluded.
A Summary of Essential Points of All Dharmas from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (Detailed items are found within the main text of the sūtra;
this is the Dharma-gate for the accomplishment of Buddhahood that Bodhisattvas training in Prajñāpāramitā should know and practice).
Mundane phenomena (*loka-dharma*) are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), phenomena without outflows (*anāsrava-dharma*).
[These consist of] the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness).
The six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind);
the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena);
and the twelve bases (the faculties and their corresponding objects).
The eighteen elements (the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses);
the four great elements (earth, water, fire, and wind);
and the four noble truths (suffering, origin, cessation, and the path).

The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death).
The six pāramitās (generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom).
The four foundations of mindfulness (body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; also called the four establishments of mindfulness).
The five faculties (the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom).
The five powers (the five faculties, when further developed, are called the five powers).

The Four Right Efforts (to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen; to prevent those not yet arisen from arising; to bring about the arising of wholesome states not yet arisen; and to increase those already arisen).
The four bases of psychic power (concentration that gathers the mind when it is slightly distracted through right effort).

The seven factors of enlightenment (the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness).
The Eightfold Path (right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right speech, right action, and right livelihood).

The nine perceptions (the perception of bloating, the perception of disintegration, the perception of being smeared with blood, the perception of festering pus, the perception of bluish discoloration, the perception of being devoured, the perception of scattering, the perception of bones, and the perception of burning).

The eight recollections (recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of generosity, recollection of the devas, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, and recollection of death).

The ten perceptions (the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of the impurity of food, the perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of cessation,
the perception of dispassion, and the perception of exhaustion).

The eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ): [1] having internal perception of form, one perceives external forms; [2] being internally without perception of form, one perceives external forms; [3] the pure liberation, which is realized through bodily witness; [4–7] the four formless attainments; and [8] the cessation of sensation and perception—these together constitute the eight.

The Eight Bases of Mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*): 1. Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. 2. Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are many, whether beautiful or ugly;

this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. 3. Being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. 4. Being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are many, whether beautiful or ugly;

this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. 5. Being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are blue and vast; through the meditation on the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), this overcomes greed for all things. 6. Being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are yellow and vast; through the meditation on the foul, this overcomes [greed] for all things.

The contemplation of the great impurity of red external forms while being internally without perception of form cures attachment to all places; the contemplation of the great impurity of white external forms while being internally without perception of form cures attachment to all places.

The Eight Liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*): 1. Possessing internal perception of form, one perceives external forms; this is the first liberation. 2. Not perceiving internal form, one perceives external forms; this is the second liberation. 3. With a mind resolved upon purity, one realizes it with the body and dwells therein; this is the third liberation. 4.

By transcending all perceptions of form, by extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation. 5. By transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. 6. By transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness;

this is the sixth liberation. 7. By transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation. 8. By transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... [the eighth liberation].

[He] dwells having fully attained the meditative absorption on the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti) from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana)—which are the same as the aforementioned spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), differing only in that they take [the object] universally as their cognitive range.
The four dhyānas (with outflows, without outflows, both with and without outflows, neither with nor without outflows).
The four formless attainments (the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception).

The nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*): (1) the first dhyāna; (2) the second dhyāna; (3) the third dhyāna; (4) the fourth dhyāna; (5) the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); (6) the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); (7) the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
(8) the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); and (9) the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).

The sixteen aspects (of contemplation): [the four aspects of suffering—contemplating suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self; the four aspects of the cause of suffering—contemplating origination, causes, conditions, and arising; the four aspects of the cessation of suffering—contemplating cessation, extinction, excellence, and escape; and the four aspects of the path—contemplating the path, right practice, track, and way].

The ten stages (the stage of right observation, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having accomplished what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata).
The four fruits (*catur-phala*: *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*).
The three vehicles (*tri-yāna*: *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*—also called *pratyekajina*—and *bodhisattva*).
The four conditions (causal condition, immediately preceding condition, objective condition, and predominant condition).

The ten similes (like a magical illusion, like a flame, like the moon reflected in water, like space, like an echo, like a city of the gandharvas, like a dream, like a shadow, like an image in a mirror, and like a transformation).

The eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*): internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of nature, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the non-apprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of existence, and emptiness of both non-existence and existence.
The three types of clear knowledge (the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the divine eye, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows).
The five eyes (the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye).

The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā): [the power of] miraculous feats, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
The four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni): loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
The four means of integration (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni): giving, affectionate speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

The four fearlessnesses (catvāri vaiśāradyāni): fearlessness regarding being perfectly awakened, fearlessness regarding the destruction of outflows, fearlessness regarding obstructive dharmas, and fearlessness regarding the path leading to the end of suffering.
The four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*: analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of eloquence).

The ten practices (*daśa-caryāḥ*: the practice of joy, the practice of benefit, the practice of freedom from malice, the practice of inexhaustibility, the practice of freedom from delusion and confusion, the practice of excellent manifestation, the practice of non-attachment, the practice of reverence, the practice of wholesome dharmas, and the practice of reality).

The ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*): patience regarding ethical discipline, patience regarding knowledge and vision, patience regarding meditative concentration, patience regarding wisdom, patience regarding liberation, patience regarding emptiness, patience regarding wishlessness, patience regarding signlessness, patience regarding impermanence, and patience regarding non-arising.

The Ten Powers (*daśabala*): (1) the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; (2) the power of knowing the retribution of karma in the past, present, and future; (3) the power of knowing all meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; (4) the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings;

(5) the power of knowing the various inclinations of beings; (6) the power of knowing the various elements (*dhātu*) of beings; (7) the power of knowing the path leading to all destinations; (8) the power of knowing the unimpeded divine eye; (9) the power of knowing the recollection of past lives free from outflows (*anāsrava*);
and (10) the power of knowing the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

The Eighteen Unshared Dharmas: No failure in physical conduct; no failure in verbal conduct; no failure in mindfulness; no divergent thoughts; no lack of concentration; no relinquishing without full awareness;
no decrease in aspiration; no decrease in vigor; no decrease in mindfulness; no decrease in wisdom; no decrease in liberation; no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation;

all bodily actions are preceded by and conform to wisdom; all verbal actions are preceded by and conform to wisdom; all mental actions are preceded by and conform to wisdom; unimpeded wisdom knows the past; unimpeded wisdom knows the future; unimpeded wisdom knows the present.
Unimpeded in the world).
Thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
The path-knowledge of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects.

all dharani-doors, and all samadhi-doors.

the constant abiding in equanimity,
suchness, and the dharma-realm.

the inconceivable realm.

The eleven knowledges (jñāna): [1] dharma-jñāna, [2] anvaya-jñāna, [3] paracitta-jñāna, [4] saṃvṛti-jñāna, [5] duḥkha-jñāna, [6] samudaya-jñāna, [7] nirodha-jñāna, [8] mārga-jñāna, [9] kṣaya-jñāna, [10] anutpāda-jñāna, and [11] yathābhūta-jñāna.
The three samādhis (with vitarka and vicāra; without vitarka and with vicāra; without vitarka and without vicāra).
The three faculties (the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known).
The three gates of liberation (emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness). The sixteen types of views (self, sentient being, life-span, living being, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, youth, agent,
causer of action, arouser, causer of arousal, experiencer, causer of experience, knower, and seer).

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the five faculties, the five powers, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path).
(Appended Note) The Four *Siddhāntas* (1. *Loka-siddhānta*; 2. *Pudgala-siddhānta*; 3. *Pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; 4. *Paramārtha-siddhānta*).

Non-arising, non-attachment, non-abiding, and non-duality.
Without abandoning and without grasping, without protection and without exertion,
without thought, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing,

Non-duality is the skillful means; non-arising is the skillful means;

When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive either correspondence or non-correspondence.
One does not cling to form that is tranquil, nor to form that is not tranquil;
form does not unite with feeling, feeling does not unite with perception,

The past world does not unite with the present world;
the present world does not unite with the future world;

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on the Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats, with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained at the stage of a learner.
They had attained the fruit of stream-entry, with Mahākāśyapa as their leader.
Furthermore, there was a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats, with Mahāprajāpatī as their leader. Additionally, there were immeasurable upāsakas.
Upāsikā, there were also immeasurable and innumerable assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that could not be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Their names were: Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Ratnagotra, Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnadatta, Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, Bodhisattva Sāradhvaja, Bodhisattva Jyotirdatta, Bodhisattva Devadatta, and Bodhisattva Śakradatta... [and so forth].
He addressed the Bodhisattvas, with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vipula-mati and others as their leaders—all of whom were Dharma-princes, capable of succeeding to the rank of Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, upon his lion throne, spread out his own *niṣīdana* and sat cross-legged, entering the sublime *samādhi* known as the King of Meditative Concentrations (*Samādhirāja*).
With correct knowledge and correct mindfulness, he emerged from the King of Meditative Concentrations in a composed manner.
Arising, he observed with his pure divine eye the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From each and every part of his body, he emitted sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light.
Each of these rays illuminated a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively until they pervaded the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Within those realms, any sentient being who encounters this light will certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, covering the entire trichiliocosm and emitting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of rays of light.
Within each ray of light appeared precious lotus flowers, and upon each flower...

All sentient beings within the three thousandfold world system—including those in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, as well as others in the perilous pits of the unfavorable states of existence—were all freed from suffering and hardship.
Upon passing away from there, they were reborn among human beings and the six heavens of the desire realm;
all of them remembered their past lives and, filled with joy and exultation, went together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves with profound purity of mind.

At that time, the Tathāgata’s feet [were visible]. Then, all the immeasurable and innumerable devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens in this trichiliocosm, down to the Cāturmahārājika devas of the desire realm, as well as all others—both humans and non-humans—beheld the Tathāgata seated upon the lion throne, his majestic radiance shining forth like a great mountain of gold.
Each of them held various kinds of immeasurable celestial flowers. They held...

They approached the Buddha and scattered [flowers] over him. By the power of the World-Honored One’s supernormal faculties, each of them saw the Buddha sitting directly before them, preaching the Dharma to them alone.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not rise from his seat;
with a joyful smile, he emitted a great radiance from the gate of his face, which illuminated the trichiliocosm as well as the Ganges-sand number of buddha-fields in the other ten directions.
In all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all sentient beings, following the Buddha’s light,
universally beheld the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions, surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
as well as all other categories of sentient and non-sentient beings; they likewise beheld Śākyamuni in this land.
The Muni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was surrounded by an assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.
At that time, in the eastern direction, extending through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a final world named Ratnāvatī.
The Buddha there was named Ratnagotra, who currently dwells there in peace and maintains his abode for the sake of all.
When the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas was expounding the Great Prajñāpāramitā, there was a Bodhisattva named Samantaprabha.
Seeing this great light, the trembling of the earth, and the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, he approached the Buddha, prostrated himself at his feet, and said:
"By what cause and by what condition has this auspicious omen appeared? Then, the Buddha Ratnagotra addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, saying:
"Good son, from here to the west, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā.
The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni, who currently dwells there in peace and stability, teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
It is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that these auspicious signs have appeared."
Having heard this, Samantaprabha requested to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Buddha Ratnagotra then bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha a thousand-stemmed golden lotus and instructed him, saying:
"Take these flowers to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides and convey my greetings to him.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha will receive these lotuses and scatter them back toward the eastern buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he will cause these lotuses to pervade all those buddha-fields, and within each lotus calyx, there shall be an emanation Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture."
Seated, he taught the Dharma associated with the Great *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Any sentient beings who heard it would surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, Samantaprabha and his retinue, having made offerings and paid homage to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, withdrew and sat to one side. Such was the final world; as for all those [worlds] previously to the east...
In each of these buddha-fields, there was a Tathāgata manifesting to the great assembly to proclaim the sublime Dharma.
Each also had a preeminent bodhisattva who, having paid homage and made offerings with reverence toward the Buddha, withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, in the southern direction, beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, there was a final world named Free from All Sorrow; the Buddha there was named Virtue Free from Sorrow.
In that [world] there is a bodhisattva named Vigatāśoka. To the west, at the end of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Upaśānta;

The Buddha there is named Vijayadatta. In the northeast, at the end of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Vyūhavyūha;
the Buddha there is named Dhyānagajavikrama. Therein dwells a bodhisattva named Virajo-vīrya.
In the southeast, at the end of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Suvibuddhavyūha, which is most excellent.
[The assembly] rejoiced. The Buddha there was named Padmavijayaśrī. There was a bodhisattva there named Padmahasta.
In the southwest, at the end of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Virajaskarāśi. The Buddha there is named Sūryamaṇḍalavyāpijayaśrī.
There is a bodhisattva there named Sūryaprabha. In the northwest, at the end of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
In the final world, named True Sovereignty (*Suvibhūta*), there is a Buddha named Supreme Single Jewel Canopy (*Ekaratnavyuha-jaya*). Therein is a bodhisattva named Jewel Victory (*Ratnavijaya*).
Below, in the final world among all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, named Lotus (*Padma*), there is a Buddha named Lotus Virtue (*Padmaguṇa*).
Therein is a bodhisattva named Lotus Victory (*Padmavijaya*). Above, in all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
In the final world-system of this realm, there is a world named *Ānanda*. The Buddha there is named *Priyaguṇa*.
A bodhisattva there named *Priyadatta*, seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, approached the Buddha, prostrated himself, and said:
"By what cause and by what condition has this auspicious omen appeared? He then requested that [the Buddha] go to the *Sahā* world-system to visit, pay homage to, and make offerings to [Śākyamuni].
Having seen that he was nourishing the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, they were filled with joy and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, this trichiliocosm Buddha-world was filled with various jewels;

diverse and wondrous flowers were strewn everywhere upon the ground, and jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies were arranged in rows everywhere, so beautifully adorned as to be most delightful, like a world of lotuses.

In the pure land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma, there dwell the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, and other immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of great majestic power who have long resided therein. (The Chapter on Dependent Origination concludes.)

The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, with..."
One should take non-abiding as the skillful means to dwell securely in the *prajñāpāramitā*, because both that which dwells and that which is dwelt upon are unattainable.
One should take non-renunciation as the skillful means to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, because the giver, the recipient, and the gift are unattainable.
One should take non-protection as the skillful means to fulfill...

Because the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended, one should fulfill the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) by employing the means of non-appropriation.
Because the characteristics of movement and immovability cannot be apprehended, one should fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) by employing the means of non-exertion.
Because physical and mental exertion and indolence cannot be [apprehended]...
Because [the dhyānas] are unattainable, one should fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) by means of non-conceptualization.
Because the presence or absence of relish (*āsvāda*) is unattainable, one should fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-attachment.
Because the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) are unattainable, one should fulfill it through non-attachment.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling in the perfection of wisdom should fulfill all dharmas by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, because such dharmas are unapprehendable.
Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one knows the six *pāramitās* as they truly are and attains great fruit.
By taking non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the means, practicing a single *pāramitā* is able to fulfill the five *pāramitās*.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain these immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable,
and rare merits should study the Prajñāpāramitā (from the point where Śāriputra poses his question regarding the meaning of what should be studied until the end of this fascicle).

At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...”
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should contemplate in this way: they do not perceive a truly existent bodhisattva;

they do not perceive practice, nor do they perceive non-practice. Why is this? Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva...
Emptiness. The Bodhisattva is named "Emptiness. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*) is empty; it is not by means of emptiness that form is empty.

Form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. The intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) is empty;

The bodhisattva is merely a name. The Buddha is merely a name. Prajñāpāramitā is merely a name. Form is merely a name;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely names. The eye-base is merely a name; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are merely names.
The form-base is merely a name; the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and dharma-bases are merely names. The eye-element is merely...

There is only a name. The realms of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are merely names. The realm of form is merely a name. The realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are merely names.
The realm of eye-consciousness is merely a name. The realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are merely names.
Eye-contact is merely a name. Ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are merely names. That which arises conditioned by eye-contact is merely a name... [and so forth].
All feelings that arise exist as mere names. All feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions exist as mere names.
The earth element exists as a mere name; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements exist as mere names. Even causes and conditions exist as mere names.
The immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition—these are merely names. All phenomena produced from conditions are merely names.

Ignorance is merely a name; formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are merely names.
The perfection of generosity is merely a name; pure ethical discipline [is merely a name].
The perfections of patience, diligence, and meditative concentration exist as mere names. Internal emptiness exists as a mere name;

external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, emptiness of the limitless, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, and the emptiness of all phenomena exist as mere names.
Emptiness, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are merely names.

The four foundations of mindfulness are merely names. The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are merely names.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is merely a name; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are merely names.
There is only a name. The Noble Truth of Suffering is only a name. The Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are only names.
The four dhyānas are only names. The four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are only names.
The eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are only names. The doors of dhāraṇī are only names. The three...
The gates of *samādhi* exist only as names. The Ground of Joy exists only as a name.

The Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud exist only as names.

The Ground of Right Contemplation exists only as a name. The Ground of the Seed-Nature, the Eighth Ground, the Ground of Vision, the Ground of Thinness, and the Ground of Separation... [exist only as names].
The stage of desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata exist as mere names.
The five eyes exist as mere names; the six supernormal powers exist as mere names; the ten powers of a Tathāgata exist as mere names;

the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha exist as mere names.
The thirty-two marks of a great man are merely names. The eighty secondary signs are merely names. The quality of non-forgetfulness is merely a name.
The state of constant abiding in equanimity is merely a name. All-knowledge is merely a name. The knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are merely names.
The knowledge of all modes of knowledge is merely a name. It is the permanent uprooting of the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Thereafter, there is only a name: the fruit of stream-entry is only a name; the once-returner, the non-returner, and the fruit of arhatship are only names;
pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is only a name; mundane dharmas are only names; supramundane dharmas are only names; contaminated dharmas are only names;
uncontaminated dharmas are only names; conditioned dharmas are only names; unconditioned [dharmas] are only names.

Śāriputra, dharmas exist as mere names. Just as "self" is a mere name—referred to as "self"—yet in reality it cannot be found, so too are sentient beings, living beings, creatures, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, youths, agents, instigators, originators, prompters, experiencers, feelers, knowers, and seers. All these are merely names.
These are also merely names, designated as "sentient beings" and so forth, up to "seers.

Because they are empty of being unapprehendable, these are merely provisional, adventitious names established in accordance with worldly convention. All phenomena are likewise; one should not cling to them.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive a self, nor even a seer, nor do they...
Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they perceive the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

With the exception of the wisdom of the Buddhas, this cannot be attained by any stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, because it is [characterized by] the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Why is that? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding...
Neither the name nor the named can be apprehended, because they are not perceived and are free from attachment. Śāriputra,
when bodhisattvas are able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner, it is called the excellent practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, suppose you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—like a forest of rice, sesame, bamboo, reeds, and sugarcane;

even the combined wisdom of all those beings would not equal one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, of the wisdom of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*. It would not even reach a hundred-thousandth part.
Not even one-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part, would suffice.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of a bodhisattva can cause all sentient beings to attain parinirvāṇa, whereas the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not do so.

A bodhisattva constantly reflects: "I shall practice all dharmas, and even until I have forever uprooted all afflictions and habitual tendencies, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and through skillful means establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not have such thoughts.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are always the true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
It is because it is by relying upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that all wholesome dharmas appear in the world.
The Bodhisattva bestows immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless wholesome dharmas upon all sentient beings, acting as a great donor;
he does not require any further repayment for the kindness of those donors. (The "Chapter on Training in Contemplation" is concluded.)
Fascicle Four, Folio 14 (Chapter on Correspondence).
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "With what phenomena is a bodhisattva mahāsattva associated such that he may be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "He is associated with the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena."
Therefore, it should be said that this is associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra, when one is associated with such emptiness as this, one does not perceive form, nor even consciousness—whether in association or non-association. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form, nor even consciousness, as being either a phenomenon subject to arising or a phenomenon subject to cessation.

Whether it be defiled phenomena or pure phenomena, one does not perceive form conjoining with feeling, feeling conjoining with perception, perception conjoining with formations, or formations conjoining with consciousness.
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that conjoins with another phenomenon, for their intrinsic nature is empty.
Why is this so? All form is empty; that is not form. All feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty;

those are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this so? All form is empty; it does not possess the characteristic of resistance. All feeling is empty; it does not possess the characteristic of experiencing. All perception is empty;
it does not possess the characteristic of grasping images. All mental formations are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of volitional activity. All consciousness is empty.
That is not a characteristic of discernment. Why is this? Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves emptiness; emptiness is itself feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Why is this? Śāriputra...
"Son, these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness. They are neither born nor extinguished; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing.
They are not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present. Śāriputra, in this emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
There is no earth element, no water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element. There is no eye-base, no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base."
There is no sphere of form; no sphere of sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomena. There is no eye-element; no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
