There is no volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, nor the arising of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
There is no cessation of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, up to and including the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. There is none.
There is no noble truth of suffering; there is no noble truth of origin, cessation, or path. There is no attainment; there is no clear realization. There is no stream-enterer;
there is no fruit of stream-entry. There is no once-returner; there is no fruit of once-returning. There is no non-returner; there is no fruit of non-returning.

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is associated with such dharmas as these, it should be said that they are associated with the perfection of wisdom."
Fascicle Five; Fascicle Six.
Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive any phenomena as either associated or dissociated.

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, having entered into the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, one does not observe form up to consciousness as being either associated or dissociated.
One does not observe form up to consciousness in relation to the past, the future, or the present as being either associated or dissociated.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a past, a future, or a present.

Therefore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not observe whether all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is associated or dissociated with all phenomena (*dharma*). Why is this?
Because one does not even perceive the existence of any phenomenon, much less observe all-knowledge in relation to them.
Regarding all phenomena, whether they are associated or dissociated, one does not contemplate whether omniscience and the Buddha are associated or dissociated.
Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of a Buddha, how much less could one contemplate whether omniscience and the Buddha are associated or dissociated?
One does not contemplate whether omniscience and awakening are associated or dissociated.
It should be so. Why? Because one does not even perceive the existence of bodhi, much less observe whether omniscience (sarvajñatā) and bodhi are associated or dissociated.
Śāriputra, omniscience is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is himself omniscience.
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is itself awakening (*bodhi*); and awakening is itself all-knowledge.
Therefore, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not cling to any phenomena as existing, non-existing, permanent, impermanent, or blissful.
Suffering, self, non-self, tranquility, non-tranquility, emptiness, non-emptiness, signlessness, having signs, wishlessness,
and having wishes (from the beginning of fascicle five, page sixteen, to the end of fascicle six).
Scroll Seven:
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of any phenomena. Why? Because one does not perceive any differentiation in the nature of phenomena.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that can manifest equal enlightenment within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
They do not perceive any phenomenon apart from the dharma-realm, nor do they perceive the dharma-realm as existing apart from all phenomena.
They do not form such thoughts as: "This phenomenon can realize the dharma-realm," or "This phenomenon cannot realize the dharma-realm. Why is this?
Therefore, one does not even perceive dharmas, much less perceive any dharma that can realize the *dharmadhātu*, or fail to realize it.
When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive all dharmas as being associated with emptiness, nor does one perceive emptiness as being associated with all dharmas.
If one can thus be associated with emptiness in this way, this is the foremost association with emptiness.
Regarding associations (*saṃprayoga*): among all associations, association with the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost. Why is this?
Because this association with the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself association with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), association with signlessness (*animitta*), and association with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
For these reasons, it is the most supreme. (The Chapter on Association is concluded.)

Ānanda, if a bodhisattva, dwelling securely in prajñā, passes away from a buddha-field in another direction and is reborn here, that bodhisattva will swiftly become associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Because of this association with the perfection of wisdom, as soon as they are reborn, profound and wondrous dharma-gates will quickly manifest before them. From that point onward, they will always...

They will swiftly attain union with the *prajñāpāramitā*. In whatever place they are born, they will always encounter the Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them, thereby enabling them to gradually bring the *prajñāpāramitā* to full completion.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva dwells in the *prajñā*, having passed away from Tuṣita Heaven, they come to be born here. This is...

Bodhisattvas, for the most part bound by only one more birth, have the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom manifest before them with mastery;
they never forget them, and likewise [they possess] all the doors of dhāraṇī.
The gateways of samādhi manifest with mastery and are never forgotten.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva dwelling in prajñā dies among humans and is reborn among humans, that bodhisattva—except for those who are non-retrogressive—possesses dull faculties;
although they diligently cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they cannot quickly attain it.

It is associated with many [dharmas]. Furthermore, regarding those who have not yet attained mastery over all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, the next answer concerns where they will be reborn after passing away from this world:
"Śāriputra, because these bodhisattvas are associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they pass away from this place and are born in other buddha-fields; from one buddha-land..."

They go to a single buddha-field. In whatever place they are born, they always encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, making offerings to them, honoring them, respecting them, and praising them, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they never depart from the Buddhas.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who, because they lack skillful means, enter the four dhyānas and are also able to practice the six pāramitās.
For the most part, because this bodhisattva has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are reborn in the long-lived heavens.

When their lifespan there is exhausted, they are born again in the human realm, where they encounter various Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them. Although they practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), [they do not fall into the extreme of tranquility].
Yet their faculties are dull and obtuse, not very clear or sharp; whatever they undertake is not extremely skillful.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who enter the four dhyānas and are also able to practice the six pāramitās;

however, because these bodhisattvas lack skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they relinquish the dhyānas and are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). You should know that such bodhisattvas are likewise...
Their faculties are dull and not very sharp; whatever they do is not extremely skillful.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; who practice the six pāramitās;
who abide in internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and who abide in suchness and abide in the dharmadhātu.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*); practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; abiding in the four noble truths;

practicing the eight liberations, the eight spheres of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten spheres of totality; and practicing the three doors of liberation and the *dhāraṇīs*.
The doors of liberation; the doors of samādhi; the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

the cultivation of the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

the cultivation of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; and the cultivation of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

Wisdom. Because this bodhisattva possesses skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are not reborn by the power of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
In whatever place they are born, they always encounter Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, whom they serve, revere, honor, and praise.
They are never separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. It should be known that this bodhisattva—this...
Within this Bhadrakalpa, they will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;

yet because these bodhisattvas possess skillful means, they are not reborn by the power of those dhyānas, immeasurables, or formless states, but instead return to birth in the desire realm—either among a great kṣatriya clan or...
Whether they be great clans of brahmins, or great clans of householders and laymen, they are born for the sake of maturing sentient beings, and not out of craving or attachment to future existence.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who enter the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.
Regarding the four formless absorptions, because this bodhisattva possesses skillful means, he does not take birth in accordance with those meditative concentrations,
the immeasurables, or the formless realms; rather, he may be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, or among the Thirty-three Gods, or among the Yāma gods, or among the Tuṣita gods,
or among the gods who Delight in Emanations, or among the gods who Wield Power over Others' Emanations.

In order to bring sentient beings to maturity and to adorn and purify the buddha-fields, they constantly encounter the Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them, never letting such encounters pass in vain.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
By virtue of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he passes away from this place and is reborn in the Brahma-world as Mahābrahmā.
His majestic power and brilliance are far more intense than those of the other Brahma-hosts, exceeding them by many hundreds of thousands of times.

From his own celestial realm, he travels through various Buddha-fields, proceeding from one Buddha-land to another. Therein, he exhorts those bodhisattvas who have not yet realized awakening to realize it.

To those who have already realized awakening but have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma, I entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth who, by virtue of their skillful means, enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they practice the six pāramitās and abide in internal emptiness. And so forth...
Up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, they abide in suchness, abide in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and even the inconceivable realm.

They practice the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path.
They abide in the four noble truths and practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive [attainments].
They cultivate the four concentrations, the ten spheres of totality, and the three doors of liberation.
They cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi. They cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

They cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They cultivate the absence of...

The quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant equanimity, and the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This bodhisattva is not born through the power of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

They manifest before, serve, attend upon, and make offerings to the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and in the presence of these Buddhas, they diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). From this...
Passing away from that realm, he was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. There, he completed his lifespan with all faculties unimpaired, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Surrounded and escorted by immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of celestial beings, he manifested supernatural powers as he came to be born among humans.
He manifested the practice of asceticism, realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers; they are not born in the desire realm, nor are they born in the form realm, nor are they born in the formless realm.

They travel through various buddha-fields, going from one buddha-field to another, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and practicing the various [virtues] of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Bodhisattva practice. Gradually and successively, they realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers and sport with mastery, traveling from one buddha-field to another.
In the buddha-fields they pass through, there are no names such as śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; there is only the true Brahma-practice of the Single Vehicle. Such is the bodhisattva.
In all buddha-fields, they make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
they practice the perfection of wisdom until it is gradually perfected, purifying buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity.
They are never indolent or negligent. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers and sport with mastery, traveling from one buddha-field to another.
In the buddha-fields they pass through, the lifespan of sentient beings is beyond calculation.
In those buddha-fields, these bodhisattvas make offerings, show respect, honor, and praise immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Awakened, they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* until it is gradually perfected; they purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity without ever becoming weary.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and sport with mastery, traveling from one world-system to another.
There are world-systems where the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are not heard. This...
The Bodhisattva goes to those worlds to extol and praise the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—causing all sentient beings to give rise to profound pure faith.

Through this, they attain benefit and peace for a long night. When that Bodhisattva passes away from this life, they are reborn in a realm where a Buddha resides, where they cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and gradually realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, apply themselves with courageous diligence;
they attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; they practice the six pāramitās;
they abide in internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities; they abide in suchness."

The dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and even the inconceivable realm; practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; abiding in the four noble truths;
practicing the eight liberations, the eight spheres of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities; and practicing the three doors of liberation. First.
All dhāraṇī-doors. All samādhi-doors. Cultivating the stage of Extreme Joy, up to the stage of Dharma Cloud.

Cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers. Cultivating the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Cultivating non-forgetfulness.

The Dharma, the nature of constant equanimity, and the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Such a bodhisattva is not born in the desire realm, nor is he born in the form realm, nor is he born in the formless realm;

rather, he is always born in places that can benefit sentient beings, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have already previously cultivated the six...

The *pāramitās*. Having first generated the mind of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they immediately enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and proceed until they realize the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have previously cultivated the six *pāramitās* as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas;
having first generated the mind of awakening, they are able to successively realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
They attain equal enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings, and enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of great nirvāṇa without remainder.
After their parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma they have taught remains in the world for one kalpa, or more than one kalpa, benefiting and bringing happiness to boundless classes of sentient beings.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who have already previously cultivated the six pāramitās...
Maitreya. Furthermore, as for the practice of other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: from the very moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they become associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Surrounded before and behind by immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas, they travel through various buddha-fields, going from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thereby bringing them to fulfillment.
Maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields.
Fascicle Eight. Fascicle Nine.
Śāriputra, there is a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and attains the four dhyānas and the four... [untranslated portion].

Immeasurable. Regarding the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and the nine successive meditative states (*navānupūrvasamāpatti*), he enters and emerges from them in forward and reverse order, sporting with mastery.
This is not within the domain of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, while the bodhisattva employs skillful means to sport with mastery by successively transcending these attainments, he remains untainted and unattached therein.
There are bodhisattvas who, although abiding in all six pāramitās, always take one particular pāramitā as their primary focus;
they cultivate it to perfection and likewise exhort all sentient beings to practice it as well.
There are bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means, manifest bodies like those of Buddhas.

They enter everywhere into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, as well as among humans and devas, speaking the true Dharma in the various languages of each class of being to bring them supreme benefit, peace, and happiness.
There are bodhisattvas who, dwelling securely in the six pāramitās, manifest emanation bodies like those of Buddhas.
They travel everywhere to Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, proclaiming the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

In the presence of various Buddhas, they listen to the sublime Dharma, purify Buddha-fields, and survey throughout the ten directions the most excellent Buddha-fields and their subtle, pure characteristics. And then...
He himself brings forth a most supremely adorned and pure buddha-field, wherein he establishes the great bodhisattvas bound to one more birth,
causing them to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
There are bodhisattvas who, dwelling securely in the six *pāramitās*, constantly act as a lamp of Dharma for sentient beings blinded by false views.
They also maintain this illumination for themselves, constantly using it to light their own way until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This lamp of Dharma they never abandon. By virtue of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas always attain the manifestation of all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, there is no room for even a momentary arising of any unwholesome karma of body, speech, or mind.
There are bodhisattvas who dwell securely in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and are able to achieve supreme knowledge.
By virtue of this knowledge, although they engage with all phenomena (dharmas), they do not apprehend any phenomenon;
although they are able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, they have no attachment to or grasping at any phenomenon, because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena is empty.
There are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and attain the purification of the five eyes.

These six kinds of pāramitās encompass all pure and wholesome dharmas—namely, the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, the wholesome dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the wholesome dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the wholesome dharmas of tathāgatas.
Śāriputra, if one were to ask correctly: "Which dharma is able to encompass all? [the answer would be these six pāramitās].
Regarding wholesome dharmas, one should answer correctly: "The profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why?
Because it gives birth to the six *pāramitās*, as well as the five eyes and other immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable supreme merits.
One who can train in such pure five eyes will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" (Volume Eight).
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are able to bring forth the six perfections of superknowledge (*abhijñāpāramitā*):
first, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of supernormal powers; second, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear;

third, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds; fourth, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of past lives; fifth, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye; and sixth, the superknowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Regarding the supernormal power of realization (*abhijñā*): Śāriputra asked, "What is the supernormal power of realization consisting of the knowledge of miraculous feats?

The Buddha said, "The bodhisattva’s supernormal power of realization consisting of the knowledge of miraculous feats gives rise to immeasurable kinds of great miraculous transformations. That is to say:

shaking the earth and all other things throughout each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; transforming one into many, and transforming many into one; appearing or disappearing at will; and moving with such swiftness..."
Unimpeded, he passes straight through mountain cliffs and walls as if through empty space. He travels across the void like a bird in flight; he emerges from and sinks into the earth as if in water;
he walks upon the surface of the water as if on solid ground. His body emits smoke and flames like a wildfire on a high plateau;
his person pours forth streams of water like the melting of the Snowy Mountains. Even the sun and moon, with their divine virtues and formidable power, cannot withstand him; with his hand—

He touches and strokes them, causing their radiance to be eclipsed, even up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. His mastery over his physical form is such that these supernormal transformations are immeasurable and boundless.
Although this bodhisattva possesses such powers of knowledge regarding the sphere of supernormal feats (*ṛddhiviṣaya-jñāna-prabhāva*), he remains entirely unattached to them.
He does not form the thought: "I shall now manifest the supernormal power of knowledge for my own amusement," nor does he do so for the amusement of others.

...except for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Śāriputra asked: "What is the supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear-knowledge (divyaśrotra-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā)?
The Buddha said: "The bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear-knowledge is supremely pure and surpasses the divine ears of humans and devas.
It can, as it truly is, hear the various sounds of sentient and non-sentient beings throughout each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. That is to say, pervading..."

They hear the sounds of the hells, the sounds of animals, the sounds of the realm of hungry ghosts, the sounds of humans, and the sounds of devas; the sounds of śrāvakas, the sounds of pratyekabuddhas, the sounds of bodhisattvas, and the sounds of tathāgatas;
the sounds of reviling and condemning birth-and-death, the sounds of praising nirvāṇa; the sounds of turning one's back on the conditioned, the sounds of heading toward bodhi;
the sounds of loathing that which is with outflows, the sounds of delighting in that which is without outflows; and the sounds extolling the Three Jewels.
The sound of [the Dharma]; the sound that subdues heterodox paths; the sound of debating and discerning [truths]; the sound of chanting and reciting the sūtras;

the sound that exhorts the severance of all evils; the sound that teaches the cultivation of all virtues; the sound that rescues and delivers from suffering and hardship; the sound of celebration, consolation, and joy. Such sounds as these.

Whether great or small, they are all able to hear them everywhere, without obstruction or hindrance. Although this bodhisattva possesses such functions of the divine ear, they have no attachment whatsoever toward them.

They do not form the thought: "I now bring forth the supernormal power of the divine ear for my own amusement, or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). They relinquish [it].
Ratnapāṇi asked, "What is the supernormal power of realizing the minds of others?

The Buddha replied, "The bodhisattva’s supernormal power of realizing the minds of others can, as it truly is, know the mental states and mental factors of other sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

That is to say, they thoroughly know whether other sentient beings possess a mind of attachment or a mind free from attachment; a mind of aversion or a mind free from aversion; a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion..."
The deluded mind; the lustful mind; the mind free from lust; the grasping mind; the mind free from grasping; the concentrated mind; the distracted mind;
the narrow mind; the broad mind; the uplifted mind; the depressed mind; the tranquil mind; the untranquil mind; the restless mind; the non-restless mind;
the concentrated mind; the unconcentrated mind; the liberated mind; the unliberated mind; the tainted mind; the untainted mind; the flawed mind; the flawless mind.
There are minds that are surpassed and minds that are unsurpassed. Although the bodhisattva possesses such applications of the knowledge of others' minds, he is entirely unattached to them.
He does not form the thought: "I now evoke the supernormal power of knowing others' minds for my own amusement."
For the sake of entertaining others, except for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Śāriputra asked:

"What is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives? The Buddha said: "The bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives can, according to reality, know all matters concerning the past lives of all sentient beings throughout as many world-systems in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. That is to say, he recollects them..."
Whether concerning oneself or others, with one mind, ten minds, a hundred minds, a thousand minds, or many hundreds of thousands of minds, they recollect various past lives;
or again, by recollecting for one day, ten days, a hundred days, a thousand days, or many hundreds of thousands of days, they recollect various past lives.
Or again, he recollects various past lives spanning one month, ten months, a hundred months, a thousand months, or many hundreds of thousands of months;
or again, he recollects various past lives spanning one year, ten years, a hundred years, a thousand years, or many hundreds of thousands of years.

Or again, one may recollect the events of former existences for one eon, ten eons, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, many hundreds of thousands of eons, or even for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
Or again, one may recollect all the events of former existences belonging to the past limit, namely: at such a time, in such a place, with such a name, and such a clan.
Such types of beings, eating such food, abiding for such a duration, having such a life limit, possessing such longevity, experiencing such pleasure, and undergoing such suffering;
passing away from there to be born here, and passing away from here to be born there;

with such physical appearances and such speech—whether briefly or in detail, whether their own or those of others—all such matters of former existences he is able to recollect. Although the Bodhisattva...
Possessing such power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he remains entirely unattached within it. He does not form the thought:

"I now manifest the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives for my own amusement, or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
Śāriputra asked: "What is the supernormal power of realization through the knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurjñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*)? The Buddha said: "The Bodhisattva’s divine eye..."
The supernormal knowledge of realization through wisdom is supremely pure and transcends the eyes of humans and devas.
It is able to see, as they truly are, the various forms and appearances of sentient and non-sentient beings throughout worlds in each of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

That is to say, it universally perceives sentient beings at the time of their birth and death—whether of exquisite or coarse appearance, superior or inferior, in happy or miserable realms—and all such various [phenomena].

From these physical forms and appearances, one further understands that among the various classes of sentient beings, there are differences in rebirth according to the power and function of their karma.

Such sentient beings, having accomplished virtuous conduct of body, virtuous conduct of speech, and virtuous conduct of mind, and having praised the causes and conditions of noble ones and right view, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, shall ascend to the happy realms—among gods or humans—and experience various sublime joys. Thus it is.

Through the causes and conditions of committing misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and holding wrong views that disparage the noble ones, one will, at the dissolution of the body after death, fall into the miserable destinies;
or be born among hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts;

or be born in remote borderlands, among lowly castes, or among classes of foul and wretched sentient beings, where one undergoes various forms of intense suffering. Such are the various distinctions in the fruits one receives.
Although a bodhisattva possesses such functions of the divine eye, they remain entirely unattached to them.

They do not form the thought: "I shall now bring forth the supernormal power of the knowledge of the divine eye for my own amusement, or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Śāriputra asked: "What is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*)? The Buddha said: "Bodhi..."

The supernormal knowledge of the realization of the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) enables one to know, as they truly are, whether the outflows of all sentient beings—whether oneself or others—in all worlds throughout the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have been exhausted or not.
This supernormal knowledge is perfected only when it relies upon the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) to sever all obscurations and habitual tendencies.
At the time of attaining the irreversible Bodhisattva stage, it is also termed [the knowledge] regarding all outflows.

It is because they have been exhausted and will never again arise before him. Although the bodhisattva has attained this supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), he does not fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha;
rather, he proceeds solely toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, as he no longer seeks any other benefit.
Although the bodhisattva possesses such application of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, he remains entirely unattached to it.

One does not form this thought: "I shall now evoke the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows for my own amusement, or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

There is a bodhisattva who, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), dwells securely in the six perfections and purifies the path to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because ultimate emptiness is without coming or going, there is no giving and no stinginess, for these are merely conventional designations.
Because it is merely a conventional designation, there is no pure ethical discipline and no violation of ethical discipline.
There is no patience and no anger, because they are merely conventional designations. There is no diligence and no laziness, because they are merely conventional designations.
There is no meditative concentration and no distraction, because they are merely conventional designations. There is no wisdom and no delusion, because they are merely conventional designations.
Thus, this bodhisattva does not cling to entering, does not cling to not entering, and does not cling to having crossed over.

He does not cling to what is not his own; he does not cling to generosity; he does not cling to stinginess; he does not cling to pure ethical discipline; he does not cling to the violation of ethical discipline;
he does not cling to patience; he does not cling to anger; he does not cling to diligence; he does not cling to laziness;

he does not cling to meditative concentration; he does not cling to distraction; he does not cling to wisdom; he does not cling to delusion. At that time, regarding such clinging, he does not [cling].
Even attachment is without anything to which one is attached. Why is this? Because one has realized that all phenomena are ultimately empty.

When the Buddha spoke of the supreme merits of the *prajñāpāramitā*, immeasurable great bhikṣus in the assembly all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. From the Blessed One’s face issued various colors.

The Light addressed Ānanda, saying: "These immeasurable bhikṣus who have risen from their seats shall, from this point forward, attain Buddhahood during the sixty-one kalpas of the Star Simile Kalpa; they shall all share the same name, namely, Tathāgata Mahādhvajaketu."
Endowed with the ten titles, these bhikṣus, after passing away from here, shall be reborn in the eastern realm of Akṣobhya Buddha.

There, in the presence of that Buddha, they shall diligently cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, there was a multitude of sixty hundred-thousand devaputras who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and its meritorious benefits as taught by the Buddha, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The World-Honored One prophesied for that Bodhisattva Awakening Mind (Bodhicitta): "He shall, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Maitreya, leave the household life with pure faith and diligently cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
The Tathāgata Maitreya will grant him a prophecy.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, the entire assembly here beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in each of the thousand Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as well as the merits of those Buddha-lands.
Magnificent and exquisitely sublime. At that time, the immeasurable classes of sentient beings in this assembly each made a vow, saying:
"By means of all the purely virtuous deeds I have cultivated, may I be reborn in those various Buddha-fields.

Then, from the Blessed One’s countenance, rays of light of various colors were emitted, and he addressed Ānanda, saying: "When these sentient beings' lives here come to an end, they shall follow [their vows]..."
By the power of their vows, they shall each attain rebirth in those respective Buddha-fields.

In the presence of those Buddhas, they shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In every place where they are born, they shall never be separated from the Buddhas.
Having diligently practiced all dharmas and the other deeds of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and attained full perfection, they shall simultaneously become Buddhas, all being identical.
The first title is: The Tathāgata King of Adornment, endowed with the ten epithets (the end of the Chapter on Successive Rebirths).
Fascicle Ten (Chapter on Praising Supreme Virtues):
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, and the rest of the assembly joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, praising and speaking of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
"O Bhagavān, among the pāramitās, those bodhisattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā are the most honored,
the most supreme, the highest, and the most wondrous; they possess great power, are able to practice the peerless dharmas,
are able to fulfill the peerless dharmas, are able to perfect the peerless dharmas, and are able to attain the peerless self."
The body— namely, the wondrously adorned body of boundless and supreme marks and signs— is able to realize the peerless and sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). World-Honored One, it is because the Tathāgata also practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
being able to practice and abide in its fulfillment, and possessing various merits, that he attains the peerless.
[He attains] form that is unequaled and peerless, as well as feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are unequaled and peerless;

he realizes the unequaled and peerless awakening, turns the unequaled and peerless wheel of Dharma, and delivers immeasurable classes of sentient beings, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
Fascicle Ten, Leaf Eleven (*Prabhūta-jihvā-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*).
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the mark of the broad and long tongue, which completely covered the trichiliocosm.

Furthermore, from this mark of the tongue, he emitted rays of light of various colors, universally illuminating Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. At that time...
"In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are each immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas who have each come to their respective Buddhas.
For what reason is there this auspicious omen? The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"In the Sahā world, there is the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who is preaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā. The light now seen is that very Buddha’s tongue."
Manifested through signs, at that time the bodhisattvas were filled with joy and leaped for gladness;

desiring to go and behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to [the Buddha], and to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, they reached the presence of this Buddha in a mere moment. At that time, the World-Honored One smiled and again emitted rays of light of various colors.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "The great multitude who have risen from their seats have already attained realization regarding all dharmas."
Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), they shall practice the bodhisattva path for sixty-eight *koṭis* of great eons in future ages.

During the Flower Accumulation Eon (*Puṣpasaṃcaya-kalpa*), they shall all attain Buddhahood, bearing the same name: the Tathāgata Awakening-Part Flower (*Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa*), fully endowed with the ten titles.
Fascicle Eleven (Chapter on Instruction and Admonition) through Fascicle Thirty-Six.

The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "By means of your eloquence, you should proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, providing instruction and admonition so that they may cultivate and study it to ultimate completion. At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas and the great...
The śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others all had this thought:

"Does the Venerable Subhūti rely on the power of his own wisdom and eloquence, or does he do so by receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power? Subhūti, knowing their thoughts, [spoke as follows].
He then addressed Śāriputra, saying: "You should know that all the teachings and instructions spoken by the disciples of the Buddhas are sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.
Why is this? When the Buddhas proclaim the essentials of the Dharma, those disciples receive the Buddha’s teaching and diligently practice and study it;
they are thus able to realize the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Therefore, whatever they proclaim is entirely non-contradictory with the true nature of phenomena."
[This would be] a contradiction. Therefore, as the Buddha has said, "It is like a lamp transmitting its light.

I shall, by relying upon the Buddha’s majesty and the Buddha’s empowerment, proclaim for the sake of the bodhisattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*; it is not by the power of my own wisdom or eloquence.
Why is this? Because the Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not [within the reach] of the various śrāvakas...
Having heard of the domain of the Pratyekabuddhas, at that time Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In this context, what dharma is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' and what dharma is called 'prajñāpāramitā'? World-Honored One, I do not perceive any dharma that can be named a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' nor do I perceive any dharma that can be named 'prajñāpāramitā.'"
"...Pāramitā. These two names are likewise not to be found. How then can I instruct the bodhisattvas? The Buddha said:
'Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is merely a name, called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Prajñāpāramitā is also merely a name, called "prajñāpāramitā. These two..."
It is called a "name. It is neither born nor extinguished; it exists only as a designation, a conceptualization, and a verbal expression.
Such a conventional name does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because it is unattainable.

When bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should correctly train in all phenomena as being conventional designations of names, conventional designations of phenomena, and conventional designations of instructions.
When practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one should not regard any phenomena as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either pure or impure, as either empty or non-empty, or as having signs or being signless.
Whether with aspiration or without aspiration; whether tranquil or not tranquil; whether secluded or not secluded;
whether conditioned or unconditioned; whether with outflows or without outflows; whether arising or ceasing; whether wholesome or unwholesome;
whether faulty or faultless; whether afflictive or non-afflictive; whether mundane or supramundane.
Whether it be defiled or pure, whether it belongs to saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, whether it is internal or external,
whether it dwells between the two, or whether it is obtainable or unobtainable.
The two names, "Bodhisattva" and "Prajñā," are not seen within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), nor are they seen within the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).

Why is this? Because when a Bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not give rise to conceptualization (*vikalpa*) or discursive differentiation (*parikalpa*) regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).
Abiding in non-conceptualization, they cultivate all phenomena, seeking only the One with right diligence.
The knowledge of all-knowledge.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "As you have said, because dharmas such as form are unapprehendable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also unapprehendable.
Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva is unapprehendable, the practice of the perfection of wisdom is likewise unapprehendable."
Much, too, is unattainable. When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should train in this manner.
(From the tenth line of scroll fifteen to the seventh line of scroll seventeen.)

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "It is as you have said. Because dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), and dharmas such as the permanence or impermanence of form, are unapprehendable, the designations (*adhivacana*) for dharmas such as form, and the designations for dharmas such as the permanence or impermanence of form, are likewise unapprehendable.
Since both the dharma and its designation are unapprehendable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also unapprehendable."
Because the *samyaksaṃbuddha* cannot be apprehended, the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended.
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should train in this manner (from the eighth leaf of scroll seventeen to the fourth leaf of scroll thirty-six).
Furthermore, Subhūti, as to what you have previously said—that you do not perceive any dharma that can be called a bodhisattva mahāsattva—it is so, it is so;
it is just as you have said. Subhūti, dharmas do not perceive dharmas; dharmas do not perceive the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
the dharma-realm does not perceive dharmas; the dharma-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm. When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom...
When practicing the pāramitās, one perceives nothing at all regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).
When there is nothing perceived, the mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; the mind does not sink into any phenomena, nor does it feel regret. Why is this?
It is because this bodhisattva does not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to not perceiving the unsurpassed [enlightenment] of the Buddhas.
“...perfectly complete enlightenment. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, for what reason does the mind not sink or become despondent regarding all phenomena?
The Buddha said, “This bodhisattva neither attains nor perceives any mental states or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Because of this, the mind does not sink or become despondent regarding all phenomena. Subhūti asked, “How is this so?”
His mind is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid. The Buddha said:

"This bodhisattva does not perceive and does not see any mental faculty (*manodhātu*) or mental consciousness faculty (*manovijñānadhātu*) throughout all things. He is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).
Subhūti, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom in any place."
One attains the name "Prajñāpāramitā," yet one does not attain a bodhisattva, nor the name "bodhisattva," nor the mind of a bodhisattva.
One should instruct and admonish all bodhisattvas in this manner, causing them to reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.
(The Chapter on Instruction and Admonition concludes.)
Fascicle 36, Leaf 7 (Chapter on Encouraging Study).

Śāriputra replied to Subhūti: "If a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās without skillful means, and dwells in the three gates of liberation, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, rather than entering the bodhisattva’s correct [path]."

Its nature is free from arising. This is called the "falling from the summit" of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, this falling from the summit is also called "arising. Śāriputra asked, "For what reason is it called 'arising'?
Subhūti replied, "'Arising' refers to attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). If a bodhisattva has attachment to the phenomena that accord with the path, it is called 'arising.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s attachment to phenomena that accord with the path? Subhūti said, "It is [the attachment] while practicing..."
When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, if one dwells upon all phenomena and gives rise to conceptual attachments, this is called a bodhisattva’s "affection for the dharmas that accord with the Path.
Such affection for the dharmas is said to be "birth," just as the digestion of old food can become a source of affliction.
How then does a bodhisattva enter the state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*)? Subhūti replied: When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*...

One does not perceive internal emptiness, nor does one depend upon internal emptiness, while contemplating external emptiness. One does not perceive external emptiness, nor does one depend upon external emptiness, while contemplating internal emptiness.
This continues until: one does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor does one depend upon the emptiness of intrinsic nature, while contemplating the emptiness of non-existence.

One does not depend upon the emptiness of intrinsic nature, while contemplating the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. One does not perceive the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

Without depending on the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, one contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). If one practices such contemplation, it is called entering the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should not be attached to the bodhicitta; "bodhicitta" is [defined as] non-attachment.
"One should not be attached to the unequaled mind; 'unequaled mind' is the name for that which should not be attached to.
One should not be attached to the vast mind; 'vast mind' is the name for that which should not be attached to. Why is this?
Because this mind is not a mind, as its intrinsic nature is pure. Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "In what way is this mind intrinsically pure? Subhūti replied:
This mind, by its very nature, is neither associated with nor dissociated from greed; it is neither associated with nor dissociated from hatred;
it is neither associated with nor dissociated from delusion; and it is neither associated with nor dissociated from the various fetters, bonds, and latent tendencies.
It is not associated with the various views, outflows, floods, yokes, or graspings, nor is it dissociated from them.
It is not associated with the Hearers, Solitary Realizers, and so forth, nor is it dissociated from them. Such is the nature of this mind: its intrinsic nature is pure.
Śāriputra asked, "Does this mind exist as a mind, or is it non-mind? Subhūti replied, "Within the state of non-mind, there is no existent nature."
“Is it possible to apprehend non-existence? Śāriputra replied, “No, Subhūti.
Subhūti answered, “Within the natureless mind, since both existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, how can one say that this mind is a mind with existence or a mind without nature?
Śāriputra asked, “What is meant by ‘mind’ and ‘non-mind’? Subhūti answered, “In regard to...”
"All dharmas are without change and without discrimination; this is called the 'non-mind-nature' of the mind. Śāriputra asked:

"Just as the mind is without change and without discrimination, is form also without change and without discrimination? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also without change and without discrimination?
And so on, up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is also without change?"
"Is it non-conceptual? He replied, "It is so. Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
You should train in this way. You should know, Subhūti, that you already abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the three vehicles are extensively explained and revealed. If a bodhisattva trains in the Prajñāpāramitā, then..."
In order to study all three vehicles exhaustively, one also attains skillfulness in the teachings of the three vehicles (*Samādāpana-parivarta*, end;
*Avasthāna-parivarta*, folio 18 of scroll 36). Scroll 37:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding all dharmas, I neither grasp nor perceive them, whether they are accumulated or dispersed."
How can it be said that these are all dharmas, or that these are the names of all dharmas? They are all without abiding, yet they are not non-abiding.
Why is this? Because the referents of the names of all dharmas do not exist at all, the names of all dharmas are without abiding, yet they are not non-abiding.
World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the Prajñāpāramitā being taught through such characteristics...
When practicing the *pāramitās*, their mind does not sink, nor do they feel regret; their mind is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid.
One should know that they already abide on the stage of non-retrogression, abiding through the skillful means of non-abiding.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: “A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not dwell in form;

they should not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this? Form is empty of the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
World-Honored One, it is not that form is separate from the emptiness of form, nor that the emptiness of form is separate from form; form does not depart from emptiness.”
Emptiness is not separate from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
This extends to the point that one should not dwell upon any of the doors of dhāraṇī or any of the doors of samādhi; they are also like this.
If a bodhisattva lacks skillful means while practicing the perfection of wisdom, [they will conceive of] "I" and "mine."
Because they are gripped and disturbed by what is grasped, the mind dwells upon form; the mind dwells upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Due to this dwelling, one applies effort toward form and applies effort toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Because of these applications of effort, one is unable to embrace the *prajñāpāramitā*, unable to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, and unable to...
One cannot fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) nor accomplish the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). A bodhisattva should contemplate all phenomena through the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
When contemplating in this way, the mind finds no place of activity within any phenomenon; this is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation. This samādhi...
This *samādhi* is subtle, wondrous, and supreme; it is vast and immeasurable, capable of gathering infinite and unimpeded functions.
It is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) that it accomplishes should not be grasped.
Why is this? Omniscience is not attained through the cultivation of grasping at signs; all grasping at signs is nothing but affliction (*kleśa*).

What are these characteristics? They are the characteristic of form, the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the characteristics of all *dhāraṇī* gates and the characteristics of all *samādhi* gates. To grasp and cling to these various characteristics is called affliction. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and cannot be grasped. (The Chapter on Non-Abiding concludes.)
Fascicle 38 (Chapter on the Characteristics of Prajñāpāramitā), Fascicle 39, Fascicle 40, Fascicle 41.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva examines with precise discernment and finds that no phenomenon exists and cannot be apprehended, this is *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within that which neither exists nor can be apprehended, what is there to be questioned or censured? At that time, Śāriputra...
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "In this regard, what dharma is non-existent and unapprehendable? Subhūti replied:
"It is the dharma of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is non-existent and unapprehendable; all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Why is this?
Because of internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā), and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā)."
Observing in this way with thorough discernment, one is able to never abandon the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, "By what cause is it possible to never abandon it?

Subhūti replied, "By knowing the *prajñāpāramitā* as it truly is—namely, that it is devoid of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*—and by knowing all phenomena as they truly are."
Because it is free from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. Śāriputra asked:
"What is the intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and what is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena? Subhūti replied:
"Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*; non-existence is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, Śāriputra. The *prajñā*...
If the *pāramitās* are devoid of the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are devoid of the characteristic of all phenomena;

if self-nature (*svabhāva*) is also devoid of self-nature, and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is also devoid of characteristic; if self-nature is also devoid of characteristic, and characteristic is also devoid of self-nature;
if both self-nature and characteristic are devoid of characteristic and self-nature, and both characteristic and self-nature are devoid of self-nature and characteristic—if, for a bodhisattva...
By training in this, one is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is this?
Because one knows that all phenomena are without arising and without accomplishment. Śāriputra asked: "For what reason are all things without arising and without accomplishment?"

Subhūti said: "Because form is empty, the production and accomplishment of form cannot be apprehended. Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, the production and accomplishment of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
This extends even to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [dharmas], and even to those dharmas that are internal, external, or between the two;
because they are empty, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [dharmas]—even those that are internal, external, or between the two—"
The production and accomplishment of the two [types of] phenomena cannot be apprehended. If a bodhisattva trains in this way, they draw near to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This bodhisattva attains purity of body, speech, and mind; they do not give rise to a mind accompanied by greed, hatred, or delusion;
they do not give rise to a mind accompanied by pride, flattery, deceit, stinginess, or craving; and they do not give rise to any mind accompanied by views or grasping. Because of this...

Because they are born [in this way], they will ultimately never fall into a woman’s womb; they will always undergo miraculous birth (*upapāduka*) and will also never be reborn in the various perilous and evil realms, except for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings as a causal condition.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If a bodhisattva, lacking skillful means, practices the perfection of wisdom while practicing with respect to form, or practicing with respect to the characteristics of form, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, or practice with respect to the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom," and so on, up to...
If one forms the thought, "That is a bodhisattva mahāsattva," this is a mode of practice characterized by apprehension;
it is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. To practice the perfection of wisdom while maintaining a mode of practice characterized by apprehension is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "If a bodhisattva, lacking skillful means, practices the perfection of wisdom while dwelling upon a conceptualization of form and resolving upon it, he exerts effort toward form.

If he dwells upon a conceptualization of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness and resolves upon them, he exerts effort toward feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Because of this exertion..."
One cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, and future suffering. Even if one forms conceptions and resolute convictions regarding śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, and their respective dharmas, and then applies oneself to those śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas,
and their dharmas through such application, by reason of that very application, one cannot be liberated from birth, old age, and sickness.
"Death and the suffering of the future. At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom through skillful means? Subhūti replied:
"If a bodhisattva possesses skillful means, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, they do not course in form, nor do they course in the characteristics of form; this is their practice."

The perfection of wisdom does not proceed by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not proceed by way of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

This extends even to not proceeding by way of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the [knowledge of] all aspects.

From the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) not practicing the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), up to the knowledge of all aspects—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Thus, by practicing the perfection of wisdom with such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one is able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*). Śāriputra, this is how a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), one does not grasp at existence, nor does one grasp at non-existence;

one does not grasp at both existence and non-existence, nor does one grasp at neither existence nor non-existence. One does not even grasp at this non-grasping. (From the seventeenth leaf of Volume 39 to the seventh leaf of Volume 41.)
The bodhisattva does not grasp at nor cling to any phenomena, nor to the prajñāpāramitā itself;
this is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of non-grasping and non-clinging. This samādhi is subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
Vast and immeasurable, it is capable of gathering boundless and unimpeded activities that are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there are other samādhis in which one constantly dwells without relinquishing them, thereby swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It should be known that those who abide in such samādhis have already received the prophecy of future buddhahood from the Buddhas of the past.
They are also prophesied by all the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present.
Although these bodhisattvas abide in such samādhis, they do not perceive these samādhis, nor do they cling to them.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Is there a distinct, truly existent bodhisattva who abides in such samādhis as these?"
"Have you already received the prediction of future enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past and present? Subhūti replied, "No, Śāriputra.
The perfection of wisdom is not different from the various samādhis; the various samādhis are not different from the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is not different from the perfection of wisdom and the [samādhis]..."
"Maudgalyāyana, the *prajñāpāramitā* and the *samādhi* are not different from the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Why is this? Because the nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is equal.
Śāriputra said, "If the nature of all phenomena is equal, can this *samādhi* be manifested? Subhūti replied, "It cannot be manifested. Śāriputra said, "..."

Śāriputra asked, "Does this bodhisattva have conceptual understanding regarding this samādhi? Subhūti replied, "He has no conceptual understanding. Śāriputra asked, "Why is there no conceptual understanding?
Subhūti replied, "Because he is without discursive differentiation (*avikalpa*). Śāriputra asked, "Why is he without discursive differentiation?
Subhūti replied, "Because the nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-dharmatā*) is entirely non-existent; therefore, within that concentration..."
Conceptual discrimination arises. Why is this? Because all phenomena and meditative concentrations are both non-existent;
within that which is non-existent, there is no basis for the arising of conceptual thoughts or understandings. At that time, the Bhagavān praised Subhūti, saying:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to study the perfection of wisdom should train in this manner, up to and including the wish to study the knowledge of all aspects."

"One should train in this way. Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva trains in this manner, is it for the sake of correctly training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, and so on, up to correctly training in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "It is for the sake of correctly training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of taking non-apprehension as the expedient."
“...up to and including training for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.

Śāriputra asked, “Regarding ‘non-apprehension,’ what dharmas are not apprehended? The Buddha said, “From the self up to the knower and the seer, they are not apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.”
Therefore, even up to the point where Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked: "What is the meaning of 'ultimately pure'?
The Buddha said: "All phenomena do not emerge and do not arise; they do not perish and are not exhausted; they are neither defiled nor pure;
they are neither attained nor conditioned. This is called the meaning of ultimate purity. At that time, Śāriputra addressed [the Buddha].
The Buddha said, "When training in this way, what dharma is one training in? The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Regarding all dharmas, there is nothing at all to be trained in.
Why is this? It is because all dharmas are not as they are grasped by foolish, ordinary worldlings; thus, there is nothing therein to be trained in.
Śāriputra said, "If that is so, how do all dharmas exist? The Buddha said, "All..."
Dharmas are such that they do not exist; yet they exist in this way. If one cannot thoroughly comprehend these dharmas that do not exist, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Śāriputra asked: "What dharmas do not exist, such that failing to comprehend them is called ignorance?

The Buddha said: "Form (*rūpa*) does not exist; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) do not exist, because of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*)."

Up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these do not exist because of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra, due to the power of ignorance and craving, they conceptually discriminate and cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; consequently, they neither know nor see.
All phenomena are of a nature of non-existence. One discriminates among phenomena;

because of this discrimination, one becomes attached to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including attachment to the knowledge of all aspects. Because of this attachment, one discriminates that phenomena are of a nature of non-existence.
This occurs because of not knowing and not seeing these phenomena. Śāriputra asked: "Regarding what phenomena does one not know?"

[He] does not see. The Buddha said: "Because he does not know and does not see form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on up to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), he falls among the ranks of foolish ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) and is unable to transcend them.
Śāriputra asked: "In what respect is he unable to transcend? The Buddha said: "He is unable to transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In...
They cannot transcend the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). They cannot transcend the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Because they cannot transcend them, they are unable to accomplish the Dharma of the Śrāvakas or the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas. They are unable to accomplish the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas or the Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
Because they do not accomplish these, they are unable to have faith and acceptance. Śāriputra asked: "In regard to what Dharma are they unable to have faith?"
[Śāriputra said: “He receives [the teaching]. The Buddha said: “Regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he is unable to believe and accept their emptiness;

even up to the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is unable to believe and accept its emptiness. Because he does not believe and accept it, he cannot abide [in it]. Śāriputra asked: “In what dharmas is he unable to abide? The Buddha said:
“That is to say, he is unable to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); he is unable to abide in the four [right efforts...]"
They cannot abide in the right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
they cannot abide in the six perfections, they cannot abide on the stage of non-retrogression, and they cannot abide in the five eyes or the six superknowledges.

They are unable to abide in the ten powers of a Buddha; they are unable to abide in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
For this reason, they are called foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), because they cling to the existence of an intrinsic nature in all phenomena, Śāriputra.
[The interlocutor] asked: "In what phenomena do they cling to an intrinsic nature? The Buddha said: "They cling to an intrinsic nature in form (*rūpa*);
they cling to an intrinsic nature in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*).

Even unto clinging to an intrinsic nature in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are unable to believe in or accept the emptiness of all phenomena. Because of this lack of faith, they are unable..."
Because they accomplish all the noble dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, they are unable to abide in those noble dharmas.

Śāriputra asked: "For what reason do some bodhisattvas train in this way, yet fail to train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and thus fail to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā-jñāna)? The Buddha said: "If a bodhisattva lacks skillful means..."
Skillfully [practicing] while conceptually adhering to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and conceptually adhering to everything from the *dhyānas* down to generosity—
training in this manner is not training in the *prajñāpāramitā*. One will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
nor even the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because of such conceptual adherence.
One should train in this way: it is not by training in the perfection of wisdom that one can accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom.
Up to and including not perceiving the knowledge of all aspects—this is training in the perfection of wisdom, which is able to accomplish the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because it takes non-apprehension as its means (*upāya*). (The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Practice of Prajñā is concluded.)
Fascicle 42 (The Chapter on Similes), Fascicle 43, Fascicle 44, Fascicle 45.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if someone were to ask: ‘Can an illusory person study the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Can an illusory person accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*)? ... up to: ‘Can an illusory person study the path-characteristics of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*)?’”
"Wisdom. Omniscience. Can it accomplish the knowledge of all modes? When I receive this question, how should I answer?
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "I shall now ask you in return: Is form different from an illusion? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Form is not different from an illusion; an illusion..."
"It is not different from form; form itself is illusion, and illusion itself is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Furthermore, is there any difference between unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and illusion? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not different from illusion; illusion is not different from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is itself illusion; illusion is itself unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Thus spoke the Buddha to Subhūti.
“Does an illusion have affliction or purification? “No, World-Honored One. “Does an illusion arise or cease? “No, World-Honored One.

“If a phenomenon has neither affliction nor purification, and neither arising nor ceasing, can such a phenomenon study the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)? “No.”
“World-Honored One,” [the Buddha] replied to Subhūti, “If a bodhisattva can train in the perfection of wisdom,
up to the knowledge of all aspects, by means of such non-apprehension as a skillful method, it should be known that this bodhisattva is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva wishes to realize the unsurpassed...”
