"World-Honored One, what is meant by the concentration characterized by the patience of being free from turbidity (*anāvila-kṣānti-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*)?

"Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this concentration, one attains the patience of being free from turbidity regarding all phenomena; therefore, it is called the concentration characterized by the patience of being free from turbidity."
“World-Honored One, what is called the ‘samādhi endowed with all excellent marks’?
Subhūti, it means that when one abides in this samādhi, there are no excellent marks of any meditative concentrations that are not fully possessed;
therefore, it is called the ‘samādhi endowed with all excellent marks. World-Honored One, what is called the ‘samādhi endowed with dhāraṇī’? Subhūti, it means that...”
When one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to sustain all the supreme qualities of the various concentrations; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi Endowed with Total Retention" (dhāraṇī).
World-Honored One, what is meant by the "Samādhi of Not Delighting in Any Suffering or Pleasure"?
"Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not take pleasure in examining the characteristics of suffering or pleasure within any meditative absorptions;
therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Not Delighting in Any Suffering or Pleasure. World-Honored One, what is called the 'Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Aspect'?
Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive..."
The modes of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are exhaustible; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi of Exhaustless Modes.
World-Honored One, what is the "Samādhi that Subdues All Right and Wrong Natures"?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding the right and wrong natures of all meditative concentrations, one subdues all views so that they do not arise at all. This is...
Therefore, it is named the samādhi that subdues all correct and erroneous natures. World-Honored One, why is it named the samādhi that severs hatred and attachment?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharmas of meditative concentration as having the characteristics of hatred or attachment.
For this reason, it is named the samādhi that severs hatred and attachment. World-Honored One, why is it named...?

“Regarding the samādhi ‘Free from Contradiction and Accordance,’ Subhūti: when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharmas of concentration as having the characteristics of contradiction or accordance. Therefore, it is called the samādhi ‘Free from Contradiction and Accordance.
“World-Honored One, what is the samādhi called ‘Stainless Radiance’? Subhūti: when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding...”
One does not perceive any meditative concentrations whatsoever, whether they be luminous or defiled;
therefore, it is called the "Stainless Luminosity Samādhi. Bhagavān, what is meant by the "Extremely Firm Samādhi"?
Subhūti, it is said that when one abides in this samādhi, all meditative concentrations become firm without exception; therefore, it is called the "Extremely Firm Samādhi."
“World-Honored One, what is called the ‘Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon’?

Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative absorptions (samādhis) to be fully endowed with merit, just as the pure full moon causes the waters of the ocean to rise.”
Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon. World-Honored One, what is meant by the Great Adornment Samādhi?

Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to accomplish various subtle, wondrous, and rare matters of great adornment; therefore, it is called the Great Adornment Samādhi. World-Honored One...
"Bhagavān, what is called the 'Lightning Flash Without Heat' (*atapanīya-vidyut-prabhā*) samādhi?
Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, it emits a cool and clear light that illuminates all classes of sentient beings, causing them to pacify all darkness, poison, and heat.
Therefore, it is called the 'Lightning Flash Without Heat' samādhi. Bhagavān, what is called the 'Able to Illuminate All Worlds'..."

The Samādhi of Illumination. Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, it illuminates all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, causing all classes of sentient beings to attain full understanding. For this reason, it is called the "Samādhi Capable of Illuminating All Worlds.
World-Honored One, what is meant by the "Samādhi Capable of Saving All Worlds"? Subhūti, [it is as follows:]
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to rescue the world from its various sorrows and sufferings;
therefore, it is called the "Samādhi Capable of Rescuing All the World. Bhagavān, what is meant by the "Samādhi of the Equality of Concentration"?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any distinction between meditative concentration and distraction.
Therefore, it is called the samādhi of the equality of concentration. Bhagavān, what is called the samādhi of the principle of the equality of the dustless and the dusty?

Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one thoroughly understands that all concentrations and all phenomena follow the principle of the equality of the dusty and the dustless; therefore, it is called "dustless."
There is the samādhi of the principle of the equality of dust. Bhagavān, what is meant by the samādhi of the principle of the equality of the non-contentious and the contentious?

Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharmas or any meditative concentrations, nor the distinctions between their characteristics and natures regarding being contentious or non-contentious;
therefore, it is called the samādhi of the equality of the non-contentious and the contentious.
The Samādhi of the Principle of Equality. "Bhagavān, what is meant by the 'Samādhi Without Dwelling, Without Signs, and Without Attachment'?
"Subhūti, it means that when one abides in this samādhi, one destroys all dwellings, relinquishes all signs, and severs all attachments, remaining without any grasping.
Therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi Without Dwelling, Without Signs, and Without Attachment.'"
The Samādhi of the Banner of Non-Attachment. "Bhagavān, what is called the 'Samādhi of Resolutely Abiding in Suchness'?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena..."
One never abandons the true mark of suchness; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi of Decisive Abiding in Suchness.
World-Honored One, what is the "Samādhi of Emerging from the Vessel"?
Subhūti, it means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations to produce merit, just as food emerges from within a vessel through the power of celestial blessings.
Therefore, it is called the samādhi of "Emerging from within a Vessel. World-Honored One, what is meant by the "samādhi that burns away all afflictions"?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it burns away all afflictions so that not even a trace of ash remains;
therefore, it is called the "samādhi that burns away all afflictions. World-Honored One, what is meant by the "Great..."?
The Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom. Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, the light of wisdom is emitted, illuminating all things;
therefore, it is called the Great Torch of Wisdom Samādhi.
Bhagavān, what is meant by the Samādhi of Producing the Ten Powers? Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes the Buddha...
The ten powers are swiftly brought to full perfection; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi that Gives Birth to the Ten Powers. World-Honored One, what is meant by the "Samādhi of Elucidation"?

Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to elucidate the essential points of the Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to be swiftly liberated from the great suffering of birth and death; therefore, it is called "Elucidation."
“Samādhi. Bhagavān, what is called the ‘samādhi that destroys misconduct of body’?
Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, although no body is perceived, one ceases misconduct of body;
therefore, it is called the ‘samādhi that destroys misconduct of body. Bhagavān, what is called the ‘samādhi that destroys misconduct of speech’?”
"Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, although no sound is perceived, verbal misconduct is stilled;
therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that destroys verbal misconduct. World-Honored One, what is called the 'samādhi that destroys mental misconduct'?
Subhūti, it is said that when one dwells in this samādhi, although no mind is perceived, [mental misconduct is stilled]."
It stills mental misconduct; therefore, it is called the "concentration that destroys mental misconduct.
"World-Honored One, what is meant by the 'concentration of skillful observation'?

"Subhūti, it means that when one abides in this concentration, one is able to skillfully observe the faculties, natures, and inclinations of all sentient beings and deliver them. Therefore, it is called 'skillful observation.'"
"Samādhi. Blessed One, what is called the 'space-like samādhi' (ākāśasama-samādhi)?
Subhūti, it means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally benefit all sentient beings with a mind as impartial as the great void.
Therefore, it is called the space-like samādhi. Blessed One, what is called 'non-attachment'?"

The "Space-like Samādhi," Subhūti: when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, just like space—unstained and unattached. Therefore, it is called the "Space-like Unstained Samādhi.
Subhūti, you should know that there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such samādhis.
This is the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
As for the mark of the Great Vehicle, it refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.

Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, although one dwells in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body, one ultimately does not give rise to any discursive thoughts associated with the body; this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Although...

Abiding in internal and external feelings, one contemplates feelings according to their nature; yet, one does not give rise to discursive thoughts associated with feelings—this is the mindfulness-establishment of feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Although abiding in internal and external mind, one contemplates the mind according to its nature; yet, one does not give rise to discursive thoughts associated with the mind—this is the mindfulness-establishment of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Although abiding in internal and external phenomena, one contemplates phenomena according to their nature; yet, one does not give rise to discursive thoughts associated with phenomena—this is the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*). It blazes forth...

Nevertheless, one exerts diligence and possesses right mindfulness and clear comprehension; this is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does one abide in the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena internally, externally, and both internally and externally, observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena? The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they minutely observe their own body, its formations..."
At the time of walking, he knows he is walking; at the time of standing, he knows he is standing; at the time of sitting, he knows he is sitting; at the time of lying down, he knows he is lying down.
In whatever way his own body is engaged in various modes of deportment, in that very way he possesses right mindfulness and awareness, clearly observing his own body.

He is rightly aware of coming and going; rightly aware of looking ahead and looking aside; rightly aware of bending and stretching; and rightly aware when putting on the saṃghāṭī, holding the robes and bowl, or eating.

Whether eating, drinking, or consuming; lying down, resting, or walking; sitting, rising, or receiving guests; waking, sleeping, speaking, or remaining silent; or entering and emerging from various meditative absorptions—in all these, he maintains mindfulness and clear comprehension.

He carefully observes his own body as it inhales and exhales, whether the breath is long or short. He carefully observes his own body as the distinct differentiation of the four elements: earth, water, fire, and wind.
He carefully observes his own body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, as being filled with various kinds of impurities.
It is filled with these [impurities]. It is externally enveloped by a thin skin. What wise person would cherish this body?
Only the foolish, deluded, and attached do so. On the path to tranquility, one observes a discarded corpse that has been dead for one day, or two days, or even up to seven days;
its body is bloated, its color has turned bluish-purple, it is putrid and rotting, and the skin is pierced, oozing pus.
Blood flows out. Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities;
not having attained liberation, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus does the Bodhisattva dwell in the contemplation of the body by observing the internal body in its various distinctions.
With ardent diligence, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension, for the sake of subduing worldly greed and sorrow, he dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body;
it is likewise so for dwelling in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena with regard to feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
All of these should be explained in detail as appropriate. This is the characteristic of the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): namely, abandoning evil, and producing the good.

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): cultivating the concentration of desire, which is the basis for the accomplishment of the exercise of abandonment; it relies on detachment, relies on non-attachment, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment.

Cultivating the concentration of energy, cultivating the concentration of mind, and cultivating the concentration of investigation, which is the basis for the accomplishment of the exercise of abandonment.
The accomplishment of practice through the bases of psychic power relies on detachment, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is dedicated to relinquishment.
These are the five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
The five powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

The seven factors of enlightenment: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation.
Cessation. Dedication to relinquishment.
The Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, dedicated to relinquishment.
The three samādhis: observing that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, the mind dwells in peace;

this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness, and is also called the samādhi of emptiness. Because one observes that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, they are all without marks;
the mind dwells in peace; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness, and is also called the samādhi of signlessness. Observing all phenomena...

Because they are empty of intrinsic characteristics, there is nothing for which one has any aspiration; the mind abides in peace, which is called the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), and is also called the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

The characteristics of the Mahāyāna are as follows: they consist of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*).

If a knowledge takes non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as its skillful means and functions by discerning the specific characteristics of the five aggregates and so forth, this is called the knowledge of phenomena. It is the knowledge of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and all conditions.

Arising—whether collectively or individually—is impermanent and so forth; this is the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*). Knowing that all phenomena are merely conventional designations is the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Knowing the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings, as well as the realization of cessation through cultivation, is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Knowing that suffering should not arise is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). Knowing that the origin [of suffering] should be permanently abandoned is the knowledge of the origin...

The knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): knowing that cessation (*nirodha*) should be realized—this is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). Knowing that the path (*mārga*) should be cultivated—this is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Knowing the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion—this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). Knowing that there will be no further rebirth in the realms of existence—this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The Tathāgata’s knowledge of all things and knowledge of all aspects is what constitutes knowledge according to reality.

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*): if those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the noble truths and have not yet obtained the fruit of the noble ones.

All faculties from the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), when belonging to those who have not yet known what is to be known, constitute the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

When those in training (*śaikṣa*) have already attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the noble truths and have attained the fruit of the noble ones, all their faculties from faith up to wisdom constitute the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*).
As for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—whether they be arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas—who have already entered [this state]...
The ten stages. If all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas possess the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom, these constitute the faculty of one who has fully understood.
The three samādhis:
if, having departed from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters [the first dhyāna]...
Abiding fully in the first dhyāna constitutes the threefold samādhi with vitarka and vicāra.
If one is in the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, or the intermediate dhyāna, this constitutes the threefold samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra.
If one is in the third dhyāna, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this constitutes the threefold samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.

The ten recollections (*daśa-anusmṛti*) are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), recollection of relinquishment (*tyāga*), recollection of the devas, recollection of peace and disenchantment, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of the body, and recollection of death.

The Buddha’s ten powers: To know, as they truly are, the characteristics of what is possible and what is impossible regarding phenomena such as cause and effect—this is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).

To know, as they truly are, the various phenomena of karma and their results experienced by all classes of sentient beings throughout the past, future, and present—this is the power of knowing the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*). To know, as they truly are, all classes of sentient beings...
The characteristic of immeasurable realms is the power of knowledge regarding the various realms (*nānādhātu-jñāna-bala*).
To know, as they truly are, the characteristics of the immeasurable inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings is the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).

To know, as they truly are, the characteristics of the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings is the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (*indriyaparāpara-jñāna-bala*). To know, as they truly are, [the characteristics] of all sentient beings...
The aspect of the practice of each practice constitutes the power of knowledge regarding the all-encompassing practice of conduct (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*).

To know, as they truly are, the characteristics of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as the defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) of sentient beings, and their faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), constitutes the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, attainments, defilement, and purification. To know, as they truly are, all that exists... [and so forth].

The power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*) is the ability to know, as they truly are, the immeasurable and innumerable characteristics of the past lives of sentient beings.

The power of knowledge concerning death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*) is the ability to know, as they truly are, the immeasurable and innumerable characteristics of the deaths and births of all classes of sentient beings.

Knowing as it truly is the permanent exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*), he dwells having personally realized and attained in this very life the taintless liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) and the taintless liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
He is able to know correctly: "Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established."
"What was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence to be taken. This is the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): if one employs the skillful means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), one declares of oneself, "I am a perfectly awakened one (*samyaksaṃbuddha*)."
Suppose someone were to raise an objection or cause me to reflect, saying: "Regarding this Dharma, you are not a Perfectly Awakened One.
In the face of such an objection, I have right view and am able to abide in peace, free from fear and dread; this is the fearlessness of being a Perfectly Awakened One.
Furthermore, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, I declare of myself: "I have eternally exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Suppose someone were to raise an objection or...
He causes [others] to reflect: "Such outflows (āsrava) have not yet been completely exhausted;
I have no basis for right view regarding that challenge, nor can I abide in peace, free from fear and dread. This is the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayaviśārada*).

If he employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to teach his disciples the dharmas that obstruct the path, and even if someone should raise an objection or cause him to reflect, saying: "By practicing this..."
Regarding the Dharma: it cannot obstruct the Path. In the face of such challenges, my right view has no cause for wavering; I abide in peace, free from fear and dread.
This is the fearlessness regarding the Dharma that does not obstruct the Path.

If, employing the method of non-apprehension, I teach the disciples the path to the exhaustion of suffering, and someone should raise an objection or attempt to remind me, saying that practicing this path cannot exhaust suffering—I [remain undaunted].
Regarding those difficulties, one possesses right view and thereby attains peaceful dwelling, free from fear and dread; this is the fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Explanation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). That is to say, from the night I first realized unexcelled, perfect,

and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) until the final moment when all that was to be done has been accomplished and I enter the remainderless nirvāṇa (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

During the night of the Great Nirvāṇa, throughout that interval, he was always free from error, free from sudden or violent sounds, free from loss of mindfulness, free from unconcentrated mind, free from diverse perceptions, and free from equanimity lacking discernment; his aspiration never regressed, and his diligence never regressed.
There is no regression in mindfulness; there is no regression in wisdom; there is no regression in liberation; there is no regression in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
All bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. All verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
All mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. Regarding the knowledge and vision arising concerning the past, they are unattached and unimpeded;

regarding the knowledge and vision arising concerning the future, they are unattached and unimpeded; regarding the knowledge and vision arising concerning the present, they are unattached and unimpeded.
Thus, among these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), there are none that do not all [proceed in this manner].
Taking non-apprehension as the means, the characteristics of the Mahāyāna refer to the various dharanī-gates of syllables. Subhūti asked the Buddha: "What are the dharanī-gates of syllables?
The Buddha said: "The equality of syllables, the equality of speech, and the equality of the principles of verbal expression."
Nature. Entering all these letter-gates constitutes the Dharani-door of letters. How does one enter these letter-gates?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they enter the letter-gate *ka*, because they realize that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; they enter the letter-gate *la*.

Because one realizes that all phenomena are free from dust and defilement, one enters the gateway of the letter *pa*. Because one realizes that all phenomena are the teaching of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one enters the gateway of the letter *dha*.
Because one realizes that all phenomena are without birth or death, one enters the gateway of the letter *na*.

Because one realizes that all phenomena are far removed from names and signs and are without gain or loss, one enters the gateway of the letter *la*. Because one realizes that all phenomena transcend the world, [one enters the gateway of the letter *ta*].
Because the causal conditions for the limb of craving never manifest, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ṭha*;

one awakens to all phenomena as being tamed, quiescent, equal to true suchness (*tathatā*), and free from conceptual discrimination. Because all phenomena are free from bondage, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ba*.
One enters the gateway of the letter *ta*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are free from feverish affliction and defilement, having attained purity.

One enters the gateway of the letter *sa*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are without obstruction. One enters the gateway of the letter *ba*, for one awakens to the fact that the path of vocal expression regarding all phenomena is severed.

One enters the gateway of the letter *ḍha*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are the immovable *tathatā*. One enters the gateway of the letter *ya*, for one awakens to the fact that... [all phenomena].
Because all phenomena are, in reality, unarisen, one enters the letter-gateway *ṣṭa*.

Because the characteristics of the subduing and sustaining of all phenomena are unapprehendable, one enters the letter-gateway *ka*. Because an agent of all phenomena is unapprehendable, one enters the letter-gateway *sa*.
Because the equality of time regarding all phenomena is unapprehendable, one enters the letter-gateway *ma*. One awakens to...
Because the nature of self and what belongs to self cannot be found in all phenomena, one enters the gateway of the letter GA.
Because the nature of grasping at formations cannot be found in all phenomena, one enters the gateway of the letter THA.
Because a locus or location cannot be found in all phenomena, one enters the gateway of the letter JA. Because the arising of all phenomena cannot be found, one enters the gateway of the letter ŚVA.
Because one realizes that the nature of peace and security of all phenomena is unattainable, one enters the gateway of the letter *da*.

Because one realizes that the nature of the realm of all phenomena is unattainable, one enters the gateway of the letter *śa*. Because one realizes that the nature of quiescence of all phenomena is unattainable, [one enters the gateway of the letter *ja*].
One enters the gateway of the letter Kha, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are like the nature of space and are ungraspable.
One enters the gateway of the letter Chaṃ, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are of an exhausted nature and are ungraspable.

One enters the gateway of the letter Ṣṭha, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena, in their sustaining of what is possible and what is impossible, are of a nature that is immovable and ungraspable. One enters the gateway of the letter Jña... [awakens to the fact that all phenomena...]
Because the nature of attachment to all phenomena cannot be apprehended, one enters the gateway of the syllable HA.

Because the nature of causes in all phenomena cannot be apprehended, one enters the gateway of the syllable PHA. Because the nature of disintegration in all phenomena cannot be apprehended, one enters the gateway of the syllable BA.
One enters the gateway of the syllable *ca*: because one realizes that the nature of desire and pleasure covering all phenomena is unattainable.
One enters the gateway of the syllable *sma*: because one realizes that the nature of being memorable in all phenomena is unattainable. One enters the gateway of the syllable *kha*:

because one realizes that the nature of being summonable in all phenomena is unattainable. One enters the gateway of the syllable *ca*: because one realizes that the nature of courage and vigor in all phenomena is unattainable.

Because the nature [of phenomena] is unapprehendable, one enters the gateway of the syllable *kṣa*. Because the thick, equal nature of all phenomena is unapprehendable, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ṭha*.
Because the accumulative nature of all phenomena is unapprehendable, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ṇa*.
One realizes that all phenomena are free from all clamor and confusion, because going, coming, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are unattainable;

thus one enters the gateway of the syllable *pha*. One realizes that all phenomena are the pervasive retribution of fruits, yet this is unattainable; thus one enters the gateway of the syllable *sa-ka*.

One realizes that all phenomena are the nature of accumulated aggregates, yet this is unattainable; thus one enters the gateway of the syllable *e-sa*. One realizes that all phenomena... [text continues]
Because the nature and characteristics of decay and old age cannot be apprehended in any phenomena, one enters the gateway of the syllable *jo*.

Because the tracks of accumulation cannot be apprehended in any phenomena, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ṭha*. Because the nature of mutual oppression cannot be apprehended in any phenomena, one enters the gateway of the syllable *ca*.
Because a final locus cannot be apprehended in any phenomena, one enters the gateway of the syllable *cha*. Subhūti!
This gateway of letters enables one to realize the ultimate limit of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Apart from these letters, which symbolize the emptiness of all phenomena, nothing further can be apprehended. Why is this?

Because the meaning of these letters cannot be proclaimed, cannot be displayed, cannot be grasped, cannot be written down or maintained, and cannot be observed, for they are free from all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). If a bodhisattva is able to listen to them...

This is the seal of the syllable-gate entrances (*akṣaramukha-mudrā*), the seals and phrases. Having heard them, one should receive and uphold them, recite and master them, thereby attaining twenty kinds of supreme merit.

One should know that this constitutes the characteristic of the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. (Fascicle 53, Leaf 19) The above concludes the response to the question regarding the characteristic of the Mahāyāna.
Below follows the response to the question regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s setting forth toward the Great [Vehicle].
“Vehicle.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “As for your question regarding how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle:
when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they proceed from one stage to the next; you should know that this is what constitutes setting out.”
The Mahāyāna. Subhūti asked: "How does one proceed from one stage to another? The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere. Why? Because all phenomena neither depart nor arrive;
they have no origin and no destination, for those phenomena are subject to no transformation or decay. Thus, regarding the stages from which he comes and to which he proceeds..."
Neither relying on nor conceptualizing them, although they cultivate the practices for purifying the stages (*bhūmi-karma*), they do not perceive those stages.

"Blessed One, what are the practices for purifying the stages of a bodhisattva? "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), they should properly cultivate ten kinds of superior practices.
First, by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, they cultivate the purification of the sublime resolve."
1. The activity of joy, because a superior mental disposition (*adhyāśaya*) cannot be apprehended. 2.
The activity of cultivating a mind of equality toward all sentient beings by taking non-apprehension as the means (*upāya*), because all sentient beings cannot be apprehended. 3.
The activity of cultivating the perfection of giving by taking non-apprehension as the means, [realizing that] the giver, the recipient, and the gift [cannot be apprehended].

4. Because things cannot be apprehended, one cultivates the practice of attending upon spiritual friends by means of non-apprehension as the skillful means, for there is no dualistic appearance between spiritual friends and evil associates. 5. By means of non-apprehension as the skillful means...
1. Cultivating the activity of seeking the Dharma, because all dharmas sought are unattainable. 2.
By means of non-apprehension as the skillful means, cultivating the activity of always delighting in leaving the household life, because the home one abandons is unattainable. 3.
By means of non-apprehension as the skillful means, cultivating the activity of loving and delighting in the Buddha’s body, because the various marks and secondary characteristics are unattainable.

8. Because [the object] can be attained; eighth, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one cultivates and elucidates the activity of the Dharma teachings, because the dharmas that are conceptually discriminated cannot be apprehended.

Ninth, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one cultivates the activity of destroying pride, because all flourishing dharmas cannot be apprehended. Tenth, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means...
Skillful means: cultivating and purifying the karma of truthful speech, because the intrinsic nature of all speech is unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the second stage, the Stainless, they should contemplate and practice eight dharmas.
To cause them to be swiftly perfected: first, the purity of moral discipline; second, knowing gratitude and repaying kindness;
third, abiding in the power of patience; fourth, receiving supreme joy; fifth, not abandoning sentient beings; and sixth, constantly giving rise to great compassion.
Seventh, toward all teachers and elders, one should serve, receive instruction from, and make offerings with a mind of reverence and faith, regarding them as if they were the Buddha.

Eighth, one should diligently seek to practice the *pāramitās*. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the third stage, the Radiant (*prabhākārī*), they should abide in five dharmas.
First, they should diligently seek extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without ever becoming weary or satisfied. Regarding that which...
First, hearing the Dharma without becoming attached to its words and letters. Second, constantly practicing the gift of Dharma with an undefiled mind;
though one extensively transforms and guides others, one does not exalt oneself. Third, planting all roots of goodness in order to adorn and purify the Buddha-land;

though one employs the dedication of merit, one does not praise oneself. Fourth, transforming sentient beings; though one does not grow weary of the boundless cycle of birth and death, one does not exalt oneself.
Fifth, although abiding in shame and remorse, one remains without attachment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the fourth stage, the Radiant Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), they should abide in ten dharmas and constantly practice them without relinquishing them. First, they should dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka).
1. Never abandoning [the practice]; 2. having few desires; 3. being content; 4. never abandoning the virtues of the *dhūta* ascetic practices;
5. never forsaking any of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*); 6. developing a deep sense of weary detachment toward all sensual pleasures; 7.
always delighting in giving rise to a mind associated with tranquility (*śamatha*); 8. relinquishing all that one possesses; 9. [and]...
The mind does not stagnate or sink. Tenth, one should have no lingering attachment toward anything that exists.
(End of Volume 53) Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), they should distance themselves from ten things:
first, they should distance themselves from household life; second, they should distance themselves from bhikṣuṇīs; third, they should distance themselves from stinginess regarding households.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from quarrels and disputes within assemblies. Fifth, one should distance oneself from praising oneself and disparaging others.
Sixth, one should distance oneself from the ten unwholesome paths of action. Seventh, one should distance oneself from arrogance born of overweening pride.
Eighth, one should distance oneself from perversions. Ninth, one should distance oneself from hesitation. Tenth, one should distance oneself from greed, hatred, and delusion. Furthermore...
Next, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī*), they should fulfill six dharmas:
first, they should fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); second, they should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
third, they should fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); fourth, they should fulfill the perfection of diligence...
The pāramitās: fifth, one should fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā; sixth, one should fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā.
Furthermore, one should distance oneself from six things: first, one should distance oneself from the mind of a śrāvaka.
Second, one should distance oneself from the mind of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*). Third, one should distance oneself from a mind of feverish affliction.
Fourth, upon seeing a beggar approach, one’s mind should not feel weary or dejected. Fifth, when relinquishing all possessions, one should have no sense of sorrow or regret.
Sixth, toward those who come seeking, one should never be arrogant or deceitful. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*),...

At the stage of the ground, one should distance oneself from twenty phenomena: first, one should distance oneself from the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, and so forth, up to the grasping at a knower and the grasping at a viewer;
second, one should distance oneself from the grasping at annihilation; third, one should distance oneself from the grasping at permanence.

Fourth, one should distance oneself from attachment to signs. Fifth, one should distance oneself from attachment to views regarding causes and so forth. Sixth, one should distance oneself from attachment to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Seventh, one should distance oneself from attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*). Eighth, one should distance oneself from attachment to the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Ninth, one should distance oneself from attachment to the elements (*dhātu*). Tenth, one should distance oneself from attachment to the truths (*satya*). Eleventh, one should distance oneself from attachment to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
12. One should distance oneself from the attachment of dwelling within the three realms. 13. One should distance oneself from attachment to all phenomena (*dharma*). 14.
One should distance oneself from attachment to all phenomena as being either conformable or non-conformable to reality.
15. One should distance oneself from attachment based on the view of a Buddha. 16. One should distance oneself from attachment based on the view of the Dharma. 17.
One should distance oneself from the attachment to views based on the Saṅgha. Eighteenth, one should distance oneself from the attachment to views based on precepts.
Nineteenth, one should distance oneself from fear of the dharma of emptiness. Twentieth, one should distance oneself from contradicting emptiness.
Furthermore, one should fulfill twenty dharmas: first, one should fulfill the thorough penetration of emptiness; second, one should fulfill the realization of non-arising...
1. One should fulfill the knowledge of signs. 2. One should fulfill the knowledge of signlessness. 3. One should fulfill the knowledge of wishlessness. 4.
One should fulfill the purity of the three spheres. 5. One should fulfill compassion for sentient beings, as well as non-attachment toward sentient beings. 6.
One should fulfill the vision of the equality of all phenomena, as well as non-attachment within that state. 7. One should fulfill the single...
8) One should fulfill the vision of all sentient beings as equal, and therein remain without attachment.

9) One should fulfill the thorough penetration of the true nature of reality, and therein remain without attachment. 10) One should fulfill the wisdom of the endurance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
11) One should fulfill the principle of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. 12) One should fulfill...
10. One should fulfill the complete eradication of conceptualization. 12. One should fulfill the distancing from all perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
13. One should fulfill the distancing from all views (*dṛṣṭi*). 14. One should fulfill the distancing from afflictions (*kleśa*). 15.
One should fulfill the stages of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). 16. One should fulfill the taming of the mental continuum (*citta-santati*). 10. [End of section].
Seventh, one should fulfill the nature of a tranquil mind. Eighteenth, one should fulfill the nature of unimpeded wisdom.
Nineteenth, one should fulfill freedom from all attachment.
Twentieth, one should fulfill the ability to manifest one's own body at will within the assemblies of Buddhas in all Buddha-fields. Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva...
When dwelling in the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), one should fulfill four dharmas:
first, one should fulfill the penetration into the mental activities of all sentient beings; second, one should fulfill the playful mastery of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
third, one should fulfill the vision of all Buddha-fields, and according to what is seen, personally adorn and purify various Buddha-fields; fourth, one should fulfill...
He fully makes offerings to and serves the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and observes the body of the Tathāgata as it truly is.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), they should fulfill four dharmas:
first, they should fulfill the knowledge that discerns the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; second, they should fulfill the purification of the Buddha-field.
Third, one should fulfill the meditative absorption on the illusion-like (*māyopama-samādhi*) and enter various concentrations repeatedly.

Fourth, one should fulfill the entry into various states of existence (*bhava*) in accordance with the ripening of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings, thereby manifesting for oneself through birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they should fulfill twelve dharmas. First, they should fulfill...
First, one should fulfill the great vow that encompasses infinite realms, causing every aspiration to be completely perfected according to its intent.
Second, one should fulfill the knowledge of the diverse languages of all classes of beings, from devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, down to humans and non-humans.
Third, one should fulfill the knowledge of unimpeded eloquence in exposition. Fourth, one should fulfill the perfection of entering the womb. Fifth, one should...
1. One should fulfill the perfection of birth. 2. One should fulfill the perfection of family. 3. One should fulfill the perfection of lineage.
4. One should fulfill the perfection of retinue. 5. One should fulfill the perfection of the physical body.
6. One should fulfill the perfection of renunciation. 7. One should fulfill the perfection of the adornments of enlightenment.
...the tree is fully endowed. Twelfth, one should fulfill the complete accomplishment and perfection of all merits.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate and purify the karma of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*)?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), practices..."
All roots of goodness—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the activity of purifying the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Bhagavān, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the activity of a mind of equality toward all sentient beings?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), brings forth the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Immeasurable. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the karma of an impartial mind toward all sentient beings.
Bhagavān, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the karma of generosity?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity toward all sentient beings without making any conceptual discriminations, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s...
Sāriputra, he cultivates the karma of generosity. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the karma of associating with spiritual friends?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees various spiritual friends exhorting and transforming sentient beings, causing them to practice the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), he immediately associates with them, reveres, makes offerings to, honors, praises, and receives instruction from them.
The True Dharma. To serve it day and night with a mind free from weariness or indolence—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the practice of attending upon spiritual friends.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the practice of seeking the Dharma? Subhūti, [it is as follows:]

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind directed toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), diligently seeks the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata and does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the activity of seeking the Dharma.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the activity of always delighting in leaving the household life? Subhūti, if—

In all places of birth, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly feel weary of the household life as a noisy and crowded prison, and always delight in the Buddha-dharma, attaining pure renunciation without anything able to obstruct them. This is the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of the practice of always delighting in renunciation.
World-Honored One, how does a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivate the practice of loving and delighting in the Buddha-body? Well...

Manifestation. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having beheld the physical form of a Buddha even for a single moment, never abandons the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the Buddha until they realize unexcelled awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the practice of cherishing the Buddha’s body.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the practice of elucidating and expounding the Dharma teachings?

Karma. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, expounds the Dharma teaching for the sake of all sentient beings—teachings that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, skillful in both words and meaning, pure, complete, and the pristine holy life—namely:
the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, and... [the rest of the list follows].
To give rise to extensive, rare, and profound discourses on the Dharma—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the activity of elucidating the teachings of the Dharma.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the activity of destroying pride?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva always maintains humility and respect, subduing the mind of arrogance, they will consequently not be born into a low-caste or inferior lineage.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the practice of destroying pride.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the practice of always speaking truthful words? Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks in accordance with what they know.
"His words and deeds correspond with one another; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the karma of constant truthful speech.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify their prohibitive precepts?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor any other factors that violate the precepts and obstruct enlightenment—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s..."
"Venerable Lord, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva recognize kindness and repay it?
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva conduct, if they do not forget to repay even a small kindness received, how much less would they fail to requite a great favor?
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to recognize kindness and repay it. Venerable Lord.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the power of patience?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is subjected to injury or insult by sentient beings, yet harbors no mind of anger or malice toward them, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the power of patience.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva experience supreme joy?"
Manifestation. If the sentient beings transformed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva have attained maturity, their bodies and minds are at ease and they experience supreme joy;
this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva experiencing supreme joy. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not forsake sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva rescues sentient beings with a mind...
They never abandon them; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon sentient beings.
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly give rise to great compassion? "Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva."

He forms this thought: "For the benefit of all sentient beings, even if I must remain in the great hells for as many immeasurable and incalculable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, undergoing various intense sufferings—whether being burned, boiled, cut, or hacked."
Whether pierced, or suspended, or ground, or pounded—undergoing such immeasurable sufferings as these for the sake of causing those beings to board the Buddha-vehicle and attain parinirvāṇa;
even until the entire realm of sentient beings is exhausted, his great compassionate heart never grows weary.
This is what it means for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva to constantly give rise to great compassion. World-Honored One, how is it that [this is] bodhi...?
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, with a mind of reverence and faith, seek instruction from and make offerings to all teachers and elders,
regarding them as if they were the Buddha. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

remains respectful and compliant toward teachers and elders without any sense of personal attachment, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to seek instruction from all teachers and elders with a mind of reverence and faith.
"One should receive offerings with the thought that it is as if serving the Buddha. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seek to practice the pāramitās?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva single-mindedly seeks to study the various pāramitās, setting aside all other matters, this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seeking to practice the pāramitās."
"Much, World-Honored One. How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seek much learning without ever becoming weary or satisfied?
Regarding the teachings they have heard, they do not cling to the words. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva exerts diligent vigor and forms this thought:
'Whether it be the True Dharma spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in this buddha-field or in the worlds of the ten directions, I shall [master] it all...'"
Listening and studying, reading and reciting, and receiving and upholding [the teachings], yet not becoming attached to the words therein—

this is what it means for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to diligently seek out extensive learning without ever being weary or satisfied, and to remain unattached to the words of the Dharma they have heard. World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly practice the gift of Dharma with an undefiled mind, such that although they extensively transform and guide others, they do not...?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, they do not even do so for their own benefit, dedicating these roots of virtue toward enlightenment;
how much less would they seek other things? Although they extensively transform and guide others, they do not rely on this as a basis for self-conceit.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to constantly practice the gift of Dharma with an undefiled mind, even while widely expounding it.

[He] transforms [them], yet does not exalt himself. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva plant various roots of goodness to adorn and purify a buddha-field, and while dedicating them, does not exalt himself?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices various roots of goodness with courageous diligence, desiring to adorn the pure lands of all Buddhas and to purify both himself and others.
Regarding the mind-field: although he acts for this purpose, he does not exalt himself;
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva plants various roots of virtue to adorn and purify the buddha-field. Although he employs dedication, he does not lift himself up.

"World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, does not grow weary of the boundless cycle of birth and death, yet does not exalt himself? Subhūti, [it is as follows:]
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to bring all sentient beings to maturity, plants roots of goodness, and purifies buddha-fields—
until even the wisdom of omniscience is fully attained— undergoes the arduous sufferings of boundless birth and death without weariness,
and likewise does not exalt themselves; this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to transform sentient beings, not to feel weary.
"Exhausted by the boundless cycle of birth and death, yet not exalting oneself—World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in a sense of shame and abashment while remaining unattached?

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva single-mindedly seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, because they possess a sense of shame and abashment, they will never for a moment give rise to mental orientations toward the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. And regarding...
Within this, there is likewise no attachment. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a sense of shame and dread of blame yet remains without attachment.
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the forest hermitage (āraṇya) and never abandon it? "Subhūti," [the Buddha replied].

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, transcends the levels of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they therefore never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to dwell in a forest hermitage and never abandon it.
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have few desires? "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva..."
O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even seek great enlightenment for his own sake, much less worldly gain, fame, or similar matters;
this is what constitutes the fewness of desires of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Bhagavān, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice contentment?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, solely for the sake of realizing all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), remains unattached to other matters, this is the contentment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva never abandon the excellence of the ascetic virtues (dhūtaguṇa)? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva always..."
The profound Dharma. To give rise to the patience of discernment—this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva never to abandon the qualities of purification (dhūta-guṇa).
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva never cast aside any of the training rules? "Subhūti," [the Buddha replied].

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva firmly maintains the precepts they have studied without wavering, yet is able to remain non-apprehensive regarding their characteristics within them, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva never to abandon the various points of training.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully manifest deep revulsion toward all sensual pleasures? If a bodhisattva...

The bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to a mind of desire toward exquisite sensual pleasures; this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward all sensual pleasures.
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly manage to give rise to a mind associated with quiescence?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena have never been produced or brought into being, this is it."
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is always able to give rise to a mind associated with tranquility. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquish all that they possess?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva never grasps at any internal or external phenomena, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to relinquish all that they possess. World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva...”

“...the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind does not become stagnant or submerged. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva never gives rise to a thought regarding any of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), this is what it means for the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind not to become stagnant or submerged.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have no longing or attachment toward anything that exists? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with respect to a single...”
To cut through all things and have no thoughts or reflections—this is for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be without attachment or longing for anything that exists.
Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the household life?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is by nature inclined to travel to the lands of the Buddhas, wherever they are born, they always delight in leaving the home life and shaving their hair.
Having shaved off his hair and beard, holding an alms-bowl and wearing the three dharma-robes, he appears as a śramaṇa;
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance himself from the household life. World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva distance himself from bhikṣuṇīs?
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should always distance himself from all bhikṣuṇīs and not associate with them.
Even if they dwell together for as long as a finger-snap, he likewise does not give rise to a contrary mind toward her.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from bhikṣuṇīs. "World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from stinginess regarding households?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus: 'I should, throughout the long night, bring about benefit and peace...'"

He delights in all sentient beings. Because these sentient beings, through the power of their own merit, have encountered such an excellent householder as a donor, I should not harbor stinginess or envy toward them.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from stinginess regarding households.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from anger and strife within assemblies? "Subhūti, if..."

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects thus: "If I am in a great assembly where there may be śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or where the essential teachings corresponding to their respective vehicles are being expounded, it may cause me to fall away from the mind of great enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Therefore, I must certainly distance myself from such assemblies. He further reflects: "Those who are prone to anger and contention can incite hatred in sentient beings."
It causes harm and leads to the performance of various evil and unwholesome karmas; such actions already contradict the paths to the happy realms, let alone the Great Enlightenment.
Therefore, one must certainly distance oneself from anger and strife. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance themselves from anger and strife within assemblies.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva distance themselves from praising themselves and disparaging others? "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva..."
The Mahāsattva perceives nothing at all within internal or external phenomena; therefore, he should remain far removed from praising himself and disparaging others.
This is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should remain far removed from praising himself and disparaging others.
"World-Honored One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva remain far removed from the ten unwholesome paths of action? "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva acts as follows..."
Reflecting on these ten unwholesome dharmas, one realizes that they still obstruct the paths to the happy realms and the noble path of the two vehicles, let alone Great Bodhi;
therefore, they should be abandoned. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance himself from the ten unwholesome paths of action.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva distance himself from overweening pride? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
The Bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that could give rise to arrogance or pride.
This is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should remain far removed from overweening pride and arrogance. "World-Honored One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva remain far removed from inversions?
"Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives that the objects of inversion are entirely unobtainable, this is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [should remain far removed from inversions]."
"One should remain far removed from inversion. World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from hesitation?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that the objects of hesitation are entirely unapprehendable, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to remain far removed from hesitation.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from craving?"

“Hatred and delusion. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive at all the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the six pāramitās? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the six kinds...”
The pāramitās transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, by abiding in these six pāramitās, the Buddhas and those of the two vehicles are able to cross over the five shores of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). What are these five? First, the past.
Second, the future; third, the present; fourth, the unconditioned; fifth, the ineffable.
These are the six perfections that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill. World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the mind of a śrāvaka?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought as this: "All..."
The mind of a śrāvaka does not realize the path to unsurpassed great bodhi; therefore, it should be abandoned.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abandon the mind of a śrāvaka. "Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abandon the mind of a pratyekabuddha?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought: 'The minds of all pratyekabuddhas are certainly...'"
"One will not be able to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Therefore, I should now distance myself from it.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance themselves from the mind of a solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha). "World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva distance themselves from a mind of feverish affliction (paridāha)?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought: 'I am terrified by the heat of saṃsāra...'"
A mind of vexation is not the path for realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, it should be abandoned.
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s abandonment of a vexed mind.
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid a mind of weariness or dejection when seeing a beggar approach? "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought: 'This weariness..."
The mind is not the path capable of realizing great enlightenment; therefore, I must now certainly distance myself from it.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing a beggar approach, feels no weariness or distress in their heart.
World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva give away all their possessions without a mind of sorrow or regret? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts in this way...
He reflects: "This mind of regret and remorse will certainly constitute an obstacle to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
therefore, I should abandon it. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of being free from regret and remorse regarding all things he has given away.
"Bhagavān, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva never deceive those who come to him seeking [gifts]? "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus: "This deceitful mind is certainly not the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, he makes this vow:
'Whatever I possess, I shall give to those who come seeking it; according to their desires, it shall not be in vain. How could I now act with deceit?"
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva never deceives those who come to him seeking help.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from grasping at a self, grasping at a sentient being, and even grasping at a knower or a viewer?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates a self, a sentient being, and even a knower or a viewer...

Because they are ultimately unattainable. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to a self and attachment to sentient beings, up to and including attachment to a knower and attachment to a viewer.
"Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to annihilation?
"Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as being ultimately non-arising and without annihilation."
For this reason, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from the clinging to annihilation.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the clinging to permanence? Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena.
Because of its impermanent nature. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from the grasping at permanence.
"Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the perception of signs?

"Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the nature of affliction is unapprehendable. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from the perception of signs. "Blessed One," [he said].
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the attachment to views such as [the view of] causes?

Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the intrinsic nature of any views whatsoever; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from the attachment to views such as [the view of] causes.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from the attachment to name-and-form?"

Manifestation. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is entirely unapprehendable, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to name-and-form.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*)?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature of the five aggregates is entirely unapprehendable, this is..."
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to the aggregates. Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to the sense bases?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the nature of the twelve sense bases is entirely unapprehendable, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to remain far removed from attachment to the sense bases. Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva...”
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to the elements (*dhātu*).

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the nature of the eighteen elements and so forth is entirely unapprehendable, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to remain far removed from attachment to the elements.
Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to the truths (*satya*)? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives...”
The nature of all truths is entirely unattainable; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to the truths.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to dependent origination?

"Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature of all dependently originated phenomena is unattainable. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed [from attachment to dependent origination]."
“Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to the grasping at dependent origination?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature of the three realms is entirely unapprehendable, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to the grasping at the three realms. Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva...”
A bodhisattva should remain far removed from all attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the nature of all phenomena as being like space and entirely unapprehendable, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to remain far removed from all attachment to phenomena.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from [the notion of] all phenomena according to reality?"

Improper adherence. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable, and that there is no such thing as a nature that is either proper or improper, this is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s avoidance of all adherence to phenomena as being either proper or improper.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid...?

Subhūti, regarding attachment to views based on the Buddha: if a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that by relying on views based on the Buddha, one cannot see the Buddha, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Buddha.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Dharma? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Because the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is realized as being invisible, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Dharma.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Saṃgha? "Subhūti," [the Buddha replied].

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the harmonious assembly is signless and unconditioned because it is invisible, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance themselves from attachment to views based on reliance upon the Saṃgha.
World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva distance themselves from attachment to views based on reliance upon the precepts?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the nature of transgression and merit...
Because both are non-existent. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from clinging to views based on the precepts.
"World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from fear of empty phenomena?
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all empty phenomena as being entirely without intrinsic nature, then the objects of fear are ultimately non-existent. This is what it means."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should remain far removed from fear of the dharma of emptiness. "World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed from contradicting emptiness?

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty, there is no contradiction between non-emptiness and emptiness; therefore, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should [remain far removed from contradicting emptiness]."
He remains far removed from contradicting emptiness. "Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the thorough realization of emptiness?

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are empty, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill the thorough realization of emptiness. "Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
