The Seven Emptinesses Layman, Ge Dinghui.
Outline of Volume 56, Leaf 14 (Praise of the Mahāyāna Chapter), through Volume 61.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Mahāyāna surpasses all those in the world—devas, humans, asuras, and so forth."
Most honored and most sublime, this Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is equal to space. For example, just as space can universally contain immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings;
and just as space neither comes nor goes, and no abiding can be perceived;
and just as space—in its prior, subsequent, and intermediate limits—is entirely ungraspable and equal throughout the three periods of time, it is therefore called the "Great Vehicle. The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, it is so, it is so. The Great Vehicle is endowed with such boundless qualities as these.

Subhūti, if all phenomena were the true nature (tathatā), were not empty, were not erroneous, were not provisional designations, but were instead truths, realities, permanent, eternal, unchanging, immutable, and possessed of an intrinsic nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be venerable or sublime, nor would it transcend the world."
All the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—regard all phenomena as not being suchness; they are false, inverted, and merely provisional designations.
They are neither truths nor realities; they are impermanent and non-eternal, subject to change and transformation, and entirely devoid of any real intrinsic nature.
Therefore, this Mahāyāna is venerable and sublime; it surpasses all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
If there were any sentient beings who possessed a truly existent nature toward whom the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, [it would not be so].
Thus, the Tathāgatas are unable to cause those sentient beings to have entered, are entering, or will enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of the wondrous nirvana without remainder,
even though the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
The sentient beings who are so addressed do not possess a real, intrinsic nature;

therefore, all Tathāgatas are able to cause those classes of sentient beings to have entered, are entering, or will enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of the supreme, wondrous nirvana that is without support.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna surpasses all devas, humans, asuras, and others, being the most honored and the most sublime.

Next, it is explained that this Mahāyāna is equal to space. For example, just as in space one cannot find the directional divisions of east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below;
so too is the Mahāyāna: one cannot find the directional divisions of east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.
Furthermore, just as in space one cannot find length, shortness, squareness, roundness, height, lowness, or obliqueness.

Just as shape and form cannot be apprehended—neither long nor short, square nor round, high nor low, nor oblique nor upright—so too it is with the Mahāyāna; neither long nor short, square nor round, high nor low, nor oblique nor upright can its shape and form be apprehended.
Furthermore, just as in space no manifest colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, black, purple, or pale green can be apprehended, so too it is with the Mahāyāna;
no manifest colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, black, purple, or pale green can be apprehended. Moreover...
Just as space is neither light nor darkness, so too is the Mahāyāna neither light nor darkness.

Furthermore, just as space is not the aggregates, bases, or elements, yet is not separate from the aggregates, bases, or elements, so too is the Mahāyāna not the aggregates, bases, or elements, yet is not separate from the aggregates, bases, or elements.
Moreover, just as space is neither obtainable nor unobtainable, so too is the Mahāyāna neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
It is unattainable. Furthermore, like empty space, it is neither expressible nor inexpressible. The Mahāyāna is likewise:
it is neither expressible nor inexpressible. Therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to empty space.
Next, regarding the statement that space can universally contain countless and immeasurable sentient beings:
Subhūti, because sentient beings do not exist, you should know that space also does not exist. Because space does not exist, you should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist.
By virtue of this principle, it is said that the Great Vehicle can universally contain countless and immeasurable [sentient beings].
One should measure infinite sentient beings. Why is this? Whether it be sentient beings, space, or the Great Vehicle—all such things as these are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, it is because sentient beings are immeasurable, innumerable, and infinite.

One should know that space is likewise immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless. Because space is immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless, one should know that the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is also immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless.
For this reason, it is said that the Great Vehicle can contain the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
If space is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless, and if the Great Vehicle is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless—all such things are non-existent because they cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, because sentient beings do not exist, you should know that space also does not exist;
because space does not exist, you should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is also non-existent.

Because the incalculable is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) is also non-existent. Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless (*ananta*) is also non-existent.
Because the boundless is non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are also non-existent. By means of this...
This is the meaning. Therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is universally able to contain and receive countless, immeasurable, and boundless sentient beings.

Why is this? Whether it be sentient beings, or space, or the Mahāyāna, or the countless, or the immeasurable, or the boundless, or all phenomena—all such things as these are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, because from the self up to the perceiver there is nothing existent, you should know that the Śrāvaka vehicle also has no existence.
Because the Śrāvaka vehicle has no existence, you should know that the Pratyekabuddha vehicle also has no existence.
Because the Pratyekabuddha vehicle has no existence, you should know that the Samyaksaṃbuddha vehicle also has no existence. Because the Samyaksaṃbuddha vehicle has no existence...
Therefore, one should know that space is also non-existent. Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Great Vehicle is also non-existent.
Because the Great Vehicle is non-existent, one should know that the innumerable, the immeasurable, and the boundless are also non-existent.
Because the innumerable, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all phenomena are also non-existent.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is universally capable of containing countless, immeasurable, and boundless sentient beings.
Why is this? Whether it be from "self" up to "seer," or whether it be the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or the Samyaksaṃbuddha-yāna.
Whether it be space, or the Great Vehicle, or that which is innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless, or all dharmas—
all these are non-existent and unobtainable (58.10).
Next, it is said that just as space cannot be seen to come, go, or abide, so too is the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti, all phenomena (dharmas) neither come nor go, nor do they abide. Why is this?
Because all phenomena, as well as their fundamental nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristics—whether in motion or at rest—cannot be apprehended. Therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
There is no coming, no going, and no abiding to be perceived. It is, for example, like space (as concluded on the third leaf of scroll fifty-nine). Next, it is said:
"Furthermore, just as the prior, posterior, and middle limits of space cannot be apprehended, so too is the Mahāyāna;
its prior, posterior, and middle limits cannot be apprehended. Because it is equal throughout the three times, it is called the 'Mahāyāna. Subhūti, regarding the past..."
The past world is empty; the future world is empty; the present world is empty.
The equality of the three times is empty of the equality of the three times. Why is this?

Because emptiness has no distinct characteristics of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or any such differentiation. Therefore, the Great Vehicle is the equality of the three times. Such is the Great Vehicle.

Within the Middle Way, neither the characteristic of equality nor the characteristic of inequality can be apprehended, because within the Mahāyāna, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, past phenomena are empty of past phenomena; future phenomena are empty of future phenomena;
present phenomena are empty of present phenomena. Why is this? Because within emptiness, past phenomena cannot be apprehended. Why?

Therefore, past phenomena are themselves emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less could past phenomena be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, future phenomena cannot be apprehended. Why is this?

Future phenomena are themselves emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less [could future phenomena be apprehended] within emptiness?
There are future dharmas that can be apprehended. Within emptiness, present dharmas cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because present dharmas are themselves empty, and the nature of emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended;

how much less could present dharmas be apprehended within emptiness? (End of leaf eleven of volume sixty). Subhūti, past-limit dharmas cannot be apprehended; future-limit dharmas cannot [be apprehended].
It can be apprehended. Yet, the phenomena of the middle period cannot be apprehended; even within the equality of the three periods of time, phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because within equality, the phenomena of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.
For what reason? Within equality, even the nature of equality itself cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be a past, future, or present within that equality?
It can be found within the Dharma, Subhūti. An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) cannot be found in the past limit;

an ordinary person cannot be found in the future limit; an ordinary person cannot be found in the middle limit. Furthermore, an ordinary person cannot be found within the equality of the three times. Why is this?
Because within that equality, ordinary persons of the past, future, and present are all unfindable. For what reason?
Within equality, even the nature of equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be the apprehension of past, future, or present ordinary beings within that equality?
This is because a self, a sentient being, and so forth, up to a knower or a viewer, cannot be apprehended.
In the past limit, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas cannot be apprehended. In the future limit, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas cannot be apprehended.
In the middle limit, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas cannot be apprehended.
Within the equality of the three times, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas likewise cannot be apprehended. Why is this so?
Within equality, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within equality, even the nature of equality itself is unapprehendable;
how much less could there be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas of the past, future, and present to be apprehended within equality? This is because of me, a sentient being.

Because even a knower or a seer cannot be apprehended, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they abide within this mark of the equality of the three times and diligently train in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

Because they are free from grasping and attachment, they swiftly attain fulfillment. This is called the Mahāyāna characteristic of the equality of the three times. (The "Chapter Praising the Mahāyāna" concludes.)
Fascicle 61, Part 2 (Chapter on Accordance).
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Tathāgata has commanded the Venerable Subhūti to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
why then does he now speak of the Mahāyāna? Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying: "Indeed..."
"Is there nothing that contradicts the Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha told Subhūti, "What you have spoken regarding the Mahāyāna is entirely in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā;
there is nothing that contradicts it. Why is this? Because all wholesome dharmas..."

The factors of enlightenment—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all such things are without exception subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti, the Great Vehicle is not other than the perfection of wisdom; the perfection of wisdom is not other than the Great Vehicle. Why is this? Because its...
Because their nature is non-dual and indivisible.
(From the seventh leaf of scroll sixty-one, the "Chapter on Non-Apprehension," to scroll seventy, Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, throughout the past, future, and present limits, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-existent."
"It can be so found, World-Honored One. Form and the other aggregates are boundless; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise boundless.
That is to say, within all dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Apart from all dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is non-existent and cannot be apprehended. Regarding all dharmas, in every manner, in every place, and in every..."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sought [them] but saw nothing at all; ultimately they could not be found. There is only a provisional name;
there is no self-nature whatsoever. Form and all other dharmas are ultimately unarisen. If they are ultimately unarisen, they cannot be called "form" and so forth.
How could I possibly instruct or admonish them by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, which is itself ultimately unarisen?
Ultimately, no bodhisattva mahāsattvas are produced. Blessed One, apart from ultimate non-production, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who can practice unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not sink into despondency, and feels no regret, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom. At that time, Śāriputra...
Ārya Subhūti was asked by Śāriputra: "For what reason do you say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unapprehendable in the past, future, and middle limits?
... For what reason do you say that one who is neither sinking nor drowning, and who feels no sorrow or regret, is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
At that time, Subhūti replied to Śāriputra: "Regarding what the Venerable One has asked, for what reason..."
Regarding the statement that the bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or middle limits:
Śāriputra, within the non-existence, emptiness, detachment, and lack of intrinsic nature of sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or middle limits.
Whether sentient beings are non-existent, whether sentient beings are empty, or whether sentient beings are detached... [sentient beings...]
They lack intrinsic nature. Whether in the past, the future, or the present, all such dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattva are non-dual and indivisible.
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent; they are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or middle limits. This is because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent;
because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached;
and because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness lack intrinsic nature. It is thus with the bodhisattva mahāsattva in the past, future, and middle limits.
All phenomena are non-dual and indivisible. Even up to the Great Vehicle, there is nothing whatsoever; it is empty, detached, and without intrinsic nature.
Within this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is unapprehendable in the past, future, or middle limits.

Whether it be that the Great Vehicle is non-existent, or that the Great Vehicle is empty, or that the Great Vehicle is detached, or that the Great Vehicle is without intrinsic nature—whether in the prior limit, the posterior limit, or...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva of the past limit, the present limit, and the middle limit—all such dharmas are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.
For this reason, I say that the bodhisattva mahāsattva of the past limit, the future limit, and the middle limit is unapprehendable.
Next, regarding the answer that because form (*rūpa*) and so forth are boundless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also boundless: Śāriputra, form is like space;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like space. Why is this? Because neither a center nor a periphery can be apprehended therein, it is called "space. For what reason?
Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, and the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty. By virtue of this...
For this reason, you should know that because form (*rūpa*) is limitless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also limitless;

because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are limitless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also limitless; and even up to the point that because the vehicles of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and the Mahāyāna are limitless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also limitless.

Next, the answer to the question "For what reason is it said that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is non-existent and unobtainable as being identical with form and so forth, yet distinct from form and so forth? is as follows: Śāriputra, form is empty of the nature of form. Why is this?
Because within the emptiness of the nature of form, form is non-existent and unobtainable. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise non-existent and unobtainable. It is not form; it is the emptiness of the nature of form. Why is this?
Because within the emptiness of the nature of form, that which is not form is non-existent and unobtainable. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise non-existent and unobtainable.

[The same applies to] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they are the emptiness of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Why is this? Because within [the emptiness of the nature of] feeling, perception, and mental formations...

Because within the emptiness of the nature of consciousness, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist and cannot be apprehended, the bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not exist and cannot be apprehended.
It is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is not the emptiness of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this?

Because within the emptiness of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Because they are attained; thus, even a bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-existent and unattainable.
Even up to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna, they are non-existent and unattainable; likewise, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also non-existent and unattainable.

Next, the answer to the question: "For what reason do you say that when one seeks a bodhisattva-mahāsattva among all phenomena, in every way, in every place, and at all times, they are entirely non-existent and ultimately cannot be found;
how then am I to instruct and admonish the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the perfection of wisdom?"—Śāriputra: [The answer follows: Śāriputra, [it is because]... (as per the original context).
Because the nature of form (*rūpa*) is empty, form does not exist and cannot be apprehended within form; form does not exist and cannot be apprehended within feeling (*vedanā*).
Because the nature of feeling is empty, feeling does not exist and cannot be apprehended within feeling; feeling does not exist and cannot be apprehended within form.
Form and feeling do not exist and cannot be apprehended within perception (*saṃjñā*). Because the nature of perception is empty, perception [does not exist... within perception...
Perception is non-existent and unattainable. Perception is non-existent and unattainable within form and feeling.
Form, feeling, and perception are non-existent and unattainable within formations, because the nature of formations is empty. Formations are non-existent and unattainable within formations;
formations are non-existent and unattainable within form, feeling, and perception. Form, feeling, perception, and formations are non-existent within consciousness...
There is nothing to be apprehended. Because the nature of consciousness is empty, consciousness is non-existent and unapprehendable within consciousness itself.
Consciousness is non-existent and unapprehendable within form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding all such phenomena, in every way, in every place, and at every time, when I seek a bodhisattva mahāsattva, I find nothing and there is nothing to be apprehended. Why is this?
Therefore, because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Next, to answer the question "For what reason is it said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has only a provisional name?
Śāriputra, the name "bodhisattva mahāsattva" is merely a temporary designation; all names for phenomena are merely temporary designations throughout the ten directions.
The three times come from nowhere and go nowhere; they likewise have no abiding place. Among all phenomena there is no name, and within names there are no phenomena.
They are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations. Why is this?
Because both all phenomena and their names are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither all phenomena nor names exist at all.
Because all things are unattainable, the name "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is likewise so. It is merely a designation applied adventitiously;
throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere.
Within the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no Bodhisattva-mahāsattva. They are neither joined nor separated; they exist only as a provisional designation.
Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists, and neither can be apprehended.
Next, the answer to the question "For what reason is it said" is as follows:
"Regarding the statement, 'We are ultimately not born,' Śāriputra, since 'self' is ultimately non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how could there be birth? ... up to ...
since 'knower' and 'seer' are ultimately non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how could there be birth? Form is ultimately non-existent."
Since they cannot be apprehended, how can there be their arising? Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately non-existent;
since they cannot be apprehended, how can there be their arising? This extends even to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna, which are ultimately non-existent.
Since they cannot be apprehended, how could there be their arising?

Next, to answer the question of why it is said that all phenomena are likewise entirely without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): Śāriputra, all phenomena are entirely devoid of an intrinsic nature of aggregation.
Why is this? Because the phenomena that arise from aggregation are empty of intrinsic nature. Form (*rūpa*) has no aggregation...
They lack an inherent nature of aggregation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness lack an inherent nature of aggregation;

even the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Mahāyāna entirely lack an inherent nature of aggregation. Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion;
all phenomena are neither pleasant nor subject to dispersion; all phenomena are neither self nor subject to dispersion; all phenomena are quiescent.
Stillness is also without loss. The detachment of all phenomena is also without loss. The emptiness of all phenomena is also without loss. The signlessness of all phenomena is also without loss.
The wishlessness of all phenomena is also without loss. The wholesomeness of all phenomena is also without loss.
The faultlessness of all phenomena is also without loss. The outflowlessness of all phenomena is also without loss. All phenomena...
Phenomena are neither defiled nor lost. All phenomena are pure and not lost. All phenomena transcend the world and are not lost.
All phenomena are unconditioned and not lost.
All phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why? Because their intrinsic nature is such.

Next, to answer the question of for what reason it is said that form and all other phenomena are ultimately unarisen: Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of form is ultimately unarisen. Why? Because it is not something produced.
The intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is ultimately unarisen... [and so forth].

It is unarisen. Why? Because it is not something produced. Even so, the intrinsic nature of the Śrāvakayāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, and the Mahāyāna is ultimately unarisen. Why? Because it is not something produced.
Next, the answer to the question, "For what reason is it said that if something is ultimately non-arising, it is not called 'form' (rūpa), etc.?
is as follows: Śāriputra, it is so; it is so. If something is ultimately non-arising, it is not called "form," etc. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature (prakṛti) of form is empty. If a phenomenon (dharma) is empty by its intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or [changing].
It is different. For this reason, if something is ultimately non-arising, it is not called "form," and so on, up to:
if something is ultimately non-arising, it is not called the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Mahāyāna.
Next, to answer the question of why it is said that one instructs and advises bodhisattvas who are ultimately unborn by means of the Prajñāpāramitā which is ultimately unborn:
Śāriputra, ultimate non-arising is itself the Prajñāpāramitā.
The perfection of wisdom is ultimate non-arising; ultimate non-arising is the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and the bodhisattva mahāsattva is ultimate non-arising. This is because they are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.
Next, to answer the question of for what reason it is said that apart from ultimate non-arising, there is no bodhisattva who can practice unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment: Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as distinct from ultimate non-arising,
nor does one perceive the bodhisattva mahāsattva as distinct from ultimate non-arising.
It is non-arising. Why? Because it is without duality and without division.
Next, to answer the question of for what reason it is said that when a bodhisattva hears this teaching, their mind does not sink, does not despair, and is neither distressed nor regretful:
Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not perceive any phenomena as existing.
He realizes its utility. He perceives all phenomena as being like magical illusions, like dream-objects, and even like transformations—none of which are truly existent.
Upon hearing it said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness, he gives rise to profound joy.
It should be known that such a bodhisattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom. (The Chapter on Non-apprehension concludes.)
Fascicle 70, Leaf 9 (Chapter on the Practice of Contemplation). Fascicle 71. Fascicle 72.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "When practicing the perfection of wisdom and contemplating all phenomena, one does not accept, grasp, cling to, or adhere to any phenomena, nor does one designate them as 'all phenomena. Why is this?"
Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and are without arising or ceasing, O Bhagavat, all dharmas are non-arisen;
thus they are not "all dharmas. Why is this? All dharmas and non-arising are non-dual and cannot be divided into two. For what reason?
Because they are by nature unarisen, they are neither one nor two, neither many nor different. Therefore, since all dharmas are unarisen, they are not "all dharmas.
World-Honored One, because all dharmas are non-dual, they are not "all dharmas. World-Honored One, all dharmas enter into the category of the non-false dharma of non-duality.

"What is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? Śāriputra, because they seek great enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, and because there is indeed enlightenment [for them], they are called 'bodhisattvas.
Because they can truly know the characteristics of all phenomena without attachment, they are further called 'mahāsattvas.'"

"What is meant by *prajñāpāramitā*? Śāriputra, it is because there is a supreme and wondrous wisdom that is distantly detached from all things that it is called *prajñāpāramitā*. This is distantly detached from all afflictions and views;
this is distantly detached from all six destinies and four modes of birth; and this is [distantly detached] from all aggregates, elements, and sense-bases."

Because it attains remoteness, it is called Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Śāriputra, because there is a supreme and wondrous wisdom that reaches far, it is called Prajñāpāramitā; this reaches far to the true nature of form.
This reaches the ultimate limit of the true nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it even reaches the ultimate limit of the true nature of all doors of dhāraṇī and the true nature of all doors of samādhi. Therefore, it is named Prajñāpāramitā.

What is the contemplation of all phenomena? Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one contemplates all phenomena as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, and neither pure nor impure.
It is not empty, nor is it non-empty; it has no marks, nor is it markless; it has no aspiration, nor is it without aspiration;
it is not tranquil, nor is it non-tranquil; it is not detached, nor is it non-detached. This is called the contemplation of all phenomena.
Fascicle 73–74. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason do you say that the non-arising of form and so forth is not form and so forth? Subhūti replied:
"Form is empty of the nature of form. Within this emptiness of nature, there is neither arising nor form. [The same applies to] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

The natures of perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. Within this emptiness of nature, there is no arising, nor are there sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
For this reason, it is said that the non-arising of form and so forth is not form and so forth.
"For what reason do you say that if form and so forth are non-dual, they are then not form and so forth?

Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra, whether it be form or non-duality, or feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or non-duality—all such things as these are entirely without association."
It is not non-associated; it is neither with form nor without form; it is neither visible nor invisible; it is neither resistant nor non-resistant.
It is entirely of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless (*animitta*). For this reason, it is said that the non-duality of form and so forth is not form and so forth.
"For what reason is it said that the bases of form and so forth are included within the category of non-dual, non-erroneous dharmas?
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra, form is not different from non-arising and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing are not different from form. Form itself is non-arising and non-ceasing;
non-arising and non-ceasing itself is form. This extends even to all doors of samādhi, which are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing."

Cessation is itself all the gateways of samādhi. For this reason, it is said that the sphere of form enters into the category of non-dual and non-erroneous dharmas, up to and including the gateways of samādhi entering into the category of non-dual and non-erroneous dharmas. (The Chapter on Contemplative Practice concludes.)
Fascicle 74, Leaf 9 (Chapter on Non-arising). Fascicle 75.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* and contemplating all phenomena (*dharmas*), one perceives that the self is non-arising because it is ultimately pure;
likewise, one perceives that the knower and the seer are non-arising because they are ultimately pure. One perceives form..."
"Non-arising, because it is ultimately pure. ... up to ... "seeing the Tathāgata as non-arising; seeing the Tathāgata’s Dharma as non-arising, because it is ultimately pure.

At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "If sentient beings and so forth are non-arising, up to the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata’s Dharma being non-arising—if this is the case, then there should be no distinction in taking birth within the six realms of existence. It should not be so."

A stream-enterer would not attain the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to: a bodhisattva would not attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor would they attain the five kinds of enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if all phenomena were definitively non-arising, for what reason would a stream-enterer cultivate the path to abandon the three fetters for the sake of the fruit of stream-entry?
For what reason would a once-returner cultivate the path to attenuate [the afflictions] for the sake of the fruit of once-returning?

For what reason does one cultivate the path for abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion? To attain the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin). For what reason does one cultivate the path for abandoning the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni)?
To attain the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala). For what reason does one cultivate the path for abandoning the five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni)?

To attain the state of an arhat. For what reason does one cultivate the path for awakening to dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)? To attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. For what reason does one cultivate [the path]? To deliver immeasurable beings.
"For the sake of all sentient beings, [the Tathāgata] practiced hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful ascetic practices and fully endured boundless varieties of intense suffering.
For what reason did the Tathāgata realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? For what reason do the Buddhas turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra: "It is not that I perceive, within dharmas that are unarisen, any..."
There are six kinds of distinctions regarding birth. It is not that I perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, anyone who can enter the clear realization of the truths;
nor do I perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, anyone who is a stream-enterer or attains the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to:
it is not that I perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, any Buddhas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
[The wheel] turns, delivering immeasurable multitudes. At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Venerable one, do you now intend to realize a phenomenon of arising by means of a phenomenon of arising?
Or do you intend to realize a phenomenon of non-arising by means of a phenomenon of non-arising? Subhūti replied:

"I truly do not intend to realize a phenomenon of arising by means of a phenomenon of arising, nor do I intend to realize a phenomenon of non-arising by means of a phenomenon of non-arising. Śāriputra said: [Śāriputra said: "... (The text continues with Śāriputra's further inquiry.)
Śāriputra said: "If that is so, do you now intend to use dharmas that arise to realize dharmas that do not arise, or do you intend to use dharmas that do not arise to realize dharmas that arise?

Subhūti replied: "I do not intend to use dharmas that arise to realize dharmas that do not arise, nor do I intend to use dharmas that do not arise to realize dharmas that arise. Śāriputra said: "If it is thus..."
"Is it that there is absolutely no attainment and no clear realization? Subhūti replied, "There is indeed attainment and clear realization, yet one does not realize by means of these two dharmas.
Rather, attainment and clear realization are provisionally designated in accordance with worldly convention;
they do not exist in the ultimate sense. It is only in accordance with worldly convention that the designation of 'stream-enterer' and 'fruit of stream-entry' is established."

There are bodhisattvas; there is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Yet, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no stream-enterer, nor even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra asked: "Are the distinctions among the six realms of existence also existent only as conventional designations (*prajñapti*) following worldly discourse, and not in the ultimate sense?
Subhūti replied: "It is so, it is so. In the ultimate sense, there is no karma."
Because they are without maturation, without arising or ceasing, and without defilement or purification. Then Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, do you now wish to cause unarisen phenomena to arise, or do you wish to cause already-arisen phenomena to arise? Subhūti replied:
"I do not wish to cause unarisen phenomena to arise, nor do I wish to cause already-arisen phenomena to arise. What, then, is...?
"Non-arising phenomena. Subhūti replied: "Form is a non-arising phenomenon; I do not wish to cause it to arise.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish to cause them to arise. This extends even to the phenomena of a Tathāgata being a non-arising phenomenon;
I do not wish to cause them to arise. Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. What, Subhūti, are 'already arisen phenomena'?"
He replied: "Form is a dharma that has already arisen; I do not wish for it to arise. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are dharmas that have already arisen;
I do not wish for them to arise. Even up to the Tathāgata-dharmas, they are dharmas that have already arisen;
I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Do you now wish for them to arise?"
"Does one wish to cause that which has already arisen to arise, or does one wish to cause that which has not yet arisen to arise?

Subhūti replied, "I do not wish to cause that which has arisen to arise, nor do I wish to cause that which has not arisen to arise. Why is this? Because these two dharmas—'arising' and 'non-arising'—are both mutually incompatible."
It is not non-associated; it is neither with form nor without form; it is neither visible nor invisible; it is neither resistant nor non-resistant.

It is entirely of one single mark, namely, the markless. For this reason, it is said that one does not wish to cause what has already arisen to arise, nor does one wish to cause what has not yet arisen to arise.
Śāriputra said: "To apply the expression 'non-arising' to dharmas that are non-arising—this is..."
Śāriputra asked, "Is it also non-arising? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is. Why is this? Form is non-arising;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-arising. Even the dharmas of a Tathāgata are non-arising. For what reason?

Because they are all empty by their very nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). For this reason, regarding dharmas that are non-arising, one utters the word 'non-arising,' yet there is no meaning of arising therein."
If the Dharma that is taught, the one who teaches, and the one who listens are all non-arising, then all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature;
whether based on the internal, the external, or both together, they cannot be apprehended.
Fascicle 75, Leaf 10 (Chapter on the Path of Purity).
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they should purify form; they should purify feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
and so on, up to purifying the path to enlightenment. Śāriputra asked: "How does one purify the path to enlightenment?"
The Venerable Subhūti replied: "The six pāramitās each have two kinds: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.

What is the mundane perfection of generosity? It is when one forms the thought, 'I give and that person receives,' employing the method of apprehending something as real, and thinks, 'I hold this merit and bestow it upon all sentient beings so that they may obtain [it].'"
This brings happiness in this world and the next, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder.
Yet, one who practices giving while clinging to the three spheres—first, the notion of a self; second, the notion of another;
and third, the notion of a gift—is said to practice the mundane perfection of generosity (*laukikī dānapāramitā*), because such practice is shared with worldly beings.
Because it does not transcend or move beyond worldly phenomena, what is the supramundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?

When practicing generosity, one purifies the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*), takes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the foremost, and dedicates the merit of the practiced giving universally to all sentient beings.
Regarding all sentient beings, one perceives nothing at all; yet, although one dedicates [the merit] together with all sentient beings toward [enlightenment], [one remains free from attachment].
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Within this, one does not perceive even the slightest mark (*nimitta*).
Because one practices giving without any attachment whatsoever, it is called the supramundane perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

It is so named because it does not act in common with the mundane world and because it is able to transcend and emerge from mundane phenomena. What is the mundane perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)?
"Much" refers to forming this thought: "For the benefit of all sentient beings, I uphold the pure precepts.
Using attainment as my means, I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may obtain peace and happiness in both this life and future lives."
Up until the attainment of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they observe the precepts while clinging to the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*): first, the notion of self;

second, the notion of others; and third, the notion of the precepts. Because they observe the precepts by clinging to these three spheres, it is called the mundane perfection of ethical discipline (*laukika-śīla-pāramitā*).
Since it functions in common with the world, it does not transcend or move beyond the mundane.
Because it is the Dharma. How is it supramundane? It is the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). When upholding the precepts, the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are purified.
With great compassion as the foremost, the merit of the upheld precepts is universally bestowed upon sentient beings.
Regarding all sentient beings, there is no apprehension of them at all. Although one dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward enlightenment, within that [dedication] one does not...
One perceives only minor signs. Because one upholds the precepts without any attachment whatsoever, it is called the supramundane pāramitā;
for it does not proceed in common with the mundane world and is able to transcend and emerge from all mundane phenomena.
When practicing these six types of pāramitās—patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—in this manner, one purifies the path to enlightenment.
This immeasurable and boundless mass of great merit is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.
Such merit is entirely brought about by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
for all wholesome dharmas arise from it and abide in reliance upon it.
Fascicle 76.

Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, has no doubt or confusion in their mind and does not become bewildered, you should know that this bodhisattva dwells in such a dwelling, never departing from mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely: the desire to rescue and protect [all beings].
"Regarding all sentient beings, one should never abandon the mental engagement of great compassion toward all sentient beings. At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If all sentient beings also constantly do not depart from this mental engagement, then there would be no distinction between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and all sentient beings.
Subhūti praised Śāriputra, saying: "It is exactly as you have said..."
It is said: "One should be able to grasp the meaning of what I have taught as it truly is. Why is this?

Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that mental attention (*manasikāra*) also does not exist. Because sentient beings lack reality, one should know that mental attention also lacks reality. Because sentient beings are empty..."
One should know that mental attention (*manasikāra*) is also empty, because sentient beings are remote. One should know that mental attention is also remote, because sentient beings are secluded.
One should know that mental attention is also secluded, because sentient beings are tranquil.

One should know that mental attention is also without cognition, because from the self up to the "seer" there is no existence, and because there is no cognition. One should know that mental attention is likewise without cognition.

Nor is it existent. Nor is there any cognition. Śāriputra, because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent and lack cognition—and so on, up to the fact that unsurpassed enlightenment is non-existent and lacks cognition—one should know that mental attention (*manasikāra*) is likewise non-existent and lacks cognition.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in such an abiding.
"One should always never abandon the mental engagement of great compassion. At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Bodhisattvas who wish to study the Prajñāpāramitā should all train according to what you have said. (The Chapter on the Pure Path concludes.)
Fascicle 77 (The Chapter on the Heavenly Kings) through Fascicle 81:
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying: "Now all the gods of the desire and form realms of this trichiliocosm have assembled here.
They are all filled with longing and yearning, desiring to hear the Venerable One proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā. Great...
"Virtue. What is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the prajñāpāramitā? How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti replied to Śakra, saying: "Kauśika, you gods have not yet generated..."
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all should now resolve to attain it.
However, those who have entered the fixed course of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*—the state of rightness free from outflows—cannot again resolve to attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because they have already established a boundary within the flow of saṃsāra.
Even if there are those who are able to resolve their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I likewise rejoice in them. Why is that?

For superior persons should seek even higher dharmas, and I do not create obstacles for sentient beings in their pursuit of the most excellent and wholesome qualities. Kausika, as for what you asked—why...
This, Kauśika, is the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and employing the method of non-apprehension (anupalambha),
contemplates form as impermanent, contemplates form as suffering, contemplates form as selfless, contemplates form as impure, and contemplates form as empty.
One contemplates form as signless; one contemplates form as wishless; one contemplates form as peaceful; one contemplates form as secluded;
one contemplates form as like a disease; one contemplates form as like an abscess; one contemplates form as like an arrow; one contemplates form as like a wound.
One contemplates form as a feverish affliction; one contemplates form as a torment; one contemplates form as subject to decay;

one contemplates form as subject to withering; one contemplates form as subject to change; one contemplates form as subject to rapid extinction; one contemplates form as fearsome; and one contemplates form as loathsome.

One contemplates that form is fraught with calamity; one contemplates that form is subject to misfortune; one contemplates that form is plagued by pestilence; one contemplates that form is afflicted by disease;
one contemplates that form is not secure; one contemplates that form is unreliable; and one contemplates that form is without arising and without ceasing.
To contemplate that form is neither defiled nor pure; to contemplate that form is unconditioned and uncreated (*asaṃskṛta*);

and to contemplate that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, up to contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unconditioned and uncreated—this is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This extends even to contemplating ignorance as unconditioned and uncreated, up to volitional formations through to old age and death.
Death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—these are unconditioned and uncreated. This is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva (concluding at folio 4 of scroll 78).

If a bodhisattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatājñāna*), contemplates internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*), as being without self or what belongs to self, signless, wishless, quiescent, and secluded.
Without arising and without cessation; without defilement and without purity; without action and without conditioning—this is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to practice the *pāramitās* of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
He cultivates the four dhyānas; he cultivates the four immeasurables; he cultivates the four formless attainments; he cultivates the eight liberations; he cultivates the eight bases of mastery;

he cultivates the nine successive attainments; he cultivates the ten universal bases; he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness; he cultivates the four right endeavors; he cultivates the four bases of psychic power;

he cultivates the five faculties; he cultivates the five powers; he cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; he cultivates the noble eightfold path; and he cultivates the three doors of liberation.
The gateways: cultivating the four noble truths; cultivating the five eyes; cultivating the six supernormal powers; cultivating the ten powers of a Buddha; cultivating the four fearlessnesses;
cultivating the four analytical knowledges; cultivating great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
cultivating the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness; cultivating the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; and cultivating all *dhāraṇī* gateways.
All gateways of samādhi; cultivating the path of all-knowledge, the knowledge of aspects, and the knowledge of all aspects—this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate in this way:
"There are only dharmas that mutually rely upon one another and provide mutual nourishment."
It increases, pervades, and overflows, being devoid of self and what belongs to a self. Furthermore, one performs this contemplation:
the mind of dedication does not merge with the bodhicitta, nor does the bodhicitta merge with the mind of dedication.
Within the bodhicitta, the mind of dedication does not exist and cannot be found; within the mind of dedication, the bodhicitta does not exist and cannot be apprehended. The bodhicitta...
Although the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, he perceives nothing at all within those phenomena;
this is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Kausika, the Bodhisattva’s mind of dedication is not a mind, and the mind of enlightenment is also not a mind.
That which is not a mind is inconceivable. One should not dedicate that which is not a mind to that which is not a mind. Furthermore...
One should not dedicate the non-mind to the inconceivable; one should not dedicate the inconceivable to the inconceivable;
nor should one dedicate the inconceivable to the non-mind. Why is this?
Because the non-mind is itself the inconceivable, and the inconceivable is itself the non-mind. Thus, these two are both non-existent.
Because there is no dedication within the state of non-existence. If one contemplates in this way, this is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Next, [the text] answers the question: "How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the *prajñāpāramitā*? Kauśika...
Kauśika, regarding the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva should not dwell upon signs as they ought to dwell.

Kauśika, whether it be the emptiness of the nature of form, the emptiness of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or the emptiness of the nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva—[all are empty].
All such things are non-dual and without division. A bodhisattva should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.

Even if the nature of the stage of a Tathāgata is empty, and the nature of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty—all such things are non-dual and without division. A bodhisattva should [dwell] in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
This is the dwelling. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti: "When practicing the perfection of wisdom, what is it that one should not dwell upon?
Subhūti replied: "When practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should not dwell upon form;
one should not dwell upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why? Because [to do so] would be by way of apprehension; therefore, one should not dwell [upon them]."
The stage of ordinary beings, up to and including the stage of a Tathāgata—one should not dwell in these. Why? Because they employ the means of apprehending something as an object.

Furthermore, Kauśika, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should not dwell on the thought, "This is form," nor should one dwell on the thought, "This is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why? Because they employ the means of apprehending something as an object.
Therefore, one should not dwell on the thought that "this is the stage of ordinary beings," up to and including "this is the stage of a Tathāgata. Why?
Because such practice is based on the expedient means of apprehending something as an object. Furthermore, Kauśika, when practicing the perfection of wisdom:
One should not dwell on form as permanent or impermanent. One should not dwell on form as pleasant or painful.
One should not dwell on form as self or non-self. One should not dwell on form as pure or impure.
One should not dwell on form as tranquil or untranquil. One should not dwell on form as detached or undetached. One should not dwell [on form].
One should not dwell on form as either empty or not empty; one should not dwell on form as having marks or being markless;

one should not dwell on form as having aspirations or being aspirationless. One should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, and so on, up to not dwelling on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having aspirations or being aspirationless. Why? Because nothing can be apprehended.

For the sake of skillful means, one should not dwell upon the stage of ordinary beings, nor even upon the stage of a Tathāgata, whether as permanent or impermanent, or with aspiration or without aspiration. Why? Because such practice takes "attainment" as its skillful means.
(From folio five of scroll seventy-nine to folio eight of scroll eighty) Furthermore, Kauśika, when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should not...

One should not dwell on the fruit of stream-entry as being an unconditioned phenomenon. One should not dwell on the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship as being unconditioned phenomena.
One should not dwell on pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as being an unconditioned phenomenon.
One should not dwell on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as being an unconditioned phenomenon. Why is this? Because it is by means of apprehending something that one acts.
Therefore, one should not dwell upon the stream-enterer as a field of merit; one should not dwell upon the once-returner, the non-returner, or the arhat as a field of merit;
one should not dwell upon the pratyekabuddha as a field of merit; and one should not dwell upon the bodhisattva, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha as a field of merit.
Why? Because they employ the means of apprehending something as an object. One should not dwell upon the first bhūmi.
The excellence of the second stage, up to and including the excellence of the tenth stage, should not be dwelled upon.

Why? Because it takes the apprehension of a referent as its means. Furthermore, Kauśika, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should not, from the very first production of the thought of awakening, dwell upon the notion: "I shall fulfill the six perfections."
Much. Up to: "I shall fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
One should not dwell on the thought, "Once my cultivation of the preparatory application is fulfilled, I shall enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
I shall abide in the bodhisattva’s stage of non-retrogression. Why? Because taking that which is apprehended as a means is not the way. One should not dwell on the thought, "I..."
Once the five supernormal powers have been perfected, one should travel through immeasurable and incalculable worlds to make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
there, one should listen to the True Dharma, reflect upon it according to reality, and extensively proclaim and reveal it for the sake of sentient beings.
One should not dwell on the thought, "I shall adorn and purify a Buddha-land such as those inhabited by the Buddhas of the ten directions," nor should one dwell on the thought, "I shall become..."
One should mature sentient beings so that they may attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, or nirvana, or the happiness of humans and gods.
One should not dwell on the thought, "I shall travel to immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields to make offerings to and praise the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones," nor should one dwell on the thought, "I shall establish immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in unsurpassed enlightenment."
One attains non-retrogression. Why is this? Because it takes "attainment" as its expedient means.
One should not dwell on the thought, "I shall master all dharanī-doors," nor take pride in the mastery of retention regarding immeasurable and boundless activities.
One should not dwell on the thought, "I shall accomplish all samādhi-doors," nor take pride in [the accomplishment of] immeasurable and boundless...
Regarding the distinctions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mastery in play, one should not dwell on the thought:
"I shall accomplish a body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, so that all sentient beings who see it will be filled with joy and never tire of beholding it. Why?
Because such an approach is based on the method of grasping at attainments. Furthermore, Kauśika, when practicing the perfection of wisdom...
At that time, one should not dwell on the aspiration: "May I obtain a pure buddha-field where there are no names or sounds for form;

no names or sounds for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so forth, until: may I obtain a pure buddha-field where there are no names or sounds for the stage of ordinary beings, nor for the dharmas [associated with them];
no names or sounds for the stage of the lineage of the seed, and so forth, up to the stage of the Tathāgata, nor for the dharmas [associated with it]. Why is this?
For this reason, because they take attainment as their skillful means. Why is that?
When all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all dharmas are entirely non-existent;
names and sounds are both unobtainable. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice regarding the Prajñāpāramitā.
Much. Regarding the characteristics of how one should or should not abide, Śāriputra then thought to himself:
"If all dharmas are such that one should not abide in them, then how should one abide in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra’s mind, said to him: "In what does the mind of the Tathāgatas abide, Śāriputra?"
He said: "The minds of all Buddhas abide nowhere. Why is this? The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in form;
it does not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, because the aggregate of form and the others cannot be apprehended. It does not abide in the sense base of the eye;
it does not abide in the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, because the sense base of the eye and the others cannot be apprehended. It does not abide in the sense base of form..."
The sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena do not abide in the eye-element, because the form-element and so forth are unapprehendable;
they do not abide in the eye-consciousness-element, nor in eye-contact, nor in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

This extends up to the non-abiding in the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mind-contact, nor in the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, because the mind-element and so forth [are likewise unapprehendable].

Because they are unattainable, one does not abide in the earth element; one does not abide in the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, because the earth element and so forth are unattainable.
One does not abide in the noble truth of suffering; one does not abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path, because the noble truth of suffering and so forth are unattainable.
One does not abide in ignorance; one does not abide in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, or craving.
Grasping, existence, birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair do not abide in inner emptiness,
nor even in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, because ignorance and the other factors are unapprehendable.
They do not abide in suchness, nor in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, nor even the inconceivable realm, because suchness and the other factors are unapprehendable.
Therefore, one does not dwell in the perfection of giving, nor even in the perfection of wisdom, because giving and the others are unapprehendable.
One does not dwell in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, because the four dhyānas and the others are unapprehendable.
One does not dwell in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities, because the eight liberations...

Because liberation and so forth are unattainable, one does not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eight branches of the noble path; for the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are unattainable.
One does not abide in the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; for the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth are unattainable.
Therefore, they do not dwell in the five eyes or the six supernormal powers, because the five eyes and so forth are unapprehendable.

They do not dwell in the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because the ten powers and so forth are unapprehendable.
They do not dwell in the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do they dwell in constant equanimity.

Because such things as the quality of non-forgetfulness are unapprehendable, one does not abide in any of the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi, because all such gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth are unapprehendable. One does not abide in omniscience.
One does not abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, because omniscience and the like are non-apprehendable.
One does not abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, because the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the like are non-apprehendable.

One does not abide in the stage of a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry or in the fruit itself; one does not abide in the stage of a once-returner, a non-returner, or a candidate for the fruit of arhatship, because the stream-enterers and the like are non-apprehendable.

Because they are unapprehendable, one does not abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor does one abide in the dharmas of a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata, because a pratyekabuddha and so forth are unapprehendable.

One does not abide in the stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and its dharmas, up to the stage of Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and its dharmas, because the stage of Extreme Joy and so forth are unapprehendable.
One does not abide in the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and its dharmas, up to the [stages of] a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata.
The stages and the dharmas, because the stage of an ordinary person and so forth cannot be apprehended.
Thus, Subhūti, the mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in any dharma whatsoever, nor does it not abide.

At that time, Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "In this way, although a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they are like the Tathāgata in that they do not dwell at all upon any phenomena, nor do they not dwell. Why is this?"
Although a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in form (rūpa),
because the aggregate of form and so forth are characterized by non-duality. Likewise, although a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom,
they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the stage of ordinary beings and their phenomena, up to and including the stage of bodhisattvas and the stage of Tathāgatas and their phenomena.

"Because the stage of ordinary beings and so forth lack the characteristic of duality, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, with respect to the perfection of wisdom, neither dwells nor does not dwell, employing the method of non-apprehension. One should train in this way. (The Chapter on the Deva King concludes.)
Fascicle 81, Leaf 7 (The Chapter on the Devaputras):
At that time, there were among those in the assembly certain devaputras who thought to themselves:
"Venerable Subhūti, although you have manifested this Prajñāpāramitā through various words and phrases, we are ultimately unable to understand it. Well.
He directly knew what was in that person’s mind and said to them: “I have not spoken a single word here, nor have you heard anything;
how then could there be any understanding? Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is entirely devoid of letters and verbal expression.

The suchness of the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated with form; it is likewise [neither associated nor dissociated] with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Nor is it associated, nor is it dissociated. The Tathāgata’s suchness is neither associated with nor dissociated from the suchness of form;
it is likewise neither associated with nor dissociated from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Tathāgata’s dharmatā is neither associated with nor dissociated from form; it is neither associated with nor dissociated from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
They are not associated. The *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated with the *dharmatā* of form (*rūpa*).

It is neither associated nor dissociated with the *dharmatā* of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*). Kauśika, the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated with that which is apart from form;
he is likewise neither associated nor dissociated with that which is apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is so. The Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated with the suchness that is apart from form;

he is likewise neither associated nor dissociated with the suchness that is apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated with the dharmatā that is apart from form;
