It is so. The Tathāgata’s suchness is neither associated nor dissociated from that which is apart from form;

it is neither associated nor dissociated from that which is apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The Tathāgata’s suchness is neither associated nor dissociated from the suchness of that which is apart from form;
it is likewise neither associated nor dissociated from the suchness of that which is apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is so. The *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated from that which is apart from form (*rūpa*).

It is also neither associated nor dissociated from that which is apart from feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated from the *dharmatā* of that which is apart from form.
It is also neither associated nor dissociated from the *dharmatā* of that which is apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is so. Even the dharmatā of the Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated from the dharmatā that is apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle;
it is likewise neither associated nor dissociated from the dharmatā that is apart from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
Kauśika, what the Venerable Śāriputra has spoken regarding all phenomena is neither separate from them nor identical to them. It is not...
Associated, not dissociated. The supernormal power of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata as the locus of reliance, because he takes non-reliance as his locus of reliance.
Fascicle 94 to Fascicle 98.
Subhūti again addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:

"Kauśika, regarding what you previously asked—where one should seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva—Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom should not be sought within form (rūpa);
it should not be sought within feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna); nor should it be sought apart from them."
One should not seek it by means of form (*rūpa*). One should not seek it apart from feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Why is this? Whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; whether it be apart from form, or apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the seeking itself—all such things are neither associated nor dissociated, and they do not possess form.
It is not formless; it is neither visible nor invisible; it is neither resistant nor non-resistant. It is entirely of one single mark, namely, the markless. Why is this?
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva is not form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
yet it is not apart from form, nor apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. All such things are utterly non-existent.
The nature [of these] cannot be apprehended. One should not seek it even within the Śrāvaka-yāna; one should not seek it within the Pratyekabuddha-yāna or the Anuttara-yāna.
One should not seek it apart from the Śrāvaka-yāna; one should not seek it apart from the Pratyekabuddha-yāna or the Anuttara-yāna.
(Up to the sixth leaf of the ninety-fifth fascicle.
Furthermore, Kauśika, one should not seek the perfection of wisdom practiced herein within the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*).
One should not seek it within the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One should not seek it apart from the suchness of form.
One should not seek it apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This extends to the point that one should not seek it within the suchness of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor should one seek it within the suchness of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. One should not seek it apart from the suchness of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Nor...
One should seek it through the suchness that is free from the vehicle of the solitary buddhas and the supreme vehicle.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the practice of the perfection of wisdom should not be sought within the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of form.
One should not seek it within the dharma-nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One should not seek it apart from the dharma-nature of form.
One should not seek it apart from the dharma-nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This applies even up to the dharma-nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle:
one should not seek it within the dharma-nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor should one seek it apart from the dharma-nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor apart from...
Seeking the Dharma-nature of Feeling, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness (up to folio four of scroll ninety-eight) [End of "Seeking Prajñāpāramitā"].
Scroll ninety-eight, folio four ("Praising the Multitude of Virtues"). Scroll ninety-nine:
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying: "The Prajñāpāramitā practiced by Bodhisattvas is great..."
"These are the perfections (pāramitās). These are immeasurable perfections. These are boundless perfections.
All stream-enterers train in these and attain the fruit of stream-entry;
likewise, all bodhisattvas train in these and are able to mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti then said:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said. Whether in the past, the present, or the future, all those who are stream-enterers attain the fruit of stream-entry by training in this;
likewise, all bodhisattvas, by training in this, are able to mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Kausika, form is great."

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva is also great. Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are great, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva is also great. Why is this?

Because the aggregates of form and so forth cannot be apprehended in their prior, subsequent, or middle limits, they are said to be "great. By virtue of that greatness, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva...
If the *pāramitās* are also said to be "great," then because the Śrāvaka vehicle is great, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by Bodhisattvas is also great.
Because the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna) are great, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by Bodhisattvas is also great.
Kauśika, because form (*rūpa*) is immeasurable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by Bodhisattvas— [is also immeasurable].
If the *pāramitās* are also immeasurable, it is because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable.
The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva is likewise immeasurable. Why is this? Because the measure of the aggregate of form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended;
therefore, they are said to be immeasurable. Just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so too is it with the aggregate of form and the others. Their measure—
It is unattainable. Even up to the immeasurable [vehicles] such as the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by the Bodhisattva is likewise immeasurable.
Kausika, because form (*rūpa*) is limitless, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by the Bodhisattva is also limitless.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are limitless, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by the Bodhisattva is...
"Much" is also limitless. Why is this? Because within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the others, neither a middle nor an end can be apprehended;

therefore, they are said to be limitless. Because those are limitless, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva is also said to be limitless, even unto the limitlessness of the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth—the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva is likewise limitless.

It is also boundless. Furthermore, Kauśika, because the object of focus for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) practiced by the bodhisattva is also boundless.
Because the object of focus of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom practiced by the bodhisattva is also boundless.
Because the object of focus of suchness (*tathatā*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom practiced by the bodhisattva is also boundless.
The practice of the perfection of wisdom is also limitless because sentient beings are limitless. Kausika, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva is likewise limitless.
As for what is called "sentient beings," Kausika, what is this a designation for?
Sakra, Lord of the Devas, replied: "Sentient beings" is not a designation for dharmas, nor is it a designation for non-dharmas; it is merely...
They are comprised of adventitious designations, comprised of names for non-existent things, and comprised of names for non-objects. Subhūti spoke again:
"Regarding the names of sentient beings spoken by the Tathāgata, is there therein any sentient being who is born or who passes away?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied: "No, Venerable One. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is pure. From that...
Because it is fundamentally non-existent [the "Chapter on Praising the Multitude of Virtues" concludes].
Folio 12 of Scroll 99: (The Chapter on Embracing).
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra and the other devas of the Desire Realm and Form Realm, as well as the ṛṣi Īśāna, were present in the assembly.
At that time, the goddesses three times cried out in a loud voice:
"Venerable Subhūti, you have excellently analyzed and revealed for us the subtle and sublime True Dharma, namely the Prajñāpāramitā. It is thus profound:
within this teaching, no dharma can be apprehended; therein, form cannot be apprehended, nor can feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended," and so forth.
There is no Śrāvaka vehicle to be found; there is no Pratyekabuddha vehicle or Supreme Vehicle (Anuttarayāna) to be found.

Although none of these dharmas can be found, there is nevertheless the provisional designation of the teachings of the three vehicles, namely: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Supreme Vehicle teaching.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the celestial beings and sages: "You should know that it is not the perfection of giving itself [that constitutes the vehicle]."

A Tathāgata can be found; yet a Tathāgata cannot be found apart from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), nor can a Tathāgata be found as being identical with the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth, nor can a Tathāgata be found apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
If a bodhisattva employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) regarding all phenomena, they should diligently train in the Prajñā[pāramitā].
The pāramitās can be correctly practiced and one should never be separated from them. You all should honor and serve those bodhisattvas as if they were the Tathāgata.
The celestial seers and others addressed the Buddha, saying: "Such is the Prajñāpāramitā."
This is most rare and extraordinary: it enables the assembly of bodhisattvas to swiftly grasp the wisdom of all-knowledge by means of non-apprehension as their expedient.
That is to say, by means of neither grasping nor rejecting form;
by means of neither grasping nor rejecting feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to neither grasping nor rejecting the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
For the sake of skillful means; for the sake of neither grasping nor rejecting the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle as skillful means.
Fascicle 100, Fascicle 101, Fascicle 102, Fascicle 103.
At that time, the World-Honored One illuminated the fourfold assembly, making them all witnesses. Thereupon, he looked toward and addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
Kauśika, if one does not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and thus receives, maintains, recites,
diligently practices, reflects upon according to principle, and expounds and disseminates this Prajñāpāramitā,
you should know that no evil Māra kings will be able to find an opportunity to cause them affliction or harm. Why is this?

They dwell well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of form; they dwell well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One cannot find an opportunity through emptiness to attain emptiness, nor can one find an opportunity through signlessness or wishlessness to attain signlessness or wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form and the others is entirely empty; thus, the afflictor, the afflicted, and the act of afflicting cannot be found.
Because they have attained it. At that time, the various devas and others all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One who receives, maintains, reads, recites, contemplates, and liberates themselves through this Prajñāpāramitā, and causes it to be widely disseminated, is indeed a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
It is by means of such a bodhisattva mahāsattva that all sentient beings are caused to forever sever [rebirth in] the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the asuras."
May those in the various perilous and evil realms, as well as all devas and humans, be forever freed from all calamities, epidemics, poverty, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and other sufferings.

Because of this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, there shall exist in the world the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel. We should always protect these and not allow anyone—whether human or non-human—to...
Afflicted by calamities and distresses, at that time the World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said, Kauśika.

Suppose the worlds of the ten directions were filled with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, without any space left between them, and suppose there were sons and daughters of good family who, throughout their entire lives, made immeasurable kinds of offerings to those fields of merit."

Furthermore, suppose there is another person who, for even a brief moment, makes offerings to a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening and does not depart from the six pāramitās.
Compared to this mass of merit, the former merit does not equal even one hundredth part;
it does not even equal one *upaniṣad* (fractional) part. Why is this? It is because [the former] does not proceed by way of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Therefore, it is because of bodhisattvas that Tathāgatas appear in the world; indeed, it is solely by reason of bodhisattvas that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas appear in the world.

For this reason, you all should always protect and make offerings to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that no calamities or afflictions may harm them. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha:
He said, "The Prajñāpāramitā is most rare. If one embraces the Prajñāpāramitā, then one embraces all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Kauśika.
You should listen attentively to the benefits and merits of the Prajñāpāramitā, both in this life and in future lives."
This bodhisattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension,
practices the six perfections throughout the long night, taking great compassion and vows as his primary guide.
If sentient beings, due to stinginess and greed, engage in strife throughout the long night, this bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena through skillful means.
He causes them to dwell securely in the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).

If sentient beings have long been transgressors of the precepts, this bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to cause them to dwell securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
If sentient beings have long been prone to anger and resentment, this bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena.
He employs skillful means to cause them to abide in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

If sentient beings have been indolent throughout the long night, this bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to cause them to abide in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
If sentient beings have had distracted minds throughout the long night, this bodhisattva [relinquishes] all internal and external phenomena...
He relinquishes everything. By skillful means, he causes those beings to abide in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

If sentient beings have long been deluded throughout the night of saṃsāra, this bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and, by skillful means, causes them to abide in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If sentient beings wander through birth and death, constantly afflicted by greed, hatred, and delusion throughout the long night...

Disturbed by the afflictions of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), and the impurities (*mala*), these bodhisattvas are able, through various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), to cause those [afflictions] to be severed and extinguished, so that beings may forever leave behind birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Alternatively, they establish them so that they abide in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Or, they establish them so that they abide in suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), up to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*). Or...
He establishes them so that they abide in the four noble truths; or he establishes them so that they abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless absorptions;
or he establishes them so that they abide in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, or the nine successive attainments.

The ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Or he establishes them so that they abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), or the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Or he establishes them so that they abide in the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*)—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Or he establishes them so that they abide in the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) or the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Or he establishes them so that...

They abide in the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or they establish others so that they may abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity.
Or they establish them so that they may abide in the knowledge of all paths, the knowledge of all aspects, or the knowledge of all things;
or they establish them so that they may abide in all doors of dhāraṇī or all doors of samādhi;

or they establish them so that they may abide in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or they establish them so that they may abide as solitary buddhas.
They awaken to bodhi; or they establish them so that they may dwell in the ten stages of a bodhisattva;
or they establish them so that they may dwell in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; or they establish them so that they may dwell in all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Such are the benefits and merits of the present life obtained through the perfection of wisdom.
Kausika, it is by means of this perfection of wisdom that a bodhisattva upholds, recites, studies, and contemplates it.

They shall transcribe and explain it, causing it to spread widely so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in future ages, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, deliver immeasurable multitudes, and establish sentient beings according to their original vows.
These are called the subsequent dharmic merits and benefits obtained from the *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, Kauśika, the *prajñā*...
If a *pāramitā* can diminish unwholesome dharmas and increase all that is wholesome,
so too this *prajñāpāramitā* can extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion, and increase their antidotes; it can extinguish name-and-form,

volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair— the entire great mass of suffering.
It increases those remedies that can extinguish all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), stains (*mala*), fetters (*bandhana*), and bonds.
It increases those remedies that can extinguish the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and even the views of a knower and a seer.

It increases those remedies that can extinguish all views of permanence, views of annihilation, views of existence, views of non-existence, and even the various evil paths of views. It increases those remedies...
It is a remedy that can extinguish all stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and delusion;
it increases their respective antidotes and can extinguish all notions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity;

it increases their respective antidotes and can extinguish all tendencies toward attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views; it increases their respective antidotes and can extinguish [all notions of] form.

Grasping. Grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. By increasing their respective antidotes, one can extinguish grasping at the sense base of the eye; by increasing their respective antidotes, one can extinguish grasping at the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
by increasing their respective antidotes, one can extinguish grasping at the sense bases of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena;
by increasing their respective antidotes, one can even extinguish grasping at the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Unsurpassed Vehicle. By increasing their respective antidotes...
It counteracts [afflictions], up to and including the cessation of the grasping for parinirvāṇa.

It increases those antidotes, can extinguish all phenomena in which Māra dwells, and can cause all wholesome things to grow. For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā possesses immeasurable and great majestic power.
Furthermore, Kauśika, such a bodhisattva causes unwholesome dharmas to cease and wholesome dharmas...
They increase. That is to say, they cause the increase of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, so that there is no diminution.
Why? Because they employ the method of non-apprehension.
They likewise cause the increase of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, so that there is no diminution. Why? Because they employ the method of non-apprehension.
For this reason, Kauśika, this bodhisattva personally practices all dharmas,
teaches others to practice all dharmas, praises all dharmas, and joyfully extols those who practice all dharmas.
Kauśika, when this bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they do so by means of the expedient of non-apprehension for the sake of all sentient beings.
Together they dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They constantly reflect:
"If I do not practice giving, I shall be born into a poor and lowly family; lacking even basic influence, by what means could I mature sentient beings or purify a Buddha-field?
How much less could I attain the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*)? If I do not guard pure ethical discipline, I shall be born among the various evil [states]."
I shall not even attain the body of a lowly human being; how much less could I mature sentient beings or purify a buddha-field?
How much more so could I ever attain the knowledge of all modes?

If I do not cultivate patience, I will be born with impaired faculties and an ugly appearance, lacking the perfect physical form of a bodhisattva, and thus I will be unable to mature sentient beings or purify [the field].
How much less could I attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)? If I were to be indolent and fail to arouse diligence, I would not even be able to attain the supreme path of a bodhisattva;
by what means then could I mature sentient beings or purify a buddha-field? How much less could I attain the knowledge of all modes?
If my mind were distracted and I did not enter meditative concentration (dhyāna), I would not even be able to give rise to the supreme samādhi of a bodhisattva.
"By what means could I mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields? How much less could I attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?
If I were without wisdom and did not study Prajñāpāramitā, I would not even be able to attain the skillful wisdom that transcends the stages of the two vehicles;
how then could I mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields? How much less could I attain the knowledge of all modes? This is the training of a bodhisattva."
Regarding the six pāramitās, one should constantly reflect: "I must not follow the power of stinginess and greed;
if I were to follow that power, my practice of giving would not reach fulfillment, and I would ultimately be unable to achieve the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
I must not follow the power of breaking the precepts; if I were to follow that power, my pure ethical discipline would not reach fulfillment, and I would ultimately be unable..."
I shall accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). I must not follow the power of anger;
if I were to follow that power, my patience would not be perfected, and I would ultimately be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes. I must not follow the power of laziness;
if I were to follow that power, my diligence would not be perfected, and I would ultimately be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.

Wisdom. I should not follow the power of mental distraction; if I were to follow that power, my meditative concentration would not reach fulfillment, and I would ultimately be unable to achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). I should not follow the power of ignorance;
if I were to follow that power, my wisdom (*prajñā*) would not reach fulfillment, and I would ultimately be unable to achieve the knowledge of all modes. This is the bodhisattva...

Without departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), one attains such benefits and virtues in this life and in future lives regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* subdues the bodhisattva, causing them to be free from arrogance, and is able to..."

Dedicating [the merit] toward the wisdom of all-knowledge. World-Honored One, because a bodhisattva relies on a worldly mind to cultivate various wholesome dharmas, and because they lack skillful means, their mind is disturbed by the grasping at "I" and "mine.

What, then, is called the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*)?
It means that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation; without abiding and without change; without defilement and without purity; without increase and without decrease;

There is no nature of sentient beings, up to and including no nature of a knower, no nature of a seer, no nature of form, and no nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

There is no nature of the eye-base, no nature of the bases of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. There is no nature of the base of forms, no nature of the bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena.

A bodhisattva newly training in the Great Vehicle should, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, sever all states of existence.
The path that cuts off conceptual proliferation; having cast off all heavy burdens, destroyed the thorns of the village, and exhausted all fetters of existence;

possessing perfect wisdom and a mind well-liberated; skillfully expounding the essentials of the Dharma—all the merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas and their assemblies of disciples, as well as the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others—all such things are gathered together and praised.
They weigh, manifest, and initiate [the merit], and dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva asked Subhūti: "If a newly trained bodhisattva contemplates all their merits and the roots of goodness they have planted, and having gathered and weighed them, manifests and initiates them—compared to other roots of goodness, are these the most supreme?"
"Excellent. Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness arising from such sympathetic joy, they together dedicate them.
How does this bodhisattva not fall into perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view? Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the merits of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples whom they recollect, does not give rise to the notion of 'merit,' [and likewise] regarding all humans and devas..."
Regarding the roots of goodness they have planted, they do not give rise to the notion of "roots of goodness.

Furthermore, regarding the mind that initiates sympathetic joy and dedicates [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they likewise do not give rise to the notion of "dedicating toward enlightenment.
This sympathetic joy and dedication initiated by these bodhisattvas is free from the perversion of perception, free from the perversion of mind, and free from the perversion of view.
Furthermore, Great Being, if one correctly understands that all phenomena associated with sympathetic joy and dedication are empty of intrinsic nature,
yet even while knowing this, is able to rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— at that time, moreover:
If one correctly understands that there are no phenomena whatsoever that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward any phenomenon, why is this?
Because all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and within emptiness, there are no phenomena of either subject or object for rejoicing or dedication.
Although they know this, they are still able to rejoice and dedicate; thus, these bodhisattvas do not give rise to attachment regarding the mind of rejoicing.
One does not cling even to the roots of virtue and merit that one rejoices in; one does not give rise to clinging toward the mind of dedication;
and one does not cling even to the unsurpassed enlightenment to which one dedicates them. By being without clinging, one does not fall into error.
Fascicle 170 (Continued from the previous fascicle: Subhūti’s Response to Maitreya Bodhisattva) up to Fascicle 172:

Furthermore, Great Being, if a bodhisattva, regarding the various meritorious deeds they perform, correctly knows them as being detached from form, detached from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on, up to correctly knowing them as being detached from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—such is correct knowledge.
One is able to correctly rejoice in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Great Being, if a bodhisattva correctly knows the various meritorious deeds associated with rejoicing as they are being cultivated, and correctly knows that these meritorious deeds associated with rejoicing are devoid of intrinsic nature;
and if one correctly knows the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and correctly knows that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is devoid of intrinsic nature...
He correctly knows all the qualities of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, while remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of those qualities of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He correctly knows the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, while remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
He correctly knows the roots of virtue cultivated by the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, while remaining detached from...

Hearing of the intrinsic nature of the roots of goodness cultivated by pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, they correctly know the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) while remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of the mind of awakening;
they correctly know the mind of dedication while remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of the mind of dedication;

and they correctly know the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening toward which it is dedicated, while remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Correctly...
Knowing that from the perfection of wisdom up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
there is a separation from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— when a bodhisattva practices in this way,
being detached from the intrinsic nature [of phenomena], they are able to correctly rejoice in and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great Being, if a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom by taking signs as the means,
and then rejoices in and dedicates all those roots of merit and virtues toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment while still taking signs,
that is not a virtuous rejoicing or dedication. If, however, one practices the perfection of wisdom without taking signs as the means...
“Maitreya, regarding all those roots of virtue and merits that are free from signs, one rejoices in them and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
this is called ‘skillful rejoicing and dedication. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva asked Subhūti:
‘How can one rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment without grasping at any signs? Subhūti replied:”
It should be understood that within the Prajñāpāramitā studied by Bodhisattvas, there are such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) whereby activities are accomplished without grasping at signs.

Apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, it is impossible to initiate meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Maitreya Bodhisattva...

Sakra said: "Do not speak thus. Why is this? Because within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the merits and roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples are all non-existent and unapprehendable;
likewise, the various meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy are also non-existent and unapprehendable. He then made the resolve...
The mind is dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment, yet it is non-existent because it is ungraspable.

In this regard, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate the merits and roots of goodness of the past Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples as being by nature already extinguished;
they should then dedicate the various meritorious deeds and acts of sympathetic joy they have performed, having generated the resolve for enlightenment.

Unsurpassed Bodhi is by nature already extinguished. If I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding it, and were to use such discrimination to skillfully initiate rejoicing and dedication, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would not permit it. Why is this?

One should not give rise to the notion of attainment, grasping at signs, or conceptual discrimination within that state when rejoicing and dedicating; for to do so is to grasp with the notion of attainment.

If one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication that involves conceptualization, has causes and conditions, involves mental engagement (*manasikāra*), and involves proliferation (*prapañca*), it is not in accordance with the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because it is mixed with poison, it constitutes slandering the Buddha, failing to follow the Buddha’s teaching, and failing to speak in accordance with the Dharma;
one should not practice or train according to what is thus taught.
Furthermore, Great Being, those sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle should perform such sympathetic rejoicing and dedication as follows:
Just as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;

and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—even so, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha does not [fall into these categories].”
They fall into the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. Since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present.
Rejoicing and dedication should also be understood in this way. Why is this? Because those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature;
they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time. Rejoicing and dedication are likewise so. That is to say, O Tathāgatas...
Because the nature of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty; because the nature of the merits of all Buddhas is empty;

because the nature of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and so forth is empty; because the nature of those roots of goodness is empty; because the nature of that which rejoices in them is empty;
because the nature of the phenomena to which they are dedicated is empty; and because the nature of the one who dedicates is empty.

Therefore, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are, they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into any of the three realms, then one is neither past, future, nor present.
This continues until, knowing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as it truly is, one does not fall into the desire [realm].
The realms are the realm of form and the formless realm. If one does not fall within the three realms, then one is neither past, future, nor present.

If one is not of the three times, then it is impossible to use the characteristics of those [realms] as a means, or to use the attainment of something as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this? Because of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Even up to the dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, its intrinsic nature is non-arising. If a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent.
Because one cannot take that non-existent dharma as a basis for rejoicing and dedicating toward that which is non-existent;
if one employs signs as a means, or employs attainment as a means, to rejoice and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment...
Subhūti, such is wrong sympathetic joy and dedication; it is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
It cannot bring all dharmas to fulfillment, nor can one realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through it. Why is this?
Because that which arises from rejoicing and dedication is mixed with various poisons, bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should form this thought:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have realized the roots of virtue and merit as they truly are;
such is the nature of these dharmas, and by relying upon these dharmas, one may generate non-erroneous rejoicing and dedication. This...
He correctly gave rise to sympathetic joy and dedicated [the merit].

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras and celestial kings, each holding various flowers, incense, and divine music, made offerings to the Buddha and said:
"Such a bodhisattva, by means of the signless (*animitta*) as a skillful means, has no..."
To attain this is the skillful means; to be free from attachment is the skillful means; to be free from volitional effort is the skillful means.
One should generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Thus they generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [the merit], not falling into either dualistic or non-dualistic dharmas.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, together with the assembly of Brahmās, raised their voices and said:
"Because these are embraced by such skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated through signs and attainments by those lacking skillful means. Then the Buddha addressed the four...
Regarding the mention of the Mahārājika devas, up to the Akaniṣṭha devas, and so forth:

suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to give rise to the bodhicitta and universally [make offerings] to all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present— from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment,
through their attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, their turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, until their entry into...
From the time after attaining parinirvāṇa in the remainder-body until the extinction of the Dharma, during that interval, all the roots of goodness practiced—
collecting and weighing them, employing the means of signs, the means of apprehension, the means of attachment,
and the means of duality and non-duality— and dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is...

"Sons of good family, those who set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening universally collect and weigh all the roots of goodness practiced by all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present—
from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until the extinction of the Dharma—
by means of the signless as a skillful method, the non-apprehensible as a skillful method, and the undefiled."
Adherence is the skillful means; non-duality and non-distinction are the skillful means.

To rejoice in and dedicate [merit] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—such a son of good family is the most eminent and supreme; he is also the most eminent and supreme among the aforementioned sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "To what extent is this rejoicing and dedication said to be the most eminent and supreme? The Buddha said: "That son of good..."

Sons of noble family, they universally regard all the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present—neither grasping nor rejecting them, neither being conceited nor disparaging them;
they do not perceive them as something attained, nor as something unattained.

Furthermore, they know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, without going or coming, and without aggregation or dispersion. They are without...
"Entering without emerging, one should form this thought: 'Just as the dharmas of the past, future, and present— suchness, the dharma-realm,

the nature of phenomena, the non-falsehood of phenomena, the immutability of phenomena, the equality of phenomena, the nature free from arising, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena,
the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm— are so, I too likewise rejoice and dedicate [the merit] in this way,' Subhūti."
I declare that the rejoicing and dedication undertaken by these bodhisattvas is the most supreme and excellent.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle should form this thought: "As is liberation, so too is form."
As with liberation, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Even as with liberation, so it is with all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) of the Buddha’s disciples and Pratyekabuddhas.
As with liberation, so it is with all sentient beings. As with liberation, so it is with the nature of all phenomena. As with liberation, so it is with all [conformable]...

Rejoicing and dedication are also like this. Just as the nature of all phenomena is without bondage and without liberation, without defilement and without purity, without arising and without ceasing, without birth and without extinction, and without grasping and without relinquishing, I now rejoice in these roots of merit and virtue and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such rejoicing is neither a subject that rejoices nor an object that is rejoiced in.
Because of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one dedicates in this way: it is neither that which can dedicate nor that which is dedicated.
This sympathetic joy and dedication thus aroused are neither transformed nor ceased, for they are without arising or ceasing.
If one accomplishes such sympathetic joy and dedication, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (The Chapter on Sympathetic Joy and Dedication is concluded.)
From the sixth leaf of fascicle 172 (Praise of the Prajñāpāramitā Chapter) to the seventh leaf of fascicle 181, Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One, is that which has been thus spoken not indeed the *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha said:
That which has been thus described is indeed the Prajñāpāramitā. Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this Prajñāpāramitā is able to provide illumination because it is ultimately pure;
it is free from attachment because no worldly dharmas can defile it; it is far removed from all cataracts of the triple world and is able to eliminate afflictions."
Because it dispels the darkness of all views; because it is the most supreme among all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);

because it can provide security by permanently severing all terrors, afflictions, and calamities; because it can bestow light by gathering in sentient beings and enabling them to attain the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*);
because it can demonstrate the Middle Way, causing those who have lost their way to depart from the two extremes; and because it can inspire...
It gives birth to the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), because it eternally severs all latent tendencies of the afflictions along with their habitual traces.
It is the mother of all Bodhisattvas, because all Buddha-dharmas arise from it. It is neither born nor extinguished, because its own-characteristic is empty.

It remains far removed from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), because it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. It can act as a refuge, because it bestows the jewels of all dharmas. It can bring about the ten [powers] of a Buddha...

It is power, because it cannot be overcome or subdued. It is able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, because it is far removed from all phenomena and is without turning back.
It is able to demonstrate that all phenomena possess no inverted nature, because it clearly reveals the emptiness of the self-nature of non-nature.
World-Honored One, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, how should sentient beings of the three vehicles speak?
"In what manner should they abide? The Buddha said, "These sentient beings should abide in this *prajñāpāramitā* as they would abide in the Buddha.
They should offer worship, pay homage, and contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* just as they would offer worship, pay homage, and contemplate the Blessed One, the Buddha.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have [arisen] from *prajñāpāramitā*."
Because the *pāramitās* have appeared. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, secretly thought to himself:
"For what reason does Śāriputra now ask about this matter? Then Śāriputra, knowing his thoughts, addressed him, saying: "Kauśika," he said.

Because the bodhisattva is embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they gather together, weigh, rejoice in, and dedicate all meritorious virtues and roots of goodness. For this reason, they inquire about this matter.
Kauśika, the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration—these births...

O blind multitude, if there were no guide with the pure eye of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you would be unable even to set out upon the correct path of a bodhisattva, much less be able to enter the city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

It is because they are embraced by this *prajñā* that giving and all other perfections attain the name of "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*). Why is this? Because one abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Only then can one fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration;
it is not by abiding in the other five that one can accomplish this matter. Therefore, among the previous five, wisdom is the most supreme.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "How does one bring forth the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said, "Not for the sake of..."
One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth form;
one should not bring forth the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Śāriputra, this is because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without disintegration, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature.
A bodhisattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
nor, up to and including, for the sake of producing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
They should practice the perfection of wisdom [without such motives].
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, "With what phenomena does such an elicitation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) coincide?
The Buddha said, "Such an elicitation of the perfection of wisdom does not coincide with any phenomena whatsoever."
Because it does not conjoin, it is named Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because such Prajñāpāramitā does not apprehend any phenomenon.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "Does such Prajñāpāramitā not conjoin with the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said: "It also does not conjoin with the knowledge of all modes."
"Wisdom. Because it cannot be apprehended therein, Blessed One, how is it that the perfection of wisdom neither joins with nor attains anything regarding all-knowledge?

Kausika, it is not the case that the perfection of wisdom joins with or attains anything regarding all-knowledge, its wisdom, its names, its characteristics, or its activities. "Blessed One, how is it that the perfection of..."

If the *pāramitās* are both conjoined with and attained to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), then, Kauśika, the *prajñāpāramitā* is, with respect to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), like names and signs:
it is without reception, without grasping, without abiding, and without cessation.
Without grasping and without relinquishing; thus, while it is attained through union, there is no attainment through union.

Regarding all phenomena, just as with their names and characteristics, there is neither receiving nor taking up, neither abiding nor ceasing, and neither grasping nor relinquishing; thus, while it is attained through union, there is no attainment through union.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha: "This Prajñāpāramitā is for the sake of all..."

The Dharma is without activity and without cessation; it is without arising and without extinction; it is without formation and without disintegration; it is without attainment and without relinquishment.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it manifests before one. Although there is union and attainment, yet there is no union and no attainment.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying, "When a bodhisattva has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, what dharmas does he not believe in?

The Buddha said, "When a bodhisattva has faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not believe in form (*rūpa*), nor does he believe in feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is because when he contemplates form and contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they are found to be unobtainable. This continues up until his faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*..."
At the time of the *pāramitās*, one does not believe in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, because one perceives that the unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is unattainable.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, with what intention do you say that the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva is called the ‘Great *Pāramitā*’?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, regarding all phenomena, a bodhisattva does not conceive of them as great, nor as small;
does not conceive of them as gathering, nor as dispersing; does not conceive of them as finite, nor as infinite; does not conceive of them as broad...”
It is not narrow; it is neither powerful nor powerless. Therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā* is called the "Great *Pāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the six *pāramitās*, gives rise to such a conception as this:
"This *prajñāpāramitā* [is] with respect to all phenomena..."

"To make it great, not small; even to the point of making it powerful, not powerless"—if a bodhisattva gives rise to such conceptions, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Furthermore, Blessed One, if a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, without relying on the six perfections, gives rise to such a conception as "this is the perfection of wisdom," [they are not practicing it].

Regarding all phenomena, to conceive of them as large or small, as gathered or dispersed, as finite or infinite, as broad or narrow, as powerful or powerless—by giving rise to such conceptions, this bodhisattva is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this, World-Honored One? If a bodhisattva gives rise to such conceptions, then this is [not] the perfection of wisdom.
Pāramitā. Regarding all phenomena, whether one conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

even if one conceives of them as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as having power or lacking power—all such cases are not the natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the Prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One, such a bodhisattva is said to have "great attainment" (*upalambha*), and is not practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Pāramitā. Why is this? Because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the perception of something to be attained.
For what reason? World-Honored One, because sentient beings are unarisen, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also unarisen.
Because sentient beings are unceasing, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also unceasing. Sentient beings...
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* also lacks intrinsic nature.
Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* also does not exist.
Because sentient beings are empty, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also empty. Because sentient beings are signless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā*...

Because sentient beings are signless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also signless. Because sentient beings are wishless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also wishless.
Because sentient beings are detached, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also detached.
Because sentient beings are quiescent, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also quiescent. Because sentient beings are unapprehendable, one should know...
The *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise unapprehendable. Because sentient beings are inconceivable, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Because sentient beings lack cognitive awareness, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* also lacks cognitive awareness.
Because the power of sentient beings is not established, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā*...
The pāramitās are likewise not established. It is with this intention that I say:
the Prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva is called the "Great Pāramitā," because even the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is unarisen, and thus the Prajñāpāramitā is also unarisen;
and because the power of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not established.
The power of the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise not established. This is called the "Great *Pāramitā*" (End of the "Praise of *Prajñā*" Chapter).
Fascicle 181-8, Leaf [Number] (The "Slandering of *Prajñā*" Chapter).
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhagavān, from where did those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas pass away to be reborn here, who are able to believe and resolve upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
How long has it been since they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
And how many Tathāgatas have they previously approached, made offerings to, and served while cultivating all dharmas?"
"For how long? How does one believe and resolve upon such profound meaning and intent of this *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said, "They have passed away from the assemblies of countless, immeasurable, and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Having come to this world, they have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they have already passed through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, and have already attended upon countless, immeasurable, and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

From their first production of the thought of enlightenment, they have constantly and diligently practiced the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

...Maitreya. Having already passed through hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta kalpas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the expedient of signlessness, non-duality, and non-apprehension, is able to correctly believe in and understand the profound meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep."
"Is there anyone who can hear or see? The Buddha said, "You are Prajñāpāramitā; in reality, there is no one who can hear or see.
Such Prajñāpāramitā is neither that which is heard nor that which is seen. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are without hearing and without seeing, for all dharmas are insentient. Subhūti then addressed [the Buddha] again:
The Buddha said, "How long must Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accumulate their practice before they are able to study and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, regarding this matter, one should explain it by making distinctions.

There are Bodhisattvas who, from the very first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], are able to study and cultivate the six *pāramitās*. These Bodhisattvas possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."

Regarding all phenomena, there is neither increase nor decrease. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from practices associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Furthermore, they are never apart from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. From one Buddha...
He proceeds to a single buddha-field and, with various sublime offerings, makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, he is able to plant many roots of goodness in the presence of those Tathāgatas. Wherever this bodhisattva takes birth, he does not fall into the womb of a mother’s belly;
his mind never dwells in association with afflictions, nor does he ever give rise to the [thoughts of] the two vehicles.

Their minds are never separated from sublime supernormal powers. From one buddha-field they proceed to another buddha-field, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields, and are able to correctly practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti, there are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they have seen many buddhas and have also practiced extensively, [do not yet possess these qualities].

Because they employ the attainment of something as a means for practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they are unable to study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds find no pleasure;
they abandon the assembly and depart. Such sons and daughters of good family, in previous lives...
It is said that they have already abandoned [the Dharma] in the past; now, upon hearing this teaching, by the power of their former habits, they abandon it once again.
Their body, speech, and mind are all in disharmony. Through such actions, they increase the karmic offenses of ignorance and evil wisdom.
Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately slander, obstruct, and discard it; thus, they commit the offense of slandering and obstructing.
Having abandoned the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they immediately commit and increase karma that brings about the deprivation of the true Dharma.
They fall into the great hells, where for many years they undergo various torments and intense, great suffering.
Because their transgression is so heavy, within this world they pass from one great hell to another great hell.
Until the fires, waters, and winds of the kalpas have yet arisen, they undergo various agonies and fierce, intense sufferings;
even when the fires, waters, and winds of this world's kalpa arise, because their karma of deprivation of the Dharma is not yet exhausted.
After death, they are reborn in another world system, within a great hell similar to this one, where they remain for many years.
Even when the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in that other world, because their karma of deprivation of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they do not pass away.
Having died, they are reborn in other worlds; thus they wander through all ten directions for incalculable eons.
When the force of their karmic offenses from depriving others of the Dharma has slightly diminished, they emerge from hell and fall into the realm of animals, remaining there for many years.
They undergo all manner of suffering, including being mangled, harmed, and coerced;
because their karma has not yet been exhausted, they pass from one perilous and evil place to another within this world until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen.
They continue to suffer all such harms and oppressions until the time when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, at which point the residual force of their karma of deprivation remains.
It is not yet exhausted. After death, they are reborn in other world-systems among the same class of beings in the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).
They pass many years in this manner, traversing throughout the animal realms of the ten directions and undergoing manifold sufferings for incalculable eons.
When the power of their karma—the sin of being destitute of the Dharma—gradually diminishes, they escape birth in the animal realm and fall instead into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Fully...
They experience the sufferings of emaciation, hunger, thirst, and so forth;

because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another within this world-system until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen. They undergo all such sufferings of emaciation, hunger, thirst, and the like.
When this world-system is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of the karma that caused their deprivation of the Dharma remains.
When their [karmic] exhaustion is complete and they have died, they are reborn in another world within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) of a similar kind.

They pass many years, traversing the ten directions for incalculable eons. When the residual force of their karma of withholding the Dharma is finally spent, although they may obtain human birth, they dwell in a lowly station;
or the body they receive has impaired faculties, and they are impoverished, withered, dull-witted, and ignorant.

Consciousness: whatever they do, people treat them with contempt; they do not hear the name of the Buddha, the name of the Dharma, the name of the Saṅgha, the name of Bodhisattvas, or the name of Pratyekabuddhas.
Or else they are born in a world of profound darkness where there is no day or night and they behold no light.
Because the karma of their deprivation of the Dharma has been created, increased, and become extremely deep and heavy, they experience such undesirable and wretched results.
It fulfills the fruit of suffering and is a karma that depletes the True Dharma; it is so extremely coarse and heavy that it cannot be compared even to the five deeds of immediate retribution.
At that time, Subhūti said to the Buddha: "Those who slander the True Dharma shall endure great suffering for a long time in future ages. It should...
Guard well the actions of body, speech, and mind. Do not slander or destroy the True Dharma, thereby falling into the three evil realms to undergo suffering for a long time.
For a vast duration, you shall not see the Buddhas, nor hear the True Dharma, nor encounter the Sangha, and you shall not be born in a land where a Buddha resides.
Even if you are born into the human realm, you will be lowly, impoverished, ugly, dull-witted, and deficient in limbs.

"His faculties are incomplete, and whatever he says, people do not believe or accept. World-Honored One, is it not because of practicing and increasing the karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma that one creates and increases such karma?

To disparage the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is to slander the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas;
it is to slander the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
it is to slander the Buddha, to slander the Dharma, and to slander the Saṅgha; it is to slander right view in the world, and it is to slander the [lay] precepts.

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—even up to and including all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and gateways of samādhis—they shall slander them.

By slandering and disparaging this mass of merit, they will thereby take upon themselves a mass of sins that is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless; they will thereby take upon themselves the great hells and the animal realm.
"In the realm of ghosts and among the human destinies, there is an incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless mass of suffering.

Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying, "By how many causes and conditions do they thus slander and revile [this teaching]? The Buddha said, "By four causes and conditions: first, being instigated and deluded by various evil māras;

They are possessed by the five aggregates and are under the influence of evil associates. Fourth, they harbor much malice, delight in practicing unwholesome dharmas, and take pleasure in self-exaltation while disparaging others.
Due to these four causes and conditions, those who are deluded slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
