Within suchness, even the mind and mental factors are unapprehendable; how much less so a mind possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, or a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion?

Furthermore, Subhūti, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know, as they truly are, that the expansive minds of all classes of sentient beings are neither expansive nor narrow.
There is no increase and no decrease; there is no going and no coming. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is non-existent.

Who could be expansive or narrow? Who could increase or decrease? Who could go or come? One knows, as it truly is, that the great mind possessed by all classes of sentient beings neither goes nor comes;
it is without arising and without cessation; it is without abiding and without change; it is without greatness and without smallness. Why is this? Because...
Therefore, because the intrinsic nature of the mind is non-existent, it neither goes nor comes; it is neither born nor extinguished;

it neither abides nor changes; it is neither great nor small. One knows, as they truly are, that all the immeasurable minds of sentient beings neither abide nor do not abide, neither go nor do not go.
Why is this? Because the nature of immeasurable minds is untainted and without support. How [could they otherwise be]?
One may say that there is abiding and non-abiding, and going and non-going.

One knows, as it truly is, that all classes of sentient beings possess minds that are invisible and non-obstructive, and that these are entirely devoid of mental characteristics. Why is this? Because all minds are empty of their own intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*).
One knows, as it truly is, that all classes of sentient beings possess minds that are formless and invisible; even the five eyes of the Buddhas do not perceive them.
One is able to see. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of all minds is empty.
One knows, as they truly are, the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion, of the minds and mental factors of all classes of sentient beings.

That is to say, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, know, as they truly are, the arising, ceasing, contraction, and expansion of the minds and mental factors—whether based on form, or based on feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness—and their grasping.
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion. "The self and the world are impermanent;
this alone is the truth, all else is delusion. "The self and the world are both eternal and impermanent;
this alone is the truth, all else is delusion. "The self and the world are neither eternal nor impermanent; this alone is the truth."

All others are deluded and false: they cling to the view that the self and the world are finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite, asserting that this alone is the truth and reality while all else is delusion and falsehood.

They cling to the view that the life-principle is identical to the body, or that the life-principle is distinct from the body, asserting that this alone is the truth and reality while all else is delusion and falsehood.
They cling to the view that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata...
"It does not exist after death. "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. This alone is the truth; all else is delusion and falsehood.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the suchness of all phenomena is the very suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas...
Suchness. That is the suchness of all sentient beings. Subhūti, whether it be the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
the suchness of all sentient beings; or the suchness of all phenomena—these are non-dual and without distinction; they are a single suchness.
Because this suchness is without differentiation, it is indestructible, inexhaustible, and cannot be conceptually differentiated. Well said.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, have realized the ultimate suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena and thereby attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For this reason, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Buddhas; she is the Mother of all Buddhas and can reveal the world to all Buddhas.
"Regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*)," Subhūti said to the Buddha, "who is able to believe in and understand the profound *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena?
The Buddha said, "Because *tathatā* is inexhaustible, it is therefore profound; for because all phenomena are inexhaustible, *tathatā* is inexhaustible."

Because the Tathāgata has realized suchness, he has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for the sake of all sentient beings, he reveals the characteristics of the suchness of all differentiated phenomena;
for this reason, he is called the "Speaker of Truth."
The Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "The profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses immeasurable characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which neither the world, nor gods, humans, or asuras can destroy.
Why is this? Because gods, humans, and asuras are themselves also characterized by these marks.
One should know that characteristics cannot destroy characteristics, and characteristics cannot fully comprehend characteristics."
All marks. All marks cannot destroy the markless; all marks cannot cognize all marks. All marks cannot destroy the markless;
all marks cannot cognize the markless. The markless cannot destroy all marks;
the markless cannot cognize all marks. The markless cannot destroy the markless. The markless...
One cannot fully comprehend signlessness. Why is this? Whether it be a sign, the absence of a sign, or both sign and absence of sign, all are non-existent.
This is because that which destroys and that which knows, the object destroyed and the object known, as well as the destroyer and the knower, are all unapprehendable.
O Son of Heaven, you should know that all signs are not produced by any phenomena; they have no attachments and are inexpressible. You should know this.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from all signs (*nimitta*). One should not ask what its signs are.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, abide in such signs;

they analyze and reveal the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for the sake of all sentient beings, they gather the signs of all phenomena and skillfully reveal them. The World-Honored One addressed the devas:

The Son said: "The Tathāgata has awakened to all phenomena as being without marks (*animitta*) exactly as they are. That which is characterized by transformation and resistance is the mark of form (*rūpa*);
the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without marks. That which is characterized by experiencing is the mark of sensation (*vedanā*);

the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without marks. That which is characterized by grasping images is the mark of perception (*saṃjñā*); the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without marks. That which is characterized by volitional activity is the mark of formations (*saṃskāra*)."

The Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are: he has realized that the characteristic of form is signless. He has realized that the characteristic of consciousness is the discernment of objects;

the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: he has realized it to be signless. The characteristic of the aggregates is a mass of suffering and affliction; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: he has realized it to be signless. The characteristic of the sense bases is the gateway for growth;
the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: he has realized it to be signless. The characteristic of the elements is manifold harm; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is...

It is signless (*animitta*). That which arises through combination is the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is, as being signless.

That which is capable of giving and relinquishing is the characteristic of generosity (*dāna*); the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is, as being signless. That which is free from feverish affliction is the characteristic of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, that this is signless (*animitta*). Absence of anger and resentment is the mark of patience (*kṣānti*);
the Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, that this is signless. Inconquerability is the mark of diligence (*vīrya*); the Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, that this is signless.

The gathering and maintaining of the mind is the mark of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, that this is signless. Absence of obstruction is the mark of wisdom (*prajñā*); the Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, that this is signless.
The Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are as being signless (*animitta*). That which is non-existent is the characteristic of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and so forth;

the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is as being signless. That which is non-perverted is the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth; the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is as being signless.

Non-falsity is the characteristic of the four noble truths; the Tathāgata has realized them as they truly are to be signless. Absence of agitation and affliction is the characteristic of the four dhyānas;
the Tathāgata has realized them as they truly are to be signless. Absence of limitation and obstruction is the characteristic of the four immeasurables.
The Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are: as signless. That which is free from clamor and confusion is the characteristic of the four formless absorptions;

the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: as signless. That which is free from bondage is the characteristic of the eight liberations; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: as signless.
That which is capable of subduing is the characteristic of the eight bases of mastery; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: as signless. It is non-distraction.
These are the characteristics of the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*); the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are as being signless (*animitta*).

Boundlessness is the characteristic of the ten spheres of totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*); the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is as being signless. That which is capable of deliverance is the characteristic of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*);
the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is as being signless. Utmost seclusion is the characteristic of the gateway of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*); the Tathāgata...
The Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is: as signless (*animitta*). That which is most tranquil is the characteristic of the signless door of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*);
the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is: as signless. Loathing all sufferings is the characteristic of the wishless door of liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*);

the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is: as signless. Proceeding toward great awakening is the characteristic of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; the Tathāgata has awakened to this as it truly is: as signless.
The ability to contemplate and illuminate is the characteristic of the five eyes; the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is, as being without marks (*animitta*).

Unobstructedness is the characteristic of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is, as being without marks. Thorough determination is the characteristic of the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*); the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is, as being without marks.
Thorough establishment is the characteristic of the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*); the Tathāgata [awakens to this as it truly is, as being without marks].
Awakening is signless. Non-interruption is the characteristic of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is as being signless.

The uprooting of sorrow and suffering is the characteristic of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is as being signless. Rejoicing in virtuous matters is the characteristic of great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*);
the Tathāgata awakens to this as it truly is as being signless. Abandoning clamor and distraction is the characteristic of great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*); the Tathāgata...
Awakening to reality as it is as being signless is the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that cannot be taken away;

the Tathāgata awakens to this as being signless according to reality. Right mindfulness is the characteristic of the quality of non-forgetfulness; the Tathāgata awakens to this as being signless according to reality.
Absence of grasping is the characteristic of the state of constant equanimity; the Tathāgata awakens to this as being signless according to reality. Manifesting...

The characteristic of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the characteristic of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). The Tathāgata realizes it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) exactly as it is. The characteristic of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) is the characteristic of thorough penetration.

The Tathāgata realizes it as being without characteristics exactly as it is. The characteristic of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the characteristic of manifesting distinct realization.
The Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are: as being without marks (*animitta*). He has universally grasped and maintained the marks of all *dhāraṇī* gates;

the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are: as being without marks. He has universally received and sustained the marks of all *samādhi* gates; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are: as being without marks.
Skillfully receiving the teaching is the mark of the fruit of the *śrāvaka*; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is: as being without marks.
It is signless (*animitta*). That which is self-awakened is the sign of the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is, as signless.
That which leads to the great fruit is the sign of the practice of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is, as signless.

That which is without equal is the characteristic of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. The Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics just as it truly is.
Regarding the characteristics of all such phenomena, he is able to realize them all as being without characteristics just as they truly are.
For this reason, I say that the Buddhas have attained unimpeded wisdom, and there is none who is their equal.

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have, without exception, relied upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize perfect awakening regarding all phenomena, whether characterized by signs or signless.
There is no real activity, because there is no agent; there is nothing accomplished, because no substantial form can be apprehended."
Therefore, the Tathāgata is able to manifest the realization of the equality of phenomena with and without marks; yet all these are without activity and nothing is accomplished therein.
To offer worship, respect, honor, and praise at all times, and to embrace and protect them without interruption, is therefore called truly knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “In what way is it that by not seeing all phenomena, one is said to demonstrate the characteristics of all phenomena?

The Buddha replied, “Because consciousness does not arise by taking any phenomenon as its object, this is called ‘not seeing all phenomena’ and is thus termed ‘demonstrating the characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to act for all...”

The Buddha reveals that the world is empty, causing all those in the world to experience the emptiness of the world, perceive the emptiness of the world, contemplate the emptiness of the world, and realize the emptiness of the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal to all Buddhas the characteristic of the emptiness of the world;
it can reveal to all Buddhas the inconceivable characteristic of the world; it can reveal to all Buddhas...
The world is characterized by detachment. It can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s tranquility;
it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s ultimate emptiness; it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s emptiness of intrinsic nature;

it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s emptiness of self-nature; it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s emptiness of both non-existence and self-nature. It can demonstrate to all Buddhas...
The world is purely characterized by emptiness. It can demonstrate to all Buddhas that the world is purely characterized by signlessness and wishlessness.
Subhūti, by such a principle, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate the true reality of the world to all Buddhas; it is called the Mother of all Buddhas.
(The Chapter on the Mother of the Buddhas concludes.)
From leaf eleven of fascicle three hundred and eight (The Chapter on the Inconceivable, etc. to leaf seven of fascicle three hundred and ten, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, is it only the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of the self-arisen Dharma, and the nature of the knowledge of all-knowledge belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that are inconceivable, immeasurable, and without..."

"Is it only the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of the self-arisen dharma, and the nature of the knowledge of all-knowledge belonging to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, that is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled?

Or are all other dharmas also inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled? The Buddha said: "It is not only the aforementioned natures of the Tathāgatas that are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled; all dharmas as well are inconceivable."
It can be measured; it is immeasurable; it is unequaled. Subhūti, within the true *dharmatā* of all phenomena, both mind and mental factors are entirely unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, all phenomena cannot be designated, they are inconceivable, they are immeasurable, they are without number, and they are of an unequaled nature.
Subhūti, this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
It is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all phenomena cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, calculable, equal, or unequal.
Subhūti, can all phenomena be apprehended within that which lacks intrinsic nature? “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is thus, it is thus.”
It is so. For this reason, all phenomena (*dharma*) are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

Because all phenomena are inconceivable, up to being unequaled, all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the self-existent Dharma, and the knowledge of all-knowledge—are likewise.
The Dharma is likewise inconceivable, even unto the Peerless (the end of the "Inconceivable Chapter").

At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The patience accomplished by one who endures, delights in, contemplates, weighs, and examines this *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the wisdom and abandonment of those [others] immeasurably and boundlessly. Why is this?

Because all the wisdom and abandonment of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) are already the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by the Bodhisattva."

Because it is a small portion of the patience [of the bodhisattva], all the knowledge and abandonment belonging to those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin), the eighth person, the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha,
are all already attained as the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) by virtue of being a small portion of the bodhisattva’s patience.
(The Chapter on Accomplishing Tasks ends.)

"Having heard the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one develops deep faith and understanding, and is further able to copy, read, recite, receive, uphold, contemplate, and practice it.
From where did such a bodhisattva pass away before coming to be born in this world? The Buddha said: "Subhūti," [he continued].
There are individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard all dharmas in previous lives, did not inquire about their profound meaning and intent.
Now born among humans, when they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds become confused and bewildered;
they waver, feel timid and weak, or even give rise to erroneous interpretations. There are such individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle.
Rāhu, although in previous lives he had heard the *prajñāpāramitā* and had even inquired about its profound meaning,
he was unable to practice in accordance with it for even one day, two days, or three, four, or five days. Now that he has been born among humans,
even if he were to hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught for one day, up to five...
Day by day, their minds become firm and steadfast, such that nothing can destroy them. Were they to depart from what they have heard, they would immediately fall away and lose it.
Why is this? Because although in previous lives they had inquired about the profound meaning and intent, they did not practice in accordance with those teachings.

Therefore, in this present life, if they encounter virtuous friends who earnestly exhort and encourage them, they will delight in hearing and receiving the Dharma; yet if they lack such virtuous friends, or...
At times they delight in hearing [the Dharma], and at other times they do not; at times they are firm, and at other times they fall away.
Their minds are fickle and unstable, advancing and retreating without constancy, like cotton wool drifting with the wind.

It should be known that such a person who has set out in the Mahāyāna has not long practiced it, has not yet extensively approached spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and has never yet made offerings to the Buddhas.
O Bhagavān, those who have never upheld, recited, copied, contemplated, or expounded the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, Subhūti,
you should know that such individuals have never practiced or studied the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, or *dāna* pāramitās,
nor have they ever practiced or studied up to and including the [perfection of] non-arising.

[They do not lead others] to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, sons of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle are unable, by means of the profound perfection of wisdom, to gather other sentient beings [into it], up to and including unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, being unable to practice in accordance with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they will, by reason of these causes and conditions, fall either to the level of a *śrāvaka* or the level of a *pratyekabuddha*, and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is like one who has set out upon the great ocean; if the ship they are riding is wrecked, it is certain that they will drown. However, if they can grasp a piece of wood...
Using vessels, life-preserving bags, and planks as their support, you should know that such persons will never perish;

they shall reach the safe shore beyond the great ocean. Subhūti, if these sons of good family can write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, taking it as their support, and furthermore can reflect...
They cultivate only the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, up to and including the cultivation of the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. Taking these as their reliance, they never midway fall back into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha,
but will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— just like a person who wishes to cross a treacherous and desolate wilderness.
...the equipment and requisites for the provisions; they will certainly reach the land of peace and happiness.

Thus, Subhūti, if these sons of good family do not embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor embrace skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will fall into the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas and will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). If, however, they can embrace [them]...

Having received this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are also able to embrace skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and do not fall into the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (End of the "Chapter on Various Similes")
From the tenth leaf of Volume Three Hundred Thirteen (Chapter on True Spiritual Friends) to the fifteenth leaf of Volume Three Hundred Sixteen, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva who is a beginner train in the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity? The Buddha said:
"One should form this thought: 'The six perfections that I cultivate shall be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings.'"
Together with all sentient beings, you should dedicate [this merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
You should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of any phenomena. Why is this?
Because if one does not grasp at any phenomena, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. You must not give rise to craving for any phenomena. Why? Because all...
"Because the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty.

Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying, "A bodhisattva mahāsattva performs a difficult task, in that they seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment while all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. Although a bodhisattva..."
Knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like reflections, like shadows, like mirages, like magical transformations,
and like cities of the Gandharvas— all being empty of intrinsic nature— they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of attaining benefit for the world,
for the sake of bringing about the welfare of the world, and for the sake of bringing about peace for the world.
Because of their joy; because they wish to rescue and deliver all the world; because they wish to act as a refuge for the world;
because they wish to act as a dwelling for the world; because they wish to act as the ultimate path for the world;
because they wish to act as an island for the world; because they wish to act as light for the world; because they wish to act as a blazing torch for the world. For...
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as guides for the world, to act as generals for the world, and to act as destinations for the world.
"Subhūti, all phenomena are entirely non-composite. That which is non-composite is not interconnected;
that which is not interconnected is unarisen; that which is unarisen is unceasing; and that which is unceasing is non-composite.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to teach all phenomena to sentient beings, they should do so by means of such characteristics of non-composition, setting out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Bodhi (the dwelling), Subhūti, is the ultimate nature of all phenomena; yet it is not [itself] all phenomena. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the characteristic of all phenomena is the same as the characteristic of the ultimate, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifest with regard to all phenomena?"
“...the Perfectly Awakened One. Why is this? World-Honored One, within the ultimate nature of all phenomena, there is no such discrimination as to say, ‘This is all phenomena.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said.
Within the ultimate nature of all phenomena, there is no such discrimination as to say, ‘This is all phenomena. This is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
This is a difficult task: although one contemplates that all phenomena possess the mark of quiescence, the mind does not sink into despondency. One forms this thought:
"Having attained manifest and equal awakening to these phenomena, I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (the ultimate path)."
Subhūti, it is like the great ocean: where the waters recede on all sides and a high, prominent land rises up, capable of being inhabited, it is called an island.
All phenomena are severed at their prior and posterior limits; because they are severed at these prior and posterior limits, all phenomena are severed.
All these phenomena are severed at their prior and subsequent limits;

they are quiescent, they are subtle and wondrous, and they are suchness—namely, emptiness, non-apprehension, the cutting off of the path, the exhaustion of craving, the remainderless, the departure from defilement, eternal cessation, and nirvāṇa (the island).
Subhūti, all phenomena have space as their destination. For the sake of all sentient beings, one proclaims and reveals that all phenomena neither go nor do not go.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is emptiness, and within emptiness there is neither going nor not going.
Why is that? Because all phenomena take emptiness as their destination; they do not [abide] in that destination.
One may transcend it. Why? Because within emptiness, neither "going" nor "not going" can be apprehended.
All phenomena take as their path that which is signless, wishless, unarisen, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified.
One cannot transcend that path. Why? Because within that which is signless and wishless, up to unstained and unpurified, [there is no such thing].
Because neither going nor not going can be apprehended. All dharmas have non-existence as their destination;
one cannot transcend that destination. Why? Because within non-existence, neither going nor not going can be apprehended.
All dharmas have illusion as their destination, they have dreams as their destination, and they likewise have the city of the gandharvas as their destination.

It is their destination. They cannot transcend that destination. Why? Because within a magical illusion, a dream, or even a city of Gandharvas, neither a destination nor a non-destination can be found. All phenomena have the immeasurable and boundless as their destination.
They cannot transcend that destination. Why? Because within the immeasurable and boundless, neither a destination nor a non-destination [can be found].
Because a destination cannot be apprehended, all phenomena have as their destination neither giving nor taking; neither raising nor lowering; neither going nor coming;
neither increasing nor decreasing; neither entering nor exiting; neither accumulating nor dispersing; and neither uniting nor separating. This is their destination.
One cannot transcend that destination. Why? Because within non-giving and non-taking, up to and including non-union and non-separation, neither a destination nor a non-destination can be apprehended.
All phenomena take as their destination the self, the sentient being, the life-force, up to and including the knower and the viewer. One cannot transcend that destination. Why? Because the self...
Sentient beings, life-principles, and even knowers or seers are ultimately non-existent; how much less can there be any attainment of going or not-going?
All phenomena have permanence as their destination, bliss as their destination, self as their destination, and purity as their destination.
One cannot transcend these destinations. Why is this? Because even permanence, up to and including purity, are ultimately...
There is nothing whatsoever that exists; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "non-going"?

All phenomena have impermanence as their destination, suffering as their destination, selflessness as their destination, and impurity as their destination. One cannot transcend these destinations. Why is this?
Because from impermanence up to impurity, these do not ultimately exist at all; how much less could there be any going or non-going?
A destination can be apprehended. All phenomena have the object of greed as their destination, the object of hatred as their destination, and the object of delusion as their destination.
One cannot transcend those destinations. Why is this? Since the objects of greed, hatred, and delusion ultimately do not exist at all, how could a destination or a non-destination be apprehended?
All phenomena have the activity of views as their [destination].
Gati. One cannot transcend that gati. Why? Because even the activity performed is ultimately non-existent; how much less can there be a gati or a non-gati to be found?

All dharmas take True Suchness as their gati, the Dharma-realm as their gati, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as their gati, the non-falsehood of nature as their gati, the non-alteration of nature as their gati, and equality as their gati.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the destination; the nature of arising is the destination; the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) is the destination; the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) is the destination;

the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the destination; the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) is the destination; and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) is the destination. One cannot transcend these destinations. Why is this?
Because within true suchness (*tathatā*), and even within the inconceivable realm, neither "destination" nor "non-destination" can ultimately be apprehended.
Therefore, all dharmas take non-movement as their destination. One cannot transcend that destination. Why?
Because within non-movement, neither "destination" nor "non-destination" can ultimately be apprehended. All dharmas take form as their destination;
they take feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as their destination; and so on, up to taking all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as their destination. Regarding those...

There is no going forth that can be transcended. Why is this? Because from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these are ultimately non-apprehendable;
how much more so, then, is there any going forth or non-going forth?

Thus, Subhūti, it is for the sake of providing a destination for the world that a bodhisattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (The "Chapter on the True Spiritual Friend" concludes.)
Fascicle 316, Leaf 16 (Chapter on Approaching Wisdom) through Fascicle 318.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Who will be able to give rise to faith and understanding in such a profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said: "It is those bodhisattvas who have long since set their minds upon and sought after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Through diligent practice, having made offerings to many Buddhas, having generated great vows, and because their roots of goodness have matured and they have been sustained by virtuous friends, they are able to give rise to faith and understanding in this Prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What is the nature, what are the characteristics, what are the marks, and what is the appearance of those who give rise to faith and understanding? The Buddha said: "It is the subduing of greed and hatred."

Its nature is the nature of delusion. Its characteristic is the state of being free from the marks of greed, hatred, and delusion. Its aspect is the state of being free from the manifestations of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Its appearance is the state of being free from the forms of greed, hatred, and delusion.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "To what destination does one who has faith and understanding in such a profound *prajñāpāramitā* proceed? The Buddha said, "One shall proceed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). If one can..."
By inclining toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one is able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.
Subhūti spoke again: "This bodhisattva performs a difficult task, in that he dons such firm armor to deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, although he performs such deeds for sentient beings, he [remains entirely...]"
He does not perceive the designation of a sentient being. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, it is so, it is so.
This armor donned by that bodhisattva does not belong to form. Why is that? Because form is ultimately non-existent; it is neither the bodhisattva nor the armor.
Therefore, it is said that this armor does not belong to form. This armor donned by that bodhisattva does not belong to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately non-existent; they are neither the bodhisattva nor the armor.
Therefore, it is said that this armor does not belong to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to:

this bodhisattva armor does not belong to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is this? Because the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are ultimately non-existent.
It is not a bodhisattva; it is not armor. Therefore, it is said that this armor does not belong to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to don such firm armor as to deliver sentient beings so that they all realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Subhūti said: "This bodhisattva does not [act] for the sake of delivering..."
They do not don the armor for the sake of liberating only a small portion of sentient beings, nor do they don the armor for the sake of seeking only a small portion of wisdom.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is. This bodhisattva dons the armor in order to rescue and deliver all sentient beings and lead them to parinirvāṇa;
he dons the armor in order to seek the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). For this reason..."
One does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This perfection of wisdom is most profound. There is no one who can practice it; there is no dharma to be practiced;
nor is there a place for its practice, nor is there anything by which it is cultivated. Why is this? It is because this perfection of wisdom is not..."

Within the profound meaning, there is not even a slight portion of a real dharma that can be apprehended as one who practices, or as the dharma practiced, or as the locus of practice, or as that by which one practices.
Blessed One, if one practices emptiness, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
if one practices all dharmas, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom; if one practices unreal dharmas, this is...
To cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to cultivate that which is non-existent;
to cultivate it is to cultivate that which is without grasping; to cultivate it is to cultivate its relinquishment.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, what is it that one cultivates by way of relinquishing? It is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom."
“Much,” Subhūti replied. “World-Honored One, to practice the elimination of form is to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To practice the elimination of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

Up to and including practicing the elimination of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is to practice the perfection of wisdom. The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "One should rely upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to verify whether a bodhisattva is non-retrogressive.
If a bodhisattva does not give rise to attachment toward the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, [he is non-retrogressive]."

One should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva. Furthermore, up to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they do not give rise to attachment; one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva.
Subhūti, when a non-retrogressive bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are not led astray by a mind of greed, nor by a mind of hatred or delusion.
Their minds are led by non-conceit and are not led by various other defiled states of mind.
They do not depart from the six perfections. Upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, terrified, or afraid;
they do not sink or become despondent, nor do they retreat or abandon it. With joy, they delight in hearing it, and they receive, uphold, and recite it.

[He] recited it until he had mastered it completely. He practiced according to what was taught. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and does not even regress or abandon it, how should this bodhisattva practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said, "This bodhisattva’s mental continuum conforms to, follows, and inclines toward [the realization of]..."
"One enters into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). One should practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner.
World-Honored One, how does one’s continuity conform to, tend toward, and enter into the knowledge of all modes?

"Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva’s continuity conforms to, tends toward, and enters into emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), wishlessness (apraṇihita), space, non-existence, and neither-arising nor ceasing."

Neither defiled nor pure: suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-false nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, the inconceivable realm, and the absence of fabrication.

Illusion, a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shimmering light, a mirage, a magical creation, and a city of Gandharvas—when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these constitute the characteristics of a bodhisattva who continuously accords with, progresses toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). Practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*...
(317) Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, regarding these characteristics..."

Furthermore, one who follows, inclines toward, and enters into emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, up to the matter of transformations, the city of Gandharvas, and practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—does that bodhisattva practice form?
Does he practice feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Up to and including the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)? The Buddha said: "That bodhisattva..."

They do not practice with regard to form; they do not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because these bodhisattvas accord with, incline toward, and enter into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
It cannot be produced; it cannot be destroyed. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it has no place of abiding. It has no direction and no domain;

it is numberless and immeasurable; it neither departs nor arrives. Subhūti, since this omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) is such that neither its number, quantity, nor its coming and going can be apprehended, and there is likewise nothing that can realize it—this omniscience cannot be characterized by form (*rūpa*).

It cannot be realized through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor can it be realized even by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because form itself is the knowledge of all aspects; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are the knowledge of all aspects;
and even the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are themselves the knowledge of all aspects. For what reason?

Why? Because whether it be the suchness of form, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness—without duality and without distinction.
Whether it be the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, or the suchness of the knowledge of all modes...
If the suchness of all phenomena is a single suchness, without duality or distinction— even the suchness of the knowledge of the paths,
the suchness of all-aspect omniscience, the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, and the suchness of all phenomena are all a single suchness,
without duality or distinction. (The Chapter on the Knowledge of the Goal concludes.)
From the thirteenth leaf of Volume 318 (Chapter on True Suchness) to Volume 321:
At that time, the various devaputras of the desire and form realms each took fragrant flowers and scattered them from afar over the Buddha. Prostrating themselves, they addressed him, saying:
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is most profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to realize, beyond the scope of discursive thought and transcending the realm of conceptualization.
Subtle, wondrous, and tranquil, it can be known by those who are wise and discerning, yet it cannot be easily believed or accepted by the world at large.
It is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
In this sutra, it is stated in all cases as follows: Form is itself the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
This is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; it is non-dual, undifferentiated, and inexhaustible.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying: "So it is, so it is! It is as you have said, O devaputras.
When I contemplate this meaning, my mind constantly inclines toward tranquility, and I do not delight in preaching the Dharma. Why is this? Because of the profound *parinirvāṇa*..."

If the *pāramitās* are themselves the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening realized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—then such unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening cannot be realized; it is not that which is realized; there is no place of realization, and no time of realization.
O sons of the gods, this Dharma is profound and subtle; it functions non-dually and cannot be fathomed by any in the world.
O sons of the gods, because space is profound, this Dharma is profound. Because *tathatā* (suchness) is profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) is profound, this Dharma is profound. And so on, up to: because the inconceivable realm is profound, this Dharma is profound.
O sons of the gods, because it is immeasurable, boundless, and profound, this Dharma is profound. It is without coming...
Because it transcends the profound, this Dharma is profound. Because it is profound in being without arising or cessation, this Dharma is profound.
Because it is profound in being without defilement or purity, this Dharma is profound. Because it is profound in being without knowledge or attainment, this Dharma is profound.
Because it is profound in being without creation or action, this Dharma is profound. At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed [the Buddha]:
The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, this profound and subtle Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping form, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning form.

It is not taught for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This continues up to: it is not taught for the sake of grasping the knowledge of the aspects of the path or all-aspect omniscience, nor for the sake of abandoning them."
"Because it is taught for the sake of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, Blessed One, sentient beings in the world mostly engage in grasping practices;

they give rise to the attachment of 'I' and 'mine,' saying: 'Form is I, form is mine; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are I, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are mine,' and so on, up to:
'The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are I, the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are mine. At that time, the Buddha...
He addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.

Devaputras, if a bodhisattva practices for the sake of grasping form, or practices for the sake of abandoning form, or practices for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness..."

If one practices for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, that bodhisattva cannot cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), nor can they cultivate the perfections from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) down to generosity (*dāna*).

Furthermore, they cannot cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "This profound and sublime Dharma..."
It accords with the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to and including the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

World-Honored One, this profound and wondrous Dharma is unimpeded regarding form; it is unimpeded regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on, up to the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
World-Honored One, this profound and wondrous Dharma is without arising and without cessation. Why is that?
Form is without arising and without cessation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation.

This extends up to the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, because they are without arising and without cessation. World-Honored One, this profound and subtle Dharma is entirely without tracks. Why is this?
The footprint of form cannot be found; the footprints of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be found;

and so on, up to the footprint of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the footprint of all-aspect omniscience cannot be found. At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Subhūti follows the Tathāgata’s birth; he is a true disciple of the Buddha. Why is this? Venerable Subhūti, all..."
As it is taught in the Dharma: because everything is in accord with emptiness. At that time, Subhūti addressed the devaputras, saying:
"In what way is Subhūti born after the Tathāgata? It is because he is born after the Tathāgata’s suchness (tathatā). Why is this so?"
The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes; the *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise, neither coming nor going.
The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of all phenomena (*dharma*); the *tathatā* of all phenomena is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata.
Such *tathatā* has no nature of *tathatā*, nor does it have a nature that is not *tathatā*. The *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise. The Tathāgata...
Suchness has permanence as its characteristic. Subhūti, suchness is likewise; it has permanence as its characteristic.
The Suchness of the Tathāgata is without change and without discrimination, pervading and operating throughout all phenomena. Subhūti, suchness is likewise;
it is without change and without discrimination, pervading and operating throughout all phenomena. The Suchness of the Tathāgata is unimpeded; the Suchness of all phenomena is likewise.
It is without obstruction; it is identical to true suchness (tathatā), being neither two nor distinct, and neither created nor produced. Such is true suchness:

its characteristic is eternally that of true suchness, and there is no time when it is not the characteristic of true suchness. Subhūti’s true suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the true suchness of the Tathāgata is not separate from the true suchness of all phenomena (sarvadharma). All phenomena...
Suchness is not separate from the Suchness of the Tathāgata; the Suchness of Subhūti is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Although it is said that he is born in accordance [with him], there is nothing to which he is born in accordance, because the Suchness of Subhūti is not different from that of the Buddha.
When this true nature of suchness was thus being explained in fascicle three hundred and twenty-two, this great trichiliocosm shook in six ways. At that time,
the devaputras of the desire and form realms scattered various kinds of incense and flowers over the World-Honored One and upon Subhūti.
Having taken his seat, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is most marvelous, World-Honored One; it is unprecedented!
The Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata by virtue of suchness. At that time, Subhūti said to the devaputras: "You should know that the Elder Subhūti..."
One follows the Tathāgata’s birth not by means of all phenomena, nor by means of the suchness of all phenomena;
one follows the Tathāgata’s birth not by being separate from all phenomena, nor by being separate from the suchness of all phenomena;
one follows the Tathāgata’s birth not by means of the conditioned, nor by means of the suchness of the conditioned.
One is born following the Tathāgata because one does not depart from the conditioned; one is born following the Tathāgata because one does not depart from the suchness of the conditioned.
One is born following the Tathāgata not by means of the unconditioned, nor by means of the suchness of the unconditioned.
One is born following the Tathāgata because one does not depart from the unconditioned, nor does one depart from the suchness of the unconditioned.
They arise in accordance with the Tathāgata. Why is this? O sons of the gods, all these dharmas are utterly non-existent.
As for those who arise in accordance, that which is the object of such arising, the process of arising in accordance, and the locus of such arising—all these are unapprehendable.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "The true thusness of all dharmas, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and even the inconceivable realm..."
All are most profound, World-Honored One. Herein, form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended; the suchness (*tathatā*) of form also cannot be apprehended. Why is this?

Because herein even form cannot be apprehended, much less can the suchness of form be apprehended. Herein, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) cannot be apprehended;
the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness also cannot be apprehended. Why is this? Because herein...
Since even feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, how much less can the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended?

This extends to the fact that the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects cannot be apprehended, nor can the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this, even the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects cannot be apprehended.

“Is it so? How much more so for the *tathatā* (suchness) of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, which could be apprehended? The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is;

it is just as you have said. When this characteristic of *tathatā* was being taught, sixty thousand bodhisattvas were forever freed from outflows (*āsrava*), their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.

In the past, he attended upon and made offerings to five hundred Buddhas. At the site of each Buddha, he gave rise to great vows and left the household life with right faith.

Although he practiced generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, he did not embrace the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor did he embrace skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Consequently, he gave rise to notions of differentiation and acted with partiality.
Diverse practices: When practicing generosity, one forms this thought: "This is generosity; these are the material goods; this is the recipient; I am able to practice giving.
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought: "This is pure ethical discipline; these are sinful actions;

Patience. This is an obstacle to patience; this is the object of patience; I am capable of practicing patience.
When cultivating diligence, one forms this thought: "This is diligence; this is laziness; this is what is to be done; I am capable of being diligent.
When cultivating meditative concentration, one forms this thought: "This is meditative concentration; this is distraction; this is what is to be done; I am [capable of it]."

They practice meditative concentration; yet, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and lack skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they engage in the distinct practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence based on the perception of diversity.

Due to these perceptions of diversity and these diverse practices, they are unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*). Because they cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty...
Because their nature is free from the state of birth, they attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), and proceed gradually until they reach the fruit of arhatship.
Śāriputra, although these bodhisattvas possess the gates of liberation— emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—

because they are far removed from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and attain the state of a śrāvaka.
*Śrāvakabhūmi*, Fascicle 323.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what cause and condition do there exist bodhisattvas who cultivate emptiness?"

Without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because they lack skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they realize the limit of reality and fall into [nirvāṇa]."

The fruit of a śrāvaka, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha— yet if bodhisattvas do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) while cultivating the gates of liberation of emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness, these bodhisattvas embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Because they possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they are able to enter the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and attain unexcelled [enlightenment].
...anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It is like a bird whose body is large but which has no wings;

Yet they fall because they lack wings. The Buddha said: "All bodhisattvas are likewise.

Although they pass through great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, diligently practicing generosity up to meditative concentration, and also cultivating the three gates of liberation, performing vast deeds, and generating a vast mind, they desire to realize the immeasurable, ungraspable, subtle, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
Subhūti, if one lacks the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and is devoid of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because such a bodhisattva has abandoned the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*);

thus, although they may recollect the aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) up to the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*) of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present...
Regarding the aggregate of wisdom and vision, they pay homage and make offerings, and practice in accordance with it;
yet, because they grasp at signs within it, they cannot correctly understand these true merits of the Tathāgatas.

Although they hear the sounds of the bodhisattva path—the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they nevertheless grasp at signs based on those sounds. Having grasped at signs, they dedicate [their merit] toward...
To supreme perfect enlightenment. This bodhisattva thus dedicates [the merit], yet does not apprehend enlightenment, nor do they abide in the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, never depart from the mind of omniscience, diligently practicing generosity up to meditative concentration, and never being separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Skillful means: although one recollects the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, one does not grasp at their signs.

Although one cultivates all the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one likewise does not grasp at their signs. Although one recollects the various [qualities] of oneself and others...
He dedicates these roots of merit and virtue together with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet he does not grasp at signs.
It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but proceeds directly toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva possesses skillful means; for he is free from...

With a mind free from signs (*animitta-citta*), they practice the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Even up to practicing the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with a mind free from signs. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that these sons of good family remain far removed from *parinirvāṇa*..."
If one seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the skillful means of the *pāramitās*, yet whether one attains it or not, why is this?
It is because one grasps at signs regarding all that is practiced, from the six *pāramitās* up to the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

“Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize. Why is this?
One must be able to realize and know the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena before one can attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
yet, the characteristics of the phenomena known by Bodhisattvas are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended. Thus the Buddha told the Bodhisattvas.
The Devaputra said: "Devaputra, you should know that I too have directly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

yet, in the ultimate sense, I do not apprehend any characteristic of phenomena that can be described as 'this is the realizer,' 'this is the realized,' 'this is the locus of realization,' 'this is the time of realization,' or 'by means of this one realizes.'"
For this reason, because all phenomena are ultimately pure, and because the conditioned and the unconditioned are ultimately empty.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "As I contemplate the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and very easy to realize.
Why is this? Because one who is able to believe and understand that there is no phenomenon that can be realized [realizes it]."
There is nothing to be realized by means of dharmas; there is no place of realization, no time of realization, nor is there anything by which realization occurs.
One who can thus have faith and resolve in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas will be able to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are ultimately empty. Within ultimate emptiness, there is—altogether—nothing whatsoever.
There is no dharma that can be called the "attainer," the "object attained," the "place of attainment," the "time of attainment," or that by which something is attained.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are empty; whether increasing or decreasing, they are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
All the dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are likewise entirely without [intrinsic nature].

They exist, yet all are unapprehendable. For this reason, as I contemplate the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, it is extremely easy to believe and understand, and very easy to realize.
One should not think that within this there is anything difficult to believe and understand, or difficult to realize. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding such emptiness of intrinsic nature...
Having developed profound faith and understanding, and having realized it without error, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this reason, it is said that this is not difficult to believe in or understand, nor is it difficult to realize.

At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "When one observes that all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and are all like space, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can believe and understand that all phenomena are equal to space, then they will easily give rise to faith and understanding regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will easily realize it.
If this were so, then there would not be [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit and sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet experiences retreat or discouragement along the way, one knows that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
At that time, Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, what do you think?"
"Are all phenomena subject to retreat or despondency regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti.
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Apart from all phenomena, is there any phenomenon that is subject to retreat or despondency regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti. At that time, Subhūti spoke to Śāriputra...

Subhūti said: "If all dharmas, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended, what dharma could be spoken of that might regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"As you have stated, within the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, there is no dharma whatsoever, nor is there any bodhisattva."
"One might say that there is falling back from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
If that were so, why did the Buddha speak of three kinds of persons who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle? He should have spoken of only one.
