Within the suchness of all phenomena, are there three distinct types of individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle?
That is to say: those who are certain to regress from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; those who are certain not to regress;
and those who are indeterminate? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti. Śāriputra, within the suchness of all phenomena...
“Are there distinctions among the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles—that is, the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the samyaksaṃbodhi vehicle?

Śāriputra replied, “No, Subhūti. “Śāriputra, within the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, is there truly any bodhisattva vehicle that is fixed or irreversible? Śāriputra replied, “No, Subhūti. “Śāriputra, one...”
"Within the suchness of all phenomena, does there truly exist a single vehicle of the Bodhisattvas who seek perfect enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti. "Śāriputra, within the suchness of all phenomena, do there exist the characteristics of one, two, or three?"
Śāriputra said, “No, Subhūti. Subhūti asked, “Śāriputra, within the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, can any phenomenon or any bodhisattva be apprehended? Śāriputra said, “No, Subhūti.
Then Subhūti said to Śāriputra, “If all phenomena, by virtue of their reality and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent, they are all—”

It is possible. How could Śāriputra have such a thought as to say that such a bodhisattva will certainly experience regression from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or that they will certainly not experience regression? To speak thus is to say it is indeterminate for such a bodhisattva.
"This is the vehicle of the śrāvakas; this is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; this is the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddha). Thus there are three;

thus there is one. Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend anything at all in any phenomena, and is also well able to believe and understand that the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is likewise entirely unapprehendable, and likewise has no [conceptual] apprehension regarding the bodhisattvas..."

One attains it; yet regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is likewise nothing to be attained. One should know that such a person is a true bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If, upon hearing it said that the suchness (*tathatā*) of all these dharmas is characterized by non-attainability, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and does not even regress or sink, they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (The Chapter on Suchness concludes.)
Fascicle 324, Leaf 13 (Bodhisattvavihāra-parivarta) through Leaf 10 of the following fascicle:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in what should they abide?"
"How should one abide? The Buddha said, "One should abide with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; one should not abide with a mind of partiality.
Furthermore, one should give rise to a mind of ultimate emptiness, non-existence, and ungraspability toward all sentient beings, and give rise to a mind of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
A bodhisattva who wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should..."
Abiding herein.
From the eleventh leaf of fascicle three hundred and twenty-five (the Chapter on Irreversibility) to fascicle three hundred and twenty-seven, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, what are the practices, marks, and signs of an irreversible bodhisattva? The Buddha said: "Subhūti, one who is able..."
"One who contemplates all phenomena as being without activity, without characteristics, and without marks—know that such a person is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If all phenomena are without activity, characteristics, or marks, then in what phenomenon does this bodhisattva [abide]?"
Because they turn back, they are called "non-retrogressive. The Buddha said: "This bodhisattva is called 'non-retrogressive' because they turn back from all dharmas.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of all dharmas is non-existent; this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not abide therein, and for this reason they are called 'turning back.'"
If a bodhisattva constantly accomplishes loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and gives rise to corresponding actions of body, speech, and mind,
one should know that this constitutes non-retrogression.
If, when entering, exiting, going, or coming, the bodhisattva’s mind is not deluded or mistaken, but always abides in right mindfulness and right situational awareness, they advance.
One should maintain dignified deportment; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, when lifting or lowering the feet, one should remain composed and mindful.
In all movements and speech, one should always be free from abruptness or violence. Know that this constitutes non-retrogression.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva, according to whatever mundane or supramundane teachings they hear, is able through skillful means to bring them into accord with the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, then in all their actions—
While performing worldly activities, they likewise enter into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*;

they do not perceive even a single thing that transcends the nature of phenomena. Even if there should be something that does not accord with the nature of phenomena, they are able to skillfully bring it into accord with the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because of this, they do not perceive anything that transcends the nature of phenomena.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has contemplated all phenomena as empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Because they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that can be apprehended, and because that which cannot be apprehended is without activity and ultimately non-arising, this is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
By attaining such patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, one is therefore termed "non-retrogressive."

The evil Māra, seeking to cause distress and ruin, said to the Bodhisattvas: "Unsurpassed enlightenment is equal to space; its intrinsic nature and specific characteristics are all ultimately empty and utterly non-existent.
Why do you undergo such fruitless toil and suffering in your quest to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
You should abandon your vow for great bodhi, lest you labor in vain through the long night for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all beings."
Sentient beings undergo diligent suffering themselves. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva hears those words, they are able to examine them thoroughly and should not believe or accept that teaching.

Although all phenomena are equal to space and their intrinsic nature and characteristics are ultimately empty, sentient beings throughout the long night of birth and death do not know, do not see, do not understand, and do not awaken; they are thus inverted and distracted.
"Though I may encounter various intense sufferings, I shall don the great armor of merit, which is empty of both intrinsic nature and characteristics like the vast void.

I shall swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall teach the Dharma as is appropriate, causing them to be liberated from the great suffering of birth and death.
It is by relying on this firm, unshakable, and irreversible mind that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly...
They correctly practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having achieved these six to some degree, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). By this, they enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva called 'non-retrogressive' because he does not retrogress, or is he called 'non-retrogressive' because he does retrogress?
The Buddha said: "He is called 'non-retrogressive' because he does not retrogress."

Furthermore, because they have transcended [the possibility of] regression, they are called "non-regressive. These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have surpassed the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
they will never again fall back into those two stages. For this reason, it is said that they are called "non-regressive" because they do not regress.
Having distanced themselves from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they definitively abandon those two stages. By means of...
For this reason, it is said that by virtue of being "reversing," one is called "non-reversing.
If a bodhisattva does not distance themselves from the great bodhicitta and does not perceive any dharma as worthy of esteem, why is this?
Because all dharmas are equal to space; their nature and characteristics are empty, for they have the meaning of non-arising. One should know this.
This is for the sake of non-retrogression.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva at the stage of non-retrogression is always a superior person and never an inferior one.
For such a Bodhisattva, all afflictions no longer manifest; moment by moment, their merit and diligence increase until they reach the unsurpassed state.
One should know that when the mind is never distracted from right and equal enlightenment at any time, this constitutes non-retrogression.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva realizes that all worldly literature and arts are comprised of frivolous speech and wrong livelihood, [this is also non-retrogression].

Therefore, the bodhisattva knows [these things] but does not engage in them. Furthermore, regarding the principles and phenomena taught in the secular and non-Buddhist treatises, there is much exaggeration and depreciation;
they do not accord with the path of the bodhisattva and are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), subsumed under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
Therefore, the bodhisattva knows this and does not delight in it; one should know that this constitutes non-retrogression.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly cultivates all dharmas, he does not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be said to retrogress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does he perceive even the slightest dharma that can be said not to retrogress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Regarding...
Regarding all dharmas subsumed within the stage of non-retrogression in which he dwells, he knows them directly and sees them directly, free from confusion and doubt.
Abiding in this stage, he purifies Buddha-fields, matures sentient beings, and cultivates all meritorious qualities.

When demonic activities arise, he is immediately able to recognize them and skillfully suppress and destroy them, ensuring they do not obstruct the meritorious qualities he is cultivating. It is, for example, like constructing a...
Regarding the "one who performs an immediate karma" (*ānantarya-kāraka*): that immediate mind constantly follows him and cannot be abandoned even until the end of his life.
Why is this? Because the intense power of the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) that give rise to the immediate karma constantly persists and cannot be suppressed even until the exhaustion of his life.
Even if other states of mind arise, they cannot obstruct it; this is the stage of non-retrogression for a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: dwelling securely in his own ground, his mind is unmoving and free from conceptual discrimination.
Neither the worldlings, nor gods, nor humans, nor asuras can turn him away. Why is this? Because the mind of this Bodhisattva is firm and steadfast.

Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and having attained sublime supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), this Bodhisattva dwells securely in his own stage (*sva-bhūmi*).
When demonic activities (*mārakarman*) arise, he immediately recognizes them and never complies with them.

Instead, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he gathers all demonic activities and places them within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), thereby eliminating them through expedient means. Regarding the dharmas of his own stage, he is without confusion or doubt. Why is this?
For this reason, one knows that all phenomena enter into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One penetrates the limit of reality as being neither one nor many;
within the limit of reality, there is no conceptual differentiation and no hesitation.

Even if such a bodhisattva were to undergo further rebirths, they would never again regress from the limit of reality toward the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Why is this? Because this bodhisattva knows...

All phenomena are empty of their own characteristics. Within this emptiness, one does not perceive any phenomenon that arises or ceases, is defiled or pure, or even undergoes a transformation of the body.
Furthermore, one does not doubt whether "I shall attain awakening" or "I shall not attain it.
This bodhisattva is, in fact, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening itself.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds the true Dharma, not begrudging even their own body or life, they should form this thought:
"All phenomena taught by the Tathāgata are empty; these are the place of refuge for all sentient beings.

By training in this, the bodhisattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and shall uproot the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress for all sentient beings, causing them to reach its end."
Ultimately leading to the peace of nirvāṇa, one should therefore protect and uphold [the Dharma], not begrudging even body or life.
For this reason, the true Dharma of all Buddhas is my own Dharma; I should protect and uphold it, not begrudging even body or life.
When I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I too shall preach that all phenomena are empty. One should know that such a person is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva, whose fame is heard everywhere.
He is able to understand all the speech, sounds, characters, and meanings of all classes of sentient beings, without confusion or doubt.

Until the end of the future, he shall never forget them. Why is this? Because he has attained the *akṣaragarbha-dhāraṇī* and other such spells, which sustain what has been spoken so that it is not forgotten.
It should be known that this constitutes a Bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive. (Non-retrogression)
The Chapter on Transformation concludes.
Fascicle 328 (The Chapter on Skillful Means), from leaf 13 of fascicle 330, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By means of these aforementioned characteristics and signs, the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva is revealed."
“O Mahāsattva, you have accomplished various kinds of sublime virtues.

I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will further explain for the Bodhisattvas the profound state, so that all Bodhisattvas may dwell therein and cultivate all dharmas to quickly bring them to fulfillment.
The Buddha said: “The profound state refers to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, and non-arising.”
Cessation, tranquil nirvāṇa, suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the limit of reality—dharmas such as these are called "profound points.
All these aforementioned names for profound points reveal that nirvāṇa is the profound point. Subhūti said:
"Is it only nirvāṇa that is called the 'profound realm,' or are all other dharmas also called profound?
The Buddha said, "All other dharmas are also called profound. Subhūti asked, "In what way are all dharmas also called profound? The Buddha said:
"Because the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is profound, all phenomena are also profound. Subhūti asked, "In what way is the *tathatā* of all phenomena profound?
The Buddha said, "The *tathatā* of all phenomena is neither identical to all phenomena nor separate from all phenomena;
for this reason, it is profound. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Buddha has, with most marvelous and subtle..."
As a skillful means for bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression, he negates all phenomena and reveals nirvāṇa;
he negates everything—whether mundane or supramundane, common or uncommon, outflowing or non-outflowing.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, they reveal nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva is able, regarding such profound points, to reflect with careful discernment,
weigh and examine them according to the principles corresponding to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and abide as it has been taught— just so...

One should study according to what has been taught. Such a bodhisattva, by giving rise to even a single thought-moment, is still able to gather boundless merit, transcend the flow of birth and death for immeasurable eons, and swiftly realize unsurpassed awakening.

How much more so if one can constantly practice the *prajñāpāramitā* without interruption, always abiding in the mental engagement associated with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti, if...
A bodhisattva who is far removed from the perfection of wisdom might practice all dharmas for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
yet, if one dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound perfection of wisdom for even a single day and night, [the latter is superior].
The merit obtained from practicing all dharmas is far greater than that; therefore, one should never be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the Buddha has taught, all that is produced through conceptual differentiation is not truly existent.
By what cause and condition is one said to obtain merit that is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless? The Buddha replied:
It is as you have said. Conceptualization and fabrication cannot give rise to true right view;

they cannot lead one to enter the state of correctness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), nor can they bring about the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including unsurpassed enlightenment.

Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have well studied internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and self-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and who abide in emptiness, act accordingly.
Just as when one examines that which is produced by conceptualization, it is empty, non-existent, false, and unreal;
in this very way, one does not depart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and one obtains merit that is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
Subhūti asked: "What is the distinction between 'immeasurable,' 'incalculable,' and 'boundless'? The Buddha said: "As for what is called 'incalculable' (*asaṃkhyeya*), its number..."
They can be apprehended. They cannot be numbered, whether within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) or the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
To say they are "immeasurable" means that their measure cannot be apprehended; they cannot be measured among the phenomena of the past, future, or present.
To say they are "boundless" means that their limit cannot be apprehended, for their boundaries cannot be fathomed. Subhūti, I have always taught that all these phenomena are empty.
As you have said, the inexhaustible, the innumerable, the immeasurable, and the boundless do not differ in their textual meaning;
they all collectively reveal the emptiness of all phenomena. Subhūti, all phenomena are empty and are all inexpressible.

It is through the skillful means of the Tathāgata that they are described as "inexhaustible," or described as "innumerable," or described as "immeasurable," or described as "boundless," or described as "empty," or described as...

It is signless; it is sometimes called wishless, sometimes called unconditioned, sometimes called non-arising, sometimes called non-ceasing, sometimes called free from defilement, sometimes called quiescence, sometimes called nirvāṇa, sometimes called suchness, sometimes called the dharma-realm, sometimes called the nature of phenomena, and sometimes called the limit of reality.
Subhūti, all such meanings are the skillful means by which the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma.
The nature of all phenomena is entirely ineffable. Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and there is nothing that can be proclaimed as ultimately empty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "Does the ineffable meaning increase or decrease? The Buddha said, "The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases.

Subhūti spoke again, "If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*) should likewise neither increase nor decrease, World-Honored One. If all phenomena neither increase nor decrease, how [is it so]..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice all dharmas and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Buddha said:
"That which is inexpressible has neither increase nor decrease; likewise, all dharmas have neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom abide in the perfection of wisdom."
Possessing great skillful means, they do not form the thought, "I am increasing or decreasing the perfection of wisdom.
They merely maintain this perception: that what is called "perfection of wisdom" is nothing but a name and a conceptual designation.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices all dharmas, they maintain this mental engagement (manasikāra) that accompanies all those dharmas, and...
Based on this, one generates the mind and roots of goodness, sharing them equally with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is meant by 'unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'? The Buddha replied, "It is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena."

This is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, because the suchness of all phenomena neither increases nor decreases, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas likewise neither increases nor decreases.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon this non-increasing and non-decreasing state, practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means; by taking this as their gateway, they gather all [virtues].
...merit. He then realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti asked: "Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, or does he realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final mind?
The World-Honored One said: "If he were to realize it by means of the initial mind..."
When one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at the moment the initial mind arises, the subsequent mind has not yet arisen; thus, there is no sense of their conjunction.
If one were to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the subsequent mind, at the moment the subsequent mind arises, the preceding mind has already ceased;

thus, there is no sense of their conjunction. In this way, when one examines the preceding and succeeding minds and mental factors through successive analysis, they lack any sense of conjunction. How [could there be such attainment]?
"How can roots of virtue be accumulated? If roots of virtue cannot be accumulated, how can a bodhisattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, I shall briefly explain a simile for you.
When a lamp is lit, is it by the initial flame that the wick is burned, or is it by the final flame that the wick is burned? [Subhūti replied,] "World-Honored One, according to my understanding..."

[Subhūti] said: "It is not the first flame that can burn the wick, yet it is not apart from the first flame. It is not the final flame that can burn the wick, yet it is not apart from the final flame.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is the wick burned? [Subhūti replied]: "World-Honored One, it is clearly seen in the world that the wick is indeed burned.
The Buddha said: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this. They do not realize [enlightenment] by means of the initial mind..."
One attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet one does not attain unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment apart from the initial thought, nor is it attained by means of a subsequent thought, nor is it attained apart from a subsequent thought.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "If a mind has already ceased, can it arise again? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
[The Buddha asked,] "If a mind has already arisen, does it have the nature of cessation? Subhūti replied, "It is so, World-Honored One; a mind has the nature of cessation."
“Is it not that which should be extinguished? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Does the mind abide as the suchness of the mind?
Subhūti replied, “It is so, World-Honored One; the mind abides as the suchness of the mind.
“Does it abide as the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Is suchness and the reality-limit profound? Subhūti replied, “It is so.”
“World-Honored One, is the mind itself suchness? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Is there a mind apart from suchness?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Is the mind itself suchness? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"No, World-Honored One. "Is there suchness apart from the mind? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
"Does suchness see suchness? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. "If a bodhisattva can practice in this way, is he practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Subhūti replied, "One who can practice in this way is practicing the profound [prajñāpāramitā]."
“Prajñāpāramitā! If a bodhisattva can practice in this way, where does he practice? Subhūti replied, “One who can practice in this way has no place of practice whatsoever. Why is this?

World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, there is no mental activity that manifests, nor is there any place where such activity manifests. Why is this? Because he dwells within True Suchness (tathatā).”
Because there is no manifestation whatsoever, nor any locus for manifestation. The Buddha asked Subhūti, "In what place does this practice occur?

Subhūti replied, "It occurs within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Within this, both manifestation and the locus of manifestation are entirely non-existent, because neither the grasper (*grāhaka*) nor the grasped (*grāhya*) can be apprehended.
[The Buddha asked: "When one practices within the ultimate truth, although one does not grasp at signs, does one still practice with signs?"
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. "Does one, while practicing within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), destroy signs?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. "Does one, while practicing within the ultimate truth, destroy the perception of signs?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. "How is it that one neither destroys signs nor destroys the perception of signs? Subhūti replied, "It is because this bodhisattva..."
He forms this thought: "I shall destroy signs and the perception of signs. Yet he does not form the thought:
"I shall destroy signlessness and the perception of signlessness," because he is without conceptual discrimination in every respect.

World-Honored One, although this bodhisattva is thus able to remain free from all conceptual discriminations, [he still possesses] the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, and the great...

Because the immeasurable and supreme qualities—such as great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and so forth—are not yet perfected, they have not realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

World-Honored One, it is because these bodhisattvas have accomplished the power of skillful means that they neither grasp nor destroy any phenomena. Why is this? Because they know the self-... of all phenomena.
Because they are empty of marks, they abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena. For the sake of liberating all sentient beings, they enter the three samādhis;
being impelled by the power of their great compassion and vows, they employ these three concentrations to bring sentient beings to maturity.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, just as you have said. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How does one enter these three samādhis?"
The stage of maturing sentient beings. The Buddha said: "A bodhisattva, dwelling in the samādhi of emptiness, perceives that sentient beings mostly cling to a self;
through the power of skillful means, he teaches them to dwell in the samādhi of emptiness.

Dwelling in the samādhi of signlessness, the bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings mostly engage with signs; through the power of skillful means, he teaches them to dwell [in the samādhi of signlessness]."

The signless samādhi. When a bodhisattva abides in the wishless samādhi and sees that sentient beings have many desires and attachments, they use the power of skillful means to instruct them so that they may abide in the wishless samādhi. At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If one enters these three samādhis within a dream, does this [contribute] to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"

"Is there an increase [in merit]? Subhūti replied, "If one enters these three samādhis during the day and thereby gains an increase in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then one who enters them in a dream likewise gains an increase. Why is that?
Because there is no difference between the daytime and the state of dreaming. Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* during the day..."

Much more so, since it is called the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, even when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in a dream, that too is called the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. [This applies to] the three *samādhis*.
"In regard to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should likewise understand that it can bring about increase.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti: 'Does the karma performed in a dream result in increase or decrease? The Buddha has taught that [all things] are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)."
They are false and unreal, like what is done in a dream. How could those karmas have increase or decrease? Subhūti replied:
Suppose someone, having taken the life of another during the day, later recalls and conceptualizes that act in a night dream, feeling deep self-congratulation and joy.
"Furthermore, suppose there is a person who dreams of taking another's life and, upon waking, feels great joy.
Regarding these two types of karma, what do you think? Śāriputra replied, "If there is no objective basis, neither volition nor karma can arise."
There must be an object of focus (*ālambana*) for volitional action (*cetanā-karma*) to arise. Regarding volitional action in a dream, upon what does it depend for its arising?

Subhūti replied: "It is so, it is so, Śāriputra. Whether in a dream or while awake, there must be the operation of discerning wisdom (*buddhi*) regarding phenomena that have been seen, heard, sensed, or known;
through this, one gives rise to either defilement or purification. If there were no phenomena seen, heard, sensed, or known, [there would be no such arising]."

The transformation of awakened wisdom is likewise neither defiled nor pure. From this it is known that whether in a dream or in the waking state, mental karma arises only when there is an object of perception;
mental karma does not arise when there is no object of perception. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"The Buddha has said that all mental karma is devoid of intrinsic nature. How can you say that it arises with an object? Subhūti replied: "Although all..."

The nature of volitional action (*cetanā-karma*) and its objective referent (*ālambana-vastu*) are both empty. Nevertheless, because one’s own mind grasps signs and engages in conceptual differentiation, it is said that volitional action arises with an objective referent.
If there were no objective referent, volitional action would not arise. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom while dreaming..."
"Taking these roots of virtue, one shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Does this Bodhisattva truly dedicate [them] toward great enlightenment? Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya has long ago received the prediction of non-retrogression; separated by only one more birth, he is certain to become a Buddha."
He is well able to answer all difficult questions. It is fitting that you now question him in this assembly.
"Venerable Śāriputra," said Subhūti, "let us respectfully inquire. Then the Bodhisattva Maitreya spoke to Śāriputra: "By what name is Maitreya called as one who can answer?

Is it by means of form (*rūpa*), or feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*)? Or is it by means of the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of form, or the emptiness of feeling..."

"Is form empty? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness empty? Form cannot answer; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot answer. The emptiness of form cannot answer;
the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot answer. Why is this so, Śāriputra?
Because I do not perceive any dharma that can answer, any dharma that is answered, the place of answering, the time of answering, or that by which one answers—all of these are likewise [unfindable]."

“I do not see it. I do not see at all any dharma that can be predicted, nor any dharma by which one is predicted, nor the place of prediction, nor the time of prediction, nor that by means of which one is predicted. This is because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty;
they are utterly non-existent, non-dual, and without distinction, for when thoroughly investigated, they cannot be apprehended. Then Śāriputra again asked Maitreya: “O Virtuous One...”
"Is the Dharma taught by you as it was realized? Maitreya Bodhisattva replied, "The Dharma I have taught is not as it was realized.
Why is this? Because the Dharma I have realized is inexpressible. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying, "By means of this Dharma, you attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Do you perceive this Dharma as being expressible? Śāriputra... [text continues]
The son replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, “It is the same with all dharmas realized by bodhisattvas.
When these bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not give rise to hesitation as to whether they will attain or fail to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They only think: ‘I shall certainly [attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.’”
Attainment (The Chapter on Skillful Means Concluded).

The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "A bodhisattva practices the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to bring sentient beings to maturity and to purify the buddha-fields, thereby swiftly bringing them to fulfillment and rapidly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Through these six perfections, they quickly attain fulfillment and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Volume 331, Leaf 13:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "When the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the great assembly.
This goddess has long since planted the roots of all virtues for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Root. Now that they have reached maturity, I grant them this prediction.
From page sixteen of fascicle three hundred and thirty-one (*Śikṣā-varga*) to fascicle three hundred and thirty-three, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has stated, a bodhisattva should not realize the emptiness of all phenomena. How...
"Why do they dwell in the emptiness of all phenomena without realizing it? The Buddha said, "When a bodhisattva contemplates the emptiness of phenomena, they first form this thought:
'I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization. Now is the time for training; it is not the time for realization.
It is like a strong man shooting upward into the sky with an arrow, and then using a subsequent arrow to strike the notch of the preceding arrow, preventing it from falling."

[They] fall away. Because they are sustained by the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva, until their roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) from causal practices have fully matured, they will never realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway.

Once the roots of virtue from causal practices for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment have all matured, it is only then that the bodhisattva realizes the limit of reality. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva...
Although they have not yet realized the ultimate reality, they do not fall away from any of the dharmas;
rather, moment by moment, their pure qualities increase, their faculties become sharp and keen, and they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One should skillfully recognize the works of Māra; one should skillfully recognize the subtle works of Māra, such as the recording and proclaiming of empty names and titles.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "What other practices of seclusion should a bodhisattva cultivate, such that the Buddha does not praise the merit of dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and practicing seclusion?
The Buddha said, "It is simply by being able to distance oneself from afflictions and evil karma, and by distancing oneself from sound..."
Hearing the mental attention of the pratyekabuddhas, one diligently cultivates the perfection of wisdom as well as all other sublime virtues;

this is called the bodhisattva’s true practice of seclusion. Subhūti, those who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should approach, serve, honor, revere, respect, and praise true and supreme spiritual friends. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "What..."

These are called true and supreme spiritual friends. The Buddha said: "One should know that from the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the realm of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) and the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*), these are the true and supreme spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.

One should know that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) act as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the illumination, the torch, the lamp, the light, and the explanation."
It is awakening; it is knowledge; it is wisdom. It is a rescue; it is a protection. It is a chamber; it is a dwelling. It is an island; it is a shore. It is a refuge;

it is a destination. It is a father; it is a mother. Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present are born from the perfection of generosity, up to and including the inconceivable realm.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "What are the characteristics of this Prajñāpāramitā, by which you exhort the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice and study it with diligence? The Buddha said, "This Prajñāpāramitā has space as its characteristic;
it has non-attachment as its characteristic; it has the signless as its characteristic. Why is this? Because Prajñā..."
Within the profound characteristics of the *pāramitās*, all phenomena and all characteristics are unapprehendable, because they are non-existent.
Subhūti asked: "Do all phenomena also possess such characteristics? The Buddha said: "All phenomena also possess such wondrous characteristics."
"Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and are devoid of all marks. Subhūti again addressed the Buddha:
"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and are far removed from all marks, then all phenomena are empty of all phenomena, and all phenomena are devoid of all phenomena.
How, World-Honored One, can sentient beings be designated, or how can they be defiled or purified? "It is not so, Subhūti."
“Is there any dharma to be apprehended within the emptiness of intrinsic nature? Nor is there any dharma to be apprehended apart from it.
How am I to understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has said? The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: “Subhūti, for a long night sentient beings have harbored the mind of ‘I’ and ‘mine.
Do they not cling to ‘I’ and ‘mine’? Is that which the mind clings to—the ‘I’ and the ‘mine’—empty and detached? “Indeed it is.”
Sentient beings do not transmigrate through birth and death due to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. Subhūti said, "So it is, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, it is in this way that sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death because of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
By this it is known that affliction is obtainable. If sentient beings were without mental attachment to a self and what belongs to a self, then there would be no affliction. If...
If there were no defilement, then there would be no transmigration through birth and death.
Since the transmigration through birth and death is indeed perceptible, one should know from this that there are dharmas of defilement. Since there is defilement, there is also purification.
Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that although sentient beings are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of all marks, defilement and purification are nonetheless perceivable.
Fascicle 334; Fascicle 335, Leaf 5.
Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there were all the sentient beings within these four continents, up to and including this great trichiliocosm.
If all were to attain human form and, throughout their entire lives, make offerings and dedicate the merit, they would obtain very great blessings.

However, the merit obtained by one who proclaims, establishes, analyzes, and reveals the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, as well as by one who dwells in the mental attention (*manasikāra*) associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is far greater than that; it is beyond measure.

Bodhisattvas should know that they ought not to engage in discourse with those who seek the state of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), does he practice a substantial dharma, or does he practice a non-substantial dharma? Subhūti replied:

Because it is not real; even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), there is likewise no solid reality.

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive even the lack of solid reality in the *prajñāpāramitā*—or indeed in anything up to the knowledge of all modes—as something to be apprehended, let alone perceive any solid reality as being apprehendable. He then addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, although they know that sentient beings do not exist at all, they nevertheless resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and don the armor of merit.

If a bodhisattva hears it said that all phenomena are detached in this way, their mind does not sink, they are not startled, not terrified, and do not feel regret."
One should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom. Fascicle 346.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "For what reason do bodhisattvas [practice] the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The mind does not sink into despondency. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Because all things are non-existent, all are detached, all are quiescent, and all are without possession or arising and ceasing, the minds of bodhisattvas do not sink into despondency regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as being unapprehendable. Unapprehendable...
These are the designations: that which causes sinking, that which is sunk, the time of sinking, the place of sinking, and the one who sinks.
By means of this sinking and for these reasons, when bodhisattvas hear such matters, their minds do not sink;
they are neither startled nor terrified, nor do they feel regret or distress.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, since the true nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in suchness (*tathatā*),
diligently practicing and training so as to swiftly abide in the stage of non-retrogression and quickly realize unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Buddha said, “Subhūti, it is just as when a transformation being (*nirmāṇa*) created by a Buddha dwells in suchness and practices...”

The conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly lead them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so that they may proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. It is the same for all bodhisattvas.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "That which is emanated by the Tathāgata does not exist at all; phenomena are apart from suchness and cannot be apprehended. Who [is it that...]"
"One dwells in suchness and practices the bodhisattva path. The Buddha said: "Suchness itself cannot be apprehended;
how much less can there be one who dwells in suchness and practices the bodhisattva path? If this were to exist as a reality, it would be impossible. Why is that?

The suchness of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation, nor is even the slightest portion of dwelling or change to be found therein. Who could possibly [apprehend] anything within it?"

Abiding thus, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying, "Although one knows that all phenomena are ungraspable, to seek awakening is an exceedingly difficult matter.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, "Kauśika," [continued].
When bodhisattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that all phenomena are without exception empty.
That is to say, they contemplate that all phenomena with form are empty; phenomena without form are also empty. They contemplate that all phenomena with visibility are empty;
phenomena without visibility are also empty. They contemplate that all phenomena with resistance are empty; phenomena without resistance are also empty. They contemplate all phenomena with...

Defiled phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) are empty; undefiled phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are also empty. One contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are also empty.

One contemplates that all mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) are empty, and supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) are also empty. One contemplates that all quiescent phenomena (*śānta-dharma*) are empty.
The non-quiescent dharmas are also empty. One contemplates that all dharmas of detachment are empty; the dharmas of non-detachment are also empty.

One contemplates that all past dharmas are empty; future and present dharmas are also empty. One contemplates that all wholesome dharmas are empty; unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas are also empty.
One contemplates that all dharmas of the desire realm are empty; the dharmas of the form and formless realms are also empty.
One contemplates that all dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*) are empty; the dharmas of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) and those that are neither of training nor no-more-training are also empty.

One contemplates that all dharmas to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) are empty; the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*) are also empty.

One contemplates that all existent dharmas (*bhava-dharma*) are empty; non-existent dharmas (*abhava-dharma*) and those that are neither existent nor non-existent are also empty. Thus one contemplates the emptiness of all such dharmas. Within the emptiness of all dharmas...
There is absolutely nothing that exists. Who could sink? Who could drown? Who could be terrified? Who could be startled? Who could doubt? Who could be obstructed?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti: "Venerable One, all that you have spoken relies upon emptiness; therefore, your words are always without obstruction.
It is like shooting an arrow upward into the void: whether near or far, it encounters no obstruction. So too is it with what the Venerable One has spoken."
Furthermore, it is thus (the "Chapter on the Praise by Vajra and Others" concludes).

The Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:

"Kauśika, because the venerable Subhūti dwells in emptiness, he does not perceive even all phenomena to be obtainable, let alone anyone who practices all phenomena. Why is this? Because he abides in all phenomena."

The dwelling of seclusion, the dwelling of tranquility, the dwelling of non-apprehension, the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness— such immeasurable and supreme dwellings,
with the exception of the dwelling of the Tathāgata, are the most excellent practices and dwellings of the perfection of wisdom in which the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas abide;
they are the highest among all the dwellings of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others.
It is supreme; it is the longest, the most venerable, the most excellent, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to dwell securely in the most supreme dwelling should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
One who wishes to dwell securely in the dwelling of a Tathāgata should study the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, countless hosts of devas and six thousand bhikṣus each took celestial incense and flowers and scattered them over the Tathāgata.
Each made this vow: "May we always abide securely in the most supreme practice and dwelling of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Then, at the moment the World-Honored One smiled, rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth. Ānanda immediately—
Rising from his seat, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying, "For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "These six thousand bhikṣus who have made these supreme vows shall, in a future kalpa known as the Star-like Kalpa, attain bodhi and be named Saṃkusumitarāja Tathāgata;
therefore, I smile. At that time, the World-Honored One praised and expounded the Prajñāpāramitā and entrusted it [to him].

Having thus instructed Ānanda, he further manifested supernatural powers before the great assembly of devas and nāgas, causing everyone to see the Tathāgata Acalā moving among the multitude and preaching the Dharma, as well as seeing the various marks and adornments of that land. Suddenly, these were no longer visible.
The Buddha asked Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you still see the Tathāgata Acalā, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, his land, and his assembly? Ānanda replied: [No.]
Ānanda said, “I no longer see them, for those matters are not within the range of these eyes.
The Buddha told Ānanda, “Just as the assembly and other such matters in that buddha-field are not the objective domain of the eyes in this land, so it is with all phenomena (*dharma*):
none are within the range of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). A phenomenon does not operate upon a phenomenon; a phenomenon does not see a phenomenon; a phenomenon does not know [a phenomenon].”
Dharma. One should know that all dharmas have no agent, no seer, and no knower; they are without movement and without action. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are devoid of activity, as the nature of both the grasper and the grasped is utterly remote.
Because all dharmas are inconceivable, as the nature of that which can be conceived is utterly remote. Because all dharmas are like...
Because things such as illusions exist only through the convergence of various conditions and appear as if they were real, all phenomena lack an agent or recipient;

they falsely manifest as if existing because they possess no solid reality. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows thus, sees thus, and practices thus, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and they likewise do not cling to the characteristics of these phenomena.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable and inexhaustible. (End of the Chapter on Entrustment.
Fascicle 347, leaf 15; (Chapter on Inexhaustibility. Fascicle 348:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How should a bodhisattva draw forth the *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha told Subhūti:
Subhūti, because all phenomena are inexhaustible, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Because all phenomena are non-existent like space, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.
By contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination as being like space and inexhaustible, they should practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

Sā. When practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive any phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either tranquil or non-tranquil, or as either secluded or non-secluded.
At that time, although the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not...
One sees all phenomena that are practiced, yet one does not see any phenomenon that is able to see those practiced phenomena.
One should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all phenomena, takes non-apprehension as the skillful means and should practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in such a manner.
At that time, when the Evil Māra saw all the bodhisattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the non-apprehension of all phenomena,
he was overcome with great anguish and distress, as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, each at his own seat.
They cannot find peace within themselves. Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattvas should constantly abide in the supreme practice and dwelling of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
(The "Chapter on the Inexhaustible" concludes.)

The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "Abiding in the perfection of generosity, one induces and includes ethical discipline, patience, and diligence."
Dhyāna-pāramitā and Prajñā-pāramitā;
abiding in Śīla-pāramitā, one draws forth Dāna-pāramitā, Kṣānti-pāramitā, Vīrya-pāramitā, Dhyāna-pāramitā,

Abiding in the perfection of patience, one draws forth and gathers the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, diligence,

The Buddha said: "Subhūti, you should know that the five pāramitās, beginning with giving, are only designated as 'pāramitās' because they are all embraced by the prajñāpāramitā. [The five beginning with giving...]"
Maitreya, by following the perfection of wisdom and being guided by its power, one swiftly proceeds toward unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If the six pāramitās are without distinct characteristics, because they are all subsumed within the prajñāpāramitā and are all brought to fulfillment through the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā, then they should be combined into a single pāramitā.
How can one speak of [the distinctions between] the pāramitās such as dāna (giving) and the others?"
It is the most supreme, the longest, the most honored, the most excellent, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is. It is by relying on this supreme *prajñāpāramitā* that one is able to enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*);

therefore, it is called 'reaching the other shore' (*pāramitā*). All are of one single flavor, their characteristics are without distinction, and they cannot be conceptually designated as such-and-such."
"This is generosity; this is pure ethical discipline," and so on, up to "wisdom. Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again:

"If, according to their ultimate meaning, all the perfections and all phenomena are devoid of such distinctions as 'this' or 'that,' superior or inferior, for what reason is wisdom said to be the foremost, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed?"

[The Bodhisattva] said, “Excellent. The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said. If one follows the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), neither the perfections (*pāramitā*) nor any phenomena (*dharma*) possess such distinctions of this or that, or superiority and inferiority.

It is only by relying on conventional linguistic usage and functional activity that one speaks of these distinctions of this or that, superiority and inferiority, and thereby designates the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) and designates the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).”
The perfections of patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from the worldly processes of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Yet, these births, aging, sickness, and deaths of sentient beings do not exist as substantial realities; they are merely conventional designations.
Why is this so? Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that all phenomena likewise have no existence. This is profound.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* thoroughly realizes that all things are utterly non-existent. It is able to extract sentient beings from the worldly functions of birth, aging, sickness, and death.

For this reason, it is said that *prajñā* is the foremost, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed. Subhūti, by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*...

[Subhūti] said: "It is much. It is able to skillfully gather all wholesome dharmas, harmoniously enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and abide immovably, using non-abiding as its skillful means.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding all wholesome dharmas, is there taking up or discarding?
The Buddha said: "In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no taking up and no discarding of any dharmas."
Subhūti asked, "How is it that there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding all phenomena? The Buddha said, "By not conceptualizing any phenomena;
in this way, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing regarding all phenomena.
Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not conceptualize any marks (*nimitta*) regarding any phenomena, nor does it conceptualize any objects of focus (*ālambana*)."
"This is the non-contemplation of all phenomena.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate any phenomena, how do the roots of goodness they have planted increase?
If the roots of goodness they have planted do not increase, how can they fulfill the perfections?"
“Pāramitā. If the pāramitās are not fulfilled, how can one attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, by not conceptualizing any phenomena, one is able to increase the roots of virtue that have been planted.
Because the roots of virtue that have been planted are increased, one is able to fulfill the pāramitās. Because the pāramitās are fulfilled...”
One is then able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Why is this?

Because by not conceptualizing any phenomena (*dharma*), one is able to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "For what reason must bodhisattvas not conceptualize any phenomena in order to be able to fully [cultivate them]?"
They cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Fascicle 353.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva conceptualizes all phenomena, they will become stained by and attached to the desire realm."
In the form and formless realms, one cannot fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva nor realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Therefore, one should diligently train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and should not contemplate with attachment to any phenomena.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
“While diligently practicing and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, in what should one abide?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is diligently practicing and studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should not abide in any phenomena (*dharma*).
Why is that? Because they do not perceive any phenomenon within which they might give rise to attachment or clinging.”
Subhūti, because it is firmly established, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which one could have any attachment toward any phenomena.
Therefore, when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one has no attachment toward any phenomena, nor toward the profound *prajñāpāramitā* itself. If a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*...
At the time of practicing Prajñāpāramitā, one gives rise to this thought: "This is Prajñāpāramitā;
it is the universal characteristic of the true reality of all phenomena. By giving rise to this thought, one then retreats from Prajñāpāramitā.
If one retreats from Prajñāpāramitā, then one retreats from all phenomena. Why is this? Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is...
The root of all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). If one regresses from the *prajñāpāramitā*, then one loses all pure dharmas.
(Fascicle 354 through Fascicle 358)
Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is universally able to encompass all phenomena (*dharma*).
If one falls away from the *prajñāpāramitā*, then one cannot encompass all phenomena. Why is this?
Because apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is impossible to universally encompass the sublime wholesome dharmas or to realize unsurpassed, perfect [enlightenment].
...equal enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva forms such a thought—dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, they will certainly receive the prediction [of enlightenment];
if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will not receive the prediction. Why is this? Because it is not...
Apart from the perfection of wisdom, one cannot receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva forms such a thought as to abide in the perfection of wisdom, they will then universally bring forth all phenomena;
if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to bring forth even a single one.
All phenomena. Why is this? It is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can lead phenomena to abide securely in wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva should form such a thought: "The Buddha knows that all phenomena have the characteristic of being without grasping."
To claim that one has personally realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment would be to fall away from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is this?
Because regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), the Tathāgata has no cognition and no realization; he has no teaching and no demonstration. For what reason?

Because the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena cannot be known or realized, and it cannot be established through conceptual designation. How, then, could there be the cognition, realization, teaching, or demonstration of any phenomenon?
If one were to say that there truly exists a conscious perceiver who can point out all phenomena, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "How should one practice the perfection of wisdom so as to remain far removed from these various faults?
The Buddha said: "All phenomena are non-existent and cannot be grasped. If phenomena are non-existent and cannot be grasped,"
Then there would be no one capable of manifesting perfect enlightenment, nor anyone capable of proclaiming or revealing it.

To practice in such a manner is to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, free from all faults. If one clings to non-existence and to dharmas that cannot be grasped, then one is removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—
One has no attachment to any phenomena and nothing to grasp therein.
If one were to have attachment to or grasp at any phenomena, one would be far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*. At that time, Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"Is the *prajñāpāramitā* distant from the *prajñāpāramitā*, or is it not distant? and so forth.
Regarding all phenomena, are they distant from all phenomena, or are they not distant?
If the perfection of wisdom were distant from the perfection of wisdom—or even if it were not distant—and this applied likewise to all phenomena.
"Even if all phenomena are either distant or not distant, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can be without attachment to the perfection of wisdom,
and even without attachment to the manifestation of all phenomena? The Buddha said, "Subhūti,
as for the perfection of wisdom, it is neither distant from nor not distant from the perfection of wisdom."

They do not distance themselves from it. For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to bring forth the perfection of wisdom without attachment, and even able to bring forth all phenomena without attachment. Why is that?

Subhūti, it is because one does not abide by means of an intrinsic nature, nor apart from an intrinsic nature, yet is able to abide in and bring forth the intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva...
When a Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not cling to any phenomena, thinking, "This is all phenomena," or "All these phenomena belong to that.
Because they do not cling to any phenomena in such a manner, [they do not apprehend them].

One is then able to bring forth all phenomena. However, if one has attachment toward any phenomena, thinking "this is a phenomenon" or "this phenomenon belongs to that," then one will not be able to bring forth and abide in supreme qualities as one wishes.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, one does not regard any phenomena as either permanent or impermanent.
Whether pleasant or painful, whether self or non-self, whether pure or impure,
whether tranquil or untranquil, whether secluded or unsecluded— because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe any such phenomena,
they are able to induce and abide in all phenomena. If, among all phenomena, there were anything...
If one observes [them], one cannot at will bring forth and abide in these sublime qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), up to and including the *dānapāramitā*;
they are practicing internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*), up to and including the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, it is marvelous!

In whatever place the profound *prajñāpāramitā* proceeds, all the other *pāramitās* and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) follow after that profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "What is the path? What is the non-path? The Buddha said: "The paths of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)."
The paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the path of self-benefit and benefit for others is the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the path of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) is the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
This is the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: it does not abide in the path of saṃsāra nor in the path of nirvāṇa.
This is the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is both the path and the non-path. Subhūti, this is the profound perfection of wisdom.
Although it can manifest all the activities performed by all phenomena, it has no attachment to these activities.
Subhūti, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* keeps bodhisattvas far removed from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

They draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet regarding all phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, because they take the abiding nature of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*) as their standard of measure.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should take the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) as their object and cultivate the six perfections for the sake of all sentient beings; they should [endow] the six perfections with...
...the *pāramitās*. They are always in mutual correspondence and never separated. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way are they always in mutual correspondence and never separated? The Buddha said:

"To contemplate all phenomena as they truly are—neither corresponding nor non-corresponding—is that which can be in constant mutual correspondence with the six *pāramitās* and never be separated from them. If...
The bodhisattva constantly reflects: "I should not abide in any phenomena. Why? Because all phenomena are neither that which abides nor that in which one abides.
Thus, this bodhisattva is able to remain in constant association with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), never being separated from them.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “How is it that when one practices the perfection of wisdom, one is protected and sustained by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present?

The Buddha said, “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices all dharmas, because they contemplate all dharmas as being unapprehendable, they are protected and sustained by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Subhūti, [it is thus].
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present do not, by means of any phenomena, hold these bodhisattva mahāsattvas in their protective mindfulness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "Although bodhisattvas train in many places, they have nothing in which to train. The Buddha said, "It is so."
"It is so. Indeed, there is no dharma whatsoever in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying, "How does a bodhisattva understand, as they truly are, the concise and detailed characteristics of all dharmas?
The Buddha said, "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the characteristic of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas."
This is the thorough understanding, both in brief and in detail, of the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

Subhūti, the suchness of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation; nor can it be designated as having duration or transformation. This is called the characteristic of the suchness of all phenomena.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, the characteristic of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, this is the understanding, as it truly is, of the brief and extensive characteristics of all phenomena.
Subhūti, the limit of formlessness is called the characteristic of the limit of reality of form;
and so on, up to the limit of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which is called the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

The characteristic of the limit of enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva understands all phenomena as they truly are according to the characteristic of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this is the concise and detailed characteristic of understanding all phenomena as they truly are.

Subhūti, the realm of form and the realm of space—this is called the dharma-realm of form. This extends up to the realm of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas and the realm of space.
This realm is called the dharma-realm of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
This entire dharma-realm is without interruption and without distinction, yet it can be provisionally designated; this is called the characteristic of the dharma-realm of all phenomena.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand it as it truly is and train therein; they should understand, as it truly is, the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena.
Fascicle 359. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “How does a bodhisattva further know the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena?
The Buddha said, “All phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed. Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If they lack intrinsic nature, then...”
There is nothing whatsoever. If there is nothing whatsoever, then it cannot be said that there is either conjunction or separation.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas understand all phenomena in this way, they are able to understand the characteristics of both the concise and the extensive.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "This is called the brief summary of the six perfections for a Bodhisattva who is newly engaged in practice."
One should always train in this; even Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages should likewise train in it.
By training in this summary of the *pāramitās*, one comes to know the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
This Dharma-gate can be entered by Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, and it can also be entered by those of middling faculties and those of fixed faculties."
They are able to enter it. Bodhisattvas of indeterminate faculties are also able to enter it, Subhūti.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in accordance with what is taught in this Prajñāpāramitā, they will be able to realize all dharmas accordingly and draw closer to the sought-after knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
All demonic activities (*mārakarman*) that arise will be extinguished as soon as they occur, and they will be sustained by all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently abide and maintain [the world], and those who proclaim the True Dharma—all of them protect and keep this in mind.
Why is this? Because there are no Buddhas of the past, future, or present who do not all arise from this very Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā should form this thought: "In the past..."
The dharmas realized by all Buddhas of the future and present—I too shall attain them;
I shall always remain inseparable from the mental engagement associated with omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva abides in accordance with what is thus taught in this *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that they have already been sustained by immeasurable true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Being thus sustained, having long cultivated all dharmas, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the stage of a youth (*kumārabhūmi*).
All his aspirations are fulfilled without exception; he constantly beholds the Buddhas, never abandoning them for even a moment;
he never forsakes any roots of goodness; he is always able to bring all sentient beings to maturity; and he also constantly adorns and purifies all [buddha-fields].
Buddha-fields. They have attained uninterrupted and inexhaustible eloquence; they have attained the dharma of sublime dhāraṇīs;

they have accomplished the most supreme and subtle form-body; they have received from all Buddhas the prophecy of perfection. According to their inclinations, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they assume various bodies within the realms of existence;
they have attained mastery, being well-versed in the gateways of objects of perception and well-versed in the gateways of modes of activity.
He is skilled in knowing the gateway of letters; skilled in knowing the gateway of non-letters; skilled in knowing speech; skilled in knowing silence;
skilled in knowing designations; skilled in knowing all phonemes; skilled in knowing all meanings; skilled in knowing all phenomena; and skilled in knowing the mental attention toward all phenomena.
He skillfully knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are empty. He skillfully knows the path of cessation. He skillfully knows the path of non-cessation.
He skillfully knows arising and ceasing. He skillfully knows abiding and changing. He skillfully knows greed, hatred, and delusion. He skillfully knows the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion.
He skillfully knows views and non-views. He skillfully knows wrong views and non-wrong views. He skillfully knows all views, obsessions, latent tendencies, fetters, and bonds. He skillfully knows...
He knows the severance of all views, obsessions, latent tendencies, fetters, and bonds. He thoroughly knows name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). He thoroughly knows causes and conditions.
He thoroughly knows conduct, liberation, and characteristics. He thoroughly knows suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He thoroughly knows the six realms of existence.

He thoroughly knows the fruit of stream-entry, up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He thoroughly knows all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). He thoroughly knows everything.
The path of wisdom. The path of the knowledge of all aspects. Skillfully knowing the faculties; skillfully knowing wisdom; skillfully knowing the past, future, and present;
skillfully knowing expedient means; skillfully knowing intentions; skillfully knowing how to regard sentient beings;

skillfully knowing the characteristics of words and meanings; skillfully knowing all noble dharmas; skillfully knowing the establishment of the expedient means of the three vehicles. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva...
Mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one attains such meritorious benefits as these.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How should one practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, "A bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena (*dharma*) as being quiescent, destructible, lacking self-mastery, essentially false, and unsubstantial."
