He likewise understands, in accordance with reality, that all other Buddha-qualities are also signless. By means of this cause and condition, he is able to universally fulfill all Buddha-qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they abide in...

Like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation—within these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha), one fulfills the perfection of pure ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

Once a bodhisattva has correctly understood these five aggregates of clinging to be like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation, they are then able to fulfill the signless (animitta) perfection of pure ethical discipline. Such is pure ethical discipline.
It is without deficiency or flaw, without blemish or impurity, and free from attachment. It is worthy of receiving offerings, praised by the wise, excellently maintained, and excellently perfected.
It is noble and untainted, subsumed within the factors of the supramundane path.
Abiding in these precepts, they are able to properly receive and uphold them:

the precepts of formal designation, the precepts obtained through the nature of phenomena, the precepts of restraint, the precepts with manifest expression (*vijñapti*), the precepts without manifest expression (*avijñapti*), the precepts of active practice, the precepts of non-active practice, the precepts of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), and the precepts that are not of dignified conduct.
Although such a bodhisattva is fully accomplished in all these precepts, they are without attachment and do not form this thought: "By me..."
By this precept, one shall be born into a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, a great householder clan, or a great merchant clan, possessing wealth, honor, and sovereignty.
One does not harbor the thought: "By means of this precept, I shall become a minor king, or a great king, or a universal monarch (cakravartin), possessing wealth, honor, and sovereignty.
One does not harbor the thought: "By means of this precept, I shall be born [in such a state]."
From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations; one shall be born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, up to the Heaven of Mahābrahmā;
one shall be born in the Heaven of Radiance, up to the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Radiance; one shall be born in the Heaven of Purity, up to the Heaven of Universal Purity;
one shall be born in the Heaven of Vastness, up to the Heaven of Vast Fruit; and one shall be born in the Heaven Free from Affliction, up to the Heaven of the Ultimate Form.
O Deva, one who possesses wealth, nobility, and sovereignty does not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall be reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space, or the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, or the Sphere of Nothingness, or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
One who possesses wealth, nobility, and sovereignty does not form such thoughts as: "By means of this precept, I shall attain the fruit of Stream-entry," and so forth, up to...
[They attain] the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*);

or they obtain the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); or they obtain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Why is this?

Because all these phenomena are signless (*animitta*), and they are all of one single mark, namely, the markless. A phenomenon that is signless cannot apprehend the signless; a phenomenon that has a mark cannot [apprehend it].
There are dharmas with marks and dharmas without marks; yet dharmas with marks cannot be apprehended as having marks, and dharmas without marks cannot be apprehended as being without marks.
For this reason, they are entirely unapprehendable. Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
They will swiftly fulfill the perfection of pure morality that is signless, enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from error,
and further attain the bodhisattva’s forbearance regarding the non-arising of phenomena. Having attained the bodhisattva’s forbearance regarding the non-arising of phenomena,

they will practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path and proceed toward the knowledge of all aspects, attaining the five superknowledges as a result of maturation, and further attaining five hundred gates of samādhi.
Abiding within five hundred dharani-doors, they further realize the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
From one buddha-field to another, they make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
Although these bodhisattvas manifest transmigration through the various realms of existence for the sake of transforming sentient beings, [they remain free from defilement].
Though they pass away, they are not defiled by the obstacles of those afflictions, karma, or retributions;
they are like a magically conjured person who, although manifesting activities such as walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, has no actual karma of coming or going.

Although they manifest various ways of benefiting sentient beings, they apprehend neither the sentient beings nor their designations at all. They are just like a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha...

He awakened, realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes, causing them to escape birth and death and realize nirvana.
Yet, there was no sentient being capable of receiving a prediction that they would next attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, that Tathāgata manifested transformation Buddhas to cause them to remain long in the world, while he himself relinquished the formations of life and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Relying upon the realm of parinirvāṇa, that emanation-body of the Buddha remains for one kalpa; having bestowed the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment upon a bodhisattva, it then enters nirvāṇa.

Although that emanation-body of the Buddha performs various deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, it has no attainment—meaning it does not attain form, nor does it attain feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not attain the sense-base of the eye.
One attains the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; one does not attain the base of form. One does not attain the bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects.

One does not attain the eye-element. One does not attain the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. One does not attain the element of form. One does not attain the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects.
One does not attain the eye-consciousness-element. One does not attain the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness. One does not attain the eye...
Contact. One does not apprehend contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, nor the various feelings produced with contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a condition.

One does not apprehend any phenomena, whether outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), nor sentient beings. This Bodhisattva is also like this: although there is that which is performed, there is nothing that is apprehended.
Thus, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Because this perfection of ethical discipline is fulfilled, they are able to encompass all the buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in suchness (*tathatā*).
Like a dream and like an echo, even unto like a conjured phenomenon, within the five aggregates of clinging, he fulfills the perfection of patience.

When that bodhisattva has correctly understood these five aggregates of clinging to be like a dream, like an echo, and even like a conjured phenomenon, he is then able to fulfill the signless perfection of patience. Subhūti, this bodhisattva...
By cultivating two kinds of patience, one is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) that is signless (*animitta*). What are these two?

First, the patience of acceptance (*adhivāsanā-kṣānti*); second, the patience of analytical observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-kṣānti*). As for the patience of acceptance, it refers to all bodhisattvas from the moment they first generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Until they are seated upon the sublime seat of awakening, during that interval, even if all classes of sentient beings were to come in competition to revile and disparage them,
using harsh and evil words to scold and insult them, and further inflict harm upon them with tiles, stones, swords, and staves.

In order to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), this bodhisattva does not give rise to even a single thought of malice or resentment, nor does he conceive the intention to retaliate.
He reflects only thus: "Those sentient beings are deeply pitiable;

their minds have been struck by the force of their own predominant afflictions (*kleśa*) such that they lack self-mastery. It is under the influence of these conditions that they have initiated such evil karma toward me. I shall now..."
One should feel resentment toward that [offender]. Yet, one should further reflect:
"It is because I have grasped these aggregates of an enemy that those sentient beings have initiated such evil karma against me; I should only reproach myself and not resent them.
When a bodhisattva examines the matter in this way, they give rise to deep compassion for those sentient beings. Such instances as these are called "accepting with composure."
Patience. Regarding the patience of contemplation: it refers to the bodhisattvas’ reflection that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions—false, unreal, and lacking self-mastery;
they are also like space, wherein no self, sentient being, up to and including a knower or a seer, can be found.
These are merely arisen from false conceptual discrimination. Who is reviling me? Who is abusing me? Who...
They insult me; who is it that inflicts various injuries upon me with tiles, stones, swords, or staves? And who is it that receives those insults and injuries?
All of this is the false conceptualization of one's own mind. I should not now give rise to groundless attachment.
Such phenomena, because they are empty of intrinsic nature and empty of ultimate reality, do not exist at all. The Bodhisattva thus examines them...
When observing, one understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as empty and quiescent as they truly are, and does not give rise to divergent conceptions regarding any phenomena.

Such categories as these are called "patience through observation" (*vipaśyanākṣānti*). Because this bodhisattva cultivates these two kinds of patience, he is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) that is signless (*animitta*), and immediately attains the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). At that time, [the bodhisattva] is well...
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "What is meant by 'the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? What is it that is severed by this?
Furthermore, what kind of wisdom is it? The Buddha said: "Subhūti, by the power of this, even the slightest portion of evil or unwholesome phenomena cannot arise."

Therefore, it is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This brings about the ultimate pacification of all afflictions such as pride, along with the notions of "I" and "mine.
It consists of accepting, in accordance with reality, that all phenomena are like dreams, echoes, and even like magical transformations.

This patience is called wisdom. Because one attains this wisdom, it is said that one has "attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas..."

"What is the distinction? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, the wisdom and the abandonment of all stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The wisdom and the abandonment of all pratyekabuddhas are also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, there is another patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
It means that one endures the fact that all phenomena are ultimately non-arising; this is the distinction.
Subhūti, because a bodhisattva accomplishes such a sublime patience, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Abiding in such a sublime, maturation-born patience of non-arising, the bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path and is able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path, never being far from it.

They are not separated from the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eight branches of the noble path;
nor are they separated from the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor are they separated from the supernormal powers that are the maturation of karma.
By not being separated from these maturation-based supernormal powers, they travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to and honoring all the Buddhas.
Buddha, World-Honored One, you mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields;
by means of the sublime wisdom associated with a single kṣaṇa, you have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they can swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of patience and thereby realize all-knowledge.
Wisdom. There is not a single Buddha-dharma that is not fully perfected.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging as being like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation.

Having understood these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are—like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical creation—and having realized their lack of substantial characteristics, one arouses vigor and applies physical and mental diligence to bring forth exceptionally swift supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
By means of these supernormal powers, one travels to the worlds of the ten directions to offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Regarding those Buddhas...
He plants the roots of all virtues, brings benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and is also able to adorn and purify various Buddha-fields.

By means of physical diligence, this bodhisattva matures sentient beings, establishing them through skillful means in the Dharma of the Three Vehicles according to what is appropriate for each, so that they may each reach ultimate realization.
Thus, Subhūti, the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom.

...the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Subhūti, because that bodhisattva initiates courageous mental diligence, they induce the diligence comprised within the noble, untainted factors of the path (*ārya-āsravāṇāṃ mārgāṅgānām*) and fulfill the perfection of diligence.
Within this, they are fully capable of encompassing all wholesome dharmas, namely:
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Abiding within these, the bodhisattva is able to fulfill the knowledge of all aspects,
forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), fully perfect the primary marks and secondary signs, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and emit—
A great radiance shone forth, illuminating the trichiliocosm and causing all worlds to tremble in six ways.
He turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma and was endowed with the thirty-two marks. All classes of sentient beings, touched by the light and beholding these manifestations, [were inspired].
Hearing the sound of the true Dharma, they all become non-retrogressive regarding the three vehicles.

Thus, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of diligence, are able to accomplish many beneficial matters for both themselves and others, swiftly perfect all Buddha-dharmas, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore:

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation—
and fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration. Having realized, in accordance with reality,
that these five aggregates of clinging are like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation, and that they lack any real characteristic, they enter [into meditative concentration].
He dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna; he enters and dwells having fully attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

He enters and dwells having fully attained the immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. He enters and dwells having fully attained the concentration of the sphere of infinite space;

he enters and dwells having fully attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He cultivates the samādhi of emptiness.
On this ground, he cultivates the signless and wishless samādhis, and even other immeasurable samādhis;
all such states he is able to personally realize, perfect, and dwell in.

Yet, regarding these dhyānas, immeasurables, formless attainments, and various samādhis, he does not give rise to attachment to their flavor, nor does he crave the fruits obtained therein. Why is this?

Therefore, this bodhisattva understands as they truly are that the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely devoid of real characteristics;
they all take the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as their own nature. One should not, by means of a signless phenomenon, become attached to a signless phenomenon.

Furthermore, one should not take the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as the intrinsic nature of phenomena, nor should one become attached to the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of phenomena.

By not becoming attached, one will ultimately never fall under the influence of various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), such as the dhyānas, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
And they are born in the realm of form and the formless realm. Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas do not apprehend anything at all within any realm;
nor do they apprehend the one who enters meditative absorption, the absorption entered, or that by which one enters it.

Thus, they swiftly fulfill and perfect the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*animitta-dhyāna-pāramitā*), transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
[Subhūti] asked: "How does one fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*animitta-dhyāna-pāramitā*) and transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?

The Buddha said: "Subhūti, it is because this bodhisattva has well studied internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), and so forth, up to the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Within these various forms of emptiness, this bodhisattva does not apprehend any phenomena; abiding therein, they do not [perceive them]."
One attains the fruit of stream-entry, but does not attain the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship;
nor does one attain pratyekabuddha enlightenment, nor any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. Why is this?
Because these very emptinesses are themselves empty. By abiding in this emptiness, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and realizes [the path].
[The Bodhisattva] enters the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*). Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what does a bodhisattva constitute 'birth,' and by what does he constitute 'departure from birth'? The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva constitutes 'birth' by means of all that is apprehended (*upalabdha*), and constitutes 'departure from birth' by means of all that is non-apprehended (*anupalabdha*). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "By what is there apprehension, and by what is there non-apprehension?"
[The Bodhisattva] attains [something]. The Buddha said: "One attains by means of all dharmas as objects of attainment;

that is, one attains by means of form (*rūpa*) as an object of attainment, and one attains by means of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as objects of attainment, even unto attaining by means of all the practices (*caryā*) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva as objects of attainment, and attaining by means of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas as an object of attainment. A bodhisattva, by means of such..."

Subhūti, these things arise from apprehension. That which is without apprehension refers to all such phenomena as being without activity, without attainment, without expression, and without demonstration. This means that regarding form (*rūpa*), there is no activity, no attainment, no expression, and no demonstration;

regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), there is no activity, no attainment, no expression, and no demonstration. Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form, and so forth...
The intrinsic nature of consciousness is such that it cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

This extends even to the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, which is without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration. Regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, there is no practice, no attainment, no explanation, and no demonstration.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas and that of all Buddhas...

Because the intrinsic nature of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated, the bodhisattva takes such non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration as "non-apprehension.
This very non-apprehension is called "departure from birth" (*niyāma*).
Subhūti, this is what constitutes the birth and departure from birth of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; it is that into which all bodhisattvas enter.

Once they have reached the stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*), they fulfill all dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).
Such a bodhisattva does not even arise according to the power of these meditative states, much less according to the power of afflictions such as greed.
If this bodhisattva, while abiding therein, performs various karmas, they may be born in the four dhyānas or wander through the various realms of existence due to the power of that karma.

This is impossible. Although this bodhisattva dwells amidst the mass of conditioned phenomena that are like an illusion, they bring about the true benefit of all sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend either the illusion or the sentient beings.

At such a time of non-apprehension, they mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable [beings].
“O Assembly, it is thus, Subhūti: when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to swiftly fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
By means of this perfection of meditative concentration, they quickly realize awakening, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Such a wheel of Dharma is called ‘non-apprehension’ and is also called ‘emptiness.’”
It is signless and wishless, and is able to bring about the unsurpassed benefit for sentient beings.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide within the five aggregates of grasping—which are like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation—and thereby fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In this way, that bodhisattva thoroughly understands all phenomena.
All are like dreams and echoes, even unto being like conjured phenomena; having thus understood this, one is then able to fulfill the signless *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive a dream.
One does not see the dreamer; one does not hear the echo, nor does one see the one who hears the echo.
This extends even to not seeing transformative phenomena, nor seeing the one who sees transformative phenomena. Why is this?
Because dreams and dreamers, echoes and those who hear echoes, and even transformative phenomena and those who see them, are all merely the inverted attachments of foolish ordinary beings.
All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not perceive dreams, nor do they perceive those who see dreams;
they do not hear echoes, nor do they perceive those who hear echoes; and so on, up to:
they do not perceive transformations, nor do they perceive those who see transformations. Why is this? Because all phenomena are...

Taking the absence of intrinsic nature as their intrinsic nature, they are neither produced nor real; they are signless and unconditioned, lacking any truly existent nature, and are equal to *nirvāṇa*.

If all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their intrinsic nature—being neither produced nor real, signless and unconditioned, lacking any truly existent nature, and equal to *nirvāṇa*—how does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?

At the time of the *pāramitās*, it is impossible for one to conceive of all phenomena as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as being established, as being real, as having characteristics, as being conditioned, as having a truly existent nature, or as not being cessation. Why is this?

Because if all phenomena possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature, were established, were real, had characteristics, were conditioned, or possessed a truly existent nature that was not cessation—[such a thing could not exist].
If that which is extinguished could be apprehended, then the practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would not be *prajñāpāramitā*.

Thus, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not cling to form, nor do they cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not cling even to all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. They do not...

They are dedicated to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas. Because they do not cling, they are able to fulfill the first bhūmi, yet they do not give rise to craving or attachment toward it.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas do not apprehend the first bhūmi; how could they then give rise to craving and attachment toward it?
Because they do not cling, they are able to fulfill the second, the third, and so on, up to the tenth bhūmi.
Yet, within this, they do not give rise to attachment. Why is that? Because these bodhisattvas do not apprehend the second bhūmi, nor even the tenth bhūmi;

how then could they give rise to attachment toward them? Although these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom. Because they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom...
Because it is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not apprehend any phenomena (*dharma*).

Although one contemplates that the perfection of wisdom encompasses all phenomena, one apprehends nothing at all regarding these phenomena. Why is this? Because these various phenomena are non-dual and indistinguishable from this perfection of wisdom.
For what reason? Because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is beyond conceptual differentiation.
It is called *tathatā* (suchness); it is called the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*).
This is because phenomena are without admixture and without distinction. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the nature of all phenomena is entirely without admixture and without distinction, how can one say that this is wholesome and that is unwholesome, that this is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that is without outflows (*anāsrava*), or that this is mundane and..."
"Whether supramundane, conditioned, or unconditioned—regarding all such immeasurable gateways to the Dharma, the Buddha said to Subhūti:
'What do you think? Within the true nature of all phenomena, is there any phenomenon that can be described as wholesome or unwholesome?'"
"Up to and including: are these conditioned or unconditioned? Is this the fruit of stream-entry? The fruit of once-returning? Up to and including:
is this the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, by this cause and condition, you should know that all dharmas are unmixed and without distinction; they are signless, unborn, unceasing, and unimpeded."

There is no speaking and no showing. Subhūti, you should know that when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any phenomena whatsoever—whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

even up to the practices of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha. Regarding the intrinsic nature of such phenomena as these, there was nothing at all to be apprehended.

Thus it is attained, Subhūti. When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime awakening and about to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should always skillfully know the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
thus they can thoroughly purify the path to great awakening and also bring all bodhisattva practices to fulfillment.
They bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, abide in this Dharma, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

They turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and, through the three vehicles and skillful means, discipline all classes of sentient beings, causing them to quickly attain liberation from the three realms of existence.
Thus, Subhūti, it is by way of non-apprehension that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas act as their method.
One should then study the *Prajñāpāramitā*; one will be able to swiftly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.
(End of the "Chapter on the Meaning of Unmixed Dharmas," folio 10 of volume 379). [The "Chapter on the Characteristics of All Merits"] begins here and extends to folio 16 of volume 383.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "How can all phenomena, which lack any substantial entity and have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and whose specific characteristics are entirely empty, be established?
How can they be designated as wholesome or unwholesome, or as contaminated or uncontaminated?"
"Is this the mundane? Is this the supramundane? Is this conditioned? Is this unconditioned?
Even so, is this the stream-enterer, up to and including the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Ordinary worldlings, foolish and uninstructed, perceive dreams and see those who dream; they perceive echoes and hear those who echo; they perceive images and see those who image."
One attains the appearance of light and shadow; one who attains the appearance of light and shadow attains a mirage;
one who attains the mirage attains an illusion; one who attains the illusion attains a city of gandharvas; one who attains the city of gandharvas attains a transformation.

One who attains these transformations clings to them through inversion, thereby performing wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. By means of these formative forces (*saṃskāra*), [the cycle continues].

Coming and going through birth and death, they transmigrate without end. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, contemplates the ultimate boundlessness of the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and abides securely in that ultimate boundlessness of the two kinds of emptiness.
For the sake of those sentient beings, he proclaims the True Dharma, saying: "All phenomena are empty; they are without self or what belongs to a self; they are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature."
Furthermore, he spoke these words: "In this, there are no phenomena whatsoever. It is by the power of your false conceptualization that you perceive all phenomena within a single phenomenon.

You should know that the nature of all phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—is established through the conjunction of various conditions, arises from inversion, and is governed by the maturation of various karmas. Why do you [perceive them otherwise]?"
Regarding these phenomena that are empty, false, and devoid of substantial reality, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the perception of them as having substantial reality.
At that time, through the skillful means of practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he delivers sentient beings.

If sentient beings are attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and their fruits, he employs various skillful means to cause them to abide in the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) and achieve formlessness (*ārūpya*).

Abiding within the truly untainted dharmas that are without view or resistance, they teach various paths to great enlightenment, providing instruction, exhortation, encouragement, and inspiration, causing beings to dwell in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes and dwells in the two kinds of emptiness that are ultimately boundless; although they know all phenomena to be like dreams and...
Like an illusion, and even like a magical transformation, they are entirely not truly existent; their intrinsic nature is empty.
Yet, they are able to establish what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, up to what is conditioned and what is unconditioned, and even that which can realize the fruit of stream-entry.
This is that which can realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, all of which is without confusion.
Subhūti, if you know this most marvelous and rare quality of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which does not exist among śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas at all.
It cannot be measured. One cannot even respond to the eloquence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, let alone be able to match it against other sentient beings.
(End of Volume Seventy-nine) Subhūti said: "What is called the most marvelous and rare dharma?"
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are both non-existent. The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they give to all sentient beings—from the Buddhas above down to the animals below—with perfect equality and without any discrimination.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and all sentient beings is [empty]."

Emptiness is entirely without differentiation; therefore, there is no thought of difference. By virtue of the absence of thoughts of difference, one shall attain the fruit of non-differentiation and non-conceptuality.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects: "I have taken up this body for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
To whoever comes seeking, I must certainly give. Upon seeing a beggar, he then reflects thus:
Now, within this context, who gives and who receives? What is the object given? By what means is it given? For what purpose is it given? And how is it given?
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is entirely unapprehendable. Why is this so? Because such phenomena [are as follows].
All things are ultimately empty. Within the dharma of emptiness, there is neither giving nor taking.

Abiding in this emptiness while practicing generosity, when one’s internal or external possessions are cut away for the sake of others, the mind is free from anger or resentment. One simply contemplates that sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely empty:
who is it that cuts me? Who is it that undergoes the cutting? And who, moreover, is observing emptiness?

Subhūti said, "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also able to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), what difference is there between them and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas?
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattva mahāsattvas and Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas both abide in the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena (*dharmāṇām aviśeṣatā*).
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they seek perfect and universal [knowledge]."
It is known. They are called the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. When they reach the ultimate state, they are named Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Regarding all phenomena, their specific and general characteristics, they illuminate them clearly without darkness;

being pure and fully endowed [with these qualities], when abiding in the causal stage, they are named the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. If they reach the resultant stage, they are named Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Awakening.
The worldly gift of Dharma and the supramundane gift of Dharma (from the fourteenth leaf of scroll three hundred and eighty to the ninth leaf of scroll eighty-one;
all are titled with their characteristics, namely the two gifts of the supramundane noble Dharma-wealth and the Dharma).
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is skillful in dharmas and skillful in syllables.

Because he is skillful in all dharmas and all syllables, he also attains skillfulness regarding the absence of syllables (*anakṣara*). By virtue of this skillfulness, he is able to teach sentient beings the dharma with syllables and the dharma without syllables;
he teaches the dharma with syllables for the sake of the dharma without syllables. Why is this? Because it is apart from syllables.

It is without words; there is no dharma distinct from the Buddha-dharma. That which transcends all words is called the true Buddha-dharma, because all dharmas and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and characterized by the emptiness of the limitless.

Subhūti said: "If all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty, empty of limits, and transcend all syllables, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and all sentient beings is ultimately unapprehendable.
How, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice all phenomena? And how does he proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Having seen that all phenomena are entirely empty, one proclaims all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings;
yet, one apprehends no sentient being at all, nor does one apprehend any phenomenon, nor any mark of emptiness."
Neither increasing nor decreasing, neither grasping nor abandoning—by reason of these causes and conditions, although one speaks of all phenomena, there is nothing that is spoken of.
Subhūti, when one contemplates all phenomena in this manner, one attains unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena.
By virtue of this knowledge, one does not destroy phenomena and is free from dualistic discrimination, thereby proclaiming the truth for the sake of all sentient beings as it truly is. (Volume 81)
Ultimately, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they preach the Dharma to all sentient beings as is appropriate.

Although they do not differentiate or dismantle the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are nonetheless able to establish sentient beings in accordance with reality, causing them to dwell securely in the stage (*bhūmi*) in which they ought to abide. Although they apprehend neither sentient beings nor any phenomena whatsoever, they nevertheless cause them—
Sentient beings are liberated from the conceptualization of false inversion and attachment. This is by means of neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this so?

Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is without bondage and without liberation. That which is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—without bondage and without liberation—is not "all phenomena.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are ultimately pure. Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding practice...
At the time of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, one dwells within the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
That is to say, Subhūti, by taking non-abiding as the skillful means, all phenomena are without abode;
all phenomena are empty and without abode. Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable.
All phenomena are empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and unapprehendable. It is not that because they lack intrinsic nature and are unapprehendable that there is anything for them to abide in.

By means of these various emptinesses, the bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the elimination of all phenomena and is also able to teach and demonstrate them to sentient beings as they truly are, yet without deviating from or transcending the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Why is this? Because the true nature of all phenomena is...
This is the dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality. This dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality are all devoid of intrinsic nature and cannot be transcended. (Volume 82)

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the realm of suchness and the limit of reality of suchness are not subject to transition or transcendence, are all phenomena different from the dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality?
The Buddha said, "All phenomena are not different from the dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality.
Subhūti said, "If all phenomena are not different from the dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality..."
How does the Blessed One establish that black dharmas bring about black maturation, namely the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts?
How does he establish that white dharmas bring about white maturation, namely humans and gods?

How does he establish that black-and-white dharmas bring about black-and-white maturation, namely certain classes of animals, hungry ghosts, and humans and gods? How does he establish that which is neither black nor...

Wholesome dharmas bring about the maturation of dharmas that are neither black nor white—namely, the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, such distinctions between cause and effect are established based on conventional truth; they are not established based on ultimate truth."
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it cannot be said that there is a distinction between cause and effect. Within the ultimate truth, the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is indivisible;
it is beyond verbal expression and demonstration. How, then, could there be a distinction between cause and effect?
Within the ultimate truth, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, because it is ultimately empty and boundlessly empty. Furthermore, Subhūti...

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "If the distinctions among the fruits of the noble ones are established based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then all foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should possess the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to and including enlightenment (*bodhi*). The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Do all foolish ordinary beings know conventional truth and ultimate truth as they truly are? Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One."
One knows them as they truly are: that they should possess the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Yet, ordinary foolish worldlings do not know the conventional truth and the ultimate truth as they truly are;

for them there is no noble path and no cultivation of the noble path. How, then, could there be the distinctions of the fruits of the noble ones? Only the noble ones are able to [know this] as it truly is.
In truth, one knows that there is the noble path within both conventional truth and ultimate truth, and there is the cultivation of the noble path;
therefore, the distinctions among the fruits of sainthood exist. Subhūti said: "If one cultivates the noble path, does one obtain the fruit of sainthood? The Buddha said: "No, Subhūti.
It is not by cultivating the noble path that one can obtain the fruit of sainthood, nor is it by not cultivating the noble path that one can obtain the fruit of sainthood. Not...
One does not attain the fruit of sainthood apart from the noble path, nor does one attain the fruit of sainthood while abiding within the noble path.
Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), neither the path nor the fruit of the path can be apprehended.

Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishes various distinctions of the fruits of sainthood for the sake of sentient beings, he does not conceptually differentiate such fruits as being within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The realms, or the unconditioned realm—thus are they established as distinctions. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is no conceptual differentiation, why does the Blessed One say that the severing of the three fetters is called the fruit of stream-entry; the attenuation of desire and hatred is called the fruit of once-returning;
the permanent exhaustion of the five lower fetters is called the fruit of non-returning; and the permanent exhaustion of the five higher fetters is called [Arhatship]?"
The fruit of arhatship consists in causing all phenomena that are subject to origination to become phenomena subject to cessation; this is called the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
The permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Buddha told Subhūti:

"What you have spoken of as the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete [enlightenment] of the Buddhas..."
“...equal enlightenment. Is such a noble fruit conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Subhūti replied, “It is entirely unconditioned; it is not conditioned.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “Within the unconditioned dharma, is there any conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*)?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti, “Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts for the sake of sentient beings...”
They proclaim all phenomena, yet do not discriminate regarding what are called the characteristics of phenomena.
They themselves have no attachment to any phenomena, and they are also able to teach others to have no attachment to any phenomena—meaning that they have no attachment to any phenomena whatsoever.
Because they are without attachment, they attain unimpededness in all places, just like the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Regarding those who have awakened to what is manifested by transformation: although they engage in all dharmas, they neither accept nor cling to their fruits, acting solely for the sake of bringing sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
Subhūti, it is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
he abides nowhere in any dharma, nor is he obstructed by anything. Why is this? Because he has thoroughly mastered the true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
(The Chapter on the Characteristics of All Meritorious Qualities ends).
Fascicle 383, leaf 17— (The Chapter on the Equality of All Dharmas)—
to fascicle 386, leaf 11.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How does one thoroughly penetrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?

The Buddha said, "To have no activity whatsoever regarding all phenomena—this is called thoroughly penetrating the true reality of all phenomena; that is, to have no conceptual discrimination regarding the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti asked, "How does one penetrate the fact that all phenomena lack any substantial entity? The Buddha told Subhūti, "Those [phenomena]..."
“Does that which is emanated by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, possess any substantial reality?
Is it based upon such substantial reality that there is defilement and purification, and the wandering through the five destinies? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.

It is not based upon that thing that there is defilement and purification, nor is there the cycle of birth and death through the five destinies. The Buddha said, “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices...”
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one thoroughly realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; it is likewise so.
One penetrates the fact that all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality. Subhūti asked: "Are all phenomena like a magical illusion?
The Buddha said: "All phenomena are like a magical illusion. (End of Scroll 83) Subhūti said: "If all phenomena are like a magical illusion..."
"Regarding those who manifest through transformation, none possess any real dharmas; nor do they possess any real saṃsāra within the five destinies, nor any real liberation from birth and death.
How then can they have the superior activity of a great being toward sentient beings? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas originally practiced the bodhisattva path, they did not perceive any sentient beings who could be liberated from the three realms. Why is this?"
Regarding all phenomena, one knows, sees, and penetrates them as being entirely like illusions and transformations, and not at all substantially existent. Subhūti asked:
"For what purpose does one practice regarding all phenomena? The Buddha told Subhūti: "If sentient beings [regard] all phenomena..."
If they were to understand that [sentient beings] are like illusions, then Bodhisattvas would not practice the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons for the sake of sentient beings.
Since sentient beings themselves are unable to know that all are like illusory transformations, for this reason, Bodhisattvas [practice] for incalculable eons.

"For the sake of all sentient beings, one practices the bodhisattva path. Subhūti said, "If all phenomena are like dreams, like illusions, and even like cities of Gandharvas, where do the sentient beings being transformed reside, so that they may be rescued and brought out [of saṃsāra]?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "The sentient beings being transformed reside in the false conceptualization of names and signs. From these..."
He delivers them by uprooting false conceptualization regarding names and signs. Subhūti asked: "What is meant by 'name' and what is meant by 'sign'?
The Buddha said: "All names are merely provisional designations. They are established as names to express various meanings, yet none of them possess true existence.
Fools and ordinary worldlings falsely cling to them; however, the bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means."
For the sake of all sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma that is free from names. What are its characteristics? Subhūti, there are two kinds of characteristics:
first, the characteristic of form; second, the characteristic of the formless. As for all forms—whether past, future, or present—

Whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near—within these momentary phenomena that are empty, foolish ordinary beings engage in conceptualization and attachment;

this is called the mark of form (*rūpa-nimitta*). Within all those formless phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), foolish ordinary beings grasp at marks and conceptualize, thereby giving rise to various afflictions; this is called the mark of the formless (*arūpa-nimitta*).

The bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means, instructs all sentient beings to distance themselves from dualistic characteristics and further teaches them to abide within the realm of signlessness,
ensuring they do not fall into the attachment of the two extremes— namely, that "this is a characteristic" and "this is signlessness."
Subhūti said, "All names and signs are merely conventional designations. How, then, can one personally advance in the wholesome dharmas and also cause others to advance?

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If, among all phenomena, there were even the slightest real entity that possessed names and signs, then a bodhisattva would not personally advance in the wholesome dharmas, nor would they cause others to advance."
Because among all phenomena there is not the slightest substantial reality in either names or characteristics, the bodhisattva,
by means of signlessness as a skillful method, is able to bring all phenomena to perfection.
All Buddha-dharmas are increased by training in signlessness, non-attention, and non-mental-application. Why is this?
Apart from the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there are no other essential dharmas to be learned.
This is because these three gateways to liberation encompass all sublime and wholesome dharmas. Thus, one who can train in these three gateways to liberation...

One is able to study the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and likewise able to study the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), even unto all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
(Fascicle 85, Leaf 5) Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he understands the dharmas such as the five aggregates, etc., exactly as they are, in their successive relations..."
[Subhūti asked: "Is it not the case that the differentiation [of phenomena] destroys the dharma-realm? And even up to:

is it not the case that all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas destroy the dharma-realm? The Buddha told Subhūti: "If there were any other dharmas obtainable apart from the dharma-realm..."

One might say that those phenomena can destroy the *dharmadhātu*; however, since no phenomenon apart from the *dharmadhātu* can be found, there is no other phenomenon capable of destroying the *dharmadhātu*.
Knowing that no phenomenon exists apart from the *dharmadhātu*, one does not establish or proclaim it as something else.

Therefore, there is nothing that can destroy the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, Subhūti, you should train in the dharma-realm as having the characteristic of being non-dual, undifferentiated, and indestructible.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If one wishes to train in the dharma-realm, in what should one train?
The Buddha said: "One should train in all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Why? Because all phenomena enter into the dharma-realm. Subhūti said:
"For what reason is it said that all dharmas enter the dharma-realm?

The Buddha replied, "Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the nature of all dharmas is such that they all enter the dharma-realm. They possess no marks of differentiation; this is not due to the Buddha's teaching. Why is this?
Because there is not a single dharma that does not enter the dharma-realm, which is signless, unconditioned, and empty of intrinsic nature. Therefore..."
"One who wishes to study the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) should study all phenomena (sarvadharma). If one studies all phenomena, one is studying the dharma-realm.
Subhūti said: "If all phenomena enter the dharma-realm, being non-dual and without distinction, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva [study it]?"
"One should train in the perfection of wisdom, and even train in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
Blessed One, it is not that within the dharmadhātu there are such various conceptual distinctions;

would it not be that by means of these conceptual distinctions, bodhisattvas act in a state of inversion, giving rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) within that which is free from conceptual proliferation? Blessed One, the dharmadhātu is not one."
All phenomena are not separate from the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is itself all phenomena, and all phenomena are themselves the dharma-realm.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so, it is so. Within the true dharma-realm, there are no various conceptual proliferations or discursive elaborations.
Subhūti, all phenomena are not the dharma-realm, yet there is no dharma-realm existing apart from all phenomena. One.
All phenomena are the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm is all phenomena.
If one perceives any phenomenon as being separate from the dharma-realm, that is not the correct way to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are the dharma-realm, yet through skillful means, they rely upon nameless and signless phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings.
This is an explanation by way of names and signs. It is like a skilled illusionist who, holding a few objects, manifests various kinds of diverse forms and appearances before a crowd.
Ignorant men and women, having seen them, are struck with wonder and amazement. Among them, those who possess wisdom reflect thus:
"How is it that this person can manifest such things? There is no real substance to be found herein, yet he causes the multitude to perceive them."
There is no real entity, yet one forms the perception of a real entity.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they do not perceive any dharma apart from the true dharmadhātu, nor do they perceive the dharmadhātu as being apart from all dharmas.
Furthermore, neither sentient beings nor the substantial entities designated as such can be apprehended; yet, through various skillful means, one is able to teach the true dharma-dhātu.

Because the true dharma-dhātu is established as being without distinction throughout its beginning, middle, and end, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to skillfully teach the true dharma-dhātu, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying the buddha-fields.
...the earth. He cultivates the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (The Chapter on the Equality of All Dharmas ends.
Volume 386, leaf 12 (The Chapter on the Immovable) through Volume 390, where Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"If all sentient beings, as well as the gifts given by sentient beings, are all unapprehendable, then for what..."
"For what reason does one practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas take the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as their measure, they practice the perfection of wisdom.

If the limit of sentient beings were different from the limit of reality, then one should not practice the perfection of wisdom; however, because the limit of sentient beings is not different [from the limit of reality]..."
The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). For this reason, one practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) for the sake of all sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If the limit of sentient beings is itself the limit of reality, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
By means of the non-disruption of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one establishes sentient beings within the reality-limit.
Blessed One, if one were to establish sentient beings within the reality-limit, that would be establishing the reality-limit within the reality-limit.
If one were to establish the reality-limit within the reality-limit, that would be establishing self-nature (*svabhāva*) within self-nature; yet, one should not establish self-nature.
Regarding intrinsic nature: how can it be said that, by means of the dharma of the non-destruction of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one establishes sentient beings within the reality-limit?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "One cannot establish the reality-limit within the reality-limit, nor can one establish intrinsic nature within intrinsic nature.
Nevertheless, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to establish sentient beings [therein]."

Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) is not different from the limit of reality. Subhūti, the limit of sentient beings and the limit of reality are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

Subhūti asked: "What is called 'skillful means' (upāyakauśalya), by which skillful means one establishes sentient beings within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without destroying the characteristics of that limit of reality? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"From the first generation of the mind of awakening, the bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means; by means of this skillful means..."
Therefore, in order to establish sentient beings within the practice of giving, he explains that there is no distinction between the prior, middle, and subsequent limits of giving.
Thus, the prior, middle, and subsequent limits of giving are all empty; the giver, the recipient, and the fruit obtained from giving are likewise all empty.
Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nothing at all exists, and nothing can be apprehended. [He] establishes them in existence...
Regarding pure ethical discipline, one should maintain deep compassion for all sentient beings.

One should abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from frivolous chatter, abstain from covetousness, abstain from malice, and abstain from wrong views.
Such phenomena as these are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; they should not [be grasped].
Regarding conceptual attachments, one should cultivate patience (*kṣānti*). Delighting in the dharma of patience, one should subdue the mind and undertake the practice of patience.
As for those phenomena toward which you feel anger, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is entirely empty; how could you give rise to anger or resentment within them?

Seeing that sentient beings are indolent in body and mind and have fallen away from diligence (*vīrya*), one should skillfully exhort and guide them so that they may arouse physical and mental diligence.

They cultivate all wholesome dharmas. Regarding the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of speech, they see that there is no dharma of indolence, no locus of indolence, no time of indolence, and no cause from which indolence could arise.
All these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and do not transcend the principle of emptiness.
Yet, seeing that the minds of sentient beings are largely distracted and agitated, and that they are unable [to remain focused] amidst the objects of desire...
Be tranquil. Through skillful means, cause yourself to enter superior samādhi; do not give rise to distraction or the conceptualization of meditative concentration.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty by their very nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, no phenomenon can be apprehended that could be called "distraction" or "one-pointedness of mind.
If one can abide in this superior concentration, all virtuous deeds will be swiftly fulfilled and perfected. Furthermore...
Acting according to their needs, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

Seeing that sentient beings have meager wisdom, are deluded and inverted, and commit various evil deeds, they employ skillful means to lead them into the gateway of supreme wisdom. They contemplate all phenomena as being empty and quiescent by nature;
thus, all their practices of body, speech, and mind proceed toward the nectar (*amṛta*), and having attained the fruit of the nectar, they shall surely [attain] the nectar itself.
This is called the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of bodhisattva mahāsattvas when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By virtue of this skillful means, they establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
yet are able not to destroy the characteristic of the limit of reality.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has realized, as it truly is, that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty,
they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and proclaim the Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if the emptiness of the internal were not empty by its very nature, or if the emptiness of the external, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, were also not empty by their very nature, then bodhisattvas would not teach sentient beings that all phenomena are empty by their very nature.
To speak in such a way would destroy the emptiness of intrinsic nature; however, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is indeed [empty].
The principle is indestructible; it is neither eternal nor annihilated. Why is this so? Because the principle of intrinsic emptiness has no direction and no location;
it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. This principle of emptiness is also called the "abiding of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*); within it, there are no phenomena.
It is without accumulation and without dispersal; without decrease and without increase; without arising and without cessation; without defilement and without purity.

This is the fundamental nature in which all dharmas abide. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell securely within it, perceiving no dharma as having a point of departure or a destination, because all dharmas fundamentally have no place of abiding. Therefore, it is called the "Abiding of Dharmas" (dharmasthiti).
Subhūti, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, all phenomena are unapprehendable.
Although bodhisattva mahāsattvas proclaim various teachings on the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of sentient beings, those sentient beings are in fact unapprehendable.
Out of compassion for those who have fallen into inverted dharmas, they deliver them and cause them to abide in non-inverted dharmas. That which is non-inverted is called "non-..."
Subhūti, within the state that is free from conceptual differentiation and free from error, there are no phenomena whatsoever. This non-existence is itself intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Abiding therein, bodhisattva mahāsattvas perceive sentient beings fallen into erroneous conceptions;
through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they cause them to attain liberation from all phenomena and also cause them to be liberated from the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

It likewise brings about liberation from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and other uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). Why is this?

Because the four foundations of mindfulness and other uncontaminated phenomena are not, like the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), without arising, without cessation, signless (*animitta*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*);
they too would have to be liberated [from themselves]. The ultimate truth is precisely intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
This is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). It is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas (the end of the eighty-seventh fascicle).
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present take this emptiness of intrinsic nature as their Buddha-eye;
there has never been one who appeared in the world apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Subhūti said, “Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice with the understanding that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they never lose or impair that emptiness of intrinsic nature;
that is to say, they do not grasp at any phenomenon as being other than the emptiness of its intrinsic nature. The Buddha told Subhūti, “So it is, so it is.
It is just as you have said: all phenomena are not other than the emptiness of their intrinsic nature; they are the emptiness of their intrinsic nature.”
They are not different from all phenomena; all phenomena are themselves intrinsic emptiness, and intrinsic emptiness is itself all phenomena.

If all phenomena were different from intrinsic emptiness, or if intrinsic emptiness were different from all phenomena, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not observe all phenomena as being different from intrinsic emptiness, nor would they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Bodhi. (Volume Eighty-Eight) Subhūti, apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), there is not a single dharma that is real or permanent, nor one that can be destroyed or severed.
Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is likewise not a single dharma that is real or permanent, nor one that can be destroyed or severed.
It is only the foolish who give rise to divergent conceptions, grasping at dharmas as being distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide...
The perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
One does not grasp at any phenomena, nor does one destroy any phenomena—whether they be empty or non-empty. Why is this?

Because all phenomena do not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy all phenomena; that is to say, "this is a phenomenon" and "this is emptiness. It is, for example, like space, which does not...
The internal space-element does not destroy the external space-element, nor does the external space-element destroy the internal space-element.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena are equally devoid of intrinsic nature and cannot be mutually destroyed;
that is to say, one cannot designate "this is empty" and "this is not empty. (End of Volume Eighty-nine) Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If all phenomena are fundamentally..."

The nature is empty. Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no distinction whatsoever. For what purpose do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell and give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, making this vow:
"I shall proceed toward and realize vast, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi"?
World-Honored One, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi of all buddhas has no dualistic mode of activity; it is not two.
The modes of practice can realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is.

Enlightenment is non-dual and without discrimination. If one practices regarding enlightenment with dualistic characteristics or engages in discrimination, one will certainly be unable to realize it."
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not practice with respect to awakening by means of dualistic marks, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination;

they give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment while abiding nowhere at all. Regarding all phenomena, they do not practice with respect to dualistic marks, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination;
they practice nothing at all, and thus are able to proceed toward and realize the vast, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti!
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that one seeks cannot be realized by practicing with dualistic characteristics.

All enlightenment is entirely without practice; that is to say, one does not practice with respect to any phenomena. Why is this? Because all enlightenment does not take names and sounds as its objective support, nor does it grasp at a self or what belongs to a self;
that is to say, one does not form the thought, "I am practicing with respect to all phenomena."
Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not proceed by way of grasping, nor does it proceed by way of relinquishing.
Subhūti said: "If it does not proceed by way of grasping, nor by way of relinquishing, where then does that bodhi proceed?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Where does the bodhi of the emanation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of all Buddhas proceed? Subhūti said:
The emanation bodies of all Buddhas are in reality non-existent; how, then, can it be said that they have a place where they act, whether taking or relinquishing?
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "In what place would the bodhi of an arhat within a dream function? Subhūti replied:

All Arhats have eternally exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*); their hindrances of lethargy and sleep (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*) and their entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are both extinguished, and they ultimately have no dreams.
How, then, could there be awakening within a dream? Wherever there is activity—whether grasping or rejecting—the Buddha said:
"The awakening of all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is also like this; it is not practiced for the sake of grasping, nor is it practiced for the sake of rejecting."
“There is no place for practice, because their intrinsic nature is empty. Subhūti said, “One does not practice regarding any phenomena;
yet without abiding in the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, one brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies buddha-fields, and attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said, “Not so, Subhūti. Although there is no place for practice regarding any enlightenment, nevertheless, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...”
O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, one must practice all dharmas and abide in the bodhisattva’s sublime supernatural powers to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields;
only then will one attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, one who wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of sentient beings.
Having cultivated all meritorious qualities until they are perfected, one then realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is utterly tranquil and non-existent.
There is not even the slightest dharma that can increase or decrease, arise or cease, be severed or eternal, be defiled or purified, attain a fruit, or realize clear observation.
One should know that because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva establishes dharmas by relying on conventional verbal expression, they speak of practicing the perfection of wisdom;
yet, having realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature as it truly is, they realize the unconditioned.
"Supreme perfect enlightenment is not the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Why? Because within the true ultimate reality, no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended.
Subhūti said: "If all phenomena are unapprehendable, how does one practice the conduct of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*), and how can one attain unsurpassed enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "In former times, you relied upon the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) to abandon..."

When one abandons all afflictions, attains the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), dwells in the concentration of immediate succession (*ānantarya-samādhi*), and realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), or the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship— did you, at that time, perceive any sentient being, or their mind, or the path, or the fruits of the paths?
“Is there anything that can be apprehended? Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said, “If at that time you apprehended nothing at all, how could you say that you have attained the fruit of arhatship? Subhūti replied, “It is spoken of in accordance with worldly convention;
it is not in accordance with the ultimate truth. The Buddha told Subhūti, “So it is, so it is. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus.”
It is according to conventional designation, not according to ultimate truth, Subhūti. It is by relying on conventional designation that all phenomena are established;
it is by relying on conventional designation that sentient beings are established, and that bodhisattvas and buddhas are established—not by relying on ultimate truth.
Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma that can increase or decrease, benefit or harm, in regard to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty.
Since bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot even find the observation of the intrinsic emptiness of all dharmas, how much less could there be any [increase or decrease] in all dharmas?

It is so, Subhūti. Thus do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and benefit sentient beings, doing so constantly and without interruption. (The "Chapter on Being Immovable" concludes.)
Fascicle 390, Leaf 18 (The Chapter on Maturing Sentient Beings), up to Fascicle 392, where Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the bodhisattva path so that it becomes fully perfected?"
"One is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Buddha told Subhūti:
