"When practicing all dharmas, if one does not apprehend any dharma and yet does not distance oneself from any dharma, then one can fulfill the cultivation of the bodhisattva path."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom,
through skillful means (upāyakauśalya), one neither unites with nor disperses any phenomena.”
"All phenomena. Why is this? Because such phenomena as these all lack an intrinsic nature that can be joined or separated.
Śāriputra said: "If all phenomena are entirely devoid of an intrinsic nature that can be joined or separated, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
One should give rise to the *prajñāpāramitā* and train therein.

If one does not train in the *prajñāpāramitā*, one will ultimately be unable to attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is so, it is so. To realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there must be skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."

Śāriputra, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if one were to perceive any dharma whose intrinsic nature (svabhāva) could be apprehended, then it would be something to be grasped.
Since no dharma is perceived whose intrinsic nature can be apprehended, what is there to be grasped?
That is to say, one does not grasp "this is the perfection of wisdom," nor even "this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) of all Buddhas."
"This is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); this is a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva or a tathāgata.
Śāriputra, one who understands, as they truly are, that the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is ungraspable—this is the "ungraspable perfection" (*agrāhya-pāramitā*).
This very ungraspable perfection is the "unobstructed perfection" (*anāvaraṇa-pāramitā*). Such an unobstructed perfection is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Pāramitā. Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in this. When training therein, they do not even apprehend that there is any dharma whatsoever with intrinsic nature to be learned;
for within such dharmas whose very nature is the absence of intrinsic nature, [they train].
What are the dharmas of ordinary beings? What are the dharmas of stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners?
What are the dharmas of arhats and pratyekabuddhas? What are the dharmas of bodhisattvas? What are the dharmas of Tathāgatas?
Since all dharmas are unapprehendable, by means of what dharma can they be designated? Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "If all dharmas..."
All are devoid of intrinsic nature; none exist as real entities. Based upon what thing could one discern:

"This is an ordinary person," "These are the dharmas of an ordinary person," and so on, up to "This is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha," or "These are the dharmas of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"?
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "What do you think? Does there truly exist any dharma at all?"
"Is it as foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp it? Śāriputra replied, "No, World-Honored One. It is only due to their perversion that foolish, ordinary worldlings hold such a view.

"Śāriputra, a practitioner of the perfection of wisdom who is skillful in means, although they contemplate all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature and entirely non-existent, nevertheless, relying upon conventional truth, they give rise to..."

They proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and proclaim it in various ways for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to attain correct understanding and remain far removed from perversion.
(End of Volume Ninety-One) Śāriputra, one does not perceive even the slightest substantial reality of sentient beings;
it is only by relying on worldly convention that one speaks of "sentient beings" as a designation. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they abide...
Abiding in the two truths, he proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings—namely, the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.

Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend a single nature, nor a diverse nature, nor a collective nature, nor a distinct nature among all phenomena, he nevertheless dons such great armor of merit."
They manifest the three realms, yet do not manifest a conditioned realm, nor do they manifest an unconditioned realm.

Although they transform sentient beings to liberate them from the three realms, they do not apprehend any sentient being at all, nor do they apprehend the designation "sentient being. There is neither bondage nor liberation;
neither defilement nor purity. The distinctions between the various realms of existence cannot be discerned; there is no karma and no afflictions, nor is there...

Regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*): how could there be a self (*ātman*) and sentient beings (*sattva*) transmigrating through the various realms, manifesting in the manifold distinctions of the three worlds?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is so, it is so. If there were classes of sentient beings that existed previously and later ceased to exist..."
If Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas were subject to faults—such as the various realms of birth and death existing first and then ceasing to exist—then Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas would indeed have faults.
However, the principle that what did not previously exist comes into being later is likewise untenable. Therefore, the Tathāgata appears in the world.
If he does not appear in the world, the characteristics of phenomena remain eternally constant and never undergo change.
Since all phenomena are like empty space, how could there be birth and death within the various realms of existence? How could there be the maturing of sentient beings to bring them to liberation?

They exist only as conventional designations. Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of such phenomena is entirely empty, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having heard this truthfully from the Buddhas of the past, act for the sake of liberating sentient beings from their inverted attachments.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. At the time of setting out, they do not form such thoughts as:
"I have already attained or shall attain this Dharma," or "I have already delivered or shall deliver those sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death to which they are attached."
He constantly reflects: "I shall certainly realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring true benefit to all sentient beings;
that is to say, I shall cause them to be liberated from delusion, error, and inversion, and from the suffering of birth and death as they wander through the various realms of existence."
Śāriputra, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas liberate sentient beings from the delusions, errors, and inversions of the various realms of birth and death, they apprehend nothing therein;
it is only in accordance with worldly convention that they say such a thing exists.
Śāriputra, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform this work, they do not apprehend either sentient beings or any phenomena whatsoever, nor do they form [such conceptualizations].
"This is the thought: 'By means of this Dharma, I shall discipline all classes of sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is called the Great Path to Bodhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
By practicing this path, how does one employ skillful means to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields? The Buddha told Subhūti: "From the very beginning..."
The generation of the mind of awakening, all dharmas practiced therein, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas constitute the Great Path to Bodhi for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

By practicing this path, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the Buddha-fields, yet they remain free from any conceptualization of "sentient beings" or "Buddha-fields. (The Chapter on Maturing Sentient Beings concludes.)
Fascicle 393-4, Leaf (The Chapter on Purifying the Buddha-field); Fascicle 394-8, Leaf.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought: "What dharma is called the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Abiding in this path, one is able to don the great armor of merit and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings. The Buddha knew his thought.
He addressed Subhūti, saying: "In sum, all dharmas are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If one does not train in all dharmas, one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: "If the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty..."
"How does one train in all phenomena? Would it not be the case, Blessed One, that you are engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena that are beyond proliferation?

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "If sentient beings were to know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not need to train in all phenomena in order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings."
They establish and proclaim [the Dharma] because sentient beings do not know that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in all phenomena and, having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, establish and proclaim them for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti, when first beginning their training, they should carefully examine the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; it is utterly non-existent.
It is so. There is only attachment to that which is produced by the coming together [of conditions]. I shall examine the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as being ultimately empty;
one should not have any attachment therein. Why is this? One should not be attached to emptiness itself.
Even emptiness cannot be apprehended within emptiness; how much less can there be an emptiness that is able to grasp at emptiness?
Subhūti, abiding in this training, one observes the various mental activities of sentient beings—that is, one carefully examines where the mental activities of these sentient beings reside.
Knowing their minds as they truly are, one realizes that they function only through the grasping of what is false and illusory, and then one reflects: "That mind..."
"Since they have already engaged in the false attachments of grasping at a self, I shall bring them to liberation; this will certainly not be difficult.
Having formed this thought, he dwells securely in the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* and provides instruction and admonition:
"Now, you should all distance yourselves from the false attachments of grasping and enter into the True Dharma, cultivating all virtuous practices. He further says: "Practice all dharmas."
However, do not rely on this and become arrogant or indolent. Why is that? Because herein there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the path to enlightenment in this manner, they take non-abiding as their skillful means;
thus, although they practice all dharmas, they abide in none of them whatsoever. Why is that? It is because...
Because their intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the modes of practice are all empty, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, although able to attain the fruit of stream-entry, does not abide therein;
although able to attain the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, he does not abide therein.
Subhūti asked: "For what reason and by what causal condition does he not abide therein? The Buddha replied:
Subhūti, there are two reasons: first, that fruit has no intrinsic nature whatsoever, such that neither the one who dwells nor the place of dwelling can be apprehended;
second, that he does not give rise to complacency regarding it, and therefore does not dwell therein. That bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"From the time I first generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at all times, there has been nothing else..."
They conceive only the thought of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; how could they dwell in any other fruit in the interim?
From the attainment of the first bhūmi until the attainment of the tenth bhūmi, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never harbor any other thoughts;
at all times their minds are undistracted, and every action of body, speech, and mind that arises is inseparable from the bodhicitta.
Together, they abide in the bodhicitta and give rise to the path of enlightenment, their minds not being disturbed by other objects. Subhūti said:
"If all things are non-arising, how can the path of enlightenment arise? The Buddha said:
"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm of all phenomena remains eternally as it is. Yet sentient beings are unable to understand this."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of benefiting others, give rise to the path to enlightenment.

By means of this path to enlightenment, they rescue sentient beings and cause them to be eternally liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death. Subhūti asked: "Is it by means of a path that has arisen that one attains enlightenment?"
"Is it by means of a path that is non-arising that one attains bodhi? Or is it by means of a path that is both arising and non-arising that one attains bodhi?
Or is it by means of a path that is neither arising nor non-arising that one attains bodhi? The Buddha said, "No.
Subhūti asked, "How then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain bodhi? The Buddha told Subhūti, "One does not attain bodhi by means of a path, nor..."
One does not attain bodhi by means of what is not the Way. Why is this? Because bodhi is itself the Way, and the Way is itself bodhi.
Subhūti said: "If all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained the path to bodhi, they should have already attained bodhi."
"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, further teach those immeasurable Buddha-dharmas to them, causing them to cultivate and realize them?
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Do you think that the Buddha attains bodhi? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha is itself bodhi, and bodhi is itself the Buddha; therefore, one should not say that the Buddha attains bodhi. The Buddha said, "It is as follows..."
It is so. How could it be said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained awakening when they have not yet perfected the path to awakening?
Subhūti, it is only when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have perfected all dharmas [that they may be said to have attained awakening].
...up until the point where, having fully perfected the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable sublime dharmas of all Buddhas, immediately thereafter,
through the sublime wisdom associated with the vajra-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) in a single kṣaṇa,

one eternally severs the continuity of the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya-vāsanā*) of both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*), and realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is then called...
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has attained great mastery over all phenomena and brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify a buddha-field?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate attainment, they constantly purify their own coarse [physical] body."
Heavyness of speech and heaviness of mind, as well as the purification of the heaviness of others' bodies, speech, and minds—
by purifying these three types of heaviness in oneself and others, one is then able to adorn and purify the Buddha-land sought.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to great vows and, with diligent vigor, cultivate all dharmas themselves and also exhort others to cultivate all dharmas. Having performed these deeds, they further make this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be far from [the Dharma]."
They are detached from all phenomena. By means of these practices and vows, they are able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields they seek (The Chapter on Adorning and Purifying Buddha-fields ends).
Fascicle 394, Leaf 9 (The Chapter on Expedient Means for the Pure Land).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed category of rightness, or do they abide in the..."
“Are they in the group of those destined for certainty? The Buddha said, “They all abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature; they do not abide in the group of those who are not destined.

Subhūti asked, “In what kind of fixed destiny of the right nature do they abide? The Buddha said, “They abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature of the Buddha-vehicle; they do not abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature of the two vehicles.
Subhūti asked, “At what time do they abide in the fixed destiny of the right nature? Is it at the initial generation of the mind? “No.”
"Is it one who has regressed from the stage? Or is it one in their final existence?

The Buddha said, "Whether it be one who has first resolved for awakening, one who has not regressed, or one in their final existence—all such abide in the fixed category of the certainty of enlightenment (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Subhūti asked, 'Once one abides in the fixed category of the certainty of enlightenment, can they still fall into the various evil destinies?
The Buddha said, 'Certainly not; they shall never again fall into the various evil destinies. Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas..."
From the first generation of the mind of awakening, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices all dharmas and subdues and eradicates all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
For this reason, it is impossible that these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas would fall into the evil destinies.

Subhūti said: "If one who has accomplished such roots of goodness and merit is no longer reborn in the various evil states, for what reason does the Blessed One frequently speak to the assembly of his own past lives—whether hundreds or thousands—in which he was also born in the various evil states?
At those times, where were those roots of goodness? The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is not that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
While others receive bodies in the miserable realms due to impure karma, [the Bodhisattva] receives such a body solely for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Subhūti, having accomplished such skillful means, he may take the body of an animal.
When a hunter approaches with the intent to cause him harm, he immediately gives rise to unsurpassed patience and compassion, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to that person. Thus, he himself—

He sacrifices his own body and life, yet does not harm others. By this cause and condition, one should know that because the bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to benefit all sentient beings and to swiftly bring great compassion to fulfillment, although he manifests in the body of an animal, he is not defiled by the faults of an animal.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Abiding in what wholesome dharma?"
Having received such a body, the Buddha told Subhūti: "All wholesome dharmas should be brought to perfection.

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should, throughout that interval, constantly train to perfect all wholesome dharmas.
Having so trained, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and forever sever all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)."
[They] continue until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "How is it that one who has accomplished all such pure, noble, and untainted dharmas is born in the evil destinies and receives the body of an animal?
The Buddha said, "When a Tathāgata manifests the body of an animal through transformation, is that a real animal that undergoes such suffering? Subhūti replied, "No."
“World-Honored One,” [he asked]. The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Although they have accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they manifest and receive various bodies such as those of animals;
yet in reality they are not those [beings], nor are they defiled by their faults. Subhūti said: “In what do they abide?”
Regarding these pure and sublime dharmas, they are able to exercise such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Abiding in the *prajñāpāramitā*, one is able to exercise such skillful means;
although one manifests various bodies throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, one does not give rise to attachment therein. Why is this? Because regarding all phenomena..."

There is nothing at all to be apprehended. One cannot apprehend that which defiles, that which is defiled, or the causal conditions for defilement, because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
Subhūti, this is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
By abiding in this, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti said: "Is it only by abiding in such a perfection..."
“If the *pāramitās* are able to act as skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), do they also abide in other dharmas? The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Are there any dharmas that do not enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*? Why, then, do you further doubt that it abides in other dharmas?
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, if their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty, how does the *prajñāpāramitā* encompass all dharmas?”

“Venerable One, it cannot be said that there is any phenomenon within emptiness that is either included or not included. Subhūti, is it not the case that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty?
“It is so, Blessed One. “Subhūti, if the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, is it not the case that all phenomena are included within emptiness?”

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty. Through the skillful means of universal contemplation of emptiness, one is able to evoke the sublime perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*).

Abiding in this perfection of supernormal powers, one further evokes the sublime super-knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the divine eye, the divine ear, the power of transformation, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*). All...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not mature sentient beings or purify buddha-fields apart from the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*).
Therefore, the perfection of supernormal powers is the path to enlightenment;

all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon this path to seek and proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, whereby they are able to personally fulfill all wholesome dharmas and also [benefit others].
He causes others to cultivate all wholesome dharmas, yet he does not give rise to attachment toward those wholesome dharmas. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all wholesome dharmas is empty; that which is empty of intrinsic nature is not something to which one can become attached.

If there were attachment, there would be a relish for flavor (*āsvāda*); because there is no attachment, there is also no relish for flavor, for within the emptiness of intrinsic nature there is no relish for flavor.
Because they have cultivated the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñāpāramitā) to full completion, they assume various bodies according to their own wishes,
remaining untainted by the defects of suffering or pleasure.
Fascicle 395. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*) are the provisions for enlightenment. All bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice..."

Regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), there is within them no conceptual differentiation or attachment; that is to say, one does not form the thought, "These are all phenomena," nor practice all phenomena for this reason or for that purpose.
These three types of conceptual differentiation and attachment are all absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.
By means of this, all phenomena that are practiced can benefit oneself and also benefit others.
Because they cause all sentient beings to emerge from birth and death and attain nirvāṇa, these are called wholesome dharmas.
They are also called the bodhisattva’s provisions for awakening (*bodhi-sambhāra*), and they are also called the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Because bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have attained, will attain, and are now attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). They also cause sentient beings [to do so].
Having already crossed the great ocean of birth and death, they have realized the bliss of nirvāṇa. (*The Chapter on Expedient Means for the Pure Land ends;
Volume 395, Folio 7, Part One: The Chapter on the Naturelessness of Self-Nature*) Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If such dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what other dharmas are the dharmas of a buddha?"
"Yes. The Buddha told Subhūti: "The qualities of a bodhisattva are themselves the qualities of a Buddha.

This means that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas awaken to all characteristics regarding all phenomena, they shall thereby attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, when Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, regarding all phenomena, in a single moment..."
Having attained manifest perfect enlightenment through corresponding sublime wisdom, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Subhūti, in this way, there is a distinction between a bodhisattva and a Buddha, just as there is a distinction between two noble ones who, though both are noble, differ in their status as those "practicing toward" (*pratipannaka*) or those "abiding in the fruit" (*phalastha*).

Furthermore, within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), while practicing with respect to all phenomena, one has not yet abandoned the obscuration of darkness and has not yet reached the further shore.
When one has not yet attained mastery and has not yet attained the fruit, one is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

When, within the path of liberation, one practices all dharmas, having already abandoned the obscuration of darkness, having reached the other shore, having attained mastery, and having attained the fruit, one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti, this is the difference between a bodhisattva and a Buddha. Although...
"While the positions differ, the dharmas have no distinction. Subhūti said, "If all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), how can there be various distinctions?

The Buddha told Subhūti, "Within the emptiness of own-characteristics, there are no persons (*pudgala*), no karma performed, and no distinctions in the results of maturation (*vipāka*) to be found. Nevertheless, sentient beings, regarding the own-characteristics of all dharmas..."

Being unable to fully comprehend the principle of emptiness, one creates various karmas due to these causes and conditions—namely, creating sinful karma, or creating meritorious karma, or creating immovable karma, or creating untainted karma. Because of creating sinful karma, one may fall into hell.
Some fall into the realm of animals; some fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. Because they perform meritorious karma, they are born in the human realm or among the gods of the desire realm.
Because they perform immovable karma, they are born in the form realm or the formless realm.

Because they perform untainted karma, they attain the fruit of a śrāvaka or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. If they know that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, they may enter into bodhi.
The stage of a Mahāsattva, or the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—the equality of the Four Noble Truths—is itself nirvāṇa.

Such nirvāṇa is not attained by means of the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path, nor is it attained by means of the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; rather, it is realized solely through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
This equanimity is called the attainment of nirvāṇa.
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands suffering yet does not give rise to a mind that clings to suffering as an object?

Although they have forever severed the origin [of suffering], they do not give rise to a mind that clings to the origin as an object. Although they have realized cessation, they do not give rise to a mind that clings to cessation as an object.
Although the mind cultivates the Path, it is able to refrain from giving rise to a mind that grasps at the Path as an object;
rather, it gives rise to a mind that accords with, inclines toward, and enters into unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Regarding all phenomena, it contemplates their true nature.

Subhūti asked, "How does one observe the true nature of all phenomena? The Buddha said, "A bodhisattva mahāsattva observes that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*).

Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, as well as all phenomena, have non-existence (*abhāva*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Such non-existence was not created by any buddha."
It is not something produced by Pratyekabuddhas; it is not something produced by Bodhisattvas; nor is it something produced by Śrāvakas on their paths or fruits.
It is solely for the sake of sentient beings who, regarding all phenomena, do not know and do not see them as they truly are—namely, that they are all empty. Subhūti asked:

"How can one designate various distinct phenomena, such as saying, 'This is hell,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'this is a human,' 'this is a deva,' or 'this is...'"?
"Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, Arhat, Pratyekabuddha—this is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
It is by virtue of these karmas that such designations are established. "World-Honored One, dharmas that lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) necessarily possess no functional activity.

How can it be said that by means of such dharmas one is born in the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts? ||| By means of such dharmas, [one is born in] the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. ||| Just as...

This Dharma gives birth to humans and devas. By means of this Dharma, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the attainment of the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, thereby liberating all sentient beings from birth and death. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is."

It is as you have said. Within phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is impossible to establish any differentiation among phenomena; there is no karma, no fruit, and no functional activity.
Foolish worldlings do not understand that all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very essence.
Through delusion and inversion, one initiates various actions of body, speech, and mind; according to the distinctions among these actions, one receives various bodies.
Based on such differences in the categories of bodies, there are conventionally designated realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans.

Subhūti, it is for the sake of rescuing foolish ordinary beings that one provisionally designates the distinctions of the stages of the noble Dharma and the Vinaya— ranging from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception—
and provisionally designates [the stages] from the Stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Yet, all phenomena have non-existence as their nature.

In phenomena that are by nature without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is truly no distinct phenomenon; there is no karma, no fruit, and no functional activity, because within that which lacks intrinsic nature, it is eternally without intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as you have said, a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature necessarily lacks functional activity.
Are all the paths of cultivation—such as the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship—not likewise without intrinsic nature?
"Is this lack of intrinsic nature [the case] for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha? Is it the lack of intrinsic nature for the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Is it the lack of intrinsic nature for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas? Subhūti replied:

All paths that are cultivated are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). From the stream-enterer and once-returner, up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, these too are devoid of intrinsic nature.
The Buddha asked: "Can a dharma that is devoid of intrinsic nature attain a dharma that is devoid of intrinsic nature?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "Subhūti, both the absence of intrinsic nature and the path—all such dharmas are non-existent."
They are associated, not dissociated; they are formless and invisible; they are non-obstructive and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Fools and ordinary worldlings, deluded and inverted, falsely conceptualize these signless phenomena and give rise to the perception of existing things.
They cling to the five aggregates, perceiving permanence within the impermanent, pleasure within suffering, and [self within the selfless]. In the absence of...

They conceive the notion of a self within what is not-self; they conceive the notion of purity within the impure; and they cling to intrinsic existence within that which is devoid of intrinsic nature.

For these reasons, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas achieve sublime skillful means to rescue sentient beings and establish them in the signless Dharma, causing them to diligently practice and train so as to attain liberation from birth and death and realize the ultimate.
“[This is] the constant bliss of nirvāṇa. Subhūti said, “Is there any phenomenon that is real and not false? The Buddha told Subhūti, “Foolish ordinary beings cling to it;

they perform various karmas. By reason of these causes and conditions, they transmigrate through the various realms of existence and cannot liberate themselves from the manifold sufferings of birth and death. There is only this inverted, false clinging. Now, for their sake, I [shall explain]...”

“Subhūti, explain this meaning at length through analogies so that it may be easily understood. For those who possess wisdom, correct understanding of the meaning of what is taught arises by means of analogies.

Subhūti, if one sees a person in a dream experiencing the pleasures of the five senses, is there therein even the slightest real thing that could cause that person to experience those sensual pleasures? Is there therein any reality?”
Is there truly a cultivation of the path? Based upon that cultivation of the path, is there the abandonment of defilement and the attainment of purity?

Regarding the various images manifested within a clear mirror and the like, do they possess any substantial reality that could serve as a basis for performing karma? Do these images possess any genuine cultivation of the path?
By relying on that cultivation of the path, is there a departure from defilement and the attainment of purity?

Regarding the various echoes produced within deep valleys and the like, do they possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma? Do these echoes possess any genuine cultivation of the path;

by relying on such cultivation of the path, is there a departure from defilement and the attainment of purity? Within various mirages, things appear as if they were water and so forth; do they possess any reality?
Can one rely on the water and such things within a mirage to perform karma? Is there any truly real cultivation of the path within those mirages;

by relying on that cultivation of the path, can one become free from defilement and attain purity? Regarding the actual characteristics manifested within all shadows and reflections, is there any substantial reality upon which one can rely to perform karma?
Within all shadows and reflections, as for their material forms and characteristics, is there any truly real cultivation of the path upon which one can rely...
In that cultivation of the path, is there a separation from defilement and an attainment of purity?

When a magician conjures illusions such as the fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, do these illusory elephants and so forth possess any real substance upon which one could rely to create karma?
Is there any genuine cultivation of the path within an illusory phenomenon? Based upon that cultivation of the path, is there any departure from defilement and attainment of purity?
Regarding the various transformation bodies emanated by the Buddha—do these transformation bodies possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma?
Within a transformation body, is there any genuine cultivation of the path? Based upon that cultivation of the path, is there any departure from defilement and attainment of purity?
"No. Do the things manifested within the City of Gandhavatī possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma?
Is there, within the City of Gandhavatī, any genuine path of cultivation? By relying on such a path of cultivation, can one become free from defilement and attain purity?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Within this city, there is absolutely no real defilement, nor..."
Regarding "purity," the Buddha said: Just as those who are defiled and those who are pure do not truly exist, for this reason, both defilement and purity are also not truly existent.
Why is this? Because sentient beings who dwell upon the notions of "self" and "mine" engage in false conceptualization, claiming that there are those who are defiled and those who are pure;
it is not those who see reality who claim that there are those who are defiled and [those who are pure].
Regarding purity: just as one who perceives reality knows that there is neither defilement nor purity, so too there is neither defilement nor purity.
(The Chapter on the Nature of Non-nature concludes.)

Outline of Volume 396, Leaf 7, through Volume 397, Leaf 15: (Chapter on Ultimate Yoga).
Subhūti said, "If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, for what reason does the Buddha sometimes speak of pure phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "I say that the equality of all phenomena is the pure phenomenon."
“World-Honored One, what is the equality of all phenomena? Subhūti, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, their nature and characteristics remain eternally constant;
this is called the equality of all phenomena. This equality is called the pure dharma.”
This is said to be "pure" based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), not based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is that?
Because within the ultimate truth, there is no conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*) and no proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); all paths of sound and names are cut off. Subhūti said:
"If all phenomena are like what is seen in a dream, like a reflection, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like a magical illusion, like a transformation..."
An emanation body is like a city of Gandharvas; although it appears as if it exists, it lacks any substantial reality.
How can one rely upon such unreal dharmas to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and make this vow, saying:
"I shall fulfill all dharmas; I shall give rise to immeasurable radiance that universally illumines the ten directions without limit"?
"World, I shall produce a single sublime voice that pervades the infinite worlds of the ten directions.

According to the mental states and mental factors of sentient beings, and according to their various inclinations, I shall preach diverse and subtle Dharma-gates for them, causing them to practice diligently so that they may realize supreme benefit and peace.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Is it not the case that the Dharma you have spoken..."
"Is it also like what is seen in a dream? Like a reflection, like an echo, even like a city of Gandharvas? Subhūti replied, "So it is, World-Honored One.

If all phenomena are like what is seen in a dream, and so forth, up to being like a city of Gandharvas, and they all lack any real substance, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva utter truthful words, saying: 'I shall fulfill...'"
All merits, which bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings—World-Honored One, these are not things seen in a dream.
To speak extensively, even the various objects manifested within the City of Fragrance (Gandhavatī) are unable to practice all dharmas, let alone fulfill them;
all other dharmas should likewise be understood as such, for neither is real. The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. Just as..."
What you have described is not a truly existent dharma; it cannot even practice all dharmas, much less fulfill those that are not truly existent.
Furthermore, Subhūti, because all dharmas are not truly existent, one cannot realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All such dharmas are merely conceptual constructions and mental fabrications. Whatever exists [is thus].
All conditioned phenomena are incapable of attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, although these various phenomena can induce the path to enlightenment, they lack the capacity to assist toward its fruition.

This is because these phenomena are unarisen, unoriginated, and devoid of intrinsic characteristics. Thus, from the first production of the thought of awakening, although the bodhisattva mahāsattvas...
They give rise to various forms of excellence in body, speech, and mind, and practice all dharmas, yet they know that all things are like what is seen in a dream,
even like a city of Gandharvas— none of them being truly existent. Furthermore, Subhūti, although these dharmas are not truly existent, if they were not perfected,
one would certainly be unable to mature sentient beings, purify a buddha-field, and realize [buddhahood].
"Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "When the Buddha realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, were the dharmas of a buddha attained said to be so by relying on conventional truth, or by relying on ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is by relying on conventional truth that they are said to be so named."
[Subhūti] replied: "It is attained, but not by relying on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If one relies on the ultimate truth, both the attainer and that which is attained are unattainable.

If it is claimed that this person attains such a dharma, then there is something attained; and for one who has something attained, there is grasping at duality, whereby one cannot attain the fruit, nor can there be clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Subhūti asked: "Is it by grasping at non-duality that one can attain the fruit and have clear realization?"
The Buddha said: "To cling to non-duality is likewise so. If there is neither duality nor non-duality, that is called attaining the fruit and is also called clear realization (abhisamaya).
Why is this? If one clings to the notion that by means of this one can attain the fruit, there is also [the error of] clear realization."
Furthermore, the grasping that one cannot attain the fruit through those [dharmas], nor that there is no clear realization (abhisamaya), is both mere conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
If one is free from conceptual proliferation, only then can it be called the equality of dharmas (dharma-samatā). Subhūti asked:
"If all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), what herein is meant by the equality of dharmas? The Buddha said: "It is where there is absolutely nothing at all."
It has no intrinsic nature, nor does it lack intrinsic nature; it cannot even be described as the nature of equality.
This is what is called the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*). You should know that since the equality of phenomena cannot be described, it cannot be known.
Apart from this equality, no phenomenon can be apprehended; apart from all phenomena, there is no equality. Subhūti, the equality of phenomena is neither ordinary beings nor noble ones (*ārya*).
[Those] cannot both practice it, because it is not their domain. Subhūti asked: "Is the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*) also not the domain within which the Buddhas practice?

The Buddha said: "The equality of phenomena is not the domain within which the noble ones (*ārya*) practice—namely, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth [stage], the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and so on, up to the Buddhas, the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
“[They] are all unable to take the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*) as their objective domain. Subhūti said:
“All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained mastery over all phenomena. How then can it be said that there is an ‘equality of phenomena’?”
"Is it not also beyond the range of the Buddhas' activity? The Buddha said: "If the nature of equality were different from the Buddha, one could say it is the range of the Buddhas' activity.
However, the nature of equality is not different from the Buddha; how then can it be said that the Buddha travels within that range?
Subhūti, you should know this: whether it be the nature of equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings, or the nature of equality of the dharmas of those who follow by faith..."

The nature of equality: whether it be the equality of phenomena for those who follow the Dharma by faith, or the equality of phenomena for those who follow the Dharma through reasoning, or even the equality of phenomena for all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—these are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless. This is the single equality.

They are non-dual and without distinction. Within this equality of all phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), since no forms of equality can be apprehended, therein the characteristics distinguishing ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) from noble ones (*ārya*) also cannot be apprehended. (End of Volume 96) Subhūti said:
"If within the equality of all phenomena, both ordinary beings and noble ones, as well as phenomena and sentient beings, are all non-existent..."
[The question on] differentiation: How do the Three Jewels appear in the world? The Buddha said:
"The Tathāgata, through skillful means regarding the Dharma, is able to establish various differentiations of dharmas within the signless.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if the Tathāgatas did not designate the differentiating characteristics of dharmas for sentient beings, would these classes of sentient beings be able to know them for themselves?"
"No. Subhūti replied, "Sentient beings are unable to know this for themselves.

The Buddha said, "Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through skillful means regarding the signless dharma, although he designates various differentiated marks for the sake of sentient beings, remains entirely unmoved within the equal dharmatā of all phenomena. Subhūti said, "So it is."
Do all foolish ordinary beings likewise remain unmoved within the mark of equality of all phenomena?
It is the same for those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-rank stream-enterers, and even up to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

"Furthermore, are all phenomena not unmoved within the equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)? The Buddha said, "All phenomena and all sentient beings do not transcend the equality of the nature of phenomena;
they are all entirely unmoved within the equality of the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the equality of the nature of all phenomena is itself the equality of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),"

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—ranging from those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), up to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—is the equal nature of phenomena.

If it were the case that because all phenomena and sentient beings are distinct and different, their nature must also be different, then the nature of phenomena would likewise have to be various and distinct for each. How, then, could one perceive [a single nature] within these variously characterized phenomena?

He establishes the single characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not discriminate among phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures? The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Is the nature of all phenomena emptiness? Subhūti replied: "So it is, World-Honored One; the nature of all phenomena is indeed [emptiness]."
"Emptiness. The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Within emptiness, can one find any distinct characteristics of dharmas?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Within emptiness, all distinct characteristics are unfindable.
The Buddha told Subhūti, "From this you should know that the nature of equality is neither all dharmas, nor is it separate from all dharmas."
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "Is the nature of equality conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "The nature of equality is neither conditioned nor unconditioned. Nevertheless, apart from conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena cannot be found;
and apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena likewise cannot be found. Subhūti, if there were a realm of the conditioned..."
If it is the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), these two realms are neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated (*viprayukta*).

They are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being signless (*animitta*). All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak thus based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), not based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth, there can be no activity of body, speech, or mind; it is not apart from them.
The conduct of body, speech, and mind can be apprehended in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
One should know that this is precisely the equality of the conditioned and the unconditioned, which is designated as the ultimate truth.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva without wavering from the ultimate truth, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying the buddha-fields.
The Earth. [One] is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
(End of the Chapter on Ultimate Yoga. Folio 16 of Volume 397. (Chapter on the Immovable Nature of Phenomena.
Subhūti, if all phenomena are equal, their nature of equality is that they are all empty by their very nature. This emptiness of nature exists within existence...
There is none. It is neither an agent nor an action. How then does the unshakable ultimate reality perform the deeds that a bodhisattva ought to perform?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "If sentient beings were to know for themselves that all phenomena are by nature empty, then the Tathāgatas would not manifest supernatural powers or perform marvelous deeds;
that is to say, within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, although there is no movement, yet..."

It causes sentient beings to distance themselves from various deluded thoughts and inversions, establishing them in the emptiness of all phenomena and liberating them from the suffering of birth and death.

This means causing sentient beings to distance themselves from all conceptualizations and also to distance themselves from the conceptualization of all phenomena, thereby establishing them in the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) and liberating them from the suffering of birth and death.
The unconditioned realm is precisely the emptiness of all phenomena; this is spoken according to worldly convention.
"It is called the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*). Subhūti asked, "By virtue of being empty of what are all phenomena said to be empty?

The Buddha told Subhūti, "By virtue of being empty of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), all phenomena are said to be empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) were to perform further transformative acts, would there be any substantial reality therein that was not empty?
Subhūti replied, "All that is transformed lacks any substantial reality whatsoever. (1)
"All things are empty. The Buddha told Subhūti: "Transformation and emptiness—these two dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed.
Both are empty because they are empty of emptiness. One should not discriminate between 'this is emptiness' and 'this is transformation. Why is this?
Because within the nature of emptiness, these two things—emptiness and transformation—cannot be apprehended, for all dharmas are ultimately empty. Furthermore..."
"Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that is not a transformation. All things that are transformations are entirely empty. Subhūti said:
"Worldly aggregates, bases, elements, dependent origination, dependently arisen phenomena, and the members of dependent origination—all these may indeed be transformations.
But what of the supramundane perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth, up to those [attained] by means of them?"
If the various types of persons (*pudgala*) are designated based on those very dharmas that constitute the fruits attained through the Dharma, would these too be transformations?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All mundane and supramundane dharmas are none other than transformations.
Nevertheless, among them, some are transformations of śrāvakas, some are transformations of pratyekabuddhas, and some are transformations of bodhisattvas."
These are emanations of the Tathāgata; some are emanations of afflictions, and some are emanations of wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, it is said that all phenomena are like magical transformations, equal and without distinction. Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the fruits of abandonment—namely, the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, or the stage of a pratyekabuddha—"
"Or the stage of the Tathāgata, which has forever severed the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions—is this also a transformation? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If these various dharmas are conjoined with the two characteristics of arising and ceasing, they are all likewise transformations. "World-Honored One, what dharma is not a transformation?
"Subhūti, if a dharma is not conjoined with the characteristic of arising and ceasing, that dharma is not a transformation. "World-Honored One, what..."
The Dharma does not conjoin with arising and ceasing. Subhūti, the non-deceptive Dharma is itself nirvāṇa. This Dharma does not conjoin with arising and ceasing;
therefore, it is not a transformation. Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said, the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is entirely empty.
There is nothing that can move it, and no duality to be found. There is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not..."
It is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). How could one say that *nirvāṇa* is not a transformation? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As you have said, there is not even the slightest dharma that is not empty of intrinsic nature.

This emptiness of intrinsic nature was not made by śrāvakas, nor made by pratyekabuddhas, nor made by bodhisattvas, nor made by Tathāgatas, nor made by anyone else. Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, its nature is eternally empty. This...
This is precisely nirvāṇa. Therefore, I say that nirvāṇa is not an emanation (*nirmāṇa*). Nirvāṇa is not a truly existent dharma;
it can be described as being without arising and without cessation, and as non-emanated (the "Chapter on the Nature of Immovable Dharmas" concludes).
Fascicle 398 (The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita); Fascicle 399, Folio 14:
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita always delighted in dwelling in forest hermitages (*araṇya*). Suddenly, he heard a voice from the sky saying: "Ho!"
"Son of good family, you may go east; you will certainly hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

According to the textual record, the first division consists of four hundred fascicles; the second division, seventy-eight fascicles;

Their doctrinal meaning is identical to that of the four hundred fascicles of the first division, though the chapter titles differ.
In some cases, a single chapter is divided into two; in others, two chapters are merged into one. Since these divisions and consolidations differ, their meanings emerge as either prolix or concise.
Although these have all been recorded according to the respective texts, they cannot avoid being presented redundantly.

Here, the chapter titles are listed in detail according to the sequence of the volumes, with the original chapter headings from the first division annotated beneath them, so that the differences may be clearly apparent and the meaning easily understood.
The various sections are cross-referenced, their titles and order being perfectly systematic; the complete scripture remains intact.

there are also those where the subsequent parts take up the threads of the first part and extend them with detailed exposition, becoming even more harmoniously integrated. Furthermore, there are occasionally elements not recorded in the first part, which are treated separately.

*Jiyi tongwen yi* (Compilation of Identical Meanings with Different Texts), one fascicle. Students perceive each subtle meaning as mutually harmonious and thus treasure its profound significance. Generally speaking, my humble intention has been to strive for brevity so that the text may circulate easily;
thus, I feared that the writing might become too prolix. On the other hand, I feared that it might be too abbreviated, lest one hold the entire scripture yet fail to grasp its essential sections.
My hope is that the substance will encompass the whole scripture while the meaning is explored through concise essentials, so that they need not carry heavy bundles upon their staffs.
May its circulation be widely disseminated; this is my aspiration. I respectfully provide this introductory preface to serve as a guide for those who come before.

Preface to the Third Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:

Now, the True Principle (tattva) is obscured when one follows the dictates of emotion, yet emotion is reflected by the Principle as its mirror. Sublime contemplation (vipaśyanā) is estranged when one pursues mere traces, yet those traces merge with contemplation through stillness.

However, when both emotion and traces are honored, one becomes addicted to provisional names and signs; thus, when the Principle and contemplation are simultaneously uprooted from these attachments, they serve as the necessary support for liberation.
Having been gradually steeped in extensive learning, the royal capital has frequently shifted its location, yet here the seat of the Sage is once again established in tranquility.

Thus, he enters the meditative concentration of "sportive play" (*vihāra-samādhi*), capturing the divine traces of his previous assemblies; he issues forth subtle and wondrous sounds, gathering the distant testimonies of former times.

He spreads the radiant moisture of the Dharma to wash and nourish the source of the mind, intending to benefit those who have not yet benefited within the realm of emotions, and to deliver those beings who have not yet been delivered.
In this chapter, the six supernatural powers are deployed within immediate stillness, and the four types of eloquence flow forth beyond the forgetting of words.
One should certainly abide in the inconceivable and attain non-discrimination. As for the case of dreaming within a dream, one is still entangled in the toil of pursuit;

yet when awakening follows awakening, there is the joy of dispelling ignorance. Why is it that the various things of the world are so dazzlingly distinct, while Suchness (tathatā) is so rarely beheld?
That which is "thus" (tathā) and "thus-ness" (tathatā) is not different from that which undergoes change. Whether entangled in afflictions or emerged from them, its nature is pure;

whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, its essence is eternal. To realize this is to return and be called a Tathāgata; to deviate from it is to flow into diversity and be termed an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
The past limit is empty and thus karmic burdens are exhausted; the future limit is empty and thus virtues are fulfilled. Thus, one opens the gate of the ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Seated upon the Vajrāsana, he is nominally beyond all phenomena; though formless, he is adorned with splendor. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he awakens without a mind.
Thus, he is able to sever the evil grasping that clings to emptiness and stagnates in emptiness, and to open the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of non-expressive provisional teaching.
The sublime manifestations of wondrous colors are brilliantly arrayed, and the perfect sounds of the Dharma are poured forth so that each may understand according to their capacity.
All of this takes Prajñā as its source and relies upon Prajñā to form its study. It is like the lofty and exquisite King of Mountains, the sovereign of all peaks;

its meaning is necessarily profound and deep, and its phrasing is likewise rich and esoteric. It consists of fifty-nine fascicles and thirty-one chapters, entirely distinct from previous works, and is titled *Dān* (Single).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery during the Táng Dynasty.

Preface to the Fourth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
Now, as for that which is cognized by consciousness, how could it ever not be consciousness? As for that which is suchness, it has never failed to be suchness.

Therefore, when both the agent of practice and the object of practice are simultaneously empty, the principle of grasping and receiving is abolished; and self-nature and the absence of nature are not different.

Then the thought of grasping is forgotten. If one forgets grasping yet still relies on something, or preserves a general outline while letting the practice collapse, or knows of vigorous cultivation yet fails to act, then one merely empties oneself in a vain attempt at victory.

Fearing that the wild-horse-like passions have not been stilled, the discourse of Vulture Peak is once again opened. Some say: "Regarding names, there is always a pressing admonition to practice; regarding reality," [it is as follows].
One must certainly be on guard against the indolence of non-practice; otherwise, one’s progress on the path may falter, and where would one find the middle way? I venture to respond:

All ordinary beings cleave to the tokens of names and forms and dwell within the abode of ignorance and craving; thus, their minds are fixed upon existence, and any deliberation necessarily deviates from the truth.
The Ultimate Reality is the opposite of this: movement and stillness are here united. Speaking from this perspective, practice is itself non-practice—non-practice.

It is neither practiced, yet it is practiced as it were; it is practiced, yet it is not practiced as it were. By means of the provisional name "Prajñā," one bestows it upon the provisional name "Bodhisattva.
This is like giving illusory dharmas to an illusory person; therefore, there is neither action nor attainment.

Is this not the morning mayfly speaking of the year, or the dream-butterfly debating the waking state? Alas, that such grasping has not yet been overturned; yet I rejoice that this teaching is just now flourishing.

The *Jian* (Gradual) [translation] consists of twenty-nine chapters and eighteen fascicles; it is the old *Xiaopin Daoxing* (Shorter Version of the Practice of the Way), which is the new *Daofengmingdu Jing* (Sutra on the Perfection of Wisdom of the Path).
The term "pin" (chapter) means a division. As these divisions vary in length, there are the *Dapin* (Large Version) and the *Xiaopin* (Small Version).

"Daoxing" refers to the first chapter within this division, which the translator selected to distinguish it as a specific scripture. "Mingdu" (Perfection of Wisdom) is simply another name for *Zhidu* (Perfection of Wisdom).
The title was originally taken from its general heading; this was truly due to the fact that the text was incomplete and deficient, which caused even the title to be erroneous.
Now that the Great Teaching has been perfected and its grand principles have been fully disseminated, may the essentials of its core methodology be restored!
Composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery during the Táng Dynasty.

Preface to the Fifth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra:

I have heard that when one is relaxed and joyful, one desires the flow of instruction while dwelling in leisure; when one is indignant and perplexed, one seeks to request further benefit upon leaving one’s seat.

How much more so for the profound compassion that nurtures from afar, the all-encompassing illumination of universal knowledge, the subtle resonance that penetrates invisibly, and the wondrous mechanism of the ultimate pivot!
How could one ever cease from expounding upon such a magnificent resonance? When the divine movement arrives, it swiftly harmonizes in a sublime gathering;
atop the Spirit Mountain, once more the subtle sound vibrates. This is truly because the path of the mind is easily overgrown with weeds and the mists of emotion are difficult to dispel;

because consciousness lingers on the appearance of phenomena as being "consciousness," and one remains ignorant that emptiness and form are identical to emptiness. How could one know that the essence of the Dharma and the suchness of the Dharma are neither one nor two?
The nature and characteristics of the Nature School (Xingzong) cannot be sought through speech or thought.

Since there is not a single thing that can be unfolded, nor anything that is not present which can be rolled up, it is truly not something that can be led by signs, nor is it something that can be followed along the tracks of sensory dust.
Thus, it is neither acting nor non-acting; it is neither abiding nor non-abiding. When one contemplates this non-dual nature—where duality is non-dual—it transcends even the name "one."
In its essence, it is one and constant; thus, when agitated, it becomes ten thousand deviations, yet when clarified, it remains as one.

Before this single suchness is delimited, meanings differentiate it; before this single meaning is easily grasped, names diversify it; before this single name is changed, appearances trade places with one another;
before this single appearance is branched out, they take up disorder. Beyond this point, there is no limit. Therefore, regarding the True Vehicle and—

The Great Mind: if one forgets dedication and sympathetic joy, then the aggregates of precept, concentration, and wisdom will perish; if one retains them, then the mind of signs and the inversion of views will persist.
Those who perceive birth-and-death are within the three realms of existence; those who cling to nirvana are followers of the two vehicles.

Therefore, by knowing that birth-and-death is empty, one transcends the triple world; by knowing that nirvana is empty, one passes beyond the two stages. This explains the bestowal of the five flowers.

Recorded: This is the realization of Bodhi. Measuring it against the seven treasures, it is a ground of profound and deep merit. The heavens offer it and the heavens protect it; though one adds the highest praise, it remains but earnest;
though one speaks of divine mantras and divine jewels, their spiritual auspiciousness is inexhaustible. I reflect that this assembly has not yet been transmitted to these lands.
It consists of twenty-four chapters in total; now ten fascicles have been translated. With tireless effort, the rhythms are harmonized; ever anew, I thirst for its veneration.
One should certainly not, because of a single down feather, disparage the accumulation of precious jewels.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery during the Táng Dynasty, Fascicle 556. *Sudharmāparivarta* (First Part: *Anutpādaparivarta*).
