○ Preface to the Sixth Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.

Originally, in controlling the path back to its source and encompassing all within its scope, and in treading upon the essential ultimate to establish one's purpose, nothing is better than to alert the ten degrees within a single act of giving, and to dispel the six obscurations through the three types of *dāna*.
Moreover, as for the grand doctrine of *prajñā*, it certainly presides over all and gazes from on high.
Truly, it is the bolt and window of the sincere mind and the pivot and axle of accumulated practice. Thus, one can encompass the ultimate reality and fill the realms of dust.

To cast it forth, there is no object; to settle it, there is no movement. With great compassion as its head and great renunciation as its tail, one calmly cultivates through the five kinds of suffering, suddenly traversing the vast sequence of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
May there be no distinction between near and far; wherever one encounters things, let them be perfected.

The resources [of this teaching] are such that they encompass both the vast and the minute; wherever one encounters them, there is necessarily abundance. By relying on the formless, one passes through eternal days;
by halting the wheel of existence, one transcends the long night. Exhausting the profound and reaching the ultimate subtlety—this is surely the realization of Prajñā.

Now there was a Heavenly King named Vaiśravaṇa, who abandoned his pleasure palace to descend and pay homage, and offered sublime words as a memorial to ascend. With every thought fixed upon this, he investigated and deliberated upon it. Thus...

Because their positions are far apart and the paths are separated, they cannot be preserved through mere visual encounter. Therefore, to guide the multitude and harmonize with the seasons, one must rely on words to provide guidance and bring about awakening.
This is the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* of the former Victorious Heavenly King (*Śakraparipṛcchā*), now translated in eight fascicles and seventeen chapters.

Its elucidation of the grand purport and its opening of the profound barriers are already established; the jewels of the Dharma shine in profusion, and the groves of meaning accumulate in interlacing layers. As for the intrinsic nature...
There are three types. Though its nature is obscure and latent, the virtues of its fruit span ten thousand regions; though its majesty is profound and not ostentatious, it shines with brilliance.
Even those who merely open their book-bags hope to find within it a standard for their character; how much more so should those who travel upon the raft of the Dharma not contemplate it?
Composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery in the Táng Dynasty.
Fascicle 566 (Chapter on Dependent Origination);
Fascicle 566-5, Leaf (Chapter on Thorough Penetration).
By practicing and training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, one is then able to thoroughly penetrate generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and diligence (*vīrya*).
The perfection of wisdom of tranquil insight, skillful means, sublime vows, power, and knowledge—
this is called the single dharma that a bodhisattva practices and studies, which enables one to penetrate all dharmas.
Fascicle 567 (Chapter on Manifesting Characteristics):
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is like the characteristics of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth.
Practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one gains faith and understanding in the threefold purity of the Tathāgata.
In this world, there is always a great fire blazing intensely; namely, greed, hatred, and delusion act as its flames, smoke, and darkness.
How may all sentient beings be caused to escape from this world? If one can penetrate the equality of all phenomena, [they shall escape].
A mind free from attachment is called renunciation.
All phenomena have no fundamental basis, yet there is the ripening of karmic fruit.
Such phenomena are empty and non-existent; they lack an independent nature and are merely false conceptualizations arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
That which is unborn appears as if born.
It is a dharma that has no name, yet names are provisionally established for it: it is called a "sentient being," it is called "prajñā," and it is said that there is one who can teach.

That is to say, there is that which is spoken, there is the listener, and there is the Dharma being heard; yet within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), these are all of one single characteristic—namely, the absence of characteristics (*animitta*)—and are entirely without distinction.
The Tathāgata has, from the very beginning, no intention to speak regarding the Dharma, nor does he form any mental resolve as to whether it is for this person or that person;
yet those whose obstructions are heavy fail to see or hear him, even though they are in close proximity to the Tathāgata.
Fascicle 567, Leaf 13 (Dharmadhātu-parivarta); Fascicle 568.
The Sovereign King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: "What is meant by the term 'Dharmadhātu'? The Buddha told the Sovereign King Vaiśravaṇa:
"You should know that the Dharmadhātu is the nature of non-falsity and the nature of non-alteration; it is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. O Devaputra!
"O King, you should know that suchness is profound and subtle; it can only be known by wisdom and cannot be expressed by words.
Why is this? Because the suchness of all phenomena transcends all letters and is beyond the realm of language, for no verbal activity can reach it.

It is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), cut off from all discrimination, without 'this' or 'that,' devoid of characteristics and signless, far removed from discursive thought and investigation, and transcending all searching."
It observes the object; it is without conceptualization and without signs, transcending these two objects. It is not that which is cognized by consciousness; it abides in non-abiding.
It is the realm of tranquil noble wisdom and non-conceptualization, as well as subsequently attained wisdom. It is devoid of self and what belongs to a self; though sought, it cannot be found.
Without grasping or abandoning, without defilement or attachment, it is pure and free from stain—supreme, foremost, and eternally unchanging in nature. If [this is] the Buddha...
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, its nature and characteristics abide eternally. O Heavenly King, you should know that this is the Dharma-realm;
it is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the True Mark, the Reality-limit of Suchness, the mark of non-discrimination, and the inconceivable realm.

It is also called the true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), as well as the non-dual dharma-realm (*advaya-dharmadhātu*) of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Varaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying: "How can one realize and attain such a dharma-realm? The Buddha told Varaprabha:

"You should know that it is the supramundane *prajñāpāramitā* and the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) thus attained that can realize and attain it. "World-Honored One, how does one realize it?"

It is attained. What is the difference in meaning? Your Majesty, King of Devas, you should know that because supramundane *prajñāpāramitā* can see according to reality, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Because subsequent wisdom thoroughly penetrates [the truth], it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).

The *prajñāpāramitā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep and subtle. The wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is coarse and shallow, and thus cannot perceive it, because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It cannot be measured by reflection (*cintā*), because it is a supramundane phenomenon (*lokottara-dharma*).

It cannot be practiced through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for Bodhisattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* remain far removed from all signs (*nimitta*), meaning they do not perceive any signs whatsoever, whether internal or external. They are free from...
The characteristic of conceptual proliferation; the characteristic of being free from discrimination; the characteristic of being free from seeking; the characteristic of being free from attachment;

the characteristic of being free from objective spheres; the characteristic of being free from cognitive objects; the characteristic of being free from all that knows and all that is known. The Most Victorious One addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If one can contemplate all phenomena as being without characteristics in this way, how should one further contemplate them? The Buddha said: "O Heavenly King, the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable."

Why is this? Because it is beyond the sphere of objects. When all sentient beings attempt to contemplate the realm of the Buddha, their minds become deranged and they lose all sense of self and other.
Why is this? Because it is of the same nature as space—incalculable and unattainable through seeking—and lies beyond the sphere of discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Even when Bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive even the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to exist.
If even these can be conceived, how much more so the realm of the Buddha? Furthermore, he does not rely upon any sublime vows;
although he practices the various *pāramitās*, he is entirely without attachment to their fruits. He likewise does not rely on or cling to any illusory phenomena, up to and including *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? Because he is free from "I" and "mine," being non-dual and undifferentiated, for his intrinsic nature is free [from such constructs].
One accords with the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not oppose *saṃsāra*. Although one remains within *saṃsāra*, one does not oppose the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The Most Victorious One asked Śvetaketu:
"How does one accord with the profound characteristics of phenomena without opposing the conventional? The Buddha said: "By acceding with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not depart from it."
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not depart from the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
yet they do not depart from phenomena while remaining free from grasping. They accord with the *prajñāpāramitā* and do not depart from the path. Why is this?
Because they possess the power of great skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful means? The Buddha said: It refers to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
Because all bodhisattvas possess the great minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they are always able to bring benefit and happiness to the sentient beings they transform.
This is the skillful means of a bodhisattva (Volume Sixty-seven).
In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, characteristics cannot be apprehended, nor can the characteristics of bodhisattvas be apprehended.
It is solely through the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) that they manifest for the sake of sentient beings, from entering the womb up to their final nirvāṇa.
Regarding these various manifestations of transformation, the gods conceive them as permanent and believe they shall not fall.

To shatter that attachment, [the Buddha] manifests entry into the womb, thereby causing those gods to give rise to the thought of impermanence. Furthermore, there are other gods who are heedless and attached to pleasure, failing to cultivate the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva exerts great diligence as if his head were on fire, destroying heedless conduct and manifesting his own downfall.
Furthermore, because certain inferior sentient beings possess few roots of virtue and are unable to behold the Buddha, he manifests as an infant and acts as a youth.
There are those who practice the noble path and are constantly able to remain detached from the mundane world; for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests the act of leaving the household life.
Furthermore, there are devas and humans who sit idly in the enjoyment of pleasure and fail to attain the Path of the Sages; for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests ascetic practices.
He also manifests various difficult and arduous ascetic practices in order to subdue non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism. There are also devas and humans who do not seek liberation.

Yet, because their faculties and natures are matured, they are profound vessels for the Dharma; for these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects.
Furthermore, there are devas and humans who delight in hearing about parinirvāṇa; for them, the Bodhisattva manifests nirvāṇa.
One should know that when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he is able to manifest such things.
Through various manifestations, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will ultimately never be born in the states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*).

A bodhisattva will ultimately never be born in the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), where one cannot benefit others because the Buddhas are not seen. Rather, they are mostly born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Manifesting the transcendence of the world to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings,
wherever a Bodhisattva is born, the Three Jewels are necessarily present due to the power of their past vows.
By practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattva is able to attain the distinctions of the ten bodies of a Tathāgata.
Fascicle 568-8, Leaf (Smṛtyupasthāna-varga):
The Bodhisattva’s Skillful Cultivation of the Mindfulness Foundations of Body, Feeling, Mind, and Phenomena; the Tathāgata’s Merits and Majestic Spiritual Power.
Fascicle 569 (Chapter on the Nature of Phenomena):
The causal nature of the Tathāgata’s *dharmatā* is profoundly deep, subtle, and inconceivable.

His meritorious spiritual power, as well as the benefit and joy he brings to others through the teachings he proclaims, are likewise so. O Heavenly King, the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata exists within the class of sentient beings.
Within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, from beginningless time, they have continued in a successive succession;

they are unstained by afflictions, pure by nature, such that the various mind, thought, and consciousness cannot give rise to them as objects, nor can other discursive thoughts, investigations, and so forth, differentiate them through false mindfulness or reflection.

It cannot be taken as an object of thought; it is far removed from false conceptualization, and ignorance does not arise therein. For this reason, it is called "signless" (*animitta*) rather than being explained through the twelve links of dependent origination.
It is not a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); it is without arising or ceasing, boundless and inexhaustible, its own characteristic eternally abiding.

"O Devaputra, when Bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus pure, unstained, unattached, and far removed from defilement. It is completely liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*).
This very nature is called the root of all Buddha-dharmas; from it arise merit and wisdom. Its original nature is luminous and pure, inconceivable."

[The Bodhisattva] deliberated: "All Buddhas fully know that the fundamental nature of sentient beings is pure, yet it is obscured by adventitious afflictions such that they are unable to awaken to and enter it.
I shall now expound the profound Prajñāpāramitā for them, to eliminate their afflictions and enable them to attain [liberation]."
One enters into the realization of the natural purity of the fundamental nature. Furthermore, one reflects thus: "These afflictions are powerless and incapable;
their own essence is false and illusory, and they contradict the pure dharma. Why is this? Because they turn their backs on all-knowledge and accord with birth-and-death.
The pure dharmatā is the root of all phenomena; its self-nature is fundamentally free from false and illusory afflictions, which all arise from erroneous thought and perversion."
It is as follows: for example, the four great elements are established in dependence upon space, yet space has no support. Afflictions are likewise:
they depend upon the *dharmatā*, yet the *dharmatā* has no support. When bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they observe and know this according to reality.
They do not give rise to opposition because they act in accordance with reality; thus, afflictions do not arise. These bodhisattvas observe afflictions and do not produce stained attachment.
If they themselves were stained by attachment, how could they teach the Dharma to enable others to attain liberation?
Furthermore, he reflects: "If there were even a single affliction within the cycle of birth and death that could benefit sentient beings, I would embrace it;
however, no such thing exists. Therefore, it is called 'annihilation'."

Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): immeasurable and boundless, yet obscured by various afflictions (*kleśa*), it follows the stream of birth and death, sinks into the six destinies, and revolves through the long night.
Because it conforms to sentient beings, it is called the "nature of sentient beings" (*sattva-dhātu*).

When bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of weary detachment, eliminate desire for the five sensory objects, extinguish all conceptual discrimination, and cultivate the unsurpassed path, at that time this nature is called...
It is called "quiescence" because it leads to renunciation and transcends all suffering.
Relying upon this very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), bodhisattvas cultivate roots of virtue and enter the three realms of existence (*trisaṃsāra*) to benefit sentient beings;
though they manifest impermanence, it is not ultimately real. Why is this? Because bodhisattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because they perceive the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it really is, they possess the power of skillful means, great compassion, and vows, and do not abandon sentient beings.

Since those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings lack such power of great compassion and vows, they do not perceive the perfectly pure *dharmatā* and are thus unable to benefit sentient beings in accordance with reality.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to contemplate the true, pure *dharmatā* in this way:
the boundless qualities and unique attributes of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas arise from this nature and emerge from this nature;
the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom of all noble ones arise from this nature. This nature is quiescent, transcending all names and signs; this nature is...

It is real; it is free from inversion; its nature is immutable; therefore, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). It is the domain of noble wisdom; therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas reflect thus: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of characteristics; all phenomena are devoid of characteristics; they are non-dual and undifferentiated. Why?

For this reason, all phenomena are devoid of characteristics; that which is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is devoid of characteristics. That which is the nature of phenomena is devoid of characteristics; sentient beings are devoid of characteristics.

That sentient beings are devoid of characteristics is identical to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) being devoid of characteristics. That the dharma-realm is devoid of characteristics is identical to all phenomena being devoid of characteristics.

Such a state of being devoid of characteristics cannot be apprehended through seeking. The suchness of the nature of phenomena and the suchness of sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction. The nature of phenomena...
Suchness. The suchness of all phenomena is non-dual and undifferentiated. The suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of the Buddhas are non-dual and undifferentiated.

The suchness of the nature of phenomena and the suchness of the three periods of time do not contradict one another. The suchness of the three periods of time is itself the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
The suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases is itself the suchness of defilement and purity. The suchness of defilement and purity is itself birth.
The *tathatā* of death and *nirvāṇa*; the *tathatā* of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*—this is the *tathatā* of all phenomena.
O Devaputra, you should know that *tathatā* is called unchanging and undifferentiated; it is without arising and without cessation, the true reality of its own nature.
To know and see it as it truly is: all phenomena do not arise. Although phenomena arise, *tathatā* remains unmoving. Although *tathatā* gives rise to all phenomena, [it does not change].
Suchness is unborn; this is called the Dharmakāya. It is pure and unchanging, equal to space. Within all the three realms, nothing can surpass it;
throughout the bodies of all sentient beings, there is none equal to it. Pure and free from defilement, it is primordially unstained.

Its intrinsic nature is luminously pure; its intrinsic nature is unborn; its intrinsic nature is unarisen. It is within the mind, intellect, and consciousness, yet it is neither mind, intellect, nor consciousness.
Its nature is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Pervading the entire realm of space and the abodes of all sentient beings, it is entirely equal.

It is immeasurable and boundless; it is neither different nor distinct. It is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is not the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, yet it is not separate from the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind. It is without birth, yet not separate from birth.
Although it runs counter to saṃsāra, it does not conform to nirvāṇa. The eye cannot see it; the ear cannot hear it; the nose cannot smell it; the tongue...

It cannot be tasted; the body cannot perceive it, and the mind cannot know it. It does not reside within the mind, intellect, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from the mind, intellect, or consciousness.

This is called the *dharmatā*. Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to penetrate this *dharmatā*, they practice with purity and can manifest physical bodies throughout the trichiliocosm. These manifested bodies are not material form (*rūpa*).

Though they are without marks, they manifest in the form of material appearances; though they do not fall within the range of the six sense faculties, they constantly transform sentient beings without rest.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and immediately attain mastery that is unshakable.
They then give rise to the activities of wisdom and sport with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting in various ways. Thus it is.
Mastery is the mark of inexhaustibility. Pervading all places, it manifests form within the formless.

With mastery, one universally observes the minds of all sentient beings and perceives the nature of the mind as it truly is. With mastery, one recollects infinite and countless eons in an uninterrupted succession.

He dwells in the signs of liberation through sovereign transformation; he possesses sovereign mastery over the exhaustion of outflows, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he does not personally realize that exhaustion of outflows;
he possesses sovereignty over the supramundane, which is the domain of noble wisdom; and he possesses sovereignty over the profound, which cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Possessing sovereign stability, he cannot be destroyed by Māra. Seated upon the Bodhi throne, he accomplishes the Buddha-dharma as the most supreme.

With sovereign compliance, he turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma. With sovereignty, he tames and transforms all sentient beings. With sovereignty, he receives his station and attains mastery over the Dharma.
If they wish to take birth, they have mastery over birth and remain free from bondage; if they wish to manifest cessation, they have mastery over cessation.
In whatever place they are born, they constantly embrace the Mahāyāna and bring the Buddha-dharmas to maturity.
If one is free from names and signs, that is equality. If dharmas are equal, there is no attachment;
since there is nothing to which one can attach, this dharma is the reality. If one clings to reality, that is itself delusion. Because of non-clinging, it is not delusion.

Although he turns the wheel of Dharma, he perceives neither speaker nor listener; although he manifests nirvana, he knows that the fundamental nature of birth and death is equal, like space, which pervades all things.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, his mind is likewise so.

The Bodhisattva is skillfully able to penetrate the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Although they speak of all phenomena, these do not exist as real entities, and thus one never grasps or clings to them.
All phenomena are without cessation; therefore, they are without arising. Why is this? Because their nature is unchanging. This is merely seen according to worldly convention.
Arising and ceasing are all false and illusory; they do not truly exist.
Those of heterodox views and external paths merely wish to sever death, yet they do not know how to sever birth. If a phenomenon does not arise, then it has no cessation.
Non-Buddhists do not know how to sever birth; they will never escape death.
Even by purely cultivating a single practice, one is born in the Pure Land. Why is this? Because within each individual practice, all practices are fully contained.
These bodhisattvas are able to produce manifold virtues and possess skillful means for transforming and delivering sentient beings.

While dwelling in this buddha-field, their bodies remain unmoving as they travel to the infinite worlds of the Buddhas. Although they perform various buddha-activities, they do so without mental effort and without conceptual discrimination.
The devas who have long resided on Vulture Peak Mountain are all bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation;
therefore, they are able to know the distinctions regarding the duration and proximity of the realms of past buddhas.
Wherever the Tathāgata dwells, there is no impurity whatsoever; that is a pure land.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time attain [their realization] precisely through the Prajñāpāramitā. (The Chapter on the Nature of Phenomena concludes.)
Fascicle 570 (Chapter on Equality):

That which grasps and that which is grasped—all afflictions that obstruct wholesome dharmas—arise based on the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). [This teaching] is able to extinguish the view of a self-body.
All latent tendencies and all afflictions are forever stilled; even the formation of vows ceases.
Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, one falsely conceives of a self, thereby giving rise to the view of a self. In reality, the nature of phenomena is equal by its very essence.
It is devoid of the grasping of subject and object and is contrary to the view of self; therefore, it constitutes an obstruction.
One should know that such a view of self does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two; being entirely without abode, it is called "quiescence," which is itself "equanimity."
To remain far removed from the view of self, to penetrate equality, and to call this "true emptiness," while practicing all types of *pāramitās*,
remaining far removed from demonic obstacles, seeing neither that which is to be practiced nor that which is to be abandoned— this is [the path].
Therefore it is called "equality. Taking all-knowledge as its object, the mind does not cease; it constantly cultivates the practice of emptiness.
By the power of great compassion, it does not abandon sentient beings; therefore it is called "equality. Regarding all phenomena, the mind’s objects are sovereign; the mind’s objects are signless.
Thus they cultivate bodhi. Because they do not perceive the signless as distinct from bodhi, it is called equality.
Their minds take the wishless as their object, yet they do not abandon the triple world. Because they do not perceive the wishless as distinct from the triple world, it is called equality.
Taking conditioned phenomena as objects is for the sake of attaining Buddha-wisdom; taking unconditioned phenomena as objects is for the sake of attaining tranquility.

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means, there is not a single thought or a single action that passes in vain without being dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Thus, although such a bodhisattva takes all phenomena as objects, they are able to remain unattached while contemplating even a single [phenomenon].
There is not a single phenomenon that does not tend toward great enlightenment. Regarding the objective sphere of a bodhisattva, there is not a single dharma that does not tend toward enlightenment.
Why is this? Because all the practices of a bodhisattva are established by means of external conditions.
O King of the Most Victorious Devas, you have practiced all the pāramitās for immeasurable kalpas and have acted as a guardian of the prajñāpāramitā for all bodhisattvas.
Having now encountered me, you shall receive my instruction;
in future ages, after further practicing the provisions for unsurpassed bodhi for immeasurable kalpas, you will subsequently realize the unsurpassed bodhi you seek.
Fascicle 570-8 (Chapter on Manifesting Signs). Śāriputra asked the Most Victorious One:

"When a Bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he should at that very moment sit upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). For what reason does he first manifest six years of ascetic practice? The [Buddha] replied: "..."
He subdued the Māras and again attained perfect enlightenment. The Most Victorious One replied: "Venerable One, you should know that in truth the Bodhisattva performed no ascetic practices.
He manifested them only for the sake of subduing the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). These non-Buddhists claimed for themselves the ability to practice asceticism;
therefore, the Bodhisattva manifested ascetic practices that surpassed theirs. For six years he endured them without a single lapse. Yet, in reality, the Bodhisattva had no [asceticism]."
During these ascetic practices, there were various hosts of devas and humans who, upon witnessing this event, became established in the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Furthermore, there were devas and humans whose power of past roots of goodness caused them to deeply delight in the Mahāyāna;

they saw the Bodhisattva seated upon a pedestal of the seven precious gems, his body and mind unmoving, with a serene countenance and a smile, having entered a supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*). After six years had passed, he finally arose from that concentration. There were devas and humans...
To those among the assembly who deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna and desired to hear it, the Bodhisattva appeared sitting upright and preaching the Dharma for six years.
Having completed those six years, he arose from his meditative absorption and, in accordance with worldly custom, went to the Immaculate River (*Vimala-nadī*) to bathe.
There, a cowherd girl offered him milk-rice, and sixty million devas, nāgas, and others each brought various kinds of fragrant and delicious drinks.
They brought food and presented it as an offering. At that time, the cowherd girls, the goddesses, the nāgas, and the others did not see one another;
each saw the Bodhisattva alone receiving their offerings. In reality, at that time, the Bodhisattva had not bathed, nor did he accept the offerings of those humans, devas, and others.
Through the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he accepted the grass mat beneath the Bodhi tree, circumambulated it seven times to the right, and sat upright with right mindfulness.
Sentient beings of inferior capacity perceived this sign;
however, the great bodhisattvas saw eighty-four thousand devaputras, each separately arranging a great lion throne, yet these devaputras did not see one another, each thinking:
The Bodhisattva sat alone upon my seat. Through his skillful means, he emitted a great radiance from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm.
All the palaces of the Māras lost their majestic splendor, and they all fell prostrate.
By the power of great compassion, the Bodhisattva causes all the hosts of Māras to be free from fear;

thus, with both terror and joy mingled in their hearts, when the Bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, he does not give rise to even a single moment of anger toward the Māras who come to disturb him.
In that single instant of mind, he is able to accord with the principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, reaching its ultimate consummation and attaining thorough penetration.

Having fully known, seen, and awakened to all that is to be known, at that time, as the Bodhisattva was about to manifest the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, the hosts of Brahmā deities, moved by compassion, made their request three times;
Śakra, Lord of Devas, likewise prepared a lion throne for the Tathāgata.
At that moment, throughout the trichiliocosm, there was not even an interval the size of a single pore, as it was filled with devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others.
It was filled to capacity. If there were sentient beings who were to be transformed by hearing the teaching on suffering, they heard the Buddha speak of suffering.
Likewise, those who were to be transformed by hearing the teachings on selflessness, tranquility, detachment, impermanence, and emptiness, were also thus transformed.
Those who were to be transformed by hearing the teachings that [all things] are like illusions, up to and including being like a city of Gandharvas, were also thus transformed. They were to hear...
Those who are to be transformed by the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—hear the Buddha speak of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
At that time, among the classes of sentient beings, some hear the Tathāgata say that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, while others hear him speak of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Some hear the teaching on the elements (*dhātu*); some hear the teaching on the sense bases (*āyatana*); some hear the teaching on suffering (*duḥkha*), and so on, up to its origin, cessation, and the path.

Some hear the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Some hear the teaching on calm abiding (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*). Some hear the teachings of the śrāvakas; some hear the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas; or some hear...
They teach the dharmas of all bodhisattvas. Thus, through their skillful means, these bodhisattvas manifest various forms of turning the wheel of Dharma;
according to the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings, each obtains benefit and happiness, and their hearts rejoice with deep gladness.
When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), the mind has no object of focus (*ālambana*) and no place of abiding.

It is, for example, like a person born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), who for eighty thousand great eons possesses only a single consciousness that has neither a place of abiding nor an object of focus.
In this same way, the bodhisattva’s mind has no object of focus and no place of abiding. Why is this?
Therefore, these bodhisattvas do not direct their minds toward the sphere of non-action; they do not conceptualize their minds toward the sphere of non-conceptualization;

they do not take their minds as objects in the sphere of the non-objectified; they do not cling to their minds in the sphere of non-attachment; they do not allow their minds to be distracted in the sphere of non-distraction;

their minds do not follow after wisdom, nor do they abide in themselves, nor do they abide in others; they do not abide relying on the eye, nor do they abide relying on the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It abides in dependence on form; it does not abide in dependence on sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena. The mind is not within, nor is it without, nor is it between the two.
The mind does not take phenomena as its object, nor does it take wisdom as its object. It does not abide in the three periods of time, nor does it abide apart from the three periods of time.
One who faithfully accepts the Prajñāpāramitā and its skillful means approaches the realm of the Buddha.

By means of this single-mindedness, one is able to penetrate all Buddha-dharmas. Because of this penetration of the Buddha-dharmas, one brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings, yet does not perceive sentient beings as distinct from the Buddha-dharmas.
Why is this? Because, in principle, sentient beings and the Buddha-dharmas are non-dual. (The "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" concludes.)

One who seeks the Dharma truly has nothing to seek. If there were truly something to be sought, it would constitute non-Dharma.
Within the reality of ultimate truth, there is not a single dharma that can arise or cease.

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), being endowed with right faith, with a mind free from negligence, and through diligent application of vigor, they immediately attain right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*). By means of this mindful wisdom, they know what exists and what does not exist.

What is meant by existence and non-existence? If one cultivates correct practice and attains right liberation, this is called "existence. If one cultivates erroneous practice and [attains] right... [text truncated]
Liberation is called "non-existence. The six faculties, such as the eye, and the six objects, such as form, exist conventionally but do not exist in the ultimate sense.
That a diligent bodhisattva can attain bodhi is called "existence"; that a lazy bodhisattva attains bodhi is called "non-existence.
To say that the five aggregates of grasping all arise from false conceptualization is called...
To say that conventional phenomena arise spontaneously without depending on causes and conditions is called "non-existence.
To say that form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to decay is called "existence. If one says it is permanent, blissful, and not subject to decay, this is called "non-existence.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. That ignorance conditions volitional formations is called "existence. If one [separates from...]

That ignorance leads to the arising of volitional formations is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*). This applies likewise up to the point where birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
That one gives alms and attains great wealth is called "existence" (*bhāva*). That one becomes impoverished is called "non-existence.
That one upholds the pure precepts and is reborn in a happy realm is called "existence. That one is reborn in an evil realm is called [non-existence].
There is no [such thing as non-existence]. Up to and including the cultivation of wisdom, which enables one to attain the state of an Arya—this is called existence.
To act as a fool—this is called non-existence. If one cultivates extensive learning and attains great knowledge—this is called existence. To become deluded—this is called non-existence.
If one cultivates right mindfulness and is able to achieve transcendence—this is called existence; failing to do so is non-existence. If one practices what is wrong...
To think that one cannot attain liberation is called "existence. To be able to attain it is called "non-existence.

To think that one can attain liberation by being free from the self and what belongs to the self is called "existence. To cling to the self and what belongs to the self while thinking one can attain liberation is called "non-existence.
If one says that space pervades all places, this is called "existence. To say that there is a real self within the five aggregates is called...

There is no [liberation] through false cultivation; only by cultivating wisdom as it truly is can one attain liberation—this is called "existence. If one could attain liberation by clinging to false wisdom, that would be called "non-existence.

By abandoning views of self and so forth, one can attain the wisdom of emptiness—this is called "existence. If one could attain the wisdom of emptiness while clinging to views of self and so forth, that would be called "non-existence.
The Bodhisattva knows the existence and non-existence of the world and is thus able to cultivate equanimity and realize it.
He realizes that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; thus, they exist conventionally. He does not give rise to the view of eternalism.
Knowing that the nature of dependent origination is entirely empty, he does not give rise to the view of nihilism. Regarding all the Buddha's teachings, he penetrates them as they truly are.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas take dwelling in saṃsāra as their joy, rather than taking nirvāṇa as their joy. Why is this? Because all Bodhisattvas take the transformation of sentient beings as their joy.
If they were to diligently cultivate virtue and quickly exhaust their outflows, they would be unable to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas, possessing the power of skillful means, remain for a long time in saṃsāra until they attain [the vision].
The Tathāgatas, immeasurable and boundless, hear and receive immeasurable and boundless true Dharma, and transform and guide immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

They do not weary of saṃsāra, nor do they delight in nirvāṇa. If one were to contemplate saṃsāra with weariness and fear, or to take pleasure in nirvāṇa, one would fall into a non-path and be unable to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; for [only by] penetrating the profound [wisdom] of the Tathāgata...
Regarding the spheres of experience: why is this not the path? Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings;
it is not the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Since they cannot fully perfect merit and wisdom, for these reasons it is not the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the Buddha Bahuśruta praised the power of his diligence, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You should cultivate your own practice."
"Do not practice what is contrary to the Way. At that time, Vijayavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is called the path practiced by a bodhisattva himself?
The Buddha said, "A bodhisattva accomplishes all merit and wisdom. By the power of great compassion, he does not abandon sentient beings.

They transform and guide others. They know that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). They contemplate all Buddha-fields as being like empty space, yet they are able to skillfully adorn and purify those Buddha-fields.
They know that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is formless, yet through skillful means (*upāya*) they manifest the adornment of the primary and secondary marks.
Knowing that intrinsic nature is empty, they are fully able to penetrate profound wisdom and, through skillful means, act for the sake of others.

He taught the Dharma: "One should not realize the fruits of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, but should diligently seek the liberation realized by the Tathāgata, never abandoning any of the bodhisattva’s path practices.
This is called the path practiced by a bodhisattva himself.
At that time, Vīryabalavat, having heard from that Tathāgata this teaching on the sphere of a bodhisattva’s practice, again addressed the Buddha Bahusruta, saying: "As I understand the Buddha..."

The meaning of what has been taught is this: a bodhisattva, being fully endowed with skillful means, perceives that all phenomena are none other than the Path—namely, the phenomena of ordinary beings, the phenomena of śrāvakas, the phenomena of pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of bodhisattvas, and the phenomena of tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have thoroughly realized it. Mañjuśrī, that power of diligence is none other than the present King Prasenajit.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, from what dharma does right faith flow forth?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, “Right faith flows forth in obtaining a true and virtuous friend. Mañjuśrī asked, “World-Honored One, from what dharma does extensive learning flow forth? The Buddha said:
“Venerable One, from extensive learning flows sublime wisdom. Venerable One, from what does generosity flow? The Buddha said: ‘From generosity flows great wealth.
From what does pure ethical discipline flow? From pure ethical discipline flows rebirth in the higher realms. From what does patience flow?’”
Patience flows forth as the acceptance of all sentient beings. What does diligence flow forth? Diligence flows forth as the accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas.
What does meditative concentration flow forth? Meditative concentration flows forth as the distancing from all distraction.
What does wisdom flow forth? Wisdom flows forth as the distancing from all afflictions. Listening to the Dharma...
What dharma flows forth from listening to the Dharma? Listening to the Dharma flows forth the distancing of oneself from all nets of doubt.
What dharma flows forth from correct inquiry? Correct inquiry flows forth the sublime wisdom that is certain regarding the Dharma. What dharma flows forth from dwelling in seclusion?

Dwelling in seclusion flows forth superior meditative concentration and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What dharma flows forth from correct cultivation? Correct cultivation flows forth the path of revulsion toward impermanence.
What phenomenon does the sound of impermanence issue forth? The sound of impermanence issues forth the non-appropriation and non-protection of objects.
What phenomenon does the sound of suffering issue forth? The sound of suffering issues forth non-arising. What phenomenon does the sound of selflessness issue forth?

The sound of selflessness issues forth the eradication of the grasping at "I" and "mine. What phenomenon does the sound of emptiness issue forth? The sound of emptiness issues forth tranquility and right mindfulness.
What does the outflow of right mindfulness produce? It produces noble vision. What does physical and mental seclusion produce?
It produces all sublime meditative concentrations and supernormal powers. What does the noble path produce? It produces the noble fruits.
What does resolute conviction produce? It produces the accomplishment of all liberations. Thus is the birth of the Buddha.
What phenomena flow forth? From the Buddha’s birth, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) flow forth.

Not contradicting correct principle and always being without dispute is called "protecting the true Dharma. Why is this? For all the foolish people of the world...
Those who adhere to various views and those who accord with correct principle constantly speak of emptiness; therefore, they together give rise to disputes in the world.
Fools cherish and value existent phenomena (*bhāva*), whereas those who accord with correct principle regard existence lightly.

The world speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, while those who accord with correct principle speak of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity; therefore, they together give rise to disputes in the world.
Those who are of the class of fools follow the worldly current; those who accord with correct reasoning go against the worldly current.

Therefore, the world collectively gives rise to disputes with them. Fools are attached to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; those who accord with correct reasoning have no attachments whatsoever.

Therefore, the world collectively gives rise to disputes with them. Those foolish people who follow the world do not practice correct reasoning, whereas those who accord with correct reasoning [do not conform] to the world.
Because they are non-contradictory, they are eternally without dispute; this is called "protecting the True Dharma.
One who does not abide in the dharma of neither-arising-nor-ceasing lacks the eloquence to preach the profound Dharma. Why is this?

Because they have distanced themselves from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they do not perceive the object of cognition, nor do they perceive the subject of cognition. Since the mind has no place of abiding, one is thus able to preach it. Not so otherwise.
Abiding in my Dharma, they do not abide in this or that, but abide solely within the pure ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Therefore, they are able to say:
"The noble son *Bhadraśrī* has cultivated the gate of the rare *dhāraṇī*; even if he were to preach the Dharma for an eon, it would never be exhausted."
This rare phenomenon transcends all words and letters; speech cannot enter it, and the mind cannot measure it. Within all internal and external phenomena, it is utterly unattainable;
there is not even the slightest dharma that can enter it. Therefore, it is called the "Dhāraṇī Door of the Non-Entry of All Dharmas. Why is this?
Because this dharma is equal, without high or low, and without entering or exiting.
Not a single syllable enters from without; not a single syllable exits from within; not a single syllable abides within this Dharma.
Furthermore, there are no syllables that perceive one another, nor is there any discrimination between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
These syllables, when spoken, do not decrease; when unspoken, they do not increase. From the very beginningless limit, they have never arisen nor been subject to destruction.
As it is with these syllables, so it is with the mind; as it is with the mind, so it is with all phenomena.
Why is this? Because phenomena transcend language and transcend conceptualization; from the very beginning, they are without arising and without cessation, and thus have no entering or exiting.
For this reason, it is called the Dharani-door of the Non-entry into All Phenomena.
If one can penetrate this dharma-door, one’s eloquence will be inexhaustible.
