Because Bodhisattvas are able to relinquish all things, when they realize unsurpassed enlightenment, they are able to exhaustively penetrate all phenomena."
He has ultimately relinquished them. Because of this ultimate relinquishment, there is no phenomenon among all dharmas that he does not directly realize, and none that he does not fully know.
In accordance with the nature of phenomena, there is nothing that he does not relinquish.
When practicing the perfection of generosity, one should first cultivate skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Although a bodhisattva may, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, constantly relinquish immeasurable and innumerable treasures and give them universally to sentient beings, if they do not dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment with the aspiration that all sentient beings together realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), [it is not true generosity]. As it is said:
This bodhisattva practices giving extensively yet gathers little merit;

although they give a small portion of material wealth to sentient beings for only a short time, they are able to dedicate it toward unsurpassed enlightenment, vowing that all sentient beings may together realize the wisdom of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Such a bodhisattva practices giving to a small degree yet gathers vast merit.
Fascicle 580: The Bodhisattva’s Quest for All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

It is not that one can realize it through the initial arising of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), nor is it that one can realize it solely through the final arising of the thought at the moment of sitting upon the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) at a later time.
Rather, it is by means of the continuity of the initial thought, continuing until sitting upon the seat of awakening...
The final mind of the seat of enlightenment arises through the successive mutual support [of preceding moments], whereby one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
There is no initial, middle, or final mind that is incapable of inducing all-knowledge and realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is because it is only by means of the successive continuity of these various minds, which suppress and sever the factors that constitute obstacles, that the goal is finally accomplished.
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, one who wishes to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi should not allow the mind to be interspersed with anything at this time.
Then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra, "To what extent is the mind said to be without interspersion? Śāriputra replied:

When improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) manifests before a bodhisattva, they are able to correctly observe that it is conducive to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and not contrary to it.
This bodhisattva is able to know as it truly is: "The improper mental attention I have now aroused can serve as an auxiliary to all-knowledge.
That is to say, the improper mental attention I have aroused is able to...
It draws forth the body of existence, causing it to persist for a long duration within saṃsāra and thereby benefiting sentient beings.

If my own body were devoid of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), which serves as its support and sustenance, it would immediately perish; it could not even bring my own practice to fulfillment, let alone benefit other sentient beings.
Up to this point is what is called the bodhisattva’s mind being free from intermixture. Furthermore, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra...

Son, if bodhisattvas are able to contemplate all phenomena—whether favorable or unfavorable—as being able to assist and lead toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), they do not treat them as merely favorable or unfavorable.
Their minds remain undisturbed by such distinctions; they do not give rise to anger toward adverse objects, nor do they give rise to attachment toward favorable objects.
Whether adverse or favorable, they are able to correctly know them both as auxiliary conditions that lead toward [the knowledge of all modes].
Wisdom. At all times and amidst all objects, his mind is free from distraction.

Although the Bodhisattva seeking omniscience dwells thus with an undistracted mind, practicing with diligence and proceeding toward the conduct of enlightenment, he is able to swiftly fulfill the provisions for enlightenment.
Other bodhisattvas, even after passing through incalculable eons, practice the bodhisattva path with distracted minds. Only then...
They attain the perfection of the provisions for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas seek omniscience;

no other mental engagements can arise in them even momentarily. Since their great mind of enlightenment is not interspersed by anything else, they cultivate the practices for enlightenment with an unadulterated mind and are able to bring them to perfection without passing through a hundred kalpas. If the mind were interspersed with other things, it would take a long time.

A continuous stream [of thought] cannot achieve accomplishment; however, even a brief continuity of an uninterrupted and unmixed mind can achieve it, because it constantly progresses from moment to moment.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "What is the nature of the uninterrupted and unmixed mind?
What kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) causes the mind to become interrupted and mixed? How does one avoid this? Śāriputra replied: "The Bodhisattva..."
One seeks omniscience through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), with no other mental engagements (*manasikāra*) intermingling in the interim and no interruptions to the mind;

this constitutes its essential nature. If there are mental engagements of the Śrāvaka vehicle or mental engagements of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle that can intermingle with the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), these are all termed "unreasonable mental engagements" for a Bodhisattva. Why is this? Because the mental engagements of the two vehicles...
This violates and harms unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. If such a mind arises and manifests before one, one will be unable to fulfill the provisions for enlightenment;
instead, one will take delight in nirvāṇa and feel aversion toward saṃsāra. A bodhisattva should therefore avoid such a person from afar.
He reflects thus: "The mental orientations of the two vehicles oppose omniscience and accord with parinirvāṇa; my mind should not be interspersed with them.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should form this thought: [I shall abandon] the mind associated with greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth."

Although they act as obstacles to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they are nevertheless conducive to the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) and do not excessively intermingle with the bodhisattva’s mind in the way that the minds seeking the stages of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka do. Why is this? Because [the afflictions such as] greed, hatred, and delusion...
It enables the continuity of birth, death, and all states of existence, and assists bodhisattvas in bringing forth all-knowledge.

That is to say, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) and take on subsequent bodies of existence to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.

Relying upon this, one practices the six perfections until they are brought to fulfillment, and even practices the immeasurable and boundless qualities of all Buddhas until they are brought to fulfillment.
Such afflictions can assist a bodhisattva in realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they are not the mental engagements of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for by those mental engagements, the Great [Vehicle] is obstructed.
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is likewise obstructed when the provisions for its attainment fail to reach fulfillment.

Therefore, when the assembly of bodhisattvas gives rise to a mind interspersed with such mental engagements (*manasikāra*), unsurpassed enlightenment becomes even more remote. Consequently, bodhisattvas whose minds are thus interspersed lack the mental engagement of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
those seeking great enlightenment should avoid them from afar so that they do not arise even momentarily. Do not allow them to cause affliction.
The mental engagement of affliction conforms to all forms of existence; it is not extremely interspersed within the mind of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva seeks great enlightenment in order to deliver sentient beings; donning the armor of diligence, they remain for a long time in saṃsāra to bring about great benefit.
One should not quickly abandon the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) with regard to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

When this mental engagement is present before one, it causes the various forms of existence (*bhava*) to continue for a long duration; based upon it, one brings to fulfillment the six perfections (*pāramitā*) as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, the assembly of Bodhisattvas should not give rise to extreme aversion toward it. Why is this?
Why? Because the fetters of existence have not yet been permanently severed, I am able to practice and thereby bring forth the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
For this reason, until the Bodhisattva has sat upon the sublime seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they do not seek to extinguish [these fetters].
Consequently, among all mental engagements (manasikāra), the Bodhisattva does not feel weary of or abandon any except those associated with the two vehicles. This is because...
Regarding the realization of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), there is nothing that does not possess the power of being an auxiliary companion.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "Is it not the case that the two vehicles also provide auxiliary power toward the knowledge of all modes? Śāriputra replied:
"The mental orientations associated with the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha provide superior auxiliary power within the stages of those two vehicles; however, regarding all [the stages of] bodhi..."

It is utterly incompatible with the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment sought by Bodhisattvas, as well as with the provisions for it—namely, the aversion to saṃsāra and the longing for parinirvāṇa, which involves abandoning great enlightenment and sentient beings.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas must certainly not give rise to the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas; for by means of such mental orientations, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood sought by Bodhisattvas...
Benefiting sentient beings, they do not conform to either [extreme].
While practicing the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), although there may be the act of relinquishing precious wealth and so forth, they have no perception of signs regarding those things.
If they were not to relinquish signs when dedicating toward enlightenment, they would wish to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
One will ultimately be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
All phenomena that possess characteristics have quantity; because phenomena with quantity have limitations, one cannot realize the limitless knowledge of all modes by taking them as objects.
A bodhisattva is able to relinquish all types of internal and external characteristics, and their mind is without—

[This is] what has been taught. Seeking to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) like the crown of the head. Fascicle 581.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to the Buddha: "If all dharmas are not truly existent, when a bodhisattva practices giving..."
"What is it that is relinquished? At the time of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, what is it that is attained? The Buddha said:

"Just as when practicing giving, there is nothing at all among all phenomena that is relinquished; so too, at the time of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there is nothing at all among all phenomena that is attained.
Those who possess wisdom should understand this correctly. Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices giving..."
At the time of giving, although there is something relinquished, no sorrow arises;

when realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, although there is something attained, there is likewise no joy, because one knows that what is relinquished and what is attained are like illusions and transformations.
Regarding the bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions practicing generosity, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva first produce the thought of enlightenment? How does a bodhisattva [produce] the second?"
The Arousing of the Mind. How does a bodhisattva abide on the stage of non-retrogression? How does a bodhisattva sit upon the seat of enlightenment?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "If a bodhisattva first arouses the mind, they transcend the stage of the arhat, for they are worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of all the world’s devas and humans.
If a bodhisattva arouses the second mind, they transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha and universally awaken to..."
Because it is the true dharma-dhātu of equality revealed by the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena;

because if a bodhisattva dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, they transcend those bodhisattvas who have not yet received a prediction and are not yet fixed, as they are certain to realize great enlightenment;

and because their mind is not interspersed with afflictions, such that once a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, they will certainly attain the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) without rising.

When Bodhisattvas sit upon the seat of enlightenment, it is impossible and out of the question that they would rise from that seat without having realized the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who sit upon the seat of enlightenment, there is certainly no case where they rise from that seat in the interim without having attained the knowledge of all modes. One should know this concerning the Bodhisattva sitting [there].
The seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This is the Tathāgata sitting upon the seat of enlightenment.

Why is this? Because such a bodhisattva will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and is thus designated as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings in accordance with reality.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, Śāriputra and the great assembly immediately beheld worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of immeasurable rivers, where countless bodhisattvas sat upon the seat of enlightenment and realized great awakening;

countless bodhisattvas had left the household life with right faith, being able to renounce all manner of things difficult to renounce and bestowing them upon sentient beings; and countless bodhisattvas had become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
Practicing the bodhisattva path, countless bodhisattvas, desiring to transform and deliver sentient beings, earnestly exhort and instruct them,

preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to diligently cultivate and study all dharmas. Although countless bodhisattvas apply themselves with diligent vigor,
seeking without interval those teachings corresponding to the *pāramitās*, countless bodhisattvas practice the various...
Having practiced various difficult asceticisms and subdued immeasurable celestial Māras and enemies, countless bodhisattvas attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, they beheld in the ten directions, in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who were proclaiming the aggregate of form for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas. Now...

Up to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the characteristics of permanence and impermanence cannot be found; even the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility cannot be found.
When the sense base of the eye is taught, up to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, the characteristics of permanence and impermanence cannot be found;
even the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility cannot be found. When the sense base of form is taught...
Up to the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), the characteristics of permanence and impermanence are unapprehendable;
even the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility are unapprehendable. He proclaims the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements (*manodhātu*);
the characteristics of permanence and impermanence are unapprehendable, and even the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility are unapprehendable. He proclaims the eye...

The various feelings produced with contact as a condition—up to and including the various feelings produced with contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions—cannot be apprehended as having the characteristics of permanence or impermanence;
nor can they be apprehended as having the characteristics of tranquility or non-tranquility.
He taught that within the earth element, and even up to the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, the characteristics of permanence and impermanence cannot be found;

and even up to the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility, they likewise cannot be found. He taught the causes and conditions, and even up to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), wherein the characteristics of permanence and impermanence cannot be found; and even up to the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility, they likewise cannot be found.

The characteristic of tranquility is also unapprehendable. He proclaims that from ignorance through formations, consciousness, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death, the characteristics of permanence and impermanence are unapprehendable; even the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility are unapprehendable.
Furthermore, he beholds countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who, desiring to benefit all bodhisattvas, [teach this].
Therefore, for many *koṭi* of eons, he does not enter parinirvāṇa. He causes those who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed *bodhicitta* to generate that resolve;
he causes those who have already generated it to never fall back; and he causes those who have not fallen back to perfect the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
For the sake of benefiting all *śrāvakas*, he remains for many eons, bringing them to maturity through skillful means so that they may realize [the goal].
Having attained the fruit of arhatship, he remains for many eons through skillful means to bring benefit to the pratyekabuddhas,
maturing them so that they may realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
he remains for many eons through skillful means to mature them according to their respective dispositions, leading them to attain parinirvāṇa or to escape the suffering of the evil realms.
Possessing the bliss of humans and devas, they employ their supernormal powers to travel to other immeasurable and boundless worlds,
using skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing such a marvel, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming, "How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You have accomplished such great majestic spiritual power that you have enabled me to behold the countless bodhisattvas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction."
The various distinctions in the practice of the bodhisattva path, the countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
and their diverse skillful means for benefiting sentient beings, are able to cause bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "By this, one is able to cultivate the perfection of the provisions and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
This applies even as far as seeing the ten directions, where it is likewise in every respect."
Fascicle 583. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Is it possible for an initial thought to be superior to a subsequent thought? The World-Honored One replied, "Excellent."
It is well that you are able to inquire about such profound meanings from the Tathāgata. Furthermore, there is the principle that an initial resolve may be superior to subsequent ones.

This refers to the fact that although the untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are free from all afflictions within themselves, they are unable to transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve their minds toward awakening and abandon their afflictions.
Although a Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the great mind of enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*)—even while [still subject to afflictions]—...
Although one has not yet severed one's own afflictions, one is able to universally transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve their minds to abandon all afflictions;
thus, through successive stages, they benefit immeasurable sentient beings. This is the sense in which the initial resolve is superior to subsequent resolves.

The great bodhicitta generated by a bodhisattva possesses extraordinary power; if it is well-cultivated, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed enlightenment and be able to bestow upon sentient beings predictions that are free from error.
This is something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not capable of bestowing as predictions to others.
"Should there be anyone capable of explaining this, they would have heard it from the Buddha. This is the meaning of how the initial mind is superior to the subsequent mind.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, "In what way is the bodhisattva’s mind superior to the untainted minds of all pratyekabuddhas and arhats?
The World-Honored One replied to Śāriputra, "Do you mean that the bodhisattva’s mind still possesses greed and hatred?"
“Is there delusion? And are there secondary afflictions such as pride? Śāriputra replied, “It is so, Blessed One.

The Blessed One further addressed Śāriputra, saying, “Do you consider that the minds of pratyekabuddhas and arhats are already free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, and free from secondary afflictions such as pride? Śāriputra replied, “It is so, Blessed One. The Blessed One—

He further addressed Śāriputra, saying: "Do you think that Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, whose outflows are forever exhausted, are at times able to enter the immeasurable states of loving-kindness and compassion, universally taking as their object the immeasurable, so as to enable all classes of sentient beings to truly attain happiness?"
"And have they abandoned suffering? Śāriputra replied, "No, World-Honored One. Those Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats possess no skillful means whatsoever;
how could their minds enter into the immeasurable states of loving-kindness and compassion, universally taking the infinite as their object?"
To cause sentient beings to attain happiness and be free from suffering, one merely forms a provisional conceptualization and contemplates in this way:
"The assembly of Bodhisattvas, having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), seeks with certainty the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they shall do so perpetually and without interruption until the end of the future. Therefore, the Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness and compassion, wishing to cause immeasurable...

"All sentient beings shall attain peace and happiness and be freed from all suffering. For those without heavy obstacles, they will indeed attain happiness and be freed from all suffering at this very moment;

how much more so when [the Buddha] attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—could he not cause all classes of sentient beings to truly attain happiness and be freed from all suffering? The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "So it is, so it is."
The minds of all bodhisattvas are superior to, more excellent than, more venerable than,
higher than, more sublime than, more exquisite than, more supreme than, and unsurpassed by the untainted minds of all pratyekabuddhas and arhats. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
even if all sentient beings in the ten directions were to exhaust all outflows, become arhats, and possess the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations...

"Even if each of his various merits, such as liberation and so forth, were to transform into ten billion demonic armies, would such countless demonic armies have the power to cause the mind of even a single non-regressive Bodhisattva to change for even a moment? Śāriputra replied: "No."
"No, World-Honored One. Such an army of Māras cannot cause even a single non-regressive Bodhisattva’s mind to undergo transformation.
The Buddha said, "It is so. You should know that the power of a Bodhisattva’s mind surpasses the minds of all Arhats who have exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*).
Śāriputra, the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can universally eclipse and surpass that of all Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas."
The mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva, conjoined with compassion, is able to cause sentient beings to attain happiness and be free from suffering.
The minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, conjoined with compassion, possess only conceptual constructs and lack practical efficacy.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are Arhats who have forever exhausted all outflows and are endowed with various merits such as supernormal powers and liberation; they are able to cast this [world] away by means of their spiritual power.
One might place the world in another direction, yet one could not cause the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo transformation.
One might, through supernatural power, dry up the waters of the great ocean, yet one could not cause the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo transformation.
One might, through supernatural power, blow apart worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that all the Kings of Mountains, Sumerus, therein become like [powdered dust].
Ash and powder cannot cause the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo transformation.

Even with supernormal powers, one might blow away world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with the masses of fire from great kalpas burning with fierce flames, yet cause them all to be instantly extinguished;
still, one could not cause the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo transformation. For this reason, the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva [is unshakable].
"Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he is the most supreme.

Śāriputra said: "With the exception of the power possessed by the mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), no one can equal the supernatural power possessed by the mind of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva. For this reason, the non-retrogressive bodhisattva..."
The supernormal powers possessed by the mind of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can only be known by a Buddha; they can only be explained by a Buddha.
Among all other supernormal powers, these are the most supreme and excellent. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is so, it is so.
Only a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows that Bodhisattva’s non-retrogressive mind and proclaims it to all sentient beings according to reality. At that time...
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "By what causes and conditions is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva unchangeable?
Śāriputra replied: "When bodhisattvas practice generosity, there is nothing that does not take the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as its object."
His mind is firm and cannot be shaken. When he thus attains the stage of non-retrogression, his mind does not undergo transformation in accordance with conditions.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who desires non-retrogression should always rely upon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Cultivate the bodhisattva practices; do not take pleasure in other vehicles. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked, "What kind of bodhisattva is surpassed by pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas?
Śāriputra replied, "One who, upon hearing the teachings concerning the superior qualities of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, conceives a heart of admiration and longing for them."
He praised the teachings of the two vehicles. Because he gave rise to such improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), he was overcome by the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked: "For what reason is this mental attention called 'improper'? Śāriputra replied:
"Because it can obstruct the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and it causes the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes to gradually diminish and recede."
Therefore, it is called improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) for a bodhisattva. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:

"If bodhisattvas give rise to mental attention associated with the two vehicles, they will be overcome by those of the two vehicles; one should know that they do not enter the ranks of the bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because bodhisattvas seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). If they give rise to [such]..."
Mental engagement associated with the vehicle contradicts one's original aspiration, for it prevents the realization of omniscience.

It is like the manifestation of afflictions in a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), which contradicts what is sought—namely, either knowledge or abandonment. One is called a "stream-enterer" because of the diligent pursuit of knowledge and abandonment;
the activity of afflictions does not possess the sense of diligent pursuit. Why is this? For a stream-enterer seeks two types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
There is one thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*) and one thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

Because both the manifestation of afflictions and the two types of seeking are destroyed [thereby], a stream-enterer should always diligently seek the thorough knowledge of wisdom and extinguish all afflictions.

Likewise, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a mental orientation associated with the two vehicles, it contradicts the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) originally sought by a bodhisattva; thus, such a person is not truly called a [bodhisattva].

At that time, the true Bodhisattva Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "When a bodhisattva wishes to realize unsurpassed enlightenment, what kind of corresponding mental attention (*manasikāra*) should they arouse?
Śāriputra replied: "They should correctly arouse a mental attention corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
One should apply the mind; abiding in this application of the mind, one practices generosity and is thus able to dedicate it toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
If one cannot dedicate the practice of generosity toward omniscience, it is not called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to be without obstruction regarding omniscience should abandon discursive conceptualization and should abide in equanimity.

that Bodhisattvas, donning the armor of great vows, proceeding toward great enlightenment, and possessing supreme skillful means and superior intention, practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), relinquishing both Dharma and wealth, free from defilement and attachment. (The Perfection of Giving)
[The division is concluded].

Fascicle 584 (The Section on the Pāramitā of Pure Ethics):
If bodhisattvas abide in the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called that which is not the domain of a bodhisattva.
They will certainly be unable to embrace the perfection of ethical discipline; this constitutes a bodhisattva’s transgression of the precepts.

If, however, bodhisattvas—even while living as householders—take the three refuges, place deep faith in the Triple Gem, and dedicate their merit toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then these bodhisattvas, even though they enjoy the five objects of sensual pleasure, remain [true to] the bodhisattva path.
They never depart from the practice of the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), and are thus called true upholders of pure discipline.
Even if they frequently give rise to improper mental attentions (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) associated with the five sensory desires,
the arising of a single thought-moment associated with unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is sufficient to utterly destroy them.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "If a bodhisattva practices the giving of gifts while seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), would they not be grasping at the knowledge of all modes?
If one gives rise to a mind of grasping, it constitutes the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
How, then, can this be called upholding the bodhisattva precepts? Śāriputra replied: "The knowledge of all modes is far removed from all marks; it is not..."
It is encompassed by spatial location. The knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is not the aggregate of form, yet it is not separate from the aggregate of form;

it is not the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This extends even to the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas:

it is not that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas, yet it is not separate from the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas. The knowledge of all modes is far removed from all signs (nimitta); no dharma can be apprehended therein.

Because there is nothing to be apprehended, it cannot be grasped. Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices generosity and upholds pure ethical discipline, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, although they seek to realize the knowledge of all modes, this is not termed being subsumed under the "clinging to rules and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
If, however, they were to dedicate these toward the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas and grasp at pure ethical discipline, those bodhisattvas [would indeed be so subsumed].
One loses the bodhisattva precepts; such a person should be known as a bodhisattva who has transgressed the precepts. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"If one violates the precepts received by a bodhisattva, is there a cause and condition through which they may be restored to purity? Śāriputra replied:

"If, having already dedicated [the roots of virtue] toward the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, one has not yet seen the noble truths nor realized the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), then there may be causes and conditions by which they can easily be restored to purity. If...
Having seen the Noble Truths and realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), their heterodox views have become so deep-seated that they are difficult to purify again.

When practicing the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), one should not adopt the pure ethical discipline of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for by means of that [latter] ethical discipline—
One cannot grasp the knowledge of all modes, nor can one bring forth the knowledge of all modes.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "What is called a bodhisattva’s upholding of the precepts? Śāriputra replied:

In whatever way a bodhisattva guards the precepts, they dedicate them all toward unsurpassed enlightenment to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, continuing without interruption until the end of the future;
this should be known as the bodhisattva’s upholding of ethical discipline.
Even if a bodhisattva, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practices pure ethical discipline until it is perfected, yet their mind—
If they dedicate [their merit] toward the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, these bodhisattvas are unable to embrace the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Although they may extensively observe the ethical discipline of the two vehicles, they can still be said to be transgressors of ethical discipline. Why is this?
It should be known that they are practicing in an improper sphere (*agocara*). What is called an "improper sphere" refers to the levels of the two vehicles; it is not the domain of bodhisattvas.
Because it is the sphere of activity. What is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva? Śāriputra replied:

One should know that the mental engagements associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom constitute the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva;
up to and including the mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, one should know these to be the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the locus: if bodhisattvas practice this locus of conduct because of their truthfulness and stability, it should be known that this constitutes the bodhisattva’s upholding of ethical discipline.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra: "If bodhisattvas set a limit for themselves in their minds, thinking, 'I shall apply myself with diligence'..."
"Having passed through that many eons, one will certainly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
What fault could there be in forming such a resolve, that one would fail to attain the knowledge of all modes? Śāriputra replied, "These bodhisattvas are weary of and terrified by saṃsāra."
One should swiftly seek awakening. Because the mind is swift, one establishes a limit; by establishing such a limit, one is unable to bring the sublime roots of virtue to maturity.

Therefore, whenever a bodhisattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they must certainly not establish a mental limit while practicing the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom. At whatever time, at whatever time...

While undergoing birth and death within the six sense bases, they practice the bodhisattva path. From time to time, the practices they cultivate—from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom—gradually reach full maturity, becoming capable of realizing the knowledge of all modes.
The Bodhisattva accomplishes the vast and sublime Dharma, universally surpassing both the Pratyekabuddhas and all Śrāvakas.
Fascicle 585. Fascicle 586. Śāriputra addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"If a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), he perceives..."

If there were even the slightest phenomenon that could be called an "agent," one should know that although such a person dwells within the dharma of a bodhisattva, they are actually abandoning all bodhisattva dharmas;
this is termed improper mental attention and is called a transgression of the precepts. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then said to Śāriputra:

...Prajñāpāramitā. There is nothing that can be transgressed. What dharma could either benefit or harm this perfection of ethical discipline?
Śāriputra replied: "There is no dharma whatsoever that can benefit or harm this perfection of ethical discipline.
If one perceives even the slightest dharma as being beneficial or harmful, one should know that such a person grasps at the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and is unable to truly embrace it. If..."
To perceive even a slight phenomenon as a "doer" is what these bodhisattvas are able to correctly relinquish.

If one upholds pure ethical discipline and dedicates it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), that is called pure ethical discipline; however, if one cannot dedicate it toward the knowledge of all modes, it is not so called.

In accordance with their diligence and in accordance with their meditative concentration, they take great compassion as the foremost of all applications toward omniscience.

They are constantly able to generate a mind that accords with and is dedicated toward the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). Such a person is called a bodhisattva endowed with ethical discipline.
Furthermore, whatever profound and subtle wisdom these bodhisattvas practice is entirely for the sake of becoming free from inversion regarding phenomena and attaining all virtues.

Skillfulness refers to skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*), skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*), skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya*), skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
In this way, a bodhisattva should cultivate skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth.
By means of such skillfulness, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings as appropriate, causing them to permanently eliminate the notion of a "sentient being."
In this way, the bodhisattva gives rise to such a sublime mind. For the benefit of self and others, they cultivate all manner of wondrous wisdom, always taking great compassion as the foremost.
They are constantly able to generate a mind that accords with the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) through corresponding dedication.
This is called a bodhisattva endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*). By means of these six perfections (*pāramitā*), the bodhisattva dedicates [their merit] toward [enlightenment].
They seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). It is by means of this pure ethical discipline that these bodhisattvas universally surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said: "Venerable sir, what dharma do you designate as the eighth? Please explain its meaning so that I may understand it."

"Uphold this according to the principle. Śāriputra said: "If, within the equality of all phenomena, one knows that equality with wisdom as it truly is and realizes that equality—by means of this wisdom, all that was to be done has been completed.

It is like a house on fire containing a heap of various jewels; suppose there is a person who enters this house seeking those jewels—at that time, two possibilities may occur for that person. First:
First, if one lacks skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one dies within the burning house; second, if one possesses skillful means, one carries the jewels and departs.
Likewise, when a bodhisattva swiftly seeks unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*):

first, if one lacks skillful means, one realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and falls into the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which is like dying in the burning house; second, if one possesses skillful means...

To say, "One should quickly realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)," is not the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because falling into the stage of the two vehicles is not the natural outflow of skillful means;

rather, it is the fruit of the natural outflow of a lack of skillful means, for one has thereby fallen away from the sought-after great enlightenment (mahābodhi). Now, for a bodhisattva who seeks great enlightenment and benefits sentient beings...
Because they seek the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they realize the limit of reality;
it is not the fruit of mere skillful means. If bodhisattvas cultivate various meritorious qualities through skillful means and give rise to such various reflections:
One should know that such a person lacks skillful means. Why is this? A bodhisattva should not desire to surpass another bodhisattva;
a bodhisattva should not treat another bodhisattva with contempt; a bodhisattva should not seek to subjugate another bodhisattva.

Toward other bodhisattvas, a bodhisattva should offer worship and respect just as one would offer worship and respect to a Tathāgata, and should likewise revere others who possess [the qualities of] existence.
Sentient beings and the mind are without distinction.
Sustained by the power of great compassion and prajñā, one does not fear the emptiness of phenomena nor realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Taking as one’s basis the perfection of pure ethical discipline, which is fully accomplished through skillful means, one should apply oneself diligently to all phenomena.

Why is this? Because if the mind gives rise to attachment, one is unable to seek after the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna);

Therefore, regarding the stages of the two vehicles, a bodhisattva should only remain distant; they should neither praise nor disparage them.
World-Honored One, I maintain that afflictions possess great merit for bodhisattvas, in that they are able to accord with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Renunciation. Thus, it should be known that such a bodhisattva has already entered the stage of non-retrogression;
for the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not abandon any sentient beings, their minds being impartial toward all.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the one who never abandons the bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there will be bodhisattvas who, through diligent practice, will gradually bring all dharmas to fulfillment and act as illuminators for the world.
Śāriputra said: "It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares; after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata..."
In the worlds of the ten directions, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who succeed the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

They proclaim immeasurable dharma-gates, causing [beings] to apply themselves with diligent vigor, to employ skillful means, to observe without error, and to remain free from all conceptual proliferation.
Through skillful means, one practices the six pāramitās as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas,
until finally realizing all-knowledge (the section on the pāramitā of pure ethical discipline is concluded).

Fascicle 589 (The Section on the Perfection of Forbearance).
Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "What is the difference between the forbearance cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattvas and the forbearance cultivated by the assembly of śrāvakas?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied: "The forbearance cultivated by the śrāvakas is called..."

The patience cultivated by Śrāvakas has limited aspects and objects of focus and is not fully perfected. The patience cultivated by Bodhisattvas is called that which possesses complete aspects and objects of focus and is most perfectly fulfilled.
Therefore, the patience of a Śrāvaka is solely for the sake of abandoning one's own afflictions and not for the sake of sentient beings;

...Maitreya.

Regarding that, what kind of mind should a bodhisattva arouse? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should not arouse attachment toward the first person, nor should they arouse aversion toward the second person.
They should arouse a mind of equanimity toward both, desiring their ultimate benefit and happiness. In this way, a bodhisattva is able to practice."

The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). One who abides in the perfection of patience should, when sentient beings come to me desiring to engage in conflict, proclaim for them that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature.
Since there is nothing to contend over within ultimate emptiness, upon hearing this, their contentious mind shall be stilled. By means of this...

Having reached the stage of skillful exhortation and practicing all dharmas, once one is firmly established therein, one takes these accumulated roots of virtue and dedicates them toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Up to this point, one should know that the bodhisattva’s mind is concentrated.
When the mind has attained concentration in all respects, it should be known as being "dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration" (dhyānapāramitā). Why?

For this reason, because they never depart from the superior mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the two vehicles are inferior to those of a bodhisattva,
as they are devoid of the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.
Then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "When śrāvakas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attain the fruit of a śrāvaka.

Likewise, when bodhisattvas abide in this meditative concentration, they realize the nature of phenomena, become free from all attachments, and attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
How can it be said that the meditative concentration of śrāvakas is definitively devoid of all [attachments]?"
Regarding the mental engagement associated with the wisdom of wisdom, the Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"Although various śrāvakas are able to enter the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments in the present, realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and achieve the fruit of a śrāvaka, they lack the Tathāgata’s superior qualities such as the powers and fearlessnesses, as well as the primary and secondary marks;
therefore, they are not called Tathāgatas. For this reason, they remain far removed [from Buddhahood]."

The mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Because they lack the qualities of a Buddha, they are called Śrāvakas. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called the supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a Bodhisattva? What is the name of such a supreme concentration? The World-Honored One replied:
"The supreme concentration of a Bodhisattva is named 'Inconceivable' (*acintya*); its power is difficult to fathom, and it can swiftly bring about realization."
Because it is the wisdom of all-knowledge, this supreme meditative concentration is also called "benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings.

When it manifests before one, it brings forth boundless skillful means, enabling the instruction and guidance of immeasurable sentient beings, and the realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
They sever all afflictions and enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, or realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to the Buddha: "I consider the various meditative concentrations attained by the *śrāvakas* to be superior to those of the bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because the *śrāvakas* fully attain the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), whereas the bodhisattvas among them attain only the first eight and do not attain [the ninth]."

Regarding the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), the Blessed One declared: "A bodhisattva also attains the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;

that is to say, having already attained mastery over this meditative state, he simply does not manifest its entry. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata does not permit the manifestation of entry into this attainment."
"Do not, by entering [this state] in the present, fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva were to enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, it would be neither the proper time nor the proper place.

When a bodhisattva sits upon the seat of enlightenment, having forever destroyed all perceptions of false appearances and realized the realm of ambrosia, only then does he enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
The Buddha said, "Bodhisattvas are truly rare; they are able to perform what is difficult to do.

That is to say, although they possess the power to realize the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) for the sake of sentient beings.

This is because, toward sentient beings, they have long contemplated their benefit and happiness, and their superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) remains ever present before them. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Bodhisattvas are peaceful..."
Abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), how does one employ skillful means to emerge from that concentration? The Blessed One addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"The bodhisattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, enters and abides in the first dhyāna, which is born of detachment and characterized by joy and bliss;
continuing in this manner up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he fully dwells therein. Regarding the dhyānas of the form and formless realms..."

Having mastered the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) through both forward and reverse sequences and by means of progressive transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*), and having become thoroughly proficient and skilled in their mastery, he enters the desire realm again with a non-concentrated mind (*asamāhita-citta*).
Why is this? It is so that he does not, by the power of meditative concentration, take birth in the long-lived heavens of the form or formless realms;

nor does he, by means of the meditative attainments of the form or formless realms, give rise to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*pratisandhi-citta*) of those planes. This is for the sake of protection.
That mind prevents [the bodhisattva] from manifesting [in higher realms], causing him to return to the desire realm with a non-concentrated mind.

By giving rise to this mind, he returns to birth in the desire realm to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and to bring forth the boundless factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Birth in the form and formless realms lacks such capacity; for those born in the two upper realms, the body and mind are dull. It is for this reason that the bodhisattva first practices [in the desire realm].
Having brought the higher meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) to full maturity, he subsequently gives rise to a lower state of mind and returns to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

There, having cultivated and accumulated the immeasurable provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) until they reach perfection, he transcends the three realms (*tridhātu*) and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
(The section on the perfection of meditative concentration is concluded.)
