In examining the principles, we find that while their manifestations differ, they all direct one toward the proper course; when one returns to the fundamental unity, all affairs are measured against it. How could this not involve melting away conceptual thought within the truth?

At this juncture, one quiets the grasping at illusory objects. Although the precepts of *dāna* and *śīla* are most solemn, and the cultivation of *kṣānti* and *vīrya* is most sharp and keen, one ultimately awakens to the favor of true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*) by taking the provisional path of the authentic teaching.
Intending to dispel the delusions of the "elephant and the touch" parable, there is once again the assembly at Lake Haṃsa;

thus, the traces of the five [Hearers] are brilliantly guided, and they ascend the Vehicle of the First [the Śrāvaka]. Refining and molding the two extremes, one gazes upon the profound and subtle mystery.
Behold! When one contemplates the four propositions, one looks up to profound stillness to conceal all sounds and cuts away the sprouts of all views;
thus the obscuring petals fall like stars. When one tears asunder the net of accumulated doubts, the veiling silk clouds are dispersed. Having realized that nature is empty, one practices constantly;

having awakened to the fact that birth is provisional, one benefits others perpetually. By this, the four Māras lose their way and the six pāramitās arrive in a multitude. Through such practice, giving is never exhausted.
That which is difficult to relinquish, he can relinquish; thus, through precepts, there is no need for further restraint. That which is difficult to protect, he can protect;

thus, through patience, there is no longer anything to be endured. That which is unbearable, he can endure; thus, through diligence, there is no longer any action to be performed. That which does not arise, he causes to arise; thus, through concentration, there is no longer any stillness to be lost.
Thus, the three marks do not interact with one another, and through this wisdom, illumination ceases; the three wheels do not revolve. Therefore, when realized, movement becomes increasingly still;
when misunderstood, stillness becomes increasingly turbulent. Phenomena are neither identical to nor separate from non-phenomena; how could practice be either one with or different from non-practice?
As for its awakening and realization, the true mind merges into a single contemplation; as for its manifestation, it is the Jewel of the Dharma.

Arranged in myriad sections, there are thus: the two wisdoms, the three bodies, the four analytical knowledges, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine meditative absorptions, and the ten powers;
further added are the eighteen unique qualities, the eighty minor marks, the knowledge of dependent origination, and the twenty modes of emptiness.
All these are manifested through the *hita* (beneficence) and perfected by the *dhāraṇī*; they are as if gathered together.
Based upon the teachings issued from the golden mouth, which manifest the jade-white tuft [of the Buddha], these have been compiled into eight fascicles.

They were not translated anew; rather, due to my own lack of talent, I have mistakenly joined the ranks of translators. Looking back upon the magnificent assembly of that former gathering, I lament that I was unable to attend;

yet, mindful of his extraordinary favor, I now set forth this record of his lingering voice. It spreads forth through the compassionate breeze and is received with veneration during this auspicious era. Intending to...

May this wondrous treasure be transmitted through the family, and may each person grasp this numinous pearl. May the dust of worldly afflictions be washed away throughout the eight regions, and may the profound nourishment of the Dharma rain down upon ten thousand generations.
May blessings protect the imperial throne, extending the longevity of the Emperor and Empress; may prosperity flow to the common people, and the teachings of the Dharma flourish and spread.
Thus, those of narrow mind may cast off their hesitation at times of alarm and terror, and those guests of arrogance may cease their slander amidst their own distress.

Were it not for those who have reverently served through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and who have heard [this teaching] repeatedly over successive generations, how could one dare to open this volume, cast aside their stinginess, and transcend words to enter into its appreciation?
How tragic! Composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery in the Táng Dynasty, Fascicle 593 (The Section on the Prajñāpāramitā).
The Bodhisattva Suvīra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, in various places you have proclaimed the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattvas.
What is the *prajñāpāramitā*? How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?
How should one practice the *prajñāpāramitā* so as to bring it to swift [completion]?”
Perfected. How does one practice the *prajñāpāramitā* so that no evil Māras can find an opportunity and all demonic activities (*mārakarman*) are fully recognized?
How does one abide in the *prajñāpāramitā* so as to swiftly perfect all the qualities of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vīra, saying: "What do you ask regarding what is called *prajñā*?"
Regarding "Pāramitā," you should know that in reality there is not even the slightest dharma that can be named "Prajñāpāramitā," because it transcends all paths of names and expressions. O Suvīra,
this profound Prajñāpāramitā truly cannot be said to be "this is Prajñāpāramitā," nor can it be said to belong to that Prajñāpāramitā.
Much more so. It cannot be said that it arises from this *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can it be said that it comes from this *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to reach far into the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called *prajñāpāramitā*.
Since even the wisdom of a Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, how much less can *prajñāpāramitā* be apprehended?
Suvīra, "prajñā" refers to the understanding of all phenomena and the knowledge of all phenomena; therefore, it is called prajñā.
How does prajñā understand and know all phenomena? It means that while phenomena are distinct and their designations are likewise distinct, no phenomenon exists apart from its designation.
Whether one understands or knows all phenomena, they are all inexpressible; yet, this conforms to what sentient beings can know.
It is so called, therefore, that it is named *prajñā*. O Well-Valiant One, as for *prajñā*, it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
It is by means of conventional designation that it is spoken of as *prajñā*. However, all phenomena (*dharma*) cannot be designated, cannot be moved, and cannot be proclaimed.
It cannot be manifested. One who knows it in this way is said to have true knowledge. Suvīra, *prajñā* (wisdom) is neither knowing nor not knowing;
it is neither here nor in any other place, and for this reason it is called *prajñā*. Suvīra, *prajñā* is that which is the range of wisdom, yet it is not the range of wisdom;
it is neither the domain of non-wisdom, nor is it the domain of wisdom, because wisdom is utterly detached from all things.
Because it is an object. If wisdom were an object, it would necessarily not be wisdom. Wisdom does not arise from non-wisdom, nor does non-wisdom arise from wisdom.

Non-wisdom does not arise from non-wisdom, nor does wisdom arise from wisdom. One does not designate something as "wisdom" by virtue of being non-wisdom, nor does one designate something as "non-wisdom" by virtue of being wisdom.
It is not by way of non-wisdom that it is called wisdom, nor is it by way of wisdom that it is called non-wisdom. Not by...
That which is non-wisdom is called "non-wisdom. Furthermore, it is not by means of wisdom that it is called "wisdom," yet it is precisely this non-wisdom that is called "wisdom.
By this very fact, what is called "wisdom" is designated as "non-wisdom. Within this context, that which is "wisdom" cannot be demonstrated such that one could say, "this is named wisdom";
it cannot be demonstrated to which [category] this wisdom belongs; it cannot be demonstrated by what this wisdom is caused; it cannot...
This demonstrates the source from which this wisdom arises; therefore, within wisdom there is no real nature of wisdom, nor does real wisdom abide within the nature of wisdom.
Both wisdom and the nature of wisdom are unattainable, and it is likewise for non-wisdom and its nature.
Wisdom is certainly not designated as "wisdom" by virtue of being non-wisdom; if it were designated as "wisdom" through being non-wisdom, then all foolish commoners would [be considered wise].

There is wisdom. If one, in accordance with reality, finds nothing to be apprehended in either wisdom or non-wisdom, and thoroughly knows wisdom and non-wisdom as they truly are, this is called wisdom.
However, the true nature of wisdom is not as it has been described. Why is this? Because the true nature of wisdom is beyond names and expressions;
wisdom is neither an object of wisdom nor an object of non-wisdom, for wisdom transcends all things.

Because it is an object, it cannot be said to be either the object of knowledge or not the object of knowledge; this is called the authentic proclamation of the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
Such characteristics of knowledge are in truth ineffable and cannot be demonstrated, yet they are explained and shown in accordance with what sentient beings can understand.
Even the knower cannot be described, for if the object of knowledge does not exist, how much less could there be a knower? If one can thus [perceive] in accordance with reality—
To know fully, to realize in accordance with reality—this is called *prajñā*.
Furthermore, Suvīra, if one can thus directly perceive and realize [this], it is called supramundane *prajñā*. Such is the supramundane *prajñā* as here described.
It cannot be described either. Why is this? Since even the mundane world does not exist, how much less could there be that which transcends it?

Since that which is transcended does not exist, how much less could there be that which transcends? Because neither the mundane nor the supramundane, nor the act of transcending nor the object transcended, can be apprehended at all, it is called "supramundane prajñā.
If anything were apprehended, it would not be called supramundane prajñā. If this prajñā...
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise unapprehendable, because it is apart from any apprehensible nature such as existence or non-existence.

Furthermore, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, "the world" is a conventional designation; there is no real world that could emerge. Rather, it is called "transcending the world" because it emerges from all designations.
Moreover, for one who transcends the world, there is in reality neither emergence nor non-emergence from the world. Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely nothing that emerges or can emerge.

Because there is not even a slight phenomenon that can be apprehended, it is called "transcending the world. Furthermore, as for "transcending the world," there is neither world nor transcending the world;

there is neither transcendence nor non-transcendence. Therefore, it is called "transcending the world. If one can understand this thus according to reality, this is what is called "transcendent prajñā.
If such prajñā were as it has been described, why would that be so? Because transcendent prajñā—
Because it transcends all paths of verbal expression, although it is called "supramundane," there is nothing from which it emerges; although it is called "prajñā," there is nothing known.
Since that which emerges and that which is known cannot be apprehended, the one who emerges and the one who knows likewise cannot be apprehended.
To know things thus, as they truly are, is called supramundane prajñā.
Because there is nothing that this prajñā does not transcend, it is therefore called supramundane prajñā. Furthermore, Suvīra, this is also called penetrating prajñā.
What does such prajñā penetrate? It is said that this prajñā penetrates nothing. If this prajñā...
That which is thoroughly penetrated is merely a conventional designation. If it is a mere designation, then it cannot be called the "thorough penetration of prajñā.
This is because within this [state], there is absolutely nothing whatsoever; there is neither "this" nor "that," nor is there anything in between.

There is no one who penetrates, no object to be penetrated, no place of penetration, no time of penetration, and no person who penetrates. For these reasons, it is called "thorough penetration. Furthermore,
Suvīra, those who possess such wisdom are able to penetrate the three realms as they truly are.
How do they penetrate the three realms as they truly are? It is by saying that what are not the three realms are called the "three realms.
Why is this? Because within them there is no realm to be penetrated; to penetrate the three realms is itself to realize them as non-realms. By being able to penetrate them in this way...
One penetrates the three realms; therefore, it is called the perfection of the wisdom of thorough penetration (*prajñā-sampad-abhisamaya*).

Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, that which is called "thorough penetration" refers to the ability to universally know all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because various phenomena arise by means of various conditions, it is called "dependent origination."
Thus, dependent origination is entirely non-existent. This is called penetrating dependent origination; this is what is meant by thoroughly knowing dependent origination.
That is to say, it can demonstrate that there is, in reality, no arising. Because there is no arising, it is termed "dependent origination."
It is equal and without arising; therefore, it is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This means that in this state, even arising does not exist, let alone cessation.

To realize dependent origination accordingly—whether in accordance with or contrary to it—is to find nothing at all obtainable, because there is no equal arising; thus it is called dependent origination.
If there is no origination, then there is no birth. If there is no birth, then there is no past, nor is there anything already born.
If there is neither past nor anything already born, then there is no cessation. If there is no cessation, then there is no knowledge of arising.

By means of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), one no longer gives rise [to further existence] nor does one realize cessation (*nirodha*). Because there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation.
It is because there is arising that cessation is conventionally designated; since there is no arising, there is therefore no cessation.

To thus know, see, penetrate, and realize all phenomena in this way is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). O Well-Valiant One, the knowledge of exhaustion refers to the exhaustion [of the outflows].

It is called "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) because it is free from ignorance. By what is it called "exhaustion"? It is called "exhaustion" by virtue of being inexhaustible; one does not perceive any dharma that can be called "exhausted.
Nevertheless, it is designated as "knowledge of exhaustion" by way of being devoid of ignorance; that is, it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" precisely because it has exhausted ignorance.
Because it thoroughly knows all dharmas characterized by ignorance, it is called "the exhaustion of ignorance. By means of this exhaustion of ignorance, it is so named.

Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): it is not that there is something among the phenomena of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*) that is exhausted or not exhausted. Rather, because one is free from non-knowledge, it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion.
By knowing these phenomena of non-knowledge as they truly are—namely, that they do not exist at all—one is said to be "free" [from them].

Through such knowledge, one knows that no distinct phenomenon of non-knowledge can be found; this is called being "free from non-knowledge. However, since the phenomena of non-knowledge are in reality unattainable, even knowledge [itself]...
It does not exist; how much less could there be any "knowledge of exhaustion"? That which can attain liberation within exhaustion is called the "knowledge of exhaustion.
O Well-Vigorous One, it is not that this *pāramitā* has even a slight portion of a distant further shore that can be attained.
If this *prajñāpāramitā* had even a slight portion of a distant further shore that could be attained, the Tathāgata would have taught a profound *prajñā*.
The *pāramitā* has a distant "other shore," yet this *prajñāpāramitā* has no distant shore that can be attained;
therefore, it is not said that this has an "other shore. Furthermore, Suvīra, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* awakens to all phenomena.
If one could awaken [to them] in such a way, that would contradict awakening. Why is this? Because herein there is no entity that can be called "awakening."
Awakening. Since there is no object to be awakened to, awakening itself is also non-existent. This means that regarding all phenomena, there is no sense of "thorough penetration.
Because awakening to the equality of the dharma-nature of all phenomena is *bodhi*, one is called *bodhi* because of thoroughly awakening to all phenomena.
How is it that this can thoroughly awaken to all phenomena? Within this, there is nothing that can be named *bodhi*; therefore, within this, there is also no thorough awakening.
Awakening. Why is this? If even a fraction of bodhi were obtainable, then one would have to obtain bodhi within bodhi.
However, within bodhi, bodhi does not exist. One should realize bodhi in this manner;

it is called "awakening" (bodha) because it is neither a matter of sequential cognition nor a matter of penetration. Although it is described in this way, it is not as it is described, because all dharmas...
It cannot be cognized; it cannot be fully realized. Furthermore, both phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because one awakens to this principle, it is called *bodhi*. Why is this? It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas can attain *bodhi*, nor is it that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas can realize *bodhi*;
for suchness (*tathatā*) as true *bodhi* cannot be realized. Not...
Because it can be manifested. It is not that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas give rise to bodhi; for bodhi has the nature of being unborn and unarisen.
O Suvīra, the "realm of sentient beings" is a designation for non-existent sentient beings. There is no nature of a sentient being within sentient beings;
because sentient beings do not exist, it is called the "realm of sentient beings. If there were a sentient being within sentient beings...

As for the nature of sentient beings (*sattva*), one should not speak of them as a "sentient-being realm" (*sattvadhātu*). To speak of a "sentient-being realm" is precisely to manifest the absence of a realm (*adhātu*).

This is because the sentient-being realm has the nature of being no-realm. If the sentient-being realm existed by way of the nature of a realm, then there would truly be a life-principle (*jīva*) identical to the body.
If the sentient-being realm existed apart from the nature of a realm, then there would truly be a life-principle distinct from the body. However, [this is not the case].
The realm of sentient beings has no intrinsic nature as a realm; it is merely designated as a "realm" by way of conventional usage.

Within the realm of sentient beings there can be no intrinsic nature of a realm, nor does the intrinsic nature of a realm contain the realm of sentient beings, nor is the intrinsic nature of a realm itself the realm of sentient beings.
There is no realm of sentient beings apart from the nature of the realms, because all phenomena lack the nature of a realm.
Furthermore, Subhānavīrya, it is with this meaning and intention in mind that I say the realm of sentient beings cannot be established as either decreasing or increasing.
Why is this? Because the realm of sentient beings is not of an existent nature; because the realm of sentient beings is devoid of sentient beings.
Just as it is impossible to designate the realm of sentient beings as either decreasing or increasing, so too it is with all phenomena:
it is impossible to designate them as either decreasing or increasing. Since all phenomena lack any real intrinsic nature, one cannot say that they decrease or increase.
If one can thus awaken to all phenomena accordingly, this is called awakening to the Buddha-dharma accordingly.
Because all phenomena are neither diminished nor fulfilled, they are designated as "Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, "Buddha-dharma" is merely a conventional designation for what is not Buddha-dharma.
There is no entity whatsoever that can cause the various Buddha-dharmas to either diminish or be fulfilled. Why is this? It is because one awakens to all phenomena accordingly.
If one can thus awaken to the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), therein no phenomenon is diminished or increased.
One should know that "all phenomena" is merely a conventional designation (*adhivacana*); for that *dharmadhātu* neither diminishes nor increases.
Why is this? Because that *dharmadhātu* is without limit. No distinction can be found between the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and that *dharmadhātu*; they do not exist as separate.

Whether the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and that realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) decrease or increase, whether they are attained or exist—such awakening to this as it is is called *bodhi*.
For this reason, it is said that among the qualities of all Buddhas, there is nothing that can be established as decreasing or increasing.

Furthermore, Subhānavīrya, if one who is free from the nature of decrease or increase can, in accordance with reality, remain without conceptual differentiation, one should know that such a person is "in accordance with reality."
The seer has no capacity for acceptance or rejection within this; such realization is called bodhi. Bodhi is precisely the characteristic of a Buddha.
What is the characteristic of a Buddha? It is that all characteristics are ultimately without characteristics; this is the characteristic of a Buddha. Why is this?
Because ultimate lack of characteristics is by nature free from the characteristics of bodhi. Such realization is [bodhi].
This is called awakening (*bodhi*). Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, although all sentient beings practice the conduct of awakening, they do not know and do not realize the true nature of phenomena;
therefore, they are not called bodhisattvas. Why is this? Because they do not know that sentient beings are not sentient beings.
If one knows that sentient beings are not of the nature of sentient beings, one practices the conduct of enlightenment and should become a bodhisattva.
However, because sentient beings are subject to perversion, they are unable to awaken to their own conduct, their own objects, and their own sphere of activity.
If one understands one's own conduct as it truly is, one will no longer engage in conduct characterized by conceptual discrimination; this is called the bodhisattva practicing non-conduct.
A bodhisattva should not give rise to conceptual activity through conceptualization.
Where there is no conceptualization, there is no activity; where one does not give rise to conceptualization, there is likewise no activity.
This is because all Buddhas and bodhisattvas practice all activities without any conceptualization.
All arrogance never arises again; regarding all phenomena, one no longer grasps at objects, no longer discriminates, and neither roams nor treads upon them.
This is called the true practice of a bodhisattva, because it takes non-action as its skillful means.
Furthermore, Suvīra, that which is "the absence of sentient beings" should be known as a designation for a bodhisattva, because they are able to eliminate all conceptualizations.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly realized that all sentient beings are not truly sentient beings;
that all sentient beings are in fact no sentient beings at all; and that all sentient beings are merely attached through inversion.
Sentient beings. All sentient beings are sentient beings conceptually imputed;
all sentient beings are sentient beings that are objects of false conceptualization; all sentient beings are sentient beings whose own nature is subject to decay;

all sentient beings are sentient beings for whom formations are conditioned by ignorance. O Well-Valiant One, there is not even the slightest real dharma that corresponds to the name "sentient being."
One might grasp at it as "self" or as "mine," yet because there is no real dharma, it can be said that all sentient beings are not real sentient beings.
That which is "not a sentient being" should be understood as a metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*) for "non-reality.

That which is "non-real" should be understood as a metaphorical designation for "non-sentient-being. If one possesses universal awakening regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one may be called a Bodhisattva.

Fascicle 594; Fascicle 595. Furthermore, O Suvīra, one who is called a "bodhisattva" is a designation for one who can correctly awaken to the fact that sentient beings are without reality and without birth.
Moreover, a bodhisattva is also able to know all phenomena as they truly are, just as a Buddha does; that is to say, according to reality.
One knows that the nature of all phenomena is without reality and without arising, and is likewise without falsity.
O Well-Valiant One, if bodhisattvas resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they should form this thought: "I have now resolved upon the mind of enlightenment; this is enlightenment."
"I now give rise to the mind of practice for the sake of attaining this bodhi. Because these [other] bodhisattvas perceive something to be attained, they are not called bodhisattvas;
they can only be called 'mad beings' (sattva). Why is this?

It is because those bodhisattvas definitively cling to the existence of that which initiates [the practice], definitively cling to the existence of the mind that is initiated, and definitively cling to the existence of bodhi."
Because their nature is that of conceptual construction (*prapañca*), they can only be called "beings who grasp at the thought of enlightenment" (*bodhicitta-saṃgrāhaka-sattva*);

they are not called "Bodhisattvas who have truly and purely generated the mind. Because they generate the thought of enlightenment through volitional effort (*abhisamskāra*), they are further called "beings of effort" (*abhisamskāra-sattva*) and are not called Bodhisattvas.
Because they generate the thought of enlightenment through applied practice (*prayoga*), they are further called "beings of practice" (*prayoga-sattva*) and are not called Bodhisattvas. Why?

For this reason, those bodhisattvas who give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) due to having something grasped can only be called "beings who have resolved their minds" (cittotpādika-sattva), but they are not called "bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One, there is no one who can truly give rise to the mind of enlightenment, because the mind of enlightenment cannot be produced;
for enlightenment is unborn and is also without mind. Those bodhisattvas merely cling to...
To resolve to attain enlightenment while failing to understand the meaning of the non-arising mind of enlightenment—that the equality of the mind is itself enlightenment—is not true resolution.
Within this state, there is no conceptual differentiation. If one differentiates between the mind and enlightenment, one becomes attached to both the mind and enlightenment.

One who resolves for enlightenment based on these two [dualistic] notions should be known as one who cannot truly resolve their mind for enlightenment. Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One, regarding enlightenment...
Mind and awakening are not distinct from one another. There is no real awakening within the mind, nor is there a real mind to be found within awakening.
Awakening and mind, according to reality and according to principle, can neither be said to be awakening nor to be mind.
Because, through realizing reality as it is, both awakening and mind are unattainable—neither arising nor non-arising—one is therefore called a Bodhisattva. One is also called...
Mahāsattva. One who is well-courageous and has entered into the Mahāyāna is called a Mahāsattva. What is meant by the Mahāyāna?
It refers to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), which is designated as the Mahāyāna. What is all-knowledge?

It refers to whatever knowledge there may be—whether conditioned knowledge or unconditioned knowledge, whether worldly knowledge or supramundane knowledge—that is capable of entering into such [realities].

He is called a *mahāsattva* because he is wise. Why is this? Because he is able to remain far removed from the great perception of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃjñā*), and because he is able to remain far removed from the great aggregate of ignorance (*avidyāskandha*), the great aggregate of formative forces (*saṃskāraskandha*), the great aggregate of unknowing (*ajñānaskandha*), and the great aggregate of suffering (*duḥkhaskandha*).
For these reasons, he is called a *mahāsattva*. Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One, he is far removed from the great...

One who possesses the perception of sentient beings is called a Mahāsattva. Although they have no apprehension of any mind or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), they are nonetheless able to understand the fundamental nature of the mind.

Although they have no apprehension of bodhi or the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), they are nonetheless able to understand the fundamental nature of bodhi. By means of this wisdom, they do not perceive bodhi as existing within the mind.
"Ti. Furthermore, one does not perceive bodhi apart from the mind, nor does one perceive a real mind within bodhi, nor does one perceive a real mind apart from bodhi.
In this way, one eliminates [such notions]. There is nothing to be cultivated, nothing to rely upon, and nothing to cling to.
Although one does not perceive a mind-nature of bodhi, one is nevertheless able to give rise to the great bodhicitta. As...
This is the generation of the bodhicitta, yet there is nothing in bodhi that is brought forth. Why is this? Because they already abide securely in great bodhi;
they do not perceive any distinction between the arising and ceasing of mind or of bodhi, nor do they perceive anyone who generates the mind and proceeds toward great bodhi.
Without views or attachments, and without conceptual differentiation, they give rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
and the mind of liberation—one should know that such a person is a true bodhisattva.

Furthermore, O Well-Valiant One, if bodhisattvas give rise to the thought of enlightenment while not being free from the perception of "mind" and the perception of "enlightenment," they are far from enlightenment and not near to enlightenment.
If one does not perceive that awakening is either near or far, it should be known that such a person is close to unsurpassed awakening and is also called one who has truly generated the bodhicitta.
It is with this meaning and intentional purpose (*saṃdhāya*) in mind that I say:

"If one can know for oneself that there are no dual characteristics, they know all Buddha-dharmas as they truly are. Why is this? Because they are able to realize and penetrate both myself and existence.
Sentient beings and all phenomena are equally devoid of intrinsic nature. Thus, one is able to universally know that all phenomena are non-dual.

One will certainly be able to realize that the self, sentient beings, and all phenomena all take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature; in principle, there is no distinction between them.
If one can understand that all phenomena are non-dual, one can then understand all Buddha-dharmas. If one can universally know that all phenomena are...
Second: one who can thoroughly know all Buddha-dharmas can, if they thoroughly know the self, thoroughly know the three realms.
Those with overweening pride cannot enter into this teaching of the Dharma, because it is not their domain and not their level.
It is essential that all sons of the Buddha arise from the self-arisen wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
only then can they diligently train in the great lion’s roar of the Teacher of Perfect Enlightenment and skillfully enjoy the unsurpassed Dharma-wealth of perfect enlightenment.
When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are about to reveal the subtle, profound, and wondrous Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to sever all doubts,
there will necessarily be such an assembly of immeasurable, boundless, and most supreme, pure merits.

According to the conventional words and phrases of the objects of knowledge as they are known, he skillfully expounds the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, causing the assembly of bodhisattvas to diligently train in the fact that the "suchness" (*yathāvadbhāva*) and "intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena are unapprehendable.
*Prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so. Regarding all [phenomena], *prajñāpāramitā*...
The Dharma is entirely without support.
All phenomena are neither within, nor without, nor in between; they abide in detachment.
All phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated. All phenomena are suchness, the non-illusory nature, and the unchanging.
The nature of difference and the nature of things as they are—this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*): they are devoid of the nature of all phenomena. Why is this? Because within all phenomena there are no all phenomena;
this non-existence is called the perfection of wisdom. All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this absence of intrinsic nature is [the perfection of wisdom].
This is called the Prajñāpāramitā: all dharmas are devoid of the self-nature of all dharmas;
this absence of self-nature is what is called the Prajñāpāramitā (ending at scroll ninety-four).
All phenomena are not the domain of all phenomena; there is no knowledge and no vision regarding all phenomena—this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
All phenomena do not abandon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena;
to have such thorough knowledge of intrinsic nature is called the perfection of wisdom. All phenomena are neither joined nor separated. This...
It is said that the perfection of wisdom is such that all phenomena neither decrease nor increase; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
It is said that the perfection of wisdom is such that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
It is said that the perfection of wisdom is such that among all phenomena there are no pure dharmas and no impure dharmas; this is called the perfection of wisdom.
All phenomena do not shift; they do not enter. This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
All phenomena are neither bound nor liberated. This is called the perfection of wisdom. All phenomena neither die nor are born;
all phenomena are neither born nor do they die. This is called the perfection of wisdom. One.
All phenomena do not undergo transmigration; there are no phenomena that transmigrate. This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
All phenomena are not subject to exhaustion; there are no phenomena that are exhausted. This is called the perfection of wisdom.
All phenomena are neither subject to arising nor subject to cessation. This is called the perfection of wisdom. All phenomena...
It is not a dharma that arises; it is not a dharma that ceases. This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
All dharmas are neither subject to transformation and decay nor are they not subject to transformation and decay. This is called the perfection of wisdom.
All dharmas are neither permanent nor impermanent, and so on, up to: neither pure nor impure. This is called the perfection of wisdom.
Prajñāpāramitā: all dharmas are neither dharmas characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they dharmas free from greed, hatred, and delusion;
this is called Prajñāpāramitā. All dharmas are not agents, nor are they instigators of action, and so on up to:
they are not knowers or perceivers; this is called Prajñāpāramitā. All dharmas are neither annihilated nor eternal.
It has limits; it is not limitless. This is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
All phenomena are neither views nor the abandonment of views; they are neither craving nor the abandonment of craving.
This is called the perfection of wisdom. All phenomena are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. This is called the perfection of wisdom. (End of Volume Ninety-five.)
Fascicle 596: Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow, their intrinsic nature is entirely non-existent.
Thus, although this *prajñāpāramitā* is conventionally described as having various intrinsic natures, in reality, no intrinsic nature of this *prajñāpāramitā* can be apprehended.
[The Buddha] proclaimed.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Although the Tathāgata has taught the Prajñāpāramitā, he has taught that the Prajñāpāramitā is not the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*).
The World-Honored One told Śāriputra, "So it is, so it is. I..."
I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*). Why? Because all phenomena are not the perfected nature.
Therefore, I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is not the perfected nature. It is, for example, like a rainbow:
although various wonderful colors appear, there is not a single reality therein. In this same way, although the *prajñāpāramitā* is [provisionally]...
It is manifested through various verbal expressions, yet that which is so manifested has no intrinsic nature that can be apprehended;
it is like space, which, though measured with various units of measurement, has never been seen to possess even as much as five finger-breadths as a perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*).
In this same way, although the *prajñāpāramitā* is provisionally manifested through various verbal expressions, not even the slightest [intrinsic nature] has ever been seen.
The intrinsic nature is the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because all phenomena are profoundly deep. The *prajñāpāramitā* is the most profound;
the *prajñāpāramitā* is deep and vast, being realized through immeasurable and boundless merit.
Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are pure by nature, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by nature.
Because all phenomena are without limit, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without limit.
One should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is without limit throughout its initial, middle, and final stages; it has no spatial domain, and its boundaries cannot be apprehended.
Therefore it is called "boundless. Because its limit cannot be apprehended, it is called "limitless. It is called "limitless" because it is boundless;
it is called "boundless" because it is limitless.
Fascicle 597. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva, relying on such dharmas, practice within the various characteristics of objects? The Buddha said:
The assembly of bodhisattvas does not even apprehend dharmas, much less non-dharmas.

Knowing that all objects of cognition are devoid of the nature of being objects, for this reason these noble beings, relying upon such dharmas, engage with the various characteristics of objects without any attachment.
Śāriputra, there are many among the classes of sentient beings who have accomplished inferior qualities;
their faith and understanding are likewise all inferior, and they are unable to plant vast roots of merit. They cannot believe in or accept such profound, vast, and untainted True Dharma.
According to their respective superior or inferior natures, each finds pleasure in their own kind; those with inferior faith and understanding—
Sentient beings who delight in inferior inclinations and understandings [attract] sentient beings with inferior inclinations and understandings;
sentient beings with vast inclinations and understandings [attract] sentient beings who delight in vast inclinations and understandings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what dharma is the sphere of activity constituted? The Buddha said, "The Prajñāpāramitā takes boundless dharmas as its sphere of activity;
it takes the emptiness of all dharmas as its sphere of activity.
Just as the realm of space and the realm of wind have no location that can be perceived, so too it does not give rise to the characteristics of dharmas."
Yet it manifests before them. In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā has nothing whatsoever that can be manifested or shown among all phenomena;
nor does it manifest before one for the sake of giving rise to the characteristics of phenomena.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, "What are the characteristics of this *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said, "This *prajñāpāramitā* is far removed from all characteristics; there is not even the slightest characteristic that can be apprehended.
Śāriputra, just as the realm of space has no place of obstruction or attachment, so too is this *prajñāpāramitā*."
There is no place for attachment. For this reason, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is no characteristic of a dharma that is non-attached which can be apprehended; however, this is spoken in accordance with the conventions and principles of worldly discourse.
He spoke thus: "The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic. Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena have non-attachment as their characteristic.
Because all phenomena are unapprehendable, they are called 'having non-attachment as their characteristic.
Not even the slightest phenomenon appears before one as a characteristic for arising, because within this [state] no characteristic can be apprehended."
It is called "signless. Because it is signless, it is described as "non-attachment.
If all phenomena possessed even the slightest sign, attachment would be found therein; however, since all phenomena are entirely devoid of signs, no attachment can be found therein.
Therefore, it is said that the characteristic of all phenomena is non-attachment. Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for all defiled phenomena, they are inverted...
Perversions manifest before one. All perversions are signless (*animitta*). All that is signless is inexpressible.
Therefore, phenomena that possess signs are themselves signless. Furthermore, Śāriputra, even all pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*) are without signs. Why is this?
If even defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*) have no signs, how much less could pure phenomena possess signs? Furthermore, Śāriputra...
Son, if one can thoroughly know the suchness of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), those defilements are entirely unapprehendable.
Yet, sentient beings give rise to these defilements due to their inversions (*viparyāsa*). All such inversions are not real.
If they are not real, they possess no substantial entity (*svabhāva*) and no real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). If one can thus thoroughly [know] them according to reality...

Knowing this is precisely what is called purity. Therefore, the two phenomena of defilement and purity both lack any inherent characteristic (*nimitta*) and are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) cling to the characteristic of non-clinging.
Moreover, Śāriputra, you should know that this characteristic of non-clinging is the sphere of activity for wisdom (*jñāna*), and it is also the sphere of activity for the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This sphere of activity of the wisdom characterized by non-attachment is also called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for this "sphere of activity," you should know that it reveals what is not a sphere of activity.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be manifested through the characteristics of a sphere of activity. Moreover, Śāriputra, as for the "objective sphere," you should know that it reveals...
It is shown that these are not the spheres of activity because the suchness and the mode of existence of all phenomena are entirely unapprehendable;
therefore, all phenomena are not the spheres of activity, as all phenomena lack the nature of being objects.
If one can thus thoroughly know all phenomena, this is called "practicing within all spheres."
Then Śāriputra said to Subhūti, "Venerable one, why do you remain silent and say nothing?
Subhūti replied, "I do not perceive any phenomena at all. Therefore, I now remain silent and say nothing. Furthermore, Śāriputra...
I do not perceive this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Nor do I perceive the assembly of bodhisattvas.
I do not perceive the speaker, nor the spoken; nor do I perceive that by which, for which, because of which, or to which [this belongs].
It is based on this that I speak. Since I perceive nothing herein, how can I proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Śāriputra, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not proceed by way of manifesting any phenomena.
...manifests before one. Furthermore, Śāriputra, since no dharma exists that manifests through the manifestation of dharmas, how could I possibly proclaim such a profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
Nevertheless, Śāriputra, if one can understand this proclaimed profound *prajñāpāramitā* as not being [attained] through manifestation...
Because such dharmas exist, they manifest before them; thus, they are able to comprehend the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and are also able to proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Suvīra, saying: "When Bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not engage with any phenomena at all.
Why is this? Because all phenomena arise from inversion;
they are not truly existent, but are false, deceptive, and illusory. It is just as if one were to engage with phenomena [as being real]."
All [those] practice perversions; all practice what is unreal. If a bodhisattva were to have any practice, it would be a practice of perversion and a practice of unreality.
Yet, bodhisattvas are not characterized by such perverse or unreal practices.
Furthermore, it is not by practicing inverted conduct or unreal conduct that a bodhisattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Moreover, O Well-Valiant One, that which is inverted and unreal is not the sphere of their practice; therefore, the bodhisattva does not act within such [states].
Furthermore, Subhānavīra, that which is called "inversion" is the attachment of deluded, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Such phenomena do not exist in the way they appear; such attachments do not correspond to their actual characteristics. Therefore, they are called inversions and unrealities.
Consequently, bodhisattvas do not engage in inversions, nor do they engage in unrealities. By means of this, the bodhisattva...
This is called "practice without inversion. If there is truly no inversion, then there is nothing to be practiced. Therefore, it is said that the practice of a bodhisattva is non-practice;
the severance of all practices is called the practice of a bodhisattva. O Suvīra, a bodhisattva does not engage in any practice of conceptualization or discursive differentiation.
The severance of all conceptualization and discursive differentiation is called the practice of a bodhisattva. As for "conceptualization," it refers to...
Regarding the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena and the conceptualization of difference: this refers to the conceptualization of distinctions among phenomena.

It is not that all phenomena can be conceptually differentiated or conceptually differentiated as distinct, because all phenomena cannot be conceptually differentiated or conceptually differentiated as distinct.
If one were to conceptually differentiate phenomena, one would thereby create a conceptualization of difference regarding them; however, all phenomena are remote [from such differentiation].
Free from conceptualization and false conceptualization. Furthermore, Subhānavīra, what is called "conceptualization" is one extreme;
"false conceptualization" is the second extreme. If bodhisattvas do not engage with either the extreme or the non-extreme, those bodhisattvas likewise do not perceive a middle.
If they were to perceive a middle, they would be engaging with the middle; if they were to engage with the middle, then...
They proceed toward the extremes. The intermediate state does not proceed, nor is it manifest or demonstrable, because it is devoid of the characteristics of proceeding.
Furthermore, Subhāṇu, that which is called "the middle" is precisely the Noble Eightfold Path. Such a noble path manifests before one without apprehending anything at all among all phenomena;
it appears before one without seeing anything at all. When there is neither cultivation nor... regarding phenomena, [it manifests].
It is abandoned. At that time, it is called the path of cessation. Regarding this path of cessation, there is neither cultivation nor abandonment of any phenomena;
it transcends both cultivation and abandonment, realizing the equal true nature of all phenomena. Furthermore, the path of cessation refers to an Arhat, a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted.
Why? Because he has abandoned the path; since it is neither cultivated nor abandoned, it is called [the path of cessation].
It is "dispelled. Since that which dispels is also non-existent, it is called "dispelling. It is called "dispelling" because one practices through dispelling.
If there were a practice of dispelling, there would be something to be attained, and it could not be called "dispelling. Here, "dispelling" refers to the nature of the practice of dispelling.
Since there is no practice here, it is called "dispelling. Because practice is non-existent, dispelling is also not existent.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take any phenomena as an object of cognition; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva knows that the nature of all objects of cognition is fundamentally remote. If one knows that the nature of objects of cognition is remote, then there is no practice.
Therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva practices non-practice.
If bodhisattvas are able to practice the perfection of wisdom, they practice by thoroughly knowing all objects of focus and by eliminating all objects of focus.
Fascicle 598, Fascicle 599, Fascicle 600.
When a bodhisattva can practice in this way, they do not practice by taking any phenomena as objects for the sake of purification. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva thoroughly knows that the intrinsic nature of the objects of all phenomena is pure.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not engage in the accumulation of any phenomena, nor do they engage in their cessation.
They do not engage in the profound, nor the shallow. They do not engage in emptiness, nor non-emptiness.
They do not engage in having signs, nor signlessness. They do not engage in having a vow, nor vowlessness. They do not engage in conditioned activity, nor unconditioned activity. Why?
For this reason, all such phenomena possess reliance and grasping, movement and fluctuation, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and craving for objects.
That is to say: "I am able to perform such movements and fluctuations; I engage in such conceptual proliferations regarding these actions;
through these actions, I crave such objects; and based on these actions, I rely upon and grasp them. In this regard, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands all such reliance and grasping.

Movement, conceptual proliferation, and craving destroy all ignorance. Because there is nothing to rely upon or grasp, and because there is no reliance or grasping, there is absolutely no activity, nor is there any storing up [of seeds].
Because there is no storing up, there is neither bondage nor liberation, nor is there any origination [of afflictions].
In this way, the bodhisattva destroys all reliance and grasping while practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Furthermore:
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they do not engage with any phenomena (*dharma*) as permanent or impermanent;

they do not engage with them as pleasant or unpleasant; they do not engage with them as self or non-self; they do not engage with them as pure or impure; they do not engage with them as empty or non-empty;
and they do not engage with them as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection, or like an echo. Why is this? Because such phenomena possess discursive investigation (*vitarka*).

There is investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*). There is application (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*). In this regard, the bodhisattva thoroughly understands all that is with investigation and analysis, with application and sustained thought;
he eliminates all formations (*saṃskāra*), fully comprehends all formations, and practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
This is called the proclamation of the conduct of bodhisattvas.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, the bodhisattva’s practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Why is this? It is called "inconceivable" because it is not produced by the mind;
it is also called "inconceivable" because it does not give rise to the mind. To claim that the mind arises is a perversion; to claim that the mind does not arise is likewise [a conceptualization].
This, too, is a perversion. To thoroughly penetrate that both the mind and mental factors are entirely non-existent is not a perversion.
Fools and ordinary worldlings are unable to realize the mind’s detachment; they lack correct knowledge, nor do they correctly know the detachment of the objects of perception.
Consequently, they cling to the thought: "The mind is the self," "The mind belongs to the self," "The mind depends upon the self," and "The mind..."
Arising from me, once that mind has been grasped, they further grasp it as virtuous, or grasp it as non-virtuous; or grasp it as pleasure, or grasp it as suffering;

or grasp it as annihilation, or grasp it as permanence. Through various gateways of Dharma, the assembly of Bodhisattvas practices the Prajñāpāramitā, remaining far removed from the inverted states of mind and mental factors, and realizes the pure nature of the mind.
Pure and luminous, within this state there is no arising of mind or mental factors whatsoever. He further reflects: "Mind and mental factors arise due to an object of perception (*ālambana*);
since he realizes that the object of perception does not exist, mind and mental factors cannot arise at all.
Since they do not arise, they neither abide nor cease, nor does he cause phenomena to undergo arising, abiding, and so forth. To be able to practice in this way is...

Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva penetrates all phenomena—whether their causes, their origins, their disappearance, or their cessation—and there is not even the slightest phenomenon that does not accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
He understands, as they truly are, the characteristics of the causes, origins, cessations, and paths of all phenomena. In one...
One neither cultivates nor abandons any phenomenon. Why is this? Because all phenomena have non-existence as their nature;
being devoid of intrinsic nature, they are not substantial entities. Since they are not substantial entities, there is neither cultivation nor abandonment.
To neither cultivate nor abandon any phenomenon is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they do not give rise to a mind associated with the characteristics of any phenomena, nor do they give rise to any concomitant mental states.

Because they are able to abide in such a pure mind, although they give rise to pervasive loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, they are able to eliminate the perception of sentient beings; regarding the perception of sentient beings, they [do not dwell upon it].
They abide without grasping, and they likewise have no attachment even toward the four Brahma-vihāras.

Having perfected sublime wisdom and skillful means, they swiftly bring the perfection of prajñāpāramitā to fulfillment. Because it is swiftly fulfilled, they then neither grasp nor cling to any phenomena.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they do not train in all phenomena; they do not train for the sake of transcending all phenomena;
they do not train in the arising of all phenomena, nor do they train in the cessation of all phenomena;

they do not train for the sake of subduing all phenomena, nor do they train for the sake of not subduing all phenomena; they do not train for the sake of gathering, suppressing, or shifting [any phenomenon].
One trains because all phenomena are such; one does not train for the sake of entering into or abiding in all phenomena (as stated in scroll ninety-eight).

When a bodhisattva trains in this manner, they do not train in any phenomenon—whether it be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, empty or non-empty, self or selfless—and they do not take any phenomenon as an object, whether it be past formations.

Whether regarding future formations or present formations, although one observes the past with the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and non-self, one does not practice with respect to the past through the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and non-self;

although one observes the future with the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and non-self, one does not practice with respect to the future through the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and non-self; although...
He observes the present through the aspects of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness, yet he does not practice with respect to the present by means of emptiness, tranquility, and selflessness.

A bodhisattva can practice in this way: although he contemplates the past as empty, selfless, devoid of "mine," impermanent, non-eternal, and lacking any dharma that remains for long or undergoes no change, he does not practice with respect to the past in such a manner. Although...
One contemplates the future as empty, selfless, devoid of what belongs to a self, impermanent, non-eternal, and lacking any quality of long-lasting stability or unchanging nature;

yet one does not act toward the future in such a manner. Although one contemplates the present as empty, selfless, devoid of what belongs to a self, impermanent, non-eternal, and lacking any quality of long-lasting stability or unchanging nature; yet one is able to act toward the present in such a manner.
Practicing in this way and abiding thus, one will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to fulfillment.

Practicing in this manner, one does not take any phenomena as objects, because all phenomena are not objects of cognition, because all phenomena are not subjects of cognition, and because no phenomenon possesses anything to be grasped; yet, it can be said that there is something therein.
Conditioned by an object of perception, there arises activity, conceptualization, and grasping.

Where there is grasping, there arise sorrow, suffering, sharp arrows of grief, lamentation, and despair. Where there is an object of perception, there arise reliance, attachment, fluctuation, and proliferation.
One who can practice in this way does not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding any phenomena.
One who can practice in this way and abide in this way cannot be obstructed by any evil Māras.
Having accomplished the sword of sharp wisdom—the *prajñāpāramitā*—they possess great power. These bodhisattvas have no basis for dependence in any place.
Cease. Why is this? If there is a basis, there is shifting; if there is shifting, there is agitation;
if there is agitation, there is conceptual proliferation. If sentient beings have a basis, shifting, agitation, and conceptual proliferation, [they do not abide in peace].
Following the movements of Māra, they have not yet escaped the realm of Māra. The Bodhisattva, however, does not rely upon any phenomena;
having realized the purification of all bases of reliance, they practice the perfection of wisdom by relying on pure and subtle insight and vision.
By this, Māra cannot find an opportunity.
One who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* does not practice with the characteristic of the conjunction or separation of all phenomena;
one does not practice with the characteristic of the purity or impurity of all phenomena. To be able to practice in this way is to neither conjoin nor [separate] with any phenomenon.
Detachment. Why is this? Because all phenomena are without conjunction or detachment. O Suvīra, "conjunction" refers to permanence; "detachment" refers to annihilation.
The nature of all phenomena does not manifest for the sake of conjunction or detachment.
If the nature of phenomena were to manifest as either conjunction or detachment, then phenomena would be obtainable; however, because they are unobtainable, the Buddha does not bestow [anything].
Furthermore, Subhūtivīra, foolish ordinary beings perceive union and separation through false views; they are bound by inversion and wander through birth and death.

Thinking that by uniting they obtain union, they abide in union and perceive union. Because they cling to the existence of union, they then cling to the existence of separation, thinking that by dispelling union they obtain separation.
Subhūtivīra, wherever there is union, there is separation. If, within union, one neither attains nor relies upon it, [one is liberated].

They do not give rise to attachment, nor do they perceive detachment. If, within detachment, one were to obtain something or rely upon it and thereby give rise to attachment, that person would then be in union with the suffering of birth and death and could not be separated from it.

The Bodhisattva contemplates the nature of all phenomena as neither joined nor detached, and does not perform any action for the sake of phenomena being either joined or detached. There may be those who train in this manner.
Abiding thus, one can swiftly fulfill all the qualities of omniscience.
Practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one does not engage in any phenomena, whether through attachment or non-attachment.

Regarding objects of perception—whether pure or impure—one perceives neither engagement nor non-engagement in any phenomena. One who can practice in this manner will swiftly fulfill [all-encompassing knowledge].
The Dharma of All-Knowledge (concluding at volume ninety-nine).
One practices the *prajñāpāramitā* by not practicing [the duality of] all phenomena as being revealed or unrevealed, tranquil or non-tranquil, pure or impure, or detached or non-detached.
One who can practice in this manner will swiftly be able to bring it to perfection.
Fulfilling the dharma of omniscience, a bodhisattva is able to practice in this way: they do not abide in any phenomena. There is no sense in which any phenomenon can be an object of abiding.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are devoid of anything to be grasped or stored. Since there is nothing to be grasped or stored, there is nothing upon which one can abide. This is excellent.
O Courageous One! Because they employ as their skillful means neither abiding nor non-abiding, it is said that all phenomena are entirely without anything upon which to abide.

Just as the four great rivers flow from Lake Anavatapta and have no sense of abiding until they enter the great ocean, so too do all these phenomena have no sense of abiding until the non-creation of all conditioned formations is exhausted.
Those bodhisattvas who hold in hand such teachings corresponding to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be known as already close to receiving a prophecy from a Buddha,
even if they have not yet received one in his presence; or else, before long,
they shall receive a prophecy from the Buddhas in their very presence.
All phenomena are without attachment and without bondage; there is not even the slightest phenomenon that manifests as attachment or bondage.
For this reason, they also possess the sense of being without liberation. O Subhānavīrya, all phenomena are without attachment, without bondage, and likewise without liberation.

What is called "attachment and bondage" refers to the clinging and fettering regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Since the nature of phenomena does not exist, it cannot be [clung to or bound].
It is said that there is attachment and there are bonds; what is called "liberation" refers to being freed from attachment and bonds. Since those two do not exist, there is no liberation.
Such a Dharma-gate cannot be grasped by the hands of sentient beings who are defiled and debased, nor can it be ensnared by the net of Māra.
This is the sphere of activity for those who are bound by fetters; it is the sphere of activity for those whose nature is disciplined and virtuous, and who possess supreme intelligence.
Regarding this profound Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even by upholding a single verse, one obtains immeasurable and boundless merit;
how much more so for one who is able to fully uphold, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to this great *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Circulate it and explain its meaning extensively for others; the merit they thereby obtain will be inconceivable.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of six hundred fascicles;
while the meaning of the *Prajñā* is the same, the phrasing differs (the detailed analysis of this meaning is recorded at the beginning of the eighth volume of the *Gangyao*).
The second part:
When practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
one attains equanimity regarding the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); and one establishes all sentient beings in the state of equality of all phenomena.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "If bodhi, or a sattva, or dharmas such as form are ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

Since this [bodhisattva] does not exist, how can one say that the dharmas such as form are themselves the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or that there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the dharmas such as form?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is.
Just as you have said, because bodhi, sattva, and dharmas such as form (rūpa) cannot be apprehended, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also cannot be apprehended.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) also cannot be apprehended, Subhūti."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this way.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what is called a "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," is form-tathatā (the suchness of form) the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
"No, World-Honored One. Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from form-tathatā? "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Subhūti, with what intention do you speak these words:
'Is it that the suchness of dharmas such as form is not the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or that apart from the suchness of dharmas such as form there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva'?
Subhūti replied to the Buddha, "Even dharmas such as form are ultimately unobtainable, because their nature does not exist; how much less so the existence of dharmas such as form?"

“Suchness. Since this suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, how can it be said that ‘the suchness of form and other phenomena is the bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ or that ‘apart from the suchness of form and other phenomena there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva’? The Buddha told Subhūti:
It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said. Because phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are unapprehendable, the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena such as form is also unapprehendable.
Because phenomena such as form and their *tathatā* are unapprehendable, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also unapprehendable.
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* they practice is...
Even the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended. Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* should train in this manner.
(See the *Subhūti-parivarta*, first volume of the *Piṇḍārtha*, folio 22; consult the sūtra text.)
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is called "prajñāpāramitā"—is it the designation for form (rūpa) that is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"No, World-Honored One. Is it the designation for the permanence of form that is a bodhisattva mahāsattva? "No, World-Honored One.
Is it the designation for the impermanence of form that is a bodhisattva mahāsattva? "No, World-Honored One. And so on, until...
"All phenomena are designations for defilement; they are designations for purification. Are these not the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Based on what meaning do you speak thus, saying that the designations for phenomena such as form are not the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Furthermore, based on what meaning do you speak thus, saying that phenomena such as form are either permanent or impermanent?"
"Is it not also the case that the designations for 'constant increase,' and so on, up to the designations for 'arising' or 'ceasing,' do not belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Subhūti said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, since even phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist, how much less can there be designations for phenomena such as form?
Since these designations do not exist, how can it be said that the designations for phenomena such as form belong [to a bodhisattva]?"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattva... even the designation for the arising and ceasing of phenomena such as form is the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said. Because phenomena such as form, as well as permanence and impermanence, are unapprehendable, the designations for phenomena such as form and the designations for permanence and impermanence are likewise unapprehendable. Phenomena and...”
Because an "additional designation" (adhivacana) cannot be apprehended, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also cannot be apprehended.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) practiced by them also cannot be apprehended, Subhūti.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this manner (refer to the *Subhūti-parivarta*,
the first fascicle of the *Piṇḍārtha*, folio 23, in conjunction with the sūtra text).
“Subhūti, it is not by departing from the conditioned that the unconditioned is designated, nor is it by departing from the unconditioned that the conditioned is designated.
(The Subhūti Chapter) Furthermore, Blessed One, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should thus examine with careful scrutiny:
“What is this perfection of wisdom? For what reason is it called ‘perfection of wisdom’?”
If it is a *pāramitā*, whose *prajñāpāramitā* is it? For what purpose is this *prajñāpāramitā* employed?
When one examines this with precise scrutiny, if no phenomenon exists and cannot be apprehended, this is the *prajñāpāramitā*. (The Chapter on Śatrujit)
Subhūti asked: "What is this 'Dharma'? In what way does one always love, delight in, and rejoice in this Dharma?

The Buddha told Subhūti: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to form and non-form; all are without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), entirely unapprehendable, indestructible, and beyond conceptual differentiation.
This is what is called 'Dharma. As for 'loving the Dharma,' it means to give rise to desire and aspiration toward this Dharma."
To "seek" means to praise the merits of this Dharma. To "rejoice in the Dharma" means to receive it with joy and faith.
To "delight in the Dharma" means to aspire to its frequent cultivation, to draw near to it, and to hold it dear.
By employing the skillful means of non-attainment, one is always able to thus love, delight in, and rejoice in it, yet without becoming arrogant or conceited.
They will certainly become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings (from the *Upamā-parivarta*).

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the six *pāramitās* that are neither bound nor liberated, they are able to realize the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is neither bound nor liberated;
this is called those who have donned the armor of the Great Vehicle that is neither bound nor liberated (from the *Abaddha-amukta-parivarta*).

The disciples of the Buddhas who are without dependence or attachment toward any phenomenon are, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), able to respond to every question and inquiry one by one with sovereignty and fearlessness.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without any basis (from the "Chapter on Detachment").
Kauśika, the dedicating mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is not a mind; the bodhicitta is also not a mind.
One should not dedicate a non-mind to a non-mind, nor should a mind dedicate itself to a non-mind.
A non-mind should not be dedicated to a mind, nor should a mind be dedicated to a mind. Why is this? Because that which is a non-mind is precisely...
It is inconceivable. That which is inconceivable is non-mind. Thus, these two kinds are both non-existent.
Within that which is non-existent, there is no sense of dedication. Kausika, the mind has no intrinsic nature. Because the nature of the mind does not exist, mental factors also do not exist.
Since both the mind and its mental factors lack intrinsic nature, the mind also lacks the sense of dedicating the mind. If...
To practice this contemplation is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva (The Chapter of Śakra).
The nature of all phenomena has no basis of reliance and no point of attachment; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are without birth and without arising.

Without knowledge and without vision, one should know that although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, it can also manifest the true reality of the world;
yet, there is nothing born, nor is there anything manifested. (Chapter on Manifesting Characteristics)

To be able to demonstrate the characteristics of the world as they are for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha means to cause the notion of "this world" not to arise, and also to cause the notion of "another world" not to arise. Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-existent.
It is truly unobtainable. There is nothing upon which one can rely to give rise to the notion of this world or another world (from the "Chapter on Manifesting Characteristics").
It is inconceivable, because conceptualization has ceased. It is immeasurable, because measurement has ceased.
It is beyond number, because numbering has ceased. It is unequaled, because equality has ceased. As for "inconceivable," it means there is only that which cannot be thought.

there is only the designation "incalculable. Regarding "the unequaled": there is only the designation "unequaled" (refer to the *Lakṣaṇaparivarta*, page sixteen of fascicle five of the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, and consult the corresponding passage in the sūtra text).
