[Chapter on Accomplishment: Neither Increasing nor Decreasing] Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and indistinguishable, they encounter no obstruction. Why is this?
Suchness and phenomena cannot be said to be one, nor can they be said to be different; they cannot be said [to be either].
Because of both [simultaneity] and non-simultaneity, a bodhisattva mahāsattva never observes the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others;

rather, with impartial compassion, they preach the Dharma. They do not observe whether the qualities of the Dharma-preacher’s lineage are good or bad, but seek only the subtle and wondrous meaning of the Dharma being taught.
Subhūti, a non-retrogressive bodhisattva possesses such various practices, marks, and signs (from the "Chapter on Non-Retrogression").
A non-retrogressive bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom penetrates the fact that all phenomena are non-existent.

They never depart from the mental engagement with awakening (*bodhicitta*) and take no pleasure in examining or discoursing upon the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), or the elements (*dhātu*).
Why is this? Because such a bodhisattva has already thoroughly contemplated the principle that the nature and characteristics of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are empty.
Because they have thoroughly mastered [this], they do not delight in examining or discoursing upon various matters. Why is this?

It is because these bodhisattvas have already well reflected upon and thoroughly mastered the fact that the nature and characteristics of all assemblies are empty. Because they have thoroughly mastered this, they do not delight in examining or discoursing upon the five matters.
Abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, these bodhisattvas do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as being superior or inferior, noble or base.

Because they dwell in the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), they do not delight in examining or discussing matters concerning thieves, for they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of gain or loss, or giving or taking away.

Because they dwell in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), they do not delight in examining or discussing military affairs, for they do not perceive any phenomena as having the characteristics of being many or few, or of gathering or dispersing. They do not delight in examining...

They discuss matters of war. This is because this bodhisattva dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena within suchness (*tathatā*), and thus does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of strength or weakness, or of attachment and aversion. They take no pleasure in observing or discussing matters concerning cities.

This is because this bodhisattva dwells in the emptiness of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and thus does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of being grasped or ungrasped, or of being good or evil. They take no pleasure in observing or discussing [such things].
He speaks of matters concerning villages. This bodhisattva dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena;

because he does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of increase or decrease, or of conjunction or separation, he takes no pleasure in examining or discoursing on matters concerning kingdoms. This bodhisattva abides securely in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Because they do not perceive any phenomena as belonging to this or that, or as having the characteristics of "this" and "that. They take no pleasure in examining or discoursing upon the matters of a self, a sentient being, or even a knower or a seer.
This is because the bodhisattva abides in ultimate emptiness and does not perceive any distinction between the existence or non-existence of a self, up to and including a seer.
They take no pleasure in examining or discoursing upon signs or auspicious matters.
This bodhisattva dwells well in the signless, because he does not perceive the differentiated marks of phenomena as being either beautiful or ugly.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing such worldly matters;
rather, he delights only in observing and discussing the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*...

Because they are largely free from all signs and are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (from the "Chapter on Turning and Not Turning"), these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, although practicing the emptiness of all phenomena, cherish the true Dharma and do not cherish what is not the Dharma;
they constantly vow to benefit all sentient beings. Although they practice the emptiness of the unapprehendable, they always praise the Three [Jewels].
Possessing the merit of jewels, they bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
Although they practice the single-flavored characteristic of the *dharmadhātu* of the suchness of all phenomena, they delight in praising the various merits of the *dharmadhātu* of suchness.
Although they know that all phenomena are ultimately empty, they cherish virtuous friends and do not cherish evil friends (*Avivartanīya-parivarta*).
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, whether by day or by night, is never apart from the mental attention of mindfulness of the Buddha, nor is he ever apart from the mental attention of hearing the Dharma.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, wherever in any land a Buddha, the World-Honored One, is currently teaching the True Dharma, he immediately travels there to take birth through the power of his vows, or travels there to hear the Dharma through the power of his supernormal faculties. Because of this—
Regarding the causes and conditions: wherever these bodhisattvas are born, they are never separated from the Buddhas and constantly hear the true Dharma without interruption or cessation.

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, although able to manifest the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, skillfully employ expedient means to arise within the desire realm.
With a mind [intent on] teaching all sentient beings the ten paths of wholesome action, they also manifest birth in the desire realm according to their vow-power.
In those buddha-fields, they make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
they hear the true Dharma and cultivate various supreme practices (from the "Chapter on Turning and Not Turning").
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protects the True Dharma, they should form this thought: "I do not protect the True Dharma of one Buddha, two Buddhas, or even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
rather, I universally uphold the True Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, so that it shall not be diminished or lost.
What is called the True Dharma of all Buddhas? It is the [teaching] of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas...
Awakening— that all phenomena, both those awakened to and those spoken of, are empty— is what is called the True Dharma of all Buddhas (see the "Chapter on Turning and Not Turning," fascicle 5,
page 38 of the *Outline*, and compare with the scriptural text).
The dedication arising from reliance on the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme dedication;
the dedication arising apart from the *prajñāpāramitā* is an inferior dedication (*Gambhīrārthapatala*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections.
Seeing that the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings is long and far-reaching, and seeing that the realm of sentient beings is infinite in number, they reflect upon this matter as follows:
"The limits of birth and death are like space; the realm of sentient beings is also like space. Although...
In reality, all sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death and attain liberation;
yet these sentient beings falsely cling to them as existing, thus circling in saṃsāra and undergoing boundless suffering. How shall I employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them?
Having reflected thus, he made this vow: "I shall practice diligently and without attachment, cultivating the six perfections."

...the Perfection of Wisdom. They bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly bring them to fulfillment so that they may quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the unsurpassed Dharma, causing them all to be liberated from the great suffering of birth and death.
Furthermore, they cause them to realize and know that both birth and death and liberation are entirely non-existent and ultimately empty. Subhūti, it is by means of this that the Bodhisattva...
These six perfections will be swiftly brought to fulfillment, and one will quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) (*Paryāya-paṭala*;
compare with the first leaf of the sixth fascicle of the *Sūtra-saṃgraha* and the corresponding scriptural passage).

Just as a bird with strong wings soars through the void, flying freely and at will without falling for a long time, though it sports within the sky, it does not rely upon the sky, nor is it obstructed by the sky; so too it is with the Bodhisattvas.
Although they repeatedly practice, approach, dwell in, and cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not [rely] therein...
They are able not to realize [the limit of reality]. Because they do not realize it, they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When all the roots of goodness cultivated through the practices for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment have fully matured, only then do they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
(Compare with the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, first leaf of the six-volume edition; consult the scriptural text.)

Abiding in conduct as inexhaustible as space, one brings forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and observes the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as they truly are.
In this way, one can swiftly bring the profound perfection of wisdom to fulfillment.
When observing the phenomena of dependent origination in such a manner, one does not perceive any phenomenon arising without a cause, nor does one perceive any phenomenon ceasing without a cause.

One does not perceive any dharma whose nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, nor that which is neither born nor extinguished (see the *Akṣayamati-parivarta*, in conjunction with the text on page 67 of fascicle 67 of the *Sūtra-śāstra*).
Subhūti asked: "How is it that one speaks of phenomena that are without name or characteristic by means of names and characteristics, yet without contradiction? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I provisionally establish names and characteristics for all phenomena in accordance with worldly convention.

I teach them through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, yet without attachment; therefore, there is nothing contradicted. If the noble ones were to be attached to names as names, or to characteristics..."

If one clings to signs, then one would likewise cling to emptiness as emptiness, cling to signlessness as signlessness, cling to wishlessness as wishlessness, cling to suchness as suchness, cling to the dharma-realm as the dharma-realm, cling to the limit of reality as the limit of reality, and cling to the unconditioned as the unconditioned.
Subhūti, all these dharmas possess only provisional names and only provisional signs; yet...
There is no reality. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in all dharmas;

yet, relying merely on provisional names and signs, he practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without any attachment therein (see the "Chapter on Skillful Means," fascicle 6, page 32 of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).

Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Once bodhisattvas have cultivated the path of the Tathāgata to full completion, would they not likewise realize and abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and cultivate their great vows.
As long as these are not yet fully perfected, they should not yet realize and abide in the limit of reality. If...
[The practice] is already perfected; one should then realize and abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Subhūti asked: "Abiding in what does one realize and abide in the limit of reality? The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Abiding in what did you attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) and the permanent liberation of the mind?

Subhūti replied: "It is not by abiding anywhere that I attained the exhaustion of all outflows and the permanent liberation of the mind. Nevertheless, my outflows were exhausted and my mind was liberated."
Liberation abides nowhere at all. The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus;
when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide nowhere at all" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*, first section;
compare with the segment of questions and answers concerning the *mārgajñatā* in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*).
Subhūti asked again: "Is the cessation of all afflictions the attainment of the unconditioned? The Buddha said: "It is so. Subhūti asked again:
"Do Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas not attain the unconditioned, yet do their afflictions cease? The Buddha said: "It is not so. Subhūti asked again:
"Is there any distinction among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)? The Buddha replied, "No.

Subhūti said, "If there is no distinction among unconditioned phenomena, for what reason does the Buddha say that the Tathāgata has eternally severed the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃtati*), whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet eternally severed them?
The Buddha said, "The continuity of habitual tendencies is not, in reality, an affliction (*kleśa*). However, for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas..."
Awakened ones have already severed their afflictions (*kleśa*); yet, there still remain slight traces resembling greed, hatred, and delusion that stir the body and speech.

This is what is called the "continuity of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-saṃtati*). In the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, these are ultimately non-existent (see the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* and the subsequent passage on the continuity of habitual tendencies;
consult the relevant sutra text).

Regarding the dharma of non-apprehension (*anupalabdha-dharma*): although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs great deeds of benefit, he ultimately does not perceive any real sentient being who attains *nirvāṇa*.
He perceives only the cessation of the manifold sufferings of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). (Refer to the "Chapter on Skillful Means" for the section on the mutual non-apprehensibility;
refer to the "Chapter on the Simile of the Tree" regarding the cessation of suffering).

Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying: "If all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, how is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having attained perfect awakening to the fact that all dharmas have non-existence as their nature, is called a 'Buddha,' and has attained sovereign mastery over all dharmas and all objective spheres? The Buddha told Subhūti: "All..."
All phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom without error. By means of this, I became detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states;
with directed thought and evaluation, born of detachment and accompanied by joy and bliss, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, fully possessed of it. Just as...

Thus, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, I entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

At that time, although I skillfully grasped the signs of the various dhyānas and their factors, I was without attachment; I did not give rise to craving for the dhyānas or their factors. Regarding all...
I did not apprehend either the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) or their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*).

At that time, regarding the four meditative absorptions, my mental aspect was pure and free from conceptual discrimination. Although I was thoroughly proficient in those meditative absorptions and their factors at that time, I did not experience their karmic fruition;
rather, relying upon meditative absorption, I brought forth supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) by means of the mind.

The divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the supernormal power of the divine eye—regarding these five supernormal powers, although I skillfully apprehend their characteristics, I am without attachment, nor do I relish them.
Within the objects of these powers, I find nothing at all; I do not engage in conceptualization, but abide as if in space.
At that time, I contemplate all phenomena as perfectly equal, having non-existence as their very nature. By means of this one...
Through the wisdom associated with each moment, one realizes unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

That is to say, these noble truths of suffering, these noble truths of its origin, these noble truths of its cessation, and these noble truths of the path are all of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Such signlessness is also non-existent. By this, one accomplishes the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four [fearlessnesses].
The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity,
as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and other immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and subtle merits— by means of his wondrous wisdom,
the Buddha establishes the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings and guides them through skillful means according to their needs, causing them to obtain supreme benefit.
[From the "Gradual Chapter" (Anupūrvika-parivarta) of the *Anāpūrṇa-sukha*, to be read in conjunction with the opening folio of the seven-fascicle version.
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see that all foolish commoners dwell upon the notion of a self where there is no self;

they dwell upon the notion of a sentient being where there is no sentient being, and so on, up to dwelling upon the notion of a knower where there is no knower, and dwelling upon the notion of a seer where there is no seer.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees these things, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to teach and transform them, causing them to abandon inverted conceptualizations and attachments, and establishing them within the nectar-like realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Abiding within this realm, [he...]
The notion of a self no longer arises, nor even the notion of a knower or seer. At that time, all agitation, distraction, conceptual proliferation, and discursive thought no longer manifest;
the mind dwells predominantly in a state of tranquility, serenity, and the realm free from conceptual proliferation (from the "Chapter on the True Teaching").
Furthermore, Subhūti, for the sake of newly ordained bodhisattvas, I have taught that nirvāṇa is not a transformation, nor is there a separate, truly existent, non-empty nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one should not hold this as a point of contention. Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what skillful means should newly ordained bodhisattvas be instructed and exhorted so that they may know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally empty? The Buddha told him:
"Subhūti, how could it be that all phenomena first exist and later cease to exist, such that they are not eternally empty?
Rather, since all phenomena neither existed previously nor do not exist subsequently, their intrinsic nature is eternally empty. You should not be terrified;
you should provide such skillful instructions and exhortations regarding emptiness. (Chapter on Emptiness)
The third section:
The devas reflect, "We shall constantly employ various skillful means to cause this bodhisattva to remain free from the dharma of lust.
From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the realization of the sought-after unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, he shall always practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*)."
One does not give rise to lustful attachment toward things that bind one to existence. Why is this?

Even practicing non-celibacy can act as an obstacle to rebirth in the Brahma Heaven, let alone to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, the Bodhisattva abandons desire and leaves the household life.

"One who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is not the case that one does not go forth [into homelessness] while practicing what is not the holy life.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Must all bodhisattvas necessarily have parents, wives, children, and various kinsmen and friends?
The Buddha said, "There may be some bodhisattvas who possess wives, children, and retinues, yet they practice the bodhisattva path."

...the practice of a Bodhisattva. There may be some bodhisattvas who have no wife or children; from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, they constantly cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and do not lose their state of perpetual youth.

Or there may be some bodhisattvas who, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), first manifest the enjoyment of the five objects of sensory pleasure, and only afterwards renounce them with weariness to diligently cultivate pure conduct, thereby attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. As...
That illusionist creates various illusions. Does that which is created by the illusion have any reality?

Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, “It is the same for a bodhisattva. Desiring to bring sentient beings to maturity, he manifests the experience of the five desires, yet in reality he is without defilement.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas give rise to a profound sense of weary detachment toward the five desires.”
He is not defiled by those faults. By means of immeasurable methods, he censures and reviles all sensual desires, thinking:
"Sensual desires are like a blazing fire; sensual desires are like filth; sensual desires are like a butcher; sensual desires are like an enemy; sensual desires are like a vessel of poison."

Desire is like a dark well; how could there be any reality in the affairs of desire? It is merely for the sake of skillful means to benefit sentient beings that these matters are manifested through transformation (from the "Chapter on Dependent Origination").
Śāriputra said, "In what places are they unable to achieve liberation? The Buddha said, "They are unable to achieve liberation from the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
consequently, they cannot accomplish the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas.
Even if they were able to achieve liberation from the three realms, they would still be unable to achieve liberation from the two vehicles. For this reason...
Unable to believe in or understand the profound Dharma (refer to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, fascicle 1, page 31; for "unable to believe and accept," consult the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).

Next, to answer from where the Great Vehicle emerges and where it abides: Subhūti, you should know that the Great Vehicle emerges from within the triple world and abides within the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
However, because it employs non-duality as its means, there is neither emergence nor abiding.
Why is this? Because these two dharmas—the Great Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes—are not...
It is neither combined nor dispersed; it is neither with form nor without form; it is neither visible nor invisible;
it is neither resistant nor non-resistant. All are of one single mark, namely, the markless (*animitta*). The markless dharma has no emergence and no abiding.

It is not that which has already emerged or already abided; it is not that which will emerge or will abide; it is not that which is currently emerging or currently abiding. Should anyone wish to cause this markless dharma...

If there were one who emerged and dwelt [in them], it would imply that True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-falsity, the immutability, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) also have emergence and dwelling. Why is this?
Because from True Suchness up to the inconceivable realm, none of them can...
One emerges from within the three realms, yet one cannot abide within the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is this?

Because true suchness (*tathatā*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of true suchness, and so on up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), which is empty of the intrinsic nature of the inconceivable realm.
For anyone who wishes for a signless dharma to have emergence or abiding, they would thereby wish for the severance of the realm, the departure from the realm, and the cessation of the realm.

The realm, the realm of peace, the realm of tranquility, the realm of non-arising, the realm of non-cessation, the realm of non-nature, the realm of signlessness, the realm of non-action, and the realm of the unconditioned.
Furthermore, there is emergence and abiding. Why is this? Because from the realm of abandonment up to the realm of the unconditioned.
None of them can emerge from the three realms, nor can they abide within the knowledge of all-knowledge. Why is this?
Because the realm of cessation is empty of the intrinsic nature of the realm of cessation, and so on, up to the unconditioned realm, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of the unconditioned realm.

If there were anyone who wished to cause the dharma of signlessness to have emergence and abiding, they would be wishing for names, conceptual designations, and conventional expressions to also have emergence and abiding.
Why is this? Because names, conceptual designations, and conventional expressions [are themselves empty].
None of them can emerge from the three realms, nor can they abide in the knowledge of all-knowledge. Why is this?
Because names, conceptual designations, and verbal expressions are empty of intrinsic nature; for names, conceptual designations, and verbal expressions are themselves empty of intrinsic nature.
Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom,

although they observe that all phenomena are non-existent and utterly unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure, there is no one who departs by means of the Great Vehicle and remains [in saṃsāra].
Nevertheless, taking non-apprehension as their skillful means, they mount the Great Vehicle and emerge from the cycle of birth and death within the triple world.

One abides within the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, without interruption and without exhaustion (see *Sukhavihāra-parivarta*,
to be consulted alongside the final folio of the two-volume *Piṇḍārtha*).
One who currently arouses a mind of non-erroneous sympathetic joy and dedication should form this thought:

"From form up to consciousness, these are equal to liberation," and so on at length until: "The knowledge of all aspects is equal to liberation. [Likewise] the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of ethical discipline.
It is equal to liberation. The resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding all phenomena is equal to liberation. The Buddhas of the three times are equal to liberation.
All phenomena of the three times are equal to liberation. All acts of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are likewise equal to liberation.
It is equal to liberation. The faculties of the Buddhas, their disciples, and the pratyekabuddhas, having matured and transformed, are equal to liberation.
The nirvāṇa attained by the Buddhas, their disciples, and the pratyekabuddhas is equal to liberation.
The dharmatā of all phenomena belonging to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas is equal to liberation. All sentient beings and all phenomena [are likewise].

And that *dharmatā* is equal to liberation (refer to the "Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication," fascicle 4, leaf 26 of the *Sūtra on the Essentials*, and likewise consult the scriptural passage on liberation).
If one perceives signs and recollects the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, all such acts are attachments (praising the category of purity).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "The profound Prajñāpāramitā is a Great Pāramitā, because it realizes that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty.
Within this Great Prajñāpāramitā, the Wheel of Dharma is turned."
Matters are entirely unattainable, because all phenomena are eternally unarisen, and thus neither that which turns nor that which is turned can be apprehended.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is a boundless *pāramitā*.
The Buddha replied: "It is so, Subhūti; it is like the great void, which has no limit. It is an equalizing *pāramitā*..."
It is the perfection of honey because the nature of all phenomena is equal. It is the perfection of detachment because it is ultimately empty.
It is the perfection that is difficult to subdue because all phenomena are unattainable.
It is the perfection of leaving no tracks because all phenomena lack a named essence. It is the perfection of space.
Because inhalation and exhalation cannot be apprehended, this is the ineffable perfection (*pāramitā*).
Because herein there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, it is the nameless perfection. Because feeling, perception, formations, and so forth cannot be apprehended, it is the non-proceeding perfection.
Because all phenomena arrive [therein], it is the unleadable perfection.
Because all phenomena are ungraspable, this is the perfection of exhaustion (*kṣayapāramitā*).
Because all phenomena are ultimately exhausted, this is the perfection of non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpādānirodhapāramitā*).

Because all phenomena have neither cessation nor arising, this is the perfection of non-action (*anabhisaṃskārapāramitā*), for no agent can be found. This is the perfection of non-cognition (*ajñānapāramitā*).
Because no knower can be apprehended, this is the perfection of immobility.
Because no one who dies or is born can be apprehended, this is the perfection of non-subjugation.
Because the subjugability of all phenomena cannot be apprehended, this is the perfection that is like a dream, like an echo, and even like a magical transformation. Because...
Because all things are like dreams, like echoes, and even like magical transformations, they are unapprehendable;
therefore, this is the perfection of non-defilement and non-purification. Because the causes of defilement and purification are unapprehendable, this is the perfection of non-staining.
Because the basis upon which they rely cannot be apprehended, it is the perfection of non-conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-pāramitā*).

Because all objects of conceptual proliferation are eternally extinguished and eliminated, it is the perfection of freedom from arrogant attachment (*nirmāna-abhiniveśa-pāramitā*), for it destroys all matters of arrogant attachment.
This is the perfection of immovability, because it abides in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
This is the perfection of freedom from attachment, because it realizes that all phenomena are not false.

This is the perfection of non-arising, because it is without conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena. This is the perfection of tranquility, because no characteristics of phenomena are apprehended. This is...
It is the perfection of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, because it eliminates all matters of the three poisons.

It is the perfection of being without afflictions, because it is free from conceptual discrimination. It is the perfection of being without sentient beings, because it realizes that all sentient beings are non-existent.
It is the perfection of being without interruption or destruction, because it can equally give rise to all phenomena.
This is the perfection of non-duality, because it is free from the two extremes.

This is the perfection of non-confusion, because all phenomena are neither corrupted nor confused. This is the perfection of non-attachment, because it transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is the perfection of non-conceptualization, because no conceptualization can be apprehended.
This is the perfection without limits, because no limits can be found among all phenomena. This is the perfection like space, because there is no obstruction regarding any phenomenon.

This is the perfection of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, because there is no attachment to the destruction and oppression of any phenomenon. This is the perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The *pāramitā* [is so called] because it realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, being free from all marks and beyond aspiration.
It is the *pāramitā* of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature, because one knows that the phenomena which are empty are unattainable.
It is the *pāramitā* of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because one knows the body...
The mind and mental phenomena are all unapprehendable; this is because it transcends all the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is the Tathāgata’s pāramitā, for it can explain all dharmas as they truly are. This is the self-arisen (svayambhū) pāramitā, for it exercises sovereign mastery over all dharmas.
This is the perfectly awakened (samyaksaṃbuddha) pāramitā, for regarding all dharmas it is able to...
Because they have perfectly awakened to all aspects (from the *Praise of Qualities* chapter):
those who, when the profound *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is being preached, depart with unpurified minds.
In accordance with that impure mind which has arisen, they will abandon this sutra;

for every step they take, their merit from so many kalpas will be diminished, and they will incur the offense of obstructing bodhi for so many kalpas. Having undergone those offenses, they will further remain for that same duration of time.
One must arouse diligent vigor, seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and practice the difficult and painful austerities of all bodhisattvas;
only then can one restore the original state (as described in the "Chapter on the Deeds of Māra").
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, dwells in accordance with the Dharma; this Dharma is precisely the profound Prajñāpāramitā (from the "Chapter on Manifesting in the World").
One should train in this way in the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, so as to be able to abide in the dharmas in which one ought to abide.
Abiding in this manner, one attains non-obstruction regarding all dharmas. Why is this?
From the very beginning, one does not grasp at any phenomena. Why is this? Because all phenomena are ungraspable.
That which is ungraspable is not a phenomenon. This is what is meant by "abiding in the time of the Dharma.
At that moment, two thousand bodhisattvas simultaneously realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). (The Chapter on Suchness)
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena, he loves and delights in the true Dharma and does not delight in what is not the Dharma.
Although he dwells in the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, he constantly extols the merits of the Triple Gem.

Although he practices the single-flavored characteristic of the suchness and dharma-realm of all phenomena, he delights in praising the various merits of that suchness and dharma-realm (from the "Chapter on the Mark of Non-retrogression").

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "What other practices of seclusion (*viveka*) should one cultivate, since the Buddha does not praise dwelling in forest hermitages (*aranyāyatana*), wildernesses, or mountain groves;
nor does he praise abandoning superior bedding and seats to dwell in contemplation and meditative seclusion?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Whether one dwells in mountain forests, empty marshes, wildernesses, or forest hermitages, or whether one resides in cities, towns, or royal capitals..."
In places that are noisy and crowded, if one can remain far removed from afflictions, evil karma, and the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and cultivating other sublime and excellent virtues, this is called the bodhisattva’s true practice of seclusion (*viveka*).
It is praised by Māra as being hidden away in mountain forests, empty marshes, vast wildernesses, and *āraṇyakas*.
To abandon superior bedding and dwellings, and to sit in quiet meditation and contemplate, is not the true practice of seclusion for Bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because such a practice of seclusion still involves distraction and confusion; that is to say, it may be mixed with evil karma and afflictions, or mixed with the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and thus one cannot diligently believe in, accept, and cultivate the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
They study, yet they cannot perfect the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
They do not give rise to affection for such practice of true seclusion; rather, they delight only in diligently cultivating the empty practices of seclusion of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
They cling to these dharmas of seclusion practiced by the two vehicles, regarding them as supreme.
Regarding those bodhisattvas praised by the Buddha who dwell in true seclusion (*praviveka*), this refers to those who, though living in a bustling environment, do not have unsettled minds.

Regarding those bodhisattvas whom the Tathāgatas do not praise as dwelling in true seclusion, this refers to those who are not secluded, whose minds are not tranquil, and who cannot practice correctly, giving rise to various false conceptualizations and attachments. (From the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*, the first leaf of the seven-fascicle *Sūtra*).
(See reference).

If one were to preach the Dharma for śrāvakas to those of the śrāvaka vehicle so that they attain the fruit of arhatship, it would still not constitute the duty a disciple of the Buddha ought to perform toward me.
However, if one can proclaim even a single verse of the profound [Dharma] for those of the bodhisattva vehicle...
The dharmas associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are precisely what I call the duties that a disciple of the Buddha ought to perform.
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for the sake of those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, expounds the *prajñāpāramitā*...
The dharmas associated with Prajñāpāramitā. Having set aside one day and night, let it be for just one day;
having set aside that, let it be for just half a day; having set aside that, let it be for just one watch; having set aside that, let it be for just the duration of a meal;
having set aside that, let it be for just a brief moment; having set aside that, let it be for just an instant; and having set aside that...
In an instant—indeed, in the mere snap of a finger—one acquires an immeasurable and incalculable mass of merit.

Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses all gifts of Dharma associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all the roots of goodness belonging to the three vehicles (as seen in the "Immovable" chapter).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "In what do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide when they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do you abide in the path and thereby attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*)? "No, World-Honored One.
"Do you abide in what is not the path and thereby attain the exhaustion of all outflows and liberation of mind? "No, World-Honored One. "Do you abide in the path..."
“Is it by abiding in what is not the path that one attains the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation of the mind? “No, World-Honored One.
“Is it by abiding in what is neither the path nor not the path that one attains the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation of the mind? “No, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said to Subhūti, “In what do you abide to attain the exhaustion of all outflows and the permanent liberation of the mind? Subhūti replied, “It is not by abiding anywhere that I attain the exhaustion of all outflows...”
"All outflows [āsrava]—the mind is forever liberated from them. Thus, having exhausted all outflows, my mind attained liberation, abiding nowhere at all.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "The bodhisattva is also like this; abiding nowhere at all, they realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). (Compare with the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta* and the two sections of the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*;
the questions therein are more detailed.)
The dharmas of marks and marklessness are established in mutual dependence; they are not ultimate (from the *Prajñāpāramitā* chapter).
The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas and all their merits have no nature of self or other; they take non-nature as their very nature.
All sentient beings have no nature of self or other; they take non-nature as their very nature (from the *Lakṣaṇa-suvibhakta*).
[Chapter on the Pure Buddha-lands] (To be consulted alongside the *Sūtra Outline* in seven fascicles, volume two, folio two).
When the Bodhisattva’s practices and vows are perfected, he purifies his respective Buddha-field.

At the time he realizes unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the sentient beings he transforms are also born in that land, where they together enjoy the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of the pure land (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*).
Sentient beings are unable to fully comprehend the principle that all things are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Consequently, they perform various actions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or untainted (*anāsrava*). Due to the performance and accumulation of wholesome karma, they are born among gods or humans;
due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome karma, they fall into the three miserable realms. Among wholesome karmas, it is through the performance [of determinate karma]...

They increase and attain birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Through untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*), there are distinctions among the noble ones (*ārya*) based on their preparatory (*prayoga*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages, as well as their lineage (*gotra*) and other such factors (as explained in the "Chapter on Teaching and Transforming," where the meaning is the same though the phrasing differs slightly; consult both).
The fourth section:
Both the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the name "bodhisattva" are without determination and have no place of abiding. Why is this?
Because these two names are both non-existent; and that which is a non-existent dharma has neither determination nor abiding.
If one dwells in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one performs the activity of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
this is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is this? One who performs such activities cannot encompass the perfection of wisdom.
Failing to encompass the perfection of wisdom, one is unable to cultivate it to completion within the perfection of wisdom.
If one is full [of grasping], one will be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes, one will be unable to gather in the sentient beings who are to be gathered. Therefore, one should not grasp at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor should one grasp at the knowledge of all modes. Why is this? This knowledge of all modes is not attained through the cultivation of grasping at signs. All...

To grasp at signs is entirely a defilement. If one were to cultivate the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) by grasping at signs, then the brahmin Jeta would have been unable to produce faith and understanding regarding that knowledge of all modes.

Although this brahmin Jeta was a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) who took refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma through the power of faith and understanding, he was nonetheless able to contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena with a degree of wisdom.

One enters into the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). Having entered it, one does not grasp at the characteristics of form (*rūpa*), nor does one grasp at the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*).
One does not view this knowledge with a mind of joy or attachment. One does not view this knowledge by means of internal form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one view this knowledge by means of external form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does one view it by means of both internal and external form.
He contemplates and perceives this wisdom; yet he does not perceive this wisdom as being separate from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Through such gates of signlessness, the brahmin Jayasena conceived a profound faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

There is no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena whatsoever; even toward nirvāṇa, there is no grasping or attachment, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is taken as the definitive standard.

The characteristic is also separated from the characterized, and the characterized is also separated from the characteristic. The characteristic is also separated from the characteristic, and the characterized [is also separated from the characterized].
They are also free from the characterized. In this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains and is swiftly able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Why is this? Because they know that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing.
Apart from dharmas that do not arise, no dharma can be apprehended (from the "Chapter on Sublime Conduct").
Kausika, it is not merely by attaining the body endowed with the marks and signs that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
rather, it is only by realizing the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) that one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Kausika, the Tathāgata...
The attainment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) necessarily has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its cause;
the Buddha’s body, endowed with the primary and secondary marks, arises merely as its locus. If one does not rely upon it, the Buddha’s body with its marks cannot arise.
Therefore, the perfection of wisdom is the direct cause that gives rise to the knowledge of all modes. This is intended so that this knowledge may be made manifest.
Because it is a continuous succession, one further cultivates and accumulates the Buddha’s body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
If this body of marks and signs were not the locus upon which omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) relies, then all devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans would not offer worship and respect with such sincerity.
It is because the body of marks and signs serves as the support for the Buddha’s omniscience that the various devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans make offerings to it.

[They] shall show reverence. After my parinirvāṇa, because my śarīra-relics all have the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as their root, if sons of good family and others make offerings to the perfection of wisdom, they are thereby making offerings to the śarīra-relics of the body of the Buddha, endowed with the marks and signs of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna). (The Chapter on Making Offerings to the Stūpa)

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have all realized suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the limit of reality, and so forth, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), thereby accomplishing the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Because of this Dharma-body, they are called Buddhas.
Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are the Dharma-body, they are the object of the world’s reverence, offerings, and the proclamation of their merits.

To take the marks of the various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, to engage in conceptual discrimination, and to rejoice in and dedicate [merit] toward unexcelled Bodhi—this is called having great attainment.
Since the past has already ceased and is non-existent, there is nothing to be found therein.
The disciples of the Buddha in the future and the present have not yet arrived and do not abide; they are likewise unattainable.

If they are unattainable, they are not objects for grasping signs. If one grasps their signs and gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedicates [merit] toward enlightenment (*bodhi-pariṇāmanā*), both fall into perversion (Chapter on Sympathetic Joy and Dedication).

One who aspires to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should, with pure faith, take up the signs of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and maintain mindfulness of them.
However, whatever signs one takes up are all termed "clinging. Why is this? Because those who take up signs are said to be clinging.
This applies whether it concerns any Tathāgata, Arhat, or Perfectly Enlightened One of the past, future, or present.

To deeply give rise to sympathetic joy toward all untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), and then to take such roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy and, together with all sentient beings, equally share them by dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is also called attachment. Why is this so?
The true nature of all phenomena is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is remote from the three periods of time.

It cannot be dedicated toward phenomena remote from the three periods of time. It cannot be grasped as a sign, nor can it be taken as an object of focus, because there is no matter that can be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are called "Manifestly and Perfectly Awakened" because they have no realization regarding any phenomena. Why is this?
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is singular and non-dual. One should know that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is not an intrinsic nature;
that which is not an intrinsic nature is itself the intrinsic nature. To be able to know it thus is to be able to remain far removed from all things.
Attachment. Among all forms of attachment, the Blessed One has taught the characteristic of non-attachment,
so that all sentient beings may, like space, be liberated from the suffering of birth and death which is like space, and attain nirvāṇa which is like space.
...and blissful. At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, I should pay homage to the profound Prajñāpāramitā; for this Prajñāpāramitā is such that no dharma can arise and no dharma can cease."
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra: "Do you perceive any dharma that can be protected? Śakra, the Lord of Devas, replied:
"I do not perceive any dharma that can be protected. Subhūti said: "It is just as with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

That which is taught as non-abiding is itself protection. If one is separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, humans, non-humans, and others who wish to cause harm or affliction will find an opportunity to do so. (The Chapter on Purity)
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is, with respect to all phenomena, neither arising nor ceasing, neither being established nor disintegrating;
it does not lean toward nor turn away from, neither attracts nor repels, neither grasps nor abandons, neither defiles nor purifies, and neither increases nor decreases.
Neither near nor far. Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are utterly non-existent and entirely unattainable;
since nothing can be apprehended among all phenomena, they are neither that which defiles nor that which is defiled. Why is this?
Non-dharmas cannot defile non-dharmas; one should know this because form (*rūpa*) is undefiled. Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also undefiled.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are undefiled, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also undefiled.
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is undefiled, form... [is undefiled].
All such phenomena are likewise without defilement.
If one does not even conceptualize them in this way, this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* (as seen in the "Chapter on Praise," folio 2b of the five-fascicle *Sūtra-śāstra*).
If one hears the *prajñāpāramitā*, and with a profound mind of reverence and faith, upholds, recites, and studies it;

if one diligently practices and trains in it, reflects upon it according to the truth, transcribes it, explains it, and causes it to spread widely—know that such a person will before long receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of great enlightenment, shall swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and shall never fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Why?
For this reason, having already seen, heard, made offerings to, and honored the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is a precursor to unsurpassed *bodhi*.
It is like the springtime when trees bearing flowers and fruit have shed their old leaves;
the branches and twigs are moistened, and it will not be long before new flowers, fruits, and leaves emerge. Why is this? Because these trees possess such new flowers...
Because the signs of the fruit appear first (from the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta*):

such is True Suchness (*tathatā*), so profound and so wondrous that only non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, Great Arhats whose vows are fulfilled, and sons of good family endowed with right view are able to give rise to faith and understanding. For their sake, the Tathāgata, relying upon himself...

The manifestation of the characteristics of the suchness that is realized reveals the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Because form (*rūpa*) is not perceived, it is called "the manifestation of the characteristic of form.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are not perceived, it is called "the manifestation of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Since consciousness does not arise by taking form as its object, this is [the manifestation].

Because one does not see form, it is called "indicating the characteristic of form. Because consciousness does not arise by taking feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as its object, this is called "indicating the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness because one does not see them" (from the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*).
The armor donned by a bodhisattva does not belong to form, nor is it for the sake of form;

it does not belong to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it for the sake of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It does not belong to the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor is it for the sake of the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

It does not belong to the level of bodhisattvas, nor is it for the sake of the level of bodhisattvas. It does not belong to the level of buddhas, nor is it for the sake of the level of buddhas. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas have no point of attachment and no purposeful action, the bodhisattva is able to don such firm armor.
By donning such firm armor, he remains without dwelling or attachment in three places. What are these three?

1. The stage of the śrāvaka; 2. The stage of the pratyekabuddha; 3. The stage of the Tathāgata (*Devastutya-parivarta*; see *Wǎngyào*, five fascicles, leaf twenty-six, which discusses what is difficult to accomplish).
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness may also be called the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the locus of the meaning of correspondence.
The nature of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is emptiness; this may also be described as immeasurable and boundless.
"Immeasurable and boundless" is a synonym for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Among all dharma-gates, there is none that is not empty.
Emptiness is inexhaustible; emptiness is immeasurable; emptiness is boundless. Although all dharma-gates possess various distinctions in their verbal expressions, their meaning is no different.
The meaning that is ineffable does not increase or decrease, yet one does not fall away from the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of true thusness (*tathatā*).
Although the perfections (*pāramitā*) do not increase or decrease, one does not fall away from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) that is sought.
If a bodhisattva dwells in such mental attention to true thusness and practices generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, then...
[From the "Chapter on the Mark of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatālakṣaṇaparivarta*) in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*]:

Approaching unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the Buddha said to Subhūti: "When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does one apprehend signs (*nimitta*) with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
"No, World-Honored One. "Even though one does not apprehend signs with respect to the ultimate truth, does one practice by means of signs? "No, World-Honored One."
“Venerable One, does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, with respect to ultimate truth, destroy signs? ‘No, World-Honored One.
Does he, with respect to ultimate truth, dispel signs? ‘No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
‘If this bodhisattva, with respect to ultimate truth, neither destroys signs nor dispels signs, how can he sever the perception of grasping at signs? Subhūti.”
He replied: "When this bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not form the thought:
'I am now destroying signs,' or 'I am now dispelling signs,' or 'I am severing the perception of signs. Nor does he train in the path that severs the perception of signs.

If a bodhisattva were to train in the path that severs the perception of signs, at that time all the Buddha-dharmas would remain unfulfilled, and he would be called one who has fallen into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."
“O Bhagavān, this is the stage of awakening. This bodhisattva has accomplished the most supreme skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*);

although he deeply understands the faults regarding all signs (*nimitta*) and the perception of grasping at signs, he does not destroy or sever them, yet he swiftly realizes the signless (*animitta*). Why is this?
Because all the Buddha-dharmas have not yet been perfected.”
If a bodhisattva reflects that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will only be attained after a long time, they should not feel fear. Why is this?
Although the number of kalpas in the past limit is immeasurable, it was formed through the accumulation of recollection and discrimination within the duration of a single moment of mind.
One should know that the number of kalpas in the future is likewise so; one should not conceive of them as being distant in time, thinking:
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is realized only after passing through a long period of time. Why is this?
Because the duration of kalpas from the prior limit to the posterior limit is all equivalent to a single moment of mind.

If bodhisattvas do not give rise to fear toward any other phenomena that may be seen, heard, sensed, or known as terrifying, it should be known that they will swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.

Therefore, one should follow the Tathāgata’s teaching of true, pure emptiness, don the armor of merit, and practice with diligent application; one should not fear any phenomena whatsoever. (From the "Chapter on Profound Merit")
[Included here for context as per the source text: Together with the *Piṇḍārtha* (Summary) in five fascicles, forty-three leaves.
(Refer to the sūtra text). Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "How does one practice emptiness? How does one manifest entry into the samādhi of emptiness? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should contemplate that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. One should perform this contemplation."
At that time, if one does not allow the mind to become distracted, one will not perceive dharmas. If one does not perceive dharmas, one will not realize them. Subhūti asked:
"How can one dwell in the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) without realizing it? The Buddha told Subhūti: "When contemplating the emptiness of dharmas, one first forms this thought:
'I should contemplate all the marks of dharmas as empty; I should not realize [this state]. Now is the time for training, not the time for realization.'"
At the time of realization, when this bodhisattva has not yet entered meditative absorption, they bind the mind to the object and embrace the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At such a time, they do not fall back from any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva abides in the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) without realizing emptiness, and likewise abides in the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*)...
Although they dwell in the stages, they do not realize signlessness.
Although all bodhisattvas practice emptiness, they do not abide in emptiness; although they manifest entry into the samādhi of emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
(See the "Chapter on Awakening to the Deeds of Māra" and compare with the first leaf of the six-volume *Jingyao* [Essential Summary], as well as the scriptural text.)
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-attachment as its characteristic. It can also be said that all other phenomena possess this characteristic of non-attachment.
Because sentient beings falsely cling to a self and what belongs to a self, it is said that there is defilement; yet, within those [phenomena],...
Regarding the absence of defilement: because sentient beings do not falsely cling to a self or what belongs to a self, it is said that there is purity;
yet within that, there is no purity whatsoever (from the "Chapter on Spiritual Friends").
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the sphere of activity of all buddhas; wishes to dwell in the exalted position of the great sages, the buddhas;
wishes to sport in the places where the buddhas sport; wishes to let out the great lion’s roar of all buddhas;
wishes to beat the unsurpassed Dharma drum of all buddhas; wishes to strike the unsurpassed Dharma bell of all buddhas; wishes to blow the unsurpassed... of all buddhas.
The Dharma Conch. Desiring to ascend to the unsurpassed Dharma throne of all Buddhas; desiring to expound the unsurpassed Dharma meaning of all Buddhas;
desiring to resolve the net of doubts of all sentient beings; desiring to enter the nectar-like Dharma realm of all Buddhas; desiring to receive the subtle and wondrous Dharma-bliss of all Buddhas;
desiring to realize the perfectly pure merits of all Buddhas; desiring, with a single voice, for the sake of all [beings] in the trichiliocosm...
Sentient beings proclaim the sublime Dharma, universally causing all to obtain great benefit;
one should train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* (The Chapter on Swift Progress).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Apart from suchness, no other dharma can be found. What dharma, then, do you teach as abiding in suchness?
Furthermore, who is said to be able to approach all-knowledge and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
And who, for whom, teaches what essential points of the Dharma? The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. It is just as you have said. Subhūti, suchness..."
Since even suchness itself cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a separate dharma that can abide in suchness?
How, then, could there be one who can approach all-knowledge, swiftly realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or even be able to teach the Dharma to others? Subhūti, you should know this:
suchness cannot abide in itself, because within it there is absolutely no distinction between a subject that abides and an object in which it abides. Suchness does not...
It can approach all-knowledge, for herein there is neither that which approaches nor that which is approached.
True Suchness cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, for herein there is no distinction between the attainer and the attained.

Postscript to the *Prajñā-piṇḍārtha*:
The Old Man of the Ash Tree says, "Having read the *Prajñā*, I have come to know that the Buddha’s wisdom universally encompasses all phenomena of both the mundane and the supramundane.

When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Worlds are infinite, and thus the gateways to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*) are likewise infinite for sentient beings."
Delusion is boundless and stubborn attachment is immeasurable; the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas are likewise immeasurable.
By these means, they enlighten, instruct, guide, lead, rescue, and deliver [beings]. Yet all of this arises from compassion (*karuṇā*) and is rooted in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

If one lacks compassion, one falls into the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); if one violates the nature of phenomena, one becomes an outsider or a heterodox practitioner, and is no longer a follower of the Buddha.
It is the Dharma. The Buddha’s Dharma must accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because form (*rūpa*) is boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.

Now, these—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and they are also called the five heaps (*pañca-rāśi*). They are one in their provisional conjunction. And...
Their functions are each distinct; for this reason, they are further called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The union of these five aggregates is what the world designates as a "person.
Thus, regarding that which is called a "person," while there is a conventional designation within the world, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no person at all;
in this way, all phenomena (*dharma*) may be understood. Now, the Great Prajñā exists within the ultimate truth, whereas in the conventional world, it is fundamentally non-existent.
Alas! Sentient beings take what does not exist to be existent and what exists to be non-existent;
thus they remain in delusion throughout long kalpas because they contravene the *dharmatā*. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this: as for that which is not non-existent...
One silently honors it; as for that which it does not possess, one regards it merely as a provisional designation.
This is how one transcends ordinary sentiments and is able to accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). To accord with the nature of phenomena is what is called *mahāprajñā*.
If a single *mahāprajñā* is expounded in as many as six hundred fascicles, why is its meaning still not fully exhausted?
Because its essential nature is subtle and elusive, its functioning is profound and mysterious, and its skillful means are boundless, it cannot be fully expressed even when proclaimed.
It is like entering the great ocean: the further one goes, the deeper it becomes, with no bottom to be reached. Or it is like observing a city of the gandharvas or a magical illusion:

those who behold them rejoice, yet cannot fathom their transformations. Nevertheless, when these are synthesized and examined through principle, they do not transcend the *dharmatā*. Therefore, it is said:
Regarding worldly dharmas, there are the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, the six consciousnesses, the four great elements,
and the twelve links of dependent origination— all these dharmas are non-dual with the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Regarding supramundane dharmas, there are the six pāramitās, the four immeasurables,

the three gates of liberation, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the ten powers, and so forth— all such dharmas [are likewise non-dual].
There is nothing that does not accord with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, yet there is no attainment. It is non-dual and without attainment;
this is the realm realized by the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas, which cannot be reached by ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, or those of the lower stages of the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, the characteristic of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is equality; its single characteristic is what is called "characteristiclessness.

Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, it is eternally pure of itself. This is its true purport. To cultivate in accordance with this, to practice in accordance with this, without ceasing or resting—this is what is called "correspondence" (*yoga*).
All various dharmas are unified by this one principle. There is neither mundane nor supramundane regarding that which is cultivated.
